  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1296.

docs.title: 00067: does one convex fit of load flows across all boundaries find more of the moved load? (SW2-15)
docs.text:
Fitting block-shaped flows to the hourly residual of all 16 Primary substations at once found far less of the moved load than the single-series 24-hour step detector. The cause is the hourly noise model, not the conservation of power, so a joint fit would have to start from the 24-hour step statistics. We injected 620 known load transfers (power moved between substations for over 1 day) and counted the share of the moved megawatts (MW) found, with every detector held to about 80 unexplained alarms on odd months. The step detector finds 0.646 (0.354 missed). The joint estimator finds 0.108 (0.892 missed), a difference of -0.538 (97.5% interval -0.605 to -0.421).

  • Finding for later experiments: a post hoc change of the loss lifts the estimator to 0.527 (-0.120 against the step detector, -0.190 to -0.084). With that change it matches the step detector for transfers with a metered receiver and a donor step of 10 noise units or more (0.92 against 0.89 of transfers found) and finds almost nothing where no receiver is metered and the step is under 6. On the 35 labelled real transfers of over 1 day it finds 4, against 7.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1298 (Experiment 67: one convex fit of load flows across all boundaries (SW2-15)).

docs.title: 00062: does removing the residual's half-hour-to-half-hour memory help the switching detector? (SW2-9)
docs.text:
Filtering the residual's short memory out before the 24-hour step makes the switching detector find fewer load transfers, because the filter shrinks a day-long step faster than it shrinks the noise. We added 620 known load transfers (power moved between substations for over 1 day) to the history of 16 Primary substations and compared the detector on the unfiltered residual with the same detector on a residual filtered by a first-order autoregressive filter. The filtered detector found 0.34 to 0.37 of the moved megawatts (MW) and the unfiltered detector 0.44 to 0.47, a range over five daily shapes of transfer. The pooled change over the three shapes that experiment 60 added was -0.097 (98.33% interval -0.132 to -0.057), so the filtered detector misses 0.63 to 0.66 of the moved MW. At 4 hours the change was -0.145 (-0.209 to -0.097).

  • Finding for later experiments: the median fitted coefficient is 0.92, so a persistent step keeps about 8% of its size after filtering, while the noise of the 24-hour step keeps about 12%. The signal-to-noise ratio of a constant step is therefore 0.52 to 0.85 of the unfiltered value for all 16 substations, which predicts the result without injecting a transfer. The interval-end misses (72 of 215 large-step constant-MW transfers for the unfiltered detector, 56 for the filtered one) are not the filter's to fix. Work on the interval end (SW2-6) or the combination of windows (SW2-13) next.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1293.

docs.title: 00066: which window and cap should the end rule of the switching detector use? (SW2-16)
docs.text:
Lengthening the end rule's search from 14 to 30 or 60 days repairs the end of transfers longer than 15.6 days and breaks some shorter ones. A rule that ends at the first return step of at least half the onset step's size beats the 14-day rule on both sets of transfers. An alarm interval runs from the step that raises an alarm (the onset step) to the opposite step (the return step) that ends it, and the cap is how many days after the onset the search for the return step may run. We added known load transfers to the power history and gave each alarm of the single-step detector D0M an interval end from the strongest opposite step within a cap. On a new set of 215 transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days, the 14-day cap found 0.013 of the moved MW and a 30-day cap 0.547, a gain of 0.534 (99% interval +0.131 to +0.780). On experiment 58's 620 transfers, of which 1.5% last over 14 days, the 30-day cap found 0.045 less (-0.070 to -0.011) and the 60-day cap 0.080 less (-0.113 to -0.035). The 4-hour window at about the same alarm rate found 0.147 less than the 24-hour window (-0.248 to -0.054). The verdict is inconclusive by the pre-registered rule, because the longer cap fails its guard on the short transfers.

  • Finding for later experiments: a post hoc rule that takes the first opposite step of at least half the onset step's size, and otherwise keeps the tracked end, gains +0.042 (+0.013 to +0.066) on the 620 transfers and +0.412 (+0.067 to +0.621) on the long set over the 14-day end rule, and the cap hardly matters for it. It needs a confirmation on a fresh draw before it becomes the benchmark. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day, D0M finds 2, the 14-day end rule 7, and the post hoc rule 8. The end rule needs up to the cap's worth of hindsight, so detectors built on it serve training-time masks and the event table for NGED, not live forecast inputs.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1297.

docs.title: 00069: why do real load transfers raise no alarm at their start? (SW2-17)
docs.text:
Half of the 24 real transfers with no alarm at their start are not a threshold problem, and accepting weaker alarms that a later step back confirms did not find more of the moved power. Of the 35 labelled real transfers over 1 day, 24 have no alarm of the single-step detector D0M within 2 hours of the start. Of those 24, 6 lie in gaps in the data, 3 where the monthly refit of the XGBoost forecast suppresses the alarm, 3 have an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start, 8 have a sharp step of 2 to 4 noise units, 2 have a spread or late step, and 2 show no step. On injected transfers, a rule that also raises a weak alarm at half the strong threshold when a matching opposite step follows within 14 days recovered 0.146 more of the moved MW than the strong alarms alone, but the strong threshold had to rise from 4.0 to 6.55 to keep 80 odd-month unexplained alarms, which lost 0.140. The net change against the benchmark was +0.007 (98.75% interval -0.014 to +0.040), and the verdict is inconclusive.

  • Finding for later experiments: the first-return end rule PF14 beat the 14-day strongest-step rule on a fresh draw, by +0.038 (+0.016 to +0.077) on 625 headline-band transfers and +0.416 (+0.059 to +0.595) on 206 long transfers, so PF14 is the benchmark end rule. The monthly refit and a 2-hour onset tolerance account for 6 of the 24 unalarmed real transfers, and a lower threshold does not address them. PF14 and the weak-alarm rule need up to 14 days of hindsight, so they serve training-time masks and the event table for NGED, not live forecast inputs.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1300.

docs.title: 00072: can a step-loss monitor find a lost inverter at the solar farms? (P35)
docs.text:
A solar farm's daily power readings show that the farm has lost 25% of its output only if the loss lasts 90 days or more, and they show a smaller or shorter loss rarely or never, so they cannot give early warning of one lost inverter. We added artificial losses to the real power of 5 of the project's 6 solar farms (farm E has too short a record) and scored three monitors, each tuned to about 0.35 false alarms per farm-year on a placebo. The change-point monitor found 0.45 of 25% losses lasting 30 days, against the 0.80 the plan required, so the verdict is refuted. It found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.26 of 10% losses lasting 90 days. A loss of 3% was found 0.02 to 0.07 of the time, against 0.00 to 0.02 when no loss was added.

  • Finding for later experiments: a farm has only 3.1 usable days a week from April to September and 2.0 from October to March, and the daily reading wanders by 6% to 11%, so a 30-day loss holds about 13 usable days. A hysteresis rule (7 usable days in a row at least 10% below normal) found 0.86 of 25% losses lasting 30 days, better than the change-point fit, after a median delay of 14.5 days. Nothing found 10% losses lasting 30 days (0.04 to 0.13).
  • A next experiment could: obtain outage notices and curtailment records from National Grid Electricity Distribution for the 6 solar farms, so that monitors are tested on more than farm A's three low months.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1305.

docs.title: 00070: does counting the neighbours that step the same way find more of the moved load? (SW2-19)
docs.text:
Counting how many neighbouring substations step in the same direction as the alarming substation finds more of the moved load on injected transfers, so the count is worth testing again on more real transfers. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain. A logistic alarm score on the substation's own 24-hour step, the largest opposite neighbour step, the number of neighbours, and the same-sign neighbour count found 0.712 of the moved MW on 615 fresh headline-band transfers per injection shape that start in even months, against 0.665 for the single-series detector with the PF14 end rule, a difference of +0.048 (97.5% interval +0.021 to +0.096) at 80 odd-month unexplained alarms for both. The verdict is supported.

  • Finding for later experiments: the gain sits in transfers with no metered receiver and a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units (68 of 537 found by PF14, against 167 of 537 found by LOGIT_SAME). Long transfers gain nothing (0.000). On the 35 labelled real transfers the score found 7 against PF14's 8.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1303.

docs.title: 00068: does refitting without the detected switching help the detector and the forecast? (SW2-5)
docs.text:
Refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the load transfers the detector found barely changed what the detector finds or the forecast error, so in these 16 series the limit on the detector is not that the forecast has learned the transfers. We ran three rounds of refitting the XGBoost model that forecasts a Primary substation's demand from weather and calendar inputs, with zero weight on the half-hours inside the intervals found on the previous round's residual, and detecting again. To test the loop we added 130 synthetic load transfers to the measured power before the model trained, and the detector found a larger share of the moved megawatts (MW), rising from 0.522 to 0.532 (+0.011, 97.5% interval +0.000 to +0.034). The forecast's mean absolute error on half-hours with no logged or labelled switching changed by -0.175% (-1.145% to +0.603%). A mask of equal volume at random times did as well.

  • Finding for later experiments: the share of the moved MW that is missed stays at 0.47 (the 130 transfers in the training data) and 0.34 (620 transfers added to the residual after the forecast) across all four rounds, so the onset step is where to look next.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1299.

docs.title: 00071: does ignoring alarms near a refit make the detector miss load transfers? (SW2-18)
docs.text:
The detector's blind spot at the monthly refit of its residual model lowered recall by about 5% of the moved power, and lifting that blind spot recovers it; bridging data gaps changes nothing. The benchmark detector PF14 raises an alarm when a substation's residual steps by 4.0 noise units or more over 24 hours, and ends the alarm interval at the first opposite step. It ignores every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its XGBoost residual model. We computed the step statistic from the model refitted on the 1st except within 24 hours of that refit, where it comes from a second model refitted on the 16th. On injected transfers that start in even months, the two-model statistic found 0.715 of the moved MW against 0.665 for PF14 (+0.050, 98.33% interval +0.012 to +0.107), at no more than 80 odd-month unexplained alarms (alarms more than 24 hours from a logged closure), and the verdict is supported. All of the gain lies in the 13% of transfers within 24 hours of a refit (+0.431 there, -0.005 elsewhere).

  • Finding for later experiments: lifting the suppression with the first model alone finds slightly more on injected transfers (+0.056), so the second model matters only for the 3 real transfers that start at a refit, where it finds 3 and the lift alone finds 2. Gap bridging changes the outcome of 0 of 1,860 transfers, because the panel holds only 3 gaps of a day or longer, and the 6 real "data gap" transfers lie on series whose residual panel has no earlier rows. The 8 sharp small steps and the 3 transfers whose alarm falls 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start are untouched.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1302.

docs.title: 00084: can the substation-limit curtailment metric rank forecasts on the pilot?
docs.text:
Two substations hold too few half-hours beyond a limit to rank forecasts, so the pilot proves the arithmetic and a ranking waits for the January 2027 delivery of about 2,500 series. We scored experiment 48's stored forecasts for Boston and Skegness by what capping the generators beneath them would have cost. The limit is 0.9, 0.75, or 0.5 times each substation's maximum export before the scored year, because the maintainer understands (unconfirmed) that NGED curtails early to keep headroom, so the published thermal limit is a reference only. At 0.9 there are 19 half-hours beyond the limit, and 81% of the best guess's avoidable cost is breach, not unneeded cuts. Every cost is a calibration to history, not a saving. The best guess is cheapest at all three limits, but at 0.9 no difference between arms is statistically significant at the 5% level. No verdict on the forecasts is drawn. The thermal limits are NGED's, Supported by NGED Open Data.

  • Write-up: the full result page.

docs.title: 00083: are the tails of the stored demand forecasts too narrow?
docs.text:
Every stored forecast of experiment 48 is too narrow in both tails, and weekly retraining has the lowest pinball loss at both levels. We built studies.tail_calibration and scored experiment 48's stored forecasts across 20 demand series. Coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927, against targets of 0.05 and 0.95. The experiment first also built a single-series curtailment-cost metric, which we withdrew because curtailment binds at a substation and not at a single meter. No verdict on the forecasts is drawn.

  • Finding for later experiments: write the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles in every prediction set.
  • Write-up: the full result page.

docs.title: 00082: do the refit offset and the same-sign neighbour count add up? (SW2-18 and SW2-19)
docs.text:
The two improvements find different missed load transfers, so using both finds about twice as much extra moved power as either alone. The combined detector XL takes the 24-hour residual step from two models refitted half a month apart (experiment 71) and scores each alarm candidate partly by the number of neighbouring substations stepping the same way (experiment 70). On fresh injected transfers that start in even months it found 0.770 of the moved MW against 0.656 for the benchmark PF14, the benchmark detector (+0.114, 98.33% interval +0.074 to +0.182; MW is megawatts, and a noise unit is the usual size of a substation's 24-hour residual step), at no more than 80 odd-month unexplained alarms. The verdict is supported.

  • Finding for later experiments: XL beats the refit-offset detector alone by +0.058 (+0.034 to +0.096) and the neighbour-count score alone by +0.064 (+0.028 to +0.127), and the share of moved MW missed falls from 0.344 to 0.230. Long transfers gain nothing. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day XL found 12 and PF14 8. The misses that remain sit mostly in transfers with a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units and no metered receiver.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1314.

docs.title: 00079: can the direction of flow be recovered at Primaries metered only in MVA? (PVDIS-7)
docs.text:
Hiding the sign of a Primary's power and recovering it finds the solar capacity to a median error of 0.09 of the capacity from the signed power (0.29 for a fit that ignores the sign) and the direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78 (0.5 is a guess), but 7 of the 8 real Primaries metered only in MVA show no reverse flow to find, and the eighth, Stickney, cannot be checked. A Primary is a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. For the 7 Primaries the reading in megavolt-amperes (MVA) can stand in for megawatts (MW) from April to September. We subtracted the output of real solar farms, scaled to each Primary's median midday power, from the power of the 8 Primaries metered in MW, threw the sign away, and fitted the magnitude of demand minus solar. The difference in median capacity error, unfolding fit minus the fit that ignores the sign, was -0.198 (99% interval -0.409 to -0.068). The balanced accuracy of the direction was 0.819 once Wrangle T1 (a Primary that exports power on most sunny days, where the fit fails) was left out. A reactive-power floor equal to 20% of midday power cut the balanced accuracy to 0.666. The verdict is partly supported.

  • Finding for later experiments: get signed power for Stickney before quoting any fitted value there, because Stickney's sunny-midday reading is about 2.4 times its typical reading and the registered fit does not explain the rise. Test any starting sign pattern for the fit on a Primary that exports power on most sunny days first. Do not read the sign recovery as valid where reactive power exceeds about 10% of midday power.
  • Write-up: the full result page.

docs.title: 00076: does experiment 64's gain beyond 10 days come from a leak? (PVDIS-5 leak check)
docs.text:
We found no route for a leak, and a refit with no solar term reproduces the gain of experiment 64's best arm at 10 days and beyond, so the gain matches the XGBoost model starting its fit at zero. Experiment 64's arm am gives the XGBoost model a base margin (a starting prediction) of solar capacity times a forecast of sunshine, and the margin is zero from 10 days, yet am still beat the best guess d0 there. The audit found a margin of exactly zero from 10 days in the training rows and in the validation rows checked, and the weights use the training window. A refit (am0) with a zero margin everywhere scores 0.102 points of capacity (95% interval -0.158 to -0.047, lower is better) below d1l, the same recipe as d0 without the radiation inputs, with no 14-day correction applied. The solar offset in training adds +0.004 (-0.012 to +0.021). The verdict is supported.

  • Finding for later experiments: compare a margin arm with a zero-margin refit, and with a refit of d1l in the same pipeline, because d1l was fitted in experiment 46's pipeline, so a refit of d1l is the next test. Score the arms without the 14-day correction as well, because the correction moves contrasts at long leads by about 0.03 points.
  • Write-up: the full result page.

docs.title: 00078: does a re-estimated solar capacity lower the error of experiment 64's best forecast? (PVDIS-5 check 2)
docs.text:
Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowers the quantile score of am, the best-scoring forecast of experiment 64, by only 0.018 points, so a capacity table refreshed once a season-year is enough. A larger finding is that XGBoost's estimated starting prediction raises the score by 0.07 to 0.10 points compared with a start at zero. Experiment 64's am is an XGBoost model for the power at a Primary substation that starts from a solar term (a base margin): the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be. That experiment held the capacity fixed. Here we re-estimated each substation's capacity before every forecast run from only the data available then, and predicted again with the same fitted models. The quantile score (lower is better; 1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity) fell by 0.018 points (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold. The fall sits mostly in May 2026, when the estimates were 13% to 31% above the held capacity. A weekly refresh made no distinguishable difference (-0.005, -0.013 to +0.003). A refit of the reference models d1l and d0 in this pipeline scores the same as the stored ones, and d0 started from a base margin of zero scores 0.071 points (-0.099 to -0.047) below the refit d0. The solar term still lowers the score by 0.100 (-0.142 to -0.061) against that zero-start d0. The verdict is small gain.

  • Finding for later experiments: score each XGBoost reference with a zero-start twin, and test a zero base margin in the production recipe, because the effect is larger than the capacity effect and needs no extra production work.
  • Write-up: the full result page.

docs.title: 00073: can the mix of solar panel orientations and the DC to AC ratio be read from a Primary's power? (PVDIS-6)
docs.text:
A fitted solar shape, a blend of east, south, and west shapes, predicts held-out power 1.3% better than all-south panels at all 8 Primary substations, but the shares in the blend are not identified, and the DC:AC search did not recover a farm's ratio once the farm sat in a Primary's power. We added made-up east-south-west output, and real solar-farm output, to the real power of the 8 Primaries and checked what each fit recovered. Without noise the orientation fit found the shares with a median error of 0.088 where guessing the fleet mix (0.2 east, 0.6 south, 0.2 west) gives 0.300. With the real series' noise added the error was 0.200, and the shares of the free fit changed by a median 0.24 between consecutive September-to-August years. On held-out 28-day blocks the blend lowered the root mean square error of daylight power by 1.3% (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%). The DC:AC search had a median absolute error of 0.055 on a farm's own output and 0.195 once the farm sat in a Primary's power, so it was dropped before any real-series fit. The verdict is partly supported, read by the pre-registered rule.

  • Finding for later experiments: use the blend as a fitted solar shape, with its shares fixed across training years, and do not publish its shares as panel orientations. A known-answer test of a linear fit must add noise, because the noise-free version cannot fail (median error 0.09 without noise, 0.20 with it). Four of 8 Primaries have a pooled west share of 0.46 to 0.58 with an interval that excludes 0.2, and a fit to rows after dark would show whether that lean is evening demand.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1304 (Experiment 73: can the mix of solar panel orientations and the DC to AC ratio be recovered?).

docs.title: 00077: does a fitted solar shape lower the error of experiment 64's best arm? (PVDIS-6b)
docs.text:
A blend of east-, south-, and west-facing solar shapes fitted to each Primary left the score of arm am unchanged. A Primary is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation. Arm am is experiment 64's best forecast, an XGBoost model that starts from an explicit solar term, the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be. The blend scored 4.466 points, against 4.467 for south-facing panels (1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity). We fitted one set of shares per Primary on rows up to 30 June 2025 and scored the forecasts on experiment 64's rows: 5 Primaries and 3 seeds. The difference was -0.001 points (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014), which excludes a gain of 0.5% of am's score (0.022 points). The shape of another Primary scored the same (+0.001, -0.006 to +0.007), as did all-south panels at the blend's tilt (-0.001, -0.014 to +0.011). The forecast sunshine mattered: the same arm given the sunshine of another date scored 0.323 points worse (-0.441 to -0.212). The verdict is refuted.

  • Finding for later experiments: improve the sunshine forecast and the capacity table, not the panel shape. A gain of 1.3% in a fit with known weather (experiment 73) did not carry into the forecast.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1308 (Experiment 77: does the fitted solar shape lower the error of arm am? (PVDIS-6b)).

docs.title: 00059: does one detector over several windows find more transfers than the best single window? (SW2-13)
docs.text:
Neither of two ways of combining four window lengths found more of the moved MW than the 24-hour window alone, and most misses of large transfers are an interval end placed outside tolerance. On injected transfers that start in even months, with every detector set to the same count of unexplained alarms on odd months, the 24-hour window finds 0.473 of the MW moved (95% interval 0.410 to 0.511). The maximum of the four windows' scores finds 0.423, and their sum finds 0.451. The maximum minus the 24-hour window is -0.050 (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.022), so the 24-hour window still misses 0.527 of the moved MW.

  • Finding for later experiments: of the 541 rows of transfers with a metered receiver and a donor step of 4.0 noise units or more, the 24-hour window misses 223, and 170 of those have a found start and an end placed outside tolerance, against 4 with no alarm. The missed ends are off by 7.5 hours at the median, against a tolerance of 6 hours for the median 32-hour transfer (the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration). The 24-hour window is the single-window benchmark for SW2-7, SW2-14, and SW2-15, and the share found by start alone is worth reporting beside the share found by start and end.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1289.

docs.title: 00060: does a step that weights each half-hour by the daily profile find more of the moved load? (SW2-7)
docs.text:
The daily shape of the moved load does not limit the 24-hour switching detector, so a shape-aware step statistic is not worth building. We added known load transfers to the power history in five daily shapes. A step weighted by each substation's predicted power found the same transfers as the constant step on every shape, including the shape the weights assume. The pooled gain in the share of the moved MW found, over the three shapes the weights do not assume, was below 0.001 (98.33% interval -0.006 to +0.008), and both detectors missed 0.53 to 0.56 of the moved MW. The two steps correlate at 0.996 wherever the constant step exceeds 3 noise units, a noise unit being the typical size of the step on a quiet day.

  • Finding for later experiments: of the 215 constant-MW transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more, 72 have an alarm at the right start and the wrong end, and 15 have no alarm at the start. Only 2 of the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day are found, against 0.355 of the injected transfers in experiment 58. The injected transfers may be easier to find than the real events, or the real events may be smaller in noise units. Paired-step intervals (SW2-6 in the research plan) are a candidate next test.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1290.

docs.title: 00058: is the recall gap without a metered receiver a step-size effect, and does a stronger veto help? (SW2-8b)
docs.text:
Much of the gap in recall between injected transfers with and without a metered receiver comes from the injected step being too small for the detector to see, and a stronger neighbour veto adds almost nothing. Of the 274 transfers without a metered receiver, 211 step by less than the alarm threshold of 4.0 noise units, against 40 of the 346 with one. Matched on the largest step of the donor and metered receivers, the gap falls from 0.33 to -0.002 (98.33% interval -0.166 to +0.119), and matched on the donor's step alone it is +0.161 (+0.013 to +0.322), so step size explains between about half and all of it. A veto of 1.0 noise units finds 0.368 against 0.355 without a veto (+0.013, 0.000 to +0.029).

  • Finding for later experiments: of the 306 transfers with a metered receiver that step by 4.0 noise units or more, 134 are still missed. SW2-7, the planned detector that models the moved load as a share of the donor's daily profile, matches the injection shape, so it needs scoring on transfers injected with a different shape, on the 14 and 35 labelled real transfers, and by bins of step in noise units.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1286.

docs.title: 00055: does a neighbour veto help the single-series switching detector?
docs.text:
A neighbour veto makes the single-series detector slightly more precise, and at the strengths tried it finds only about 1 point more of the injected transfers. With the veto the 24-hour threshold fell from 4.00 to 3.70 noise units at the same rate of unexplained alarms, and the detector found 0.363 of 620 injected transfers against 0.355 without it (+0.008, 98.75% interval -0.003 to +0.022). The verdict is inconclusive, and a stronger veto than 1.5 noise units was not tried.

  • Finding for later experiments: the veto removes 35% of the unexplained 24-hour alarms and 20% of the alarms a logged closure explains, a ratio of 1.8. It loses 2 of the 220 transfers found without it and gains 7, raises the precision of the real alarms by about 3 points at 24 hours and 6 to 7 points at 4 hours, and loses 6 and gains 2 of 300 transfers that start near a bank holiday. The gain sits in the transfers with no metered receiver, but those transfers have a smaller injected step (median 16% of the donor's load against 55%), so the next experiment re-cuts recall by step size first.
  • Series status: experiments 43, 47, and 55 found no detector change that raises recall by more than about 1 point at the 24-hour window.
  • Write-up and pull request: the full result page, PR #1282.

docs.title: 00053: does the UKV forecast the solar anomaly better than ENS? (PVDIS part 8b)
docs.text:
We asked whether the Met Office UKV, a 2 km weather model that runs to 2 to 5 days ahead, forecasts how sunny each half-hour will be better than the European ensemble forecast (ENS), at the 5 Primary substations that decide experiment 46's verdict. Each forecast's output of a generic solar fleet was compared with the satellite-based CAMS estimate, as a departure from the forecast's own monthly average, on 72 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The run is post hoc and was not pre-registered: the brief and the PVDIS-8 plan fixed the arms, the lead bands, the 1% margin and the 15-fold month-block cross-validation beforehand, while the ukv3w control and the t54_late variant were chosen after seeing results. The UKV alone was worse than ENS in every lead band (correlation lower by 0.034 to 0.364 within 54 hours). A blend with weights fitted on the earlier 15 months cut the cross-validated mean squared error by 3.8% to 13.8% in every band within 54 hours, which gives the verdict small gain. In the validation year the blend's correlation gain was smaller than its uncertainty: +0.019 (-0.000 to +0.038) at 0 to 6 hours and +0.011 (-0.006 to +0.027) over 0 to 54 hours, with 3 of 6 origin-month blocks favouring the blend, and at 48 to 54 hours its validation mean squared error (0.0382) was worse than ENS's (0.0337). The blend gained nothing beyond 54 hours. Forming 3-hour window means from the UKV, as ENS delivers its flux, scored slightly better than the native hourly values, so the UKV's time resolution is not what limits it. On 14 days of overlap with CAMS, the live MOGREPS-UK ensemble was also no better than ENS.

  • Findings that bear on later experiments: the one UKV we found with a matched history is the CEDA archive, which is not the live product and is licensed for non-commercial use, so the gain is a ceiling; the demand contrasts at 0 to 48 hours were not run, because the gain is a ceiling from a non-live product and its interval over 0 to 54 hours includes zero; the manager decides.
  • Write-up: result.

docs.title: 00056: does Flexpectation v1 need special handling for Primary substations metered only in MVA?
docs.text:
At sunny middays the best-guess forecast has 5.6 percentage points less skill at the 8 Primary substations metered only in MVA than at the 8 metered in MW, but the 95% interval (-5.0 to 14.6) includes zero, so the verdict is inconclusive. The experiment found no evidence that Flexpectation v1 needs special handling, and could not rule out a loss of up to about 15 percentage points. An MVA meter records the magnitude of the power with no sign, so a substation whose net flow embedded solar pushes through zero loses the direction of flow. The experiment fitted nothing. It took the forecasts that experiment 33 stored for July 2025 to June 2026, and compared the quantile score of the best-guess forecast of Primary-substation demand with that of a simple rule-based forecast, manual_heuristic, at each group of 8. Skill is the percentage by which the best guess's quantile score is lower. At sunny middays (April to September, 10:00 to 13:30 UTC) the skill is 15.9% at the MW substations and 10.3% at the MVA substations.

  • Finding for later experiments: skill is lower at the MVA group all year (a gap of 10.5 percentage points, 2.1 to 17.5), not specifically at middays, and one MW substation with 31% skill accounts for most of that gap (3.8 percentage points without it; checked after seeing the results).
  • Near-zero flow: 1.5% of the MVA group's half-hours have power within 10% of capacity of zero, against 2.5% of the MW group's, and the best guess's skill on them is 18.8% in the MVA group against 46.1% in the MW group (gap 27.4 percentage points, -0.3 to 48.2). At sunny middays, leaving those half-hours out cuts the gap from 5.6 to 2.0 percentage points.
  • Write-up: result, PR #1284.

docs.title: 00054: does UKV, learned from its own history, help the wind-farm forecast?
docs.text:
Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to a wind-farm forecast that already uses the European Centre's ensemble (ENS) lowered the error by about 0.2 points of the farms' capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead, a small but real gain, so the verdict is small gain. The error is the quantile score, and 1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity. We trained XGBoost models for three metered wind farms, each on its own forecast history, and the gain at 24 to 54 hours after the ENS run's 00 UTC start is -0.198 points (95% interval -0.316 to -0.069), against a decision threshold of 0.15. The UKV data come from the CEDA research archive, not the live feed, so the result is an upper limit on what a service could get.

  • Finding for later experiments: a shuffled-UKV placebo differs from ENS alone by no more than 0.04 points, and UKV alone scores 0.88 points worse than ENS alone. W1 gains clearly (-0.413), W2 probably gains (-0.198, interval -0.378 to -0.000), and W3 shows no gain (+0.018); all three reads are exploratory. The ENS-only model scored 0.218 better than the ERA5-trained best guess at these leads, an unresolved difference (-0.472 to +0.069; exploratory).
  • A next experiment could: build a matched history of the live UKV for the farms, or test UKV at lead day 0 on Open-Meteo's live history.
  • Write-up: result.

docs.title: 00064: does demand minus forecast solar match the best guess? (PVDIS-5)
docs.text:
Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset (a fixed amount added to every tree prediction) beat d0, the best-guess recipe of experiment 33, by 0.15 points of capacity. Subtracting the forecast solar from an XGBoost model trained on gross demand (metered power plus the panels' output) was not shown to score within 0.10 points of d0. The verdict is supported. We built four Primary demand forecasts that each carry an explicit solar term. The solar term is the panels' capacity times a calibrated forecast of the sunshine anomaly from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS). We scored the forecasts on 5 Primary substations over daylight half-hours of April to September. The starting-offset arm am scores -0.152 points (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111) against the best guess d0 and -0.300 (-0.407 to -0.198) against its placebo twin, which is the same arm given the solar shape of another date. At leads under 48 hours the gain is -0.272 (-0.420 to -0.145).

  • Finding for later experiments: the fitted weight on the ENS shift is -0.60 to -0.29, well short of -1, and the slope on the true-sunshine shift stays at about -0.73 when the lagged-power and cloud-proxy columns are removed, which points to noise in the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) sunshine estimate or a mismatch between its shape and the panels' output; the diagnostic does not separate the two, and the cloud-proxy columns absorb about 0.15 of the slope at leads under 2 days. The weight was set to zero beyond 10 days, where the ENS anomaly has a correlation of 0.03 with CAMS.
  • Arm b: training on gross demand and subtracting the forecast solar scores +0.105 (-0.090 to +0.292) against d0, so it is not shown to match, and it is worse than d0 from 6 days.
  • What is untested: a capacity table current for the validation year (the capacity held is 5% to 19% below experiment 45's 2025/26 constants), more than one summer in the weights, and the live service supplying a base margin.
  • Write-up: result, PR #1294.

docs.title: 00074: do same-time sunshine analogues add anything once the solar forecast is explicit? (AN1)
docs.text:
Telling the XGBoost model of a Primary substation's power about sunshine, in either of two ways, lowered its daylight error by 0.09 to 0.15 points of capacity, and the two ways help in different conditions, so the next test needs more forecast weeks. A Primary substation steps 33 kV or 66 kV down to 11 kV, and 1 point is 1% of its capacity. The explicit forecast of the solar panels' output, given to the model as a starting offset, wins at leads under 2 days (the time from the forecast start to the half-hour forecast) and on cloudy rows. Analogues, which are recent days at the same time of day with similar sunshine, match it on sunny rows and in August and September. The verdict is inconclusive. We refitted the XGBoost model every month for 5 Primary substations and scored the daylight half-hours of April to September. The explicit offset scored 0.149 points lower than the same monthly refit without sunshine information (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104), and 3 analogues scored 0.095 points lower (-0.185 to -0.007). The analogues scored 0.054 points higher than the offset (-0.053 to +0.161). Adding the analogues to the offset scored 0.066 points lower than the offset alone (-0.149 to +0.015). A gain of 0.05 points would be worth porting, but the half-width of 0.08 could neither show nor rule out a gain of that size.

  • Finding for later experiments (exploratory, 95%): one analogue scores as well as three (-0.008, -0.037 to +0.019) and five score worse (+0.034, +0.014 to +0.060). Matched analogues beat random days on sunny rows (-0.188, -0.307 to -0.060) and lose to them on cloudy rows (+0.137, +0.002 to +0.293).
  • What is untested: the analogue gain on top of the offset with a second validation year, and analogues matched on the day type alone.
  • Write-up: result, PR #1306.

docs.title: 00063: does a linear joint fit of baseline, solar, and transfers beat the Flexpectation v1 baseline? (SW2-10)
docs.text:
In hindsight, the solar part of a joint fit lowers the error of a Primary substation's median forecast by about a third of a point, but the tests that check whether each part comes out at the right size could not be passed. "In hindsight" means the weather and sunshine inputs are estimates of the past that do not exist at forecast time. The verdict is inconclusive. We fitted one linear model per substation: a weather baseline without radiation inputs, plus the embedded-solar capacity times the CAMS (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service) sunshine shape, plus a share of the donor's power for each labelled switching job. We compared it with the Flexpectation v1 baseline outside switching, at 5 Primaries, and then added known solar-farm output and known transfers to check what the fit recovered.

  • Headline result: C1, the joint fit's mean absolute error minus the Flexpectation v1 baseline's, is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), against a threshold of 0.35. The sunshine is a past estimate and the capacity is fitted on the same power, so the figure is a ceiling.
  • Finding for later experiments: the injection gates could not be passed, because of the test design. CAMS sunshine matches a real solar farm's anomaly with a slope of 0.65 to 0.87, so the 0.76 recovery of an injected capacity reflects how well CAMS sunshine matches a real farm, and the fit's own regressor shape is recovered at exactly 1.000. A placebo transfer share has a 95th percentile of 0.63 for donors under 3 MW at 6 to 12 hours and 0.14 for donors over 5 MW, so a gate of 0.10 needs a scale set by donor size. The plan's filter on observed weeks left 2 event-Primary pairs, and 7 once events were allowed in any week.
  • A next experiment could: keep the positive control, scale the share gate by donor size, use intervals of 24 hours or longer, allow events in unobserved weeks, and cover all 8 Primaries.
  • Write-up and pull request: result, PR #1292.

docs.title: 00057: does UKV, learned from its own history, help the solar-farm forecast?
docs.text:
Giving the Met Office's UK Variable-resolution (UKV) weather forecast to a solar-farm forecast that already uses the ensemble forecast of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ENS) lowered the error by only about 0.03 points of the farms' capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead, whose 95% interval includes zero, so the verdict is inconclusive. The error is the quantile score, and 1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity. We trained XGBoost models for six metered solar farms, each on its own forecast history, and the difference at 24 to 54 hours after the ENS run's 00 UTC start is -0.035 points (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), against a decision threshold of 0.10. The UKV data come from the CEDA research archive, not the live feed, so any gain would be an upper limit.

  • Finding for later experiments: UKV helps the solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms of experiment 54, and a gain above 0.12 points is ruled out. UKV alone scores 0.40 points worse than ENS alone, and the shuffled-UKV placebo and the 3-hourly UKV control differ from the plain arms by under 0.03 points. After UKV's upgrade of 2026-01-21 the ENS-plus-UKV model beats the ENS-only model by 0.133 points (95% interval -0.262 to -0.017; exploratory).
  • A next experiment could: try a source of a different kind, such as a satellite-based nowcast at lead day 0, since a second numerical forecast adds little at these leads.
  • Write-up: result.

docs.title: 00048: weekly retraining of the demand model, checked on the runs experiment 34 left out
docs.text:
Refitting the Primary demand model weekly, with no error correction, scored 0.20 points of capacity below the best setup tested earlier (5.44 against 5.64) on 292 daily forecast runs that experiment 34 had not scored. Scores are the quantile score in percentage points of capacity, and the earlier setup, called the stack, is a model fitted once with a 14-day error correction. The experiment refitted the XGBoost demand model (N1) weekly and monthly for 16 Primary substations and for 2 bulk supply point (BSP) and 2 grid supply point (GSP) substations. It refitted the weather-to- power model monthly for 6 solar and 3 wind farms. The verdict is supported. A 7-day or 14-day error correction was not shown to help a refitted model, and monthly refitting changed solar and wind scores by 0.04 points or less.

  • Headline result: weekly minus the stack -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.04); weekly minus monthly -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.03); the 7-day correction on the weekly model +0.16 (-0.06 to +0.36, worse, unresolved).
  • Finding for later experiments: at the 2 BSP and 2 GSP substations weekly retraining gained 0.66 points over the stack (-1.23 to -0.27), more than predicted, on 4 series. The 7-day correction window was 0.09 worse than the 14-day window. The Primary gain is fragile: it rests on 12 months, three series carry most of it (without D8 the interval includes zero), and the 292 runs share their months with experiment 34's 73, so a second validation year is the open test.
  • Write-up and pull request: result, PR #1269 (Experiment 48: does weekly retraining still win on the runs experiment 34 left out?).

docs.title: Research plan of the ML experiments
docs.text:
This page lists the ml-experiments that are planned or proposed, sorted by priority. The research log holds the finished experiments, their verdicts, and the lessons so far. The design under test is on the staged probabilistic forecast page. In this plan, CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score, MAE is the mean absolute error, ENS is the ECMWF ensemble, ERA5 and CAMS are estimates of past weather, stage 1a is stage 1 as the experiments train it, and ECC-Q is ensemble copula coupling by sorting quantiles. The maintainer adds proposals to this page, and the ML experiment manager orders them, merges proposals that test the same hypothesis, and discards the ones an earlier result has answered.

Each planned experiment has a result.md with status planned, committed before any code runs. An idea that has no folder yet is marked "proposed" and carries a tentative id, P1, P2, and so on, which the sections below use as headings. A proposal receives its numeric id when its plan is committed, and the tentative id then disappears. A lower number in the "Priority" column runs sooner.

Id Question Priority Waits for State SW2-11 With the labelled switching removed from the training targets, does the best-guess architecture forecast the normal running arrangement as well outside switching as the plain best guess, and does a switching magnitude paired with each lagged power input, or a lag corrected by that magnitude, improve it? 2 RT2 (experiment 48), for the architecture Proposed; picks the v1 NRA candidate SW2-12 How much of SW2-11's NRA skill is lost when the switching labels come from the detector instead of NGED's logs? 3 SW2-11 and SW2-8 Proposed P2 Can summaries of the stage 1a residuals over recent days separate a change in a substation's embedded solar capacity since the stage 1a XGBoost model was trained from a fixed error in the irradiance input? 2 Nothing Experiment 00007 (static CAMS correction) was inconclusive and experiment 00009 (CAMS-trained stage 1a) refuted a gain of 0.2 points; the slope statistics are still proposed and need a plan PVDIS-T What is the unmetered solar capacity behind each Primary metered in MW, with error bars and outside checks? 2 The maintainer's review of this plan Proposed; a study under docs/studies/, season-year table first from experiment 00040's outputs, weekly after PVDIS-4

docs.title: Deferred until the first results are in
docs.text:
These proposals wait for a decision on the shape of the production model. Each keeps its section below, and a result may promote it.

Id Question Priority Waits for State P11 Do ensemble statistics (the member mean, spread, and percentiles of temperature and irradiance) beat control-member rows? 5 Nothing Deferred; an ERA5-trained stage 1 cannot take ensemble spread as an input, and experiment 00018 found the staged chain level with N1 for demand P13 Does a stage 1 trained on ENS early leads beat the ERA5-trained stage 1 at long leads, and how much skill remains with ERA5, CAMS, or short-lead fields as inputs? 5 Nothing Deferred; 00001 found no gain beyond day 6, and 9 generator series cannot resolve smaller gains P14 Which coupling step, ECC-Q or the Schaake shuffle, gives better coherence scores at short and long leads? 5 The scoring harness and experiment 00016 Deferred; no consumer needs coherent members yet P15 For solar and wind, does a shared stage 2 calibrator with a learned blend let a second weather product already on disk (CEDA UKV or Open-Meteo) enter without retraining? 5 A decision on the shape of the production model Deferred; run for solar and wind only, ENS against ENS plus one product, because demand depends less on weather than generation does P16 Does the ENS backfill (2021-03 to 2024-03) give an extra validation fold, or improve the single-stage or stage 2 models? 5 The maintainer, who runs the fetch on a cloud machine Deferred; tracked in issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history), and the 51-member fetch cannot run autonomously because it needs a cloud machine in us-west-2

docs.title: Proposals in detail
docs.text: Resolution limits. The sections below flag the experiments whose planned contrasts the available sample cannot resolve. The sample is 16 Primary substations, 9 generator series, and one validation year with 12 months, and it resolves gains of roughly 0.3 points of capacity or more.

docs.title: P2: embedded-solar capacity from lagged residuals
docs.text:
The embedded-solar proposal rests on one follow-up check of experiment 00006's residuals, which motivated two different questions. Experiment 00007 then ran a first test and was inconclusive. The check was run by the 00006 session on CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location, and its figures and script are in the write-up of PR #1202 (Experiment 6: which input features work best for the ERA5-trained demand model). It was not pre-registered. At Primary substation 12, the median-error Primary substation, the residual of the chosen-feature stage 1a XGBoost model averaged -5.3 points of capacity from 08:00 to 16:59 in the June, July, and August of the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), against -1.0 at night. In July 2025, a linear fit on 431 daylight hours explained 25.5% of the hourly residual's variance with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), 3.8% with ERA5 shortwave, and 43.3% with both. Across the 14 Primary series that have CAMS values, CAMS alone explained more than ERA5 alone in all 14: a median of 23.7% against 2.9%, and 39.8% with both. In one series the error is a level shift that irradiance does not explain, and in another the residual correlates positively with CAMS irradiance.

The check cannot yet say whether the cause is embedded solar capacity or an error in ERA5's irradiance. At Primary substation 12 the joint fit gives coefficients of opposite sign and similar size for ERA5 and CAMS, and CAMS minus ERA5 alone explains 33.9%, so much of the residual tracks the difference between the two irradiance products. Stage 1a has already learned an irradiance response from ERA5, so a fixed error in ERA5's cloud field would produce the same pattern without any change in solar capacity. Daytime lighting load and behaviour on sunny days could also contribute. At Primary substation 12, CAMS explains 25% of the variance on weekdays and 10% on weekends, so the weekday mix matters too. The check has no time dimension, because it covers one month, one seed, and one fold, and with hourly autocorrelation the effective sample is far below 431 hours. Because stage 1a already uses ERA5 shortwave, the comparison of 25.5% with 3.8% is not like for like, and the partial R² of CAMS given ERA5 would be a fairer figure.

Experiment 00007 was the cheap first test of an irradiance error against a capacity change. It added CAMS irradiance to ERA5 shortwave and fitted a static correction on one year of residuals. The correction removed 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual against the 50% planned, and one substation sets the pooled figure, so the verdict is inconclusive. A further test could compute the three candidate statistics on residuals from walk-forward (out-of-fold) stage 1a fits, because residuals from a model fitted on the same period are shrunk and would look different in operation.

The three candidate statistics each compare what stage 1a predicted with what the substation metered. Each uses the residual, the metered power over capacity minus stage 1a's prediction at the observed weather.

  • The solar slope: regress the residual on irradiance over the trailing 14 to 28 days, in daylight hours only. A more negative slope means more embedded solar than stage 1a learned. The slope mixes capacity change, irradiance error, and other demand that varies with irradiance, so the regression could use the clear-sky index with day-of-week and temperature controls. Noise in the estimation irradiance biases the slope towards zero.
  • The sunny-minus-cloudy daytime residual: the mean residual on sunny days minus the mean on cloudy days at matched hours, with a named clear-sky-index threshold. A day-minus-night residual is not a substitute. Commercial load is daytime-heavy, electric-vehicle charging and storage are night-heavy, and heat pumps are daytime and seasonal, so their trends would appear as false solar change.
  • The change from the same calendar window a year earlier: this year's 28-day slope minus the slope in the same 28 days of the previous year. A ratio of the 28-day to the 365-day slope is unstable, because the slope is seasonal and the denominator can be near zero or change sign.

The correction could be given to stage 2 as a linear offset, not as a tree feature. Gradient-boosted trees cannot extrapolate beyond their training range, and embedded solar capacity grows steadily, so a product of the slope and the forecast shortwave would still be held flat by a tree. A linear term, in stage 1b or in stage 2, would extrapolate correctly, and the tree feature would be the comparison arm. The slope is estimated against observed irradiance and applied to forecast irradiance, which differ in bias and scale, so the conversion has to be stated. The past-weather source used at lag times has to be available at forecast time, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, and training has to use that same source. CAMS is observed after the fact and has no forecast, so the CAMS satellite-derived irradiance can feed the statistics only at lag times. The CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location comes from PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations), which covers the 22 series of experiment 00003 (16 Primary demand series, 4 bulk-supply and grid-supply point flows, and 2 non-demand series, a battery and a biofuel generator). The experiment could compute each statistic from ERA5 alone and from CAMS and ERA5 together.

A decision rule could be fixed before any fit. One candidate: the trend in the monthly change from a year earlier is negative at 70% or more of the substations in the top quartile of registered embedded solar capacity per unit of substation capacity, with a block-bootstrap 95% interval that excludes zero, and it is absent in the night-time residuals. A second candidate: the linear-offset arm lowers the confirmation-year daylight quantile score at Primary substations by at least 0.2 points of capacity, with a month-block bootstrap interval that excludes zero. Otherwise the hypothesis is refuted. The thresholds are proposals for the planning step to confirm.

Resolution limit. The top quartile of 16 Primary substations by embedded solar capacity is 4 substations, so a rule of "70% of them" means 3 of 4, which no interval can support. The slope statistics need more substations or a continuous measure of capacity.

docs.title: SW2: switching-event detection
docs.text:
The SW2 line improves the switching-event detector first, scored by event-level F1 against a labelled set of visible events, and leaves the use of the detector until the detector works. The detector serves two purposes later. The first is a lower forecast error, if switching periods act as unexplained noise for the XGBoost model and corrupt its lagged power inputs. The second, and the more important to NGED, is a forecast under the normal running arrangement (NRA), into which NGED can add its own switching. The switching events roadmap page proposes building that forecast by excluding switching periods from the training target. An event table for NGED is a third purpose, at lower priority. The production detector has to run on power alone, because the switching logs exist only for the trial area, so the logs are used here for evaluation only.

The line reopens a question that experiment 00038 closed, because experiment 00038 tested a different use of the detector. Experiment 00038 masked detected switching from the history of the error correction that runs after the XGBoost model, and the mask made the forecast worse. No experiment has yet masked switching from an XGBoost training target or from a lagged input. Experiment 00037 confirmed 37 of 612 logged closures of 2 hours to 60 days as visible in its own residual, and scored its detectors on the 18 of them in the validation months. That reference set is small, about 6 of the 37 are expected by chance, and the label was built from the residual the detectors use, so a detector that shares the residual's blind spots is flattered by the label. The line therefore starts by building a reference set independent of the detectors.

The full labeller design is in the private file data/ml-experiments/briefs/sw2_labeller_design.md.

docs.title: SW2-4 to SW2-9: detector iterations
docs.text:
Each iteration tests one change to the detector against the experiment 43 scoreboard, tuned on injections and odd months, scored on even months, with recall weighted by the MW moved as the headline from SW2-7 onwards. The order below is a proposal, by expected gain per hour of work, for the plan of each iteration to confirm:

  • SW2-5 (done, experiment 68): three rounds of refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the detected intervals changed the share of the moved MW found by +0.011 and the forecast error by -0.175%, and a random mask did as well.
  • SW2-6 (done, experiment 61): pairing the onset and return steps into one alarm score finds less than D0M at the same alarm rate, but taking the end of D0M's interval from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days finds 0.19 more of the moved MW.
  • SW2-7 (done, experiment 60): a step statistic that weights each half-hour by the expected power found the same transfers as the constant step on five injection shapes, so the step's shape does not limit the 24-hour detector. About a third of the transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more have the right onset and the wrong end, which SW2-6 (paired-step intervals) addresses.
  • SW2-8 (done, experiment 55): a single-series detector first, with neighbour balance as a sense check, not a gate. Every single-series alarm stands. A metered neighbour's opposite step raises the alarm's confidence and names the receiver, a same-sign step on the neighbours vetoes the alarm as a common-mode weather or calendar miss, and an alarm with no metered neighbour keeps its single-series confidence. Experiment 00043 found the neighbour-balance detector D1, which uses the neighbour test as a gate, finding almost none of the injected transfers without a metered receiver. The sum of the neighbourhood's residuals and a subset-sum over neighbours for a split feed the confidence score.
  • SW2-9 (done, experiment 62): whitening, experiment 00037's proposed F4, an autoregressive model of order 1 per series and hour of day fitted to the residual. The filtered detector found less of the moved MW (-0.097 at 24 hours), because the filter shrinks a day-long step faster than the noise of the 24-hour step.

docs.title: SW2-11 and SW2-12: a v1 forecast under the normal running arrangement
docs.text:
Retrain the best-guess architecture so that it never learns to predict an abnormal running arrangement, and pick the v1 NRA candidate from three arms. SW2-11 uses experiment 00041's labelled switching, and SW2-12 repeats the experiment with the detector's labels, which is what Flexpectation v2 will have. The gap between the two runs is the skill lost without a labelled set.

  • The architecture is the winner of RT2 (experiment 00048). Weekly retraining without the error correction is the leading candidate. If the winner keeps an error correction, the correction's history leaves out switching half-hours and looks back far enough to hold 14 unmasked days, and the write-up reports the unmasked days per window and how often the fallback to the last full correction fired.
  • The arms: the plain architecture with nothing removed; the NRA arm, with logged switching removed from the training targets; and the NRA arm plus, for each lagged power input, the signed MW moved by any switching event at that lag. A fourth arm replaces each lag by the lag minus that MW, because a tree model cannot easily subtract one column from another.
  • The labels in SW2-11 are experiment 00041's visible events, conserved or one-sided, which two Sonnet labellers and an Opus adjudicator found in the telemetry at NGED's logged times. The target mask removes each event's interval from the training targets of its donor and receivers, and the magnitudes are the events' labelled MW moved.
  • The labels in SW2-12 come from the best detector after SW2-8.
  • Scoring uses the same rows in every arm and in both runs: half-hours outside NGED's logged closures and outside the labelled events, where the metered target is the NRA target. A secondary metered view scores every half-hour and decides nothing.
  • Threshold. The target mask needs a detector at training time only, so the NRA arm is adopted when its interval does not show it worse than the plain arm. The magnitude arms need a detector on the serving path, so they need a gain whose interval excludes zero. Experiment 00044 bounded a perfect detector's gain at 0.34% of the best guess's quantile score under the NRA view, so the gains are expected to be small.

docs.title: PVDIS: separating embedded solar from Primary demand
docs.text:
The PVDIS line estimates how much unmetered solar capacity sits behind each Primary substation, how that capacity changes over time, and whether an explicit solar term improves or explains the net demand forecast. The line serves three purposes, and the second matters about as much as the first:

  • Skill: a lower error in the net demand forecast at each substation.
  • Explanation: a forecast that NGED can read as demand minus solar. A solar term that leaves the error level but splits the forecast into parts an engineer recognises is still worth keeping, so experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) tested non-inferiority as well as gain.
  • Capacity: a time series of unmetered solar capacity per Primary. NGED holds almost no information on unmetered solar today, so an estimate with honest error bars is useful even when the estimate is far from perfect.

The capacity estimate runs offline, weekly or monthly, and the production forecast only reads the latest capacity table. Nothing in this line adds a fitting step to the serving path. Experiment 73 (PVDIS-6) found that the mix of panel orientations behind each Primary, the quantity the UniversalSolarFleetNode sketched in differentiable physics would fit, is not stable across season-years, so the explicit solar forecast keeps one south-facing shape.

Experiments 00039 and 00040 are parts 1 and 2 of the series, and the parts below follow the exploratory protocol in the ml-experiment skill. Opus plans each part after reading the result of the part before, so the designs below are proposals that each part's plan may change. Experiment 00039 fitted one capacity per Primary per season-year, from a calendar and temperature demand term minus one CAMS-driven solar shape. On real solar-farm output injected into the real demand, the half-hourly fit recovered a median 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818) of the injected capacity, and a fit on daily sums recovered 0.854 (0.815 to 0.866). Experiment 00040 compared six fits, which differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows, and took the six-arm capacity C as its estimate. C recovered a median 0.992 (0.951 to 1.032) of the injected capacity. Experiment 00040 also attached a bound on the error that an undetected demand load would cause, of 0.18 to 0.23 at five Primaries. A demand load that rises with sunshine cannot be told apart from solar.

The Opus review of experiment 00040 recommended stopping the series, publishing a season-year capacity table, and not using capacity as a forecast feature; the parts below continue because the goals changed. That review judged the series against the questions it had then: whether a further experiment could narrow the capacity bound, and whether capacity improves the forecast score. Four experiments (00007, 00009, 00022, and 00031) found small or no gains from solar inputs. The maintainer has since added two goals: a forecast that explains itself, and a capacity series that changes week by week for NGED. Experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) rested on the explanation goal and on what differs from those four experiments, not on a claim that the review missed the forecast question. The same review found that the daily fit is about 2.6 times more exposed than C to an undetected day-long load, so every part reports C as the capacity and keeps the daily fit as a cross-check.

Rules shared by every part:

  • Substations. Only the 8 Primaries metered in MW, each carrying its status from the earlier review into every result: Kirton is reported only as a range (1.2 to 4.4 MW), because its daylight cloud load was flagged in 6 of 7 season-years; Wrangle T1 is excluded from any claim that a Primary is free of a confound; Trusthorpe is marked low-power. The 8 Primaries metered only in MVA fold solar into the magnitude of the flow, and experiment 00039 fitted a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. Experiment 00079 (PVDIS-7) treats them separately.
  • Service areas. TimeSeriesMetadata.area_wkt holds one polygon per Primary. Wrangle T1 and Wrangle T2 are two transformers at one substation, feeding different circuits, and share one polygon. Each transformer keeps its own capacity fit, and any comparison against an outside count of solar uses the sum of the two against the shared polygon. Before any outside comparison, a check reports overlaps and gaps between neighbouring polygons, whether each Primary's location falls inside its own polygon, and how the union of the polygons compares with the two BSPs' area.
  • Irradiance. CAMS for past weather, because the past-weather solar study found the CAMS solar estimate the most accurate of the products it compared. ENS for forecasts. Where a capacity fitted on CAMS is applied to ENS, the ENS irradiance is first calibrated against CAMS, by lead, on data from the fold's training window only.
  • Capacity used in a forecast is a real-time vintage. A forecast experiment reads the capacity that a fit truncated at the fold's training end would give, never a path smoothed over the whole record. A path fitted once over all data passes information from later weeks back to earlier weeks through the penalty and the constraint.
  • Switching is masked. The logged closures, padded by 24 hours, are removed from every capacity fit until SW2-0b's labels exist. A transfer moves a share of the donor's net load, including the donor's solar, so an unmasked transfer looks like a step in capacity. The logs miss some real switching, so unlogged transfers remain a source of false steps.
  • Known answers first. Every capacity method is scored on experiment 00039's injection harness before its result on the real series is trusted.
  • Loads that track sunshine are a named confound. Seaside visitor load at the coastal Primaries (Skegness, Ingoldmells, Chapel St Leonards, and Trusthorpe), irrigation pumping, cooling of crop stores, and air conditioning all rise on sunny days and bias the fitted capacity low. Daytime domestic load falls on sunny days, as people go outside, and biases the fitted capacity high. Each write-up reports the coastal Primaries separately and compares school-holiday weeks with term-time weeks.

docs.title: PVDIS-T: the capacity table, a study
docs.text: Publish a season-year capacity table now, built from experiment 00040's outputs with no refit, and replace it with PVDIS-4's weekly series once that part has run. NGED's need is to improve on almost no information, so the season-year table is useful before the weekly series exists. The study reports C as the capacity, keeps sampling uncertainty separate from the named systematic scenarios, and carries each Primary's status from the earlier review. The joint fit of experiment 00063 read the same capacities.

docs.title: P11: ensemble statistics as inputs
docs.text: The arms are the member mean, spread, and 10th and 90th percentiles of temperature and irradiance, against rows from the control member only. The planned contrast is the statistics arm against the control-member arm.

docs.title: P13: perfect-prognosis and ceiling checks
docs.text:
Experiment 00001 found no gain from ERA5 training beyond day 6. The arms are the ERA5-trained stage 1, a stage 1 trained on ENS early leads, and ceiling inputs (ERA5, CAMS, both, and each product's short-lead fields).

Resolution limit. 9 generator series cannot resolve gains smaller than about 0.3 points of capacity, and few solar farms share a weather cell.

docs.title: P14: coupling
docs.text: The coupling step turns calibrated quantiles back into 51 coherent members. The arms are ECC-Q with the interpolation, tail, and tie rules of the staged forecast roadmap page, and the Schaake shuffle, scored by the variogram score and the CRPS of summed solar farms in a weather cell, by lead band.

docs.title: P15: a second weather product already on disk
docs.text:
Blending products is the maintainer's strongest hunch for improving the forecast, and it can be tested before any ingest. CEDA UKV and products downloaded from Open-Meteo are already on disk. The CEDA UKV archive differs statistically from the live feed, so a result may not carry over. The arms are ENS alone; ENS plus the second product with the shared calibrator and the learned blend; the per-product-columns control; a fixed equal-weight mixture; and a learning curve at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months of the second product's history, rotated across seasons. The planned contrast is ENS plus the second product against ENS alone, with a safe-entry check at 1 and 2 months (the interval lies inside plus or minus 0.15 points).

Resolution limit. With 9 generator series, a safe-entry interval of plus or minus 0.15 points is not reachable at 1 or 2 months of history. The experiment compares ENS alone with ENS plus one product, and does not run the learning curve.

docs.title: P16: a longer ENS history
docs.text: The ENS backfill from Source Cooperative (2021-03 to 2024-03) could give an earlier validation fold, and the full fetch cannot run autonomously. Issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history) describes the fetch. The archive is in us-west-2. Fetching the control member alone is about 530 GB and 4 to 5 hours, and fetching all 51 members is about 30 TB, which needs a cloud machine in that region and the maintainer's approval of the cost. The issue also ties autonomous use of the fetch to the scorer-protection work in issue 958. Every experiment since 00003 scores the same year on the same 16 series, so choices tuned there overfit it, and an earlier fold is the remedy. For demand, a longer training history has hurt so far, so the backfill is valuable first as validation data.

docs.title: Does an ERA5-trained weather-to-power model beat the same model trained on ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether a model that turns weather into solar or wind farm output works better when it is trained on estimates of past weather than when it is trained on archived weather forecasts. We trained one model each way for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, gave both the same 51 weather forecasts for the days ahead, and compared their errors over 53 weekly forecast runs in one held-out year. Training on estimates of past weather gave the smaller error for forecasts up to 6 days ahead, and the benefit was not shown beyond that.

Verdict: supported up to day 6, not supported beyond. Stage 1a (one XGBoost model per series, trained on ERA5 (a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) and CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite estimate of sunlight), no calendar and no power-history columns) applied to the 51 members of ENS (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast) and averaged has a smaller error than the same columns trained on ENS weather, for lead bands up to 6 days, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, in one held-out year (fold A, 53 weekly runs). The planned contrasts were revised after two scientific reviews, so they are not pre-registered. The full write-up is the study README in studies/stage1_pilot/README.md.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
Every arm except c0 gets the same columns, and none is a calendar column or a power lag. Solar zenith and azimuth carry the time of day and the time of year.

  • Solar farms (9 columns): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth.
  • Wind farms (6 columns): wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, wind_dir_sin_10m, wind_dir_cos_10m, wind_dir_sin_100m, wind_dir_cos_100m. The wind farms' ERA5 cells have no temperature or pressure on disk.
  • ens_trained_plus_s1 adds one column, stage1a_prediction.
  • The *_calendar arms (the first run) add hour_sin, hour_cos, doy_sin, and doy_cos (solar 13 columns, wind 10).
  • c0, the production control, has 24 columns: categorical_precipitation_type_surface, dew_point_temperature_2m, downward_short_wave_radiation_flux_surface, geopotential_height_500hpa, local_day_of_week, local_day_of_week_cos, local_day_of_week_sin, local_time_of_day_cos, local_time_of_day_sin, local_time_of_year_cos, local_time_of_year_sin, local_utc_offset_minutes, power_lag_24h, power_lag_48h, power_lag_168h, power_lag_336h, pressure_reduced_to_mean_sea_level, pressure_surface, temperature_2m, windchill, wind_direction_10m, wind_direction_100m, wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m.

docs.title: Planned contrasts (revised)
docs.text:
• P1 (s1_memberavg minus ens_trained) is material up to day 6 for both technologies. Wind -3.18, -4.04, and -2.37 points at 0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 days, and 3 to 6 days; solar -1.23, -1.41, and -0.73. At 7 to 10 and 11 to 15 days neither passes.
  • P2 (adding stage 1a's prediction as a column to ens_trained) is not material anywhere. Solar -0.06 (-0.12 to -0.01), wind +0.02 (+0.01 to +0.03) over all leads.
  • Beyond day 6 stage 1a is within about 1 point of climatology.

docs.title: What else the study found
docs.text:
• Averaging the 51 members is associated with a much larger drop in error for the ERA5-trained model (-0.70 solar, -2.23 wind) than for the ENS-trained model (-0.15, -0.22). With the control member alone, ERA5 training is associated with lower error at 0 to 2 days and higher error at 7 to 15 days.
  • Removing hour and day-of-year columns lowered the ENS-trained error by 1.13 (solar) and 3.40 (wind) points and the ERA5-trained error by 0.23 (solar) and 0 (wind). The first run's control, with 24 production columns, looked like it memorised calendar position.

docs.title: Effect of the feature lists (post hoc)
docs.text:
Removing the hour and day-of-year columns helped the ENS-trained model a lot and the ERA5-trained model little. The first run gave every arm those four calendar columns, and the production control also had 24 production columns including power lags. The table gives each change in mean absolute error over all leads, in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals. Every row is post hoc. The first run's arms are the *_calendar arms, scored on the same cases.

change solar wind ERA5-trained, calendar columns removed (F1) -0.23 (-0.47 to -0.08) +0.03 (-0.08 to +0.15) ENS-trained, calendar columns removed (F2) -1.13 (-1.71 to -0.65) -3.40 (-4.81 to -1.97) ENS-trained, 24 production columns replaced by the common columns (E13) -0.49 (-0.70 to -0.29) -1.99 (-2.73 to -1.31)
  • The ENS-trained model with calendar columns is the one that does worse. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, once per lead, so a model given the calendar position can learn the weather of that day rather than a weather-to-power relation.
  • The first run's headline against the production control was largely this effect. The common feature list, with no calendar column, is used in every arm of the revised contrasts.

docs.title: Gains in the tails (exploratory)
docs.text:
For wind, the gain from ERA5 training is much larger on the largest outputs; for solar it is larger in points at short leads but uncertain. The tail is the cases where observed power exceeds the series' 90th percentile of cleaned power in stage 1a's training window (20,020 solar and 9,747 wind cases per seed). The table gives s1_memberavg minus ens_trained in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals, against the same contrast on all cases.

lead band wind, top decile wind, all cases solar, top decile solar, all cases 0 to 24 h -16.54 (-18.82 to -12.81) -3.18 -2.99 (-7.73 to +0.23) -1.23 1 to 2 days -17.56 (-20.63 to -13.17) -4.04 -3.52 (-6.24 to -0.89) -1.41 3 to 6 days -8.46 (-11.47 to -5.18) -2.37 -1.76 (-4.52 to +0.78) -0.73 7 to 10 days -1.22 (-2.46 to -0.08) -0.45 -0.19 (-3.60 to +2.91) -0.30 11 to 15 days +0.12 (-1.17 to +1.56) -0.61 +0.58 (-2.70 to +3.73) -0.12 all leads -6.14 (-7.66 to -4.33) -1.70 -1.05 (-3.93 to +1.25) -0.57
  • Relative to each arm's own error, the wind gain is about 12% in the tail and 10% overall. The top-decile error of ens_trained is 53.22 points and of s1_memberavg 47.08, against 17.09 and 15.39 over all cases. At 0 to 24 h the tail gain is 42% of the error against 27% overall.
  • For solar the relative gain is smaller in the tail (4% against 7% over all leads), and every solar tail interval over all leads and at 0 to 24 h and 3 to 6 days spans zero.
  • Tail errors are large for every forecast, and the weather input is associated with most of them. era5_ceiling has a top-decile error of 13.16 (wind) and 18.43 (solar) points. Without a second model, both ERA5-trained and ENS-trained forecasts miss most of the largest wind outputs.
  • The control member alone gives the same tail result for wind (-6.95, -8.39 to -5.23), so averaging the members is not needed for the tail gain, unlike the all-cases gain.
  • Selecting on the observed value truncates the outcome, so slopes on this subset are not comparable across studies; only paired differences are reported. Tail pinball loss, exceedance Brier scores, and reliability for the probabilistic forecasts are in the stage 2 experiment.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• The first run compared against a control that memorised calendar position, and the headline was revised after two Opus reviews. The revised contrasts were chosen after seeing the first run.
  • One held-out year, nine generators in two weather regions, fold A only, 24 decisions without a multiple-comparison correction.
  • ENS is biased against ERA5 (10 m wind 13% to 15% slower, shortwave 7% brighter). Mapping ENS onto ERA5 before stage 1a is untested.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Give every arm the same feature columns, and add a control without calendar columns whenever the training rows repeat a valid time.
