  • Holiday, five arms: the holiday name as a categorical (England and Wales, from the holidays package); the holiday flag with day-before and day-after flags; the signed days to the nearest holiday, clipped at 7; the signed days to 25 December, clipped at 14; a bridge-day flag (a working day between a holiday and a weekend). Holidays are known years ahead.
  • Trailing temperature, four arms: the mean temperature over the previous 24 hours; 72 hours; 7 days; and exponentially weighted means with half-lives of 12 hours, 72 hours, and 7 days. The window ends at the valid time. At forecast time the window straddles analysis and forecast weather and would be built from one member's trajectory.
  • Heating degree-hours: the mean over 24 and 72 hours of the excess of 15.5 °C over the temperature.
  • Sun position: day length and hours since sunrise (local); and the sine and cosine of the azimuth. Sun elevation is 90 degrees minus the zenith, a monotone function a tree treats as the same column, so it is not tested.
  • UTC offset: 0 or 1 hour.
  • Windchill: the Environment Canada formula, equal to the temperature above 10 °C or below 4.8 km/h, and the product of the wind speed and the shortfall of temperature below 15.5 °C. Both are implemented inside the experiment script only.
  • COVID: a 0/1 indicator for 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, reading 0 in every validation month; an arm that excludes those training rows; and an arm with recency sample weights (half-life 2 years).
  • Spatial mean: the 3 by 3 block mean replaces the nearest cell for every weather column.

Extra inputs from an Opus consultation. Taken: the exponentially weighted temperatures, the heating degree-hours, the spatial block mean, the bridge-day flag, and the replacement for windchill. Not taken, and listed in the write-up as untested: an embedded-solar proxy (needs an outside capacity series), school terms (dates must be collected by hand), cooling degree-hours, temperature change over 24 hours, snow, humidity, days since the clock change, sporting events, and the substation-type fields.

Planned contrasts (mean absolute error of the median, points of capacity, one model per series; the interval resamples whole validation months). P1 to P7 are scored on the selection fold. P8 and P9 are scored on the confirmation fold, and P8 is the one contrast the frozen set must pass.

  • P1: W plus clock minus W.
  • P2: W plus clock plus one harmonic minus W plus clock.
  • P3: W plus clock plus the holiday flags minus W plus clock.
  • P4: W plus clock plus the 24-hour trailing mean minus W plus clock.
  • P5: W plus windchill (the formula) minus W.
  • P6: W plus clock plus the COVID indicator minus W plus clock.
  • P7: W plus clock with recency weights minus W plus clock.
  • P8: the frozen set selected on the selection fold minus W plus clock.
  • P9: the selected set trained from 2023-09 minus the same set trained from 2019-09.

Every other number is exploratory and labelled so: the add-one-in arms against W and against W plus clock, the drop-one-out, the pooled configurations, the second selection fold, and the breakdowns by type, hour, and season. A month-by-half-hour climatology (ClimatologyForecaster) is the reference row. Absolute scores are reported for every arm.

Not tested here. Lagged power, forecasting from ENS weather, and downloaded COVID series (Oxford stringency, Google mobility).

docs.title: Changes to the plan
docs.text:
The plan below is as committed before the first fit, with these changes made afterwards.

  • Selection and confirmation folds. Selection used the validation years 2024-07 to 2025-06 and, for a replication, 2023-07 to 2024-06. The Primary set was written into this page before the confirmation year (2025-07 to 2026-06) was scored, and the planned set was scored once. The BSP and GSP sets, the discarded all-series set, the pooled models, the Christmas control, and the importance fits were also scored on the confirmation year and are post hoc. The plan's original wording scored the main fold first.
  • The set was selected on the Primary series. The first all-series selection was replaced before the confirmation year was scored.
  • Added arms: the BSP and GSP sets, a graded lockdown indicator, a masking ablation of the time of year, production's unguarded windchill, and the Christmas-window control.
  • Drop-one-out ran on the Primary set on the selection year only.

docs.title: Experiment 7: does a static CAMS correction remove the stage 1a daytime residual?
docs.text:
We asked whether the daytime error of a demand forecast comes from a fixed error in its estimate of sunlight, or from changes in how much embedded solar generation (solar panels connected to the distribution network, such as rooftop panels) is installed. We fitted a fixed correction, using the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) satellite-based estimate of sunlight as a second estimate, to one year of the forecast's errors. We then checked how much of the next year's daytime error the correction removed. The correction removed 46.6% of the squared daytime error, but a fixed bias alone removed 39.1% and one substation set the pooled figure, so the test could not separate the two explanations.

This is the cheap first test that decides whether to carry out the later steps of proposal P2 (the embedded-solar-capacity proposal) in the research plan. The result says whether the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model tracks a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input (the sunlight estimate that stage 1a was trained on), or a change in embedded solar capacity that a correction with fixed coefficients cannot follow. The plan was committed before the code ran; the Results section reports the run. ERA5 is a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather. Stage 1a is an XGBoost model per series that turns weather into power. In the body below, "P2" also names one of the 13 substations.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: residual tables and figures only, under this experiment's private folder. Nothing enters a Delta table.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Designs that would test the hypothesis defensibly: two. A linear correction of the residuals answers the question cheaply and is the planned design. Retraining the XGBoost model with CAMS as a feature is the later P4.
  • Callers that need searching for: none, because the script reads 00006's stored predictions and the CAMS download from PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations).

The experiment is medium: it uses a new data source and a new method, but touches nothing stored for production. It gets one Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code, and one of the write-up.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The residuals come from 00006's out-of-fold fits. The residual is the metered power over effective capacity minus the median forecast of the chosen arm, times 100, averaged over the three seeds of the finals stage. Each validation year was forecast by a model trained on data ending a week before that year starts, so no residual comes from a fit that saw its own row. The two years are 2024-07 to 2025-06 (year A, fold select_2024) and 2025-07 to 2026-06 (year B, fold confirm_2025). Half-hours are averaged to the hour ending at the CAMS time stamp, as in e00006_solar_residual.py, and only daylight hours (solar zenith below 80 degrees) are kept.

The correction is fitted on year A and scored on year B, per substation. Each correction is an ordinary least-squares fit of the hourly residual on the columns below, with its coefficients frozen after year A. Scoring on year B is the walk-forward test of a static correction. The substations are the Primary series that have CAMS values (14 planned; one has no year A rows, so 13 are scored).

Arm Fitted columns Role none nothing The uncorrected forecast shift intercept A fixed daylight bias era5 intercept, ERA5 shortwave What stage 1a could already learn cams intercept, CAMS irradiance CAMS alone era5+cams intercept, ERA5 shortwave, CAMS irradiance The headline arm cams-era5 intercept, CAMS minus ERA5 shortwave One coefficient on the difference

Two planned contrasts, both on year B. The first is the share of the daylight mean squared residual removed by era5+cams against none. The second is the partial R squared of CAMS given ERA5, that is 1 - SSE(era5+cams) / SSE(era5). A third quantity, the mean absolute error of the median, is read for the same arms because it is the metric the other experiments report. The stability ratio is the out-of-sample share removed divided by the share removed when the same correction is fitted on year B itself. A ratio near 1 means the relation is stable. A low ratio means the coefficients drift between the years.

The interval resamples whole months, each with all 13 scored substations. Weather is shared across substations and hours within a day, so the block is a month of year B with every substation in it. The 98.33% interval (Bonferroni across the three interval conditions) comes from 10,000 resamples of the 12 months, rescored from the frozen coefficients. With 12 blocks the tails are coarse, and the write-up says so. The write-up also reports the share removed for each substation, and the share removed with each substation left out in turn. The script does not run the leave-one-month-out repeat that an earlier draft of the plan mentioned.

The stability ratio is pooled. Its numerator is the out-of-sample share removed and its denominator is the share removed by the same correction fitted on year B. A denominator below 5% makes the ratio undefined, and the outcome is then inconclusive.

Share removed Stability ratio Outcome 50% or more 0.8 or more P4 gate, if the three interval conditions also hold 50% or more 0.5 to 0.8 Inconclusive 20% to 50% 0.5 or more Inconclusive 20% or less, or any share below 0.5 P2 capacity-change statistics

CAMS is a lag-time input only. CAMS is observed after the fact and has no forecast, so a stage 1a trained on it could use it only for the past. Its latency at forecast time is not checked here. A positive gate is a necessary condition for P4 and does not show that the input is available in time. ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, so the ERA5 column is also a lag-time input in this test.

Year B's residuals come from a model trained on year A. The confirm_2025 model saw year A, so it may already have absorbed part of a fixed ERA5 error, and the stability ratio then measures that model change as much as any drift. Year B is also 00006's confirmation fold, and the July 2025 exploration in e00006_solar_residual.py has already looked at one month of it. The arm and the seeds of the chosen forecast were selected on folds that include year A. The write-up repeats all three points. The expected sign of the CAMS coefficient is negative, as at P12 in that exploration. CAMS and ERA5 shortwave are collinear, so the write-up reports the partial R squared and not the two coefficients. A linear fit on irradiance cannot capture a response that is nonlinear in cloud, so a low share removed is weaker evidence than a high one.

Confounds the write-up has to discuss. A fixed error in ERA5's cloud field and a fixed embedded-solar capacity both give a static relation, so a positive gate says the relation is stable over one year and does not exclude capacity. The stability ratio is the only evidence against capacity drift in this test.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The gate does not open for P4, and does not close for P2: the outcome is inconclusive. The planned share removed was 50% or more. The result is 46.6%, with a 98.33% month-block interval of 38.4% to 53.1% that straddles 50%. The stability ratio is 0.84, so the relation held across the two years. A fixed irradiance error gives a stable relation, and a steady capacity gives one too. The plan's table calls a share of 20% to 50% with a ratio of 0.5 or more "inconclusive". Seven conditions held: the partial R squared is above zero, the MAE gain against the shift is at least 0.3 points (0.73), and the stability ratio is at least 0.8. The lower bound of the share's interval is above 25% (38.4%). One condition failed: the share removed is below 50%.

Arm Share of daylight squared residual removed Daylight MAE of the median (points of capacity) Uncorrected 0% 8.78 Fixed daylight shift 39.1% 7.52 ERA5 shortwave 40.0% 7.41 CAMS 42.7% 7.11 ERA5 and CAMS 46.6% 6.80 CAMS minus ERA5 (one coefficient) not scored 7.00

The out-of-sample figures use 13 Primary substations, not the 14 planned. One substation has no 2024-07 to 2025-06 residual, so it has nothing to fit on. Fitting each correction on the scored year gives 55.8%, from which the stability ratio of 0.84 follows.

Most of what the correction removes is a fixed daytime bias, and one substation sets the pooled figure. The shift arm alone removes 39.1%, so CAMS adds 7.5 percentage points of share on top. Substation P2 has a mean absolute error of 34.1 points before correction, against a median of 5.8 at the other substations, and its shift alone removes 64.5%. Without P2 the pooled share is 18.2%, and an 18.2% share would sit in the plan's P2-capacity branch. The median substation's share is 34.4%. The correction makes the next year worse at 2 of the 13 substations (P13 and P15), removes almost nothing at P16 (1.2%), and has its largest partial R squared at P3 (0.41).

What this means for the follow-up work. CAMS carries information that ERA5 shortwave lacks at all 13 substations (partial R squared above zero), so a CAMS-trained stage 1a (P4) is worth a test of its own, with the substation that sets the pooled figure treated separately. The result does not show that the residual is an irradiance error and not a change in capacity. A growing capacity and a fixed ERA5 cloud error both give a stable relation, and the model behind year B was trained on year A, so it may have absorbed part of the error. The slope statistics of P2 should wait for that follow-up.

Caveats. The 98.33% interval resamples 12 months, so its tails are coarse. The MAE is of the hourly mean residual in daylight hours, not of half-hours. Year B is 00006's confirmation fold, and the earlier July 2025 exploration had already looked at part of it. CAMS has no forecast and its latency at forecast time was not checked.

Script: ml-experiments/00007-cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual/e00007_correction.py.

docs.title: Do summaries of recent power help the stage 2 calibrator?
docs.text:
We asked whether giving the second step of a demand forecast a few summaries of recent power, such as the minimum, mean, and maximum over the last 24 hours, helps when it already has the individual recent readings. We added six such summaries and compared the forecast error for the Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) up to 48 hours ahead. The summaries changed the error by about 0.02 points of capacity, which cannot be told apart from no change.

Verdict: inconclusive. Adding the six summaries to 00005's L3 calibrator changed the quantile score for leads up to 48 hours by -0.02 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.14 to +0.13), so the prediction of at least -0.15 failed and the interval does not exclude zero. The plan below was committed before any fit, and the results above it were written after the run. A point of capacity is 1% of the series' effective capacity.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Adding the summaries to L3 did not change the score by a resolvable amount. Up to 48 hours ahead, the Primary substations' quantile score (twice the mass-weighted pinball loss, an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score; smaller is better) was 5.31 for L3, 5.29 for S1, 5.59 for S2, 5.65 for S3, 5.93 for S4, 7.11 for R0c, and 8.14 for day-type climatology. Over all leads the scores were 6.36, 6.29, 6.46, 6.49, 6.73, 7.47, and 8.21. The refitted L3 matched 00005's L3 exactly to two decimals (5.31 up to 48 h, 6.36 over all leads), so the pipeline reproduces 00005.

All four planned contrasts, Primary substations. Negative means the first arm is better, and the intervals are at 98.75%.

  • C1 (primary), S1 minus L3: -0.02 up to 48 h (-0.14 to +0.13), 7 of 12 months and 8 of 16 series negative. Over all leads -0.06 (-0.18 to +0.06). The difference is slightly negative from 1 to 2 days onward (-0.04 to -0.08), and no band excludes zero.
  • C2, S2 minus L3: +0.29 up to 48 h (+0.11 to +0.51), 0 of 12 months negative. Replacing the raw power lags with summaries is worse at short leads, and the loss shrinks to +0.04 at 7 to 10 days.
  • C3, S3 minus L3: +0.35 up to 48 h (+0.15 to +0.58), 0 of 12 months negative.
  • C4, S4 minus R0c: -1.18 up to 48 h (-1.83 to -0.58), 12 of 12 months and 16 of 16 series negative, and -0.74 over all leads (-1.19 to -0.37). Summaries alone, without any ERA5 residual, recover about two thirds of the 1.80 points that L3 gains over R0c (exploratory E3).
  • Exploratory, S1 minus S2: -0.31 up to 48 h (95% interval -0.45 to -0.19), so the raw power lags are worth keeping even when the summaries are present.

The prediction's second clause, a gain within plus and minus 0.15 from 3 to 6 days onward, held for C1. C1 was -0.04 (-0.16 to +0.07) at 3 to 6 days, -0.08 (-0.22 to +0.02) at 7 to 10 days, and -0.08 (-0.23 to +0.09) at 11 to 15 days. That clause could not change the verdict.

The BSP and GSP results are descriptive, from two series each. Up to 48 h, C1 was +0.10 (-0.08 to +0.31) for the two bulk supply points and -0.25 (-0.69 to +0.23) for the two grid supply points. C4 was -0.04 (-0.23 to +0.15) for the bulk supply points and -1.57 (-3.09 to -0.62) for the grid supply points.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• C1 to C3 are ceilings. L3, S1, S2, and S3 use ERA5 weather at lag times in their residual columns, which production does not have in time. Only S4 uses recent power alone, and its gain over R0c is the deployable result. S4 still uses the stage 1 statistics of 00005's stage 1a, whose inputs are ERA5-trained.
  • C2 and C3 change several inputs at once. Each drops inputs and adds the summaries, so a loss cannot be attributed to either change.
  • The residuals are partly in-sample when the calibrator trains. This is shared with 00005 and affects L3, S1, S2, and S3 alike.
  • The same-weekday summary goes stale with lead. It covers the previous week's day at leads under a day and a day about a week old at leads near 6 to 7 days. The 48 half-hours start at UTC midnight, so each window holds the previous day's last half-hour stamp and 47 of the target day's own half-hours.
  • The reviews used Sonnet. The plan and the code each had one fresh Sonnet review. The code review found no lookahead: it overwrote power and residual with 99 from the origin onward and found every input unchanged.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• Keep the raw power lags. Replacing them with summaries cost 0.29 points up to 48 h.
  • Summaries alone recover about two thirds of L3's gain over no recent power. Daily minimum, mean, and maximum power beat no recent power by 1.18 points up to 48 h, and score 0.62 worse than L3 (E2).
  • An effect of 0.15 points is near this design's resolution. The C1 interval is 0.27 points wide, so a larger fold or more series would be needed to resolve it.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Question. Experiment 00005 found that recent power helps most when the stage 2 calibrator receives it (arm L3), as four raw power lags (24, 48, 168, and 336 hours before the target), the four stage 1a residuals at those lag times (the lag anomalies), and five residuals measured at the newest observation. Raw lags are single half-hours and are noisy. This experiment asks whether the minimum, mean, and maximum of a whole day of power are a better summary.

Series, rows, and folds. The same as 00005. The headline is the 16 Primary substations. The 2 bulk supply points and 2 grid supply points are reported separately as descriptive results. The rows are the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 (ECMWF ENS runs at 00:00 UTC every fifth day from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30), with nothing scored on or after 2026-07-01. The fitting seeds are 0, 1, and 2. The stage 1a models and the calibrator's training statistics are 00005's, read from its work folder without refitting, so every arm sees identical stage 1 inputs. Training window from 2023-09.

The six summaries. All are computed from observed power over effective capacity, using only observations up to the newest half-hour before the forecast's initialisation time T. Missing half-hours are ignored, and a window with fewer than 24 observed half-hours gives null. Weekdays are UTC weekdays.

  • Last 24 hours: the minimum, mean, and maximum of the 48 half-hours ending at T - 0.5 h.
  • Same weekday: the minimum, mean, and maximum of the 48 half-hours of the most recent UTC calendar day that falls on the target's weekday and whose last half-hour is no later than T - 0.5 h. For a lead of under a day this is the previous week's day; for a longer lead it is the latest complete such day.

Neither summary depends on weather, so both are available at forecast time. The five residuals and the four lag anomalies use ERA5 weather at the lag time, which production does not have in time, so every arm that keeps them is a ceiling, as 00005's lagged arms were.

Arms. All use the calibrator of 00005 (one multi-quantile XGBoost model per series, depth 4, eta 0.05, 300 rounds, the 9 levels, inputs of the 51 members' mean, standard deviation and 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles, and the lead). No arm has a calendar column.

  • L3 (base): 00005's recent-origin inputs. Refitted here, to check that the pipeline reproduces 00005's scores.
  • S1 (add): L3 plus the six summaries.
  • S2 (replace power lags): the five residuals, the four lag anomalies, and the six summaries. The four raw power lags are dropped.
  • S3 (summaries replace all lags): the five residuals and the six summaries. No raw lag and no lag anomaly.
  • S4 (power summaries only, no ERA5 residual): the six summaries and no residual. This is the only arm whose recent-power inputs are fully available at forecast time.
  • R0c, R2: 00005's lag-free calibrator and day-type climatology, as references.

Planned contrasts (quantile score, points of capacity, Primary substations, read at 98.75% because four are planned):

  • C1 (primary): S1 minus L3.
  • C2: S2 minus L3 (do summaries beat raw power lags).
  • C3: S3 minus L3 (do summaries beat all the lag columns).
  • C4: S4 minus R0c (do summaries help when no ERA5 residual is available).

C1 to C3 are scored over leads up to 48 hours (the decision scope) and by lead band. C2 and C3 are bundle contrasts: each drops inputs and adds the summaries, so a loss cannot be attributed to either change. The exploratory contrast S1 minus S2 isolates the raw power lags. Because L3 and S1 keep the ERA5 residuals, C1 to C3 are ceilings, and a supported verdict reads "supported as a ceiling"; C4 is the contrast that can support a claim about production. The same four are computed for the BSP and GSP series and reported as descriptive. The second clause of the prediction (the gain from 3 to 6 d onward) is descriptive and cannot change the verdict. The 98.75% level is a uniform Bonferroni convention across the four contrasts, although only C1 decides the verdict. The rule is asymmetric on purpose: a difference between 0 and +0.15 is inconclusive. C1 uses the refitted L3, which runs through the same code as S1. The refit must reproduce 00005's L3 score up to 48 h within 0.05 points; if it does not, the write-up says so and the cause is investigated before any result is reported. The same-weekday summary goes stale as the lead grows (a week old at short leads, about a day old at 6 to 7 d), so results are reported by lead band. Everything else, such as S4 minus L3 and S1 minus S2, is exploratory, read at 95%, and labelled so. The write-up reports the number of series (by series sign) and of months that agree with each mean, and the absolute score of every arm by lead band.

Calendar guard. The calibrator has no calendar column, and no arm uses early stopping, so no inner split is needed.

Reviews. A fresh Sonnet reviewer reads the plan, another reads the code for leakage (the summaries must use only data before T, and the same-weekday window must end before T), and another checks the write-up against the printed report.

Size. Medium. (1) Storage: new prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/, nothing in the production tables. (2) The production serving path is not touched. (3) No degradation rule is touched. (4) More than one design could test the hypothesis, such as adding or replacing, and the arms cover both. (5) The new code is a copy of 00005's calibrator with one added input function; its callers are all inside this folder. The mutation pass does not apply, because no production logic changes.

docs.title: Not tested here
docs.text: Summaries of weather, generator series, a second fold, and summaries in stage 1b.

docs.title: Does a stage 1a trained on CAMS irradiance beat one trained on ERA5 shortwave, for demand?
docs.text:
We asked whether training a weather-to-power demand model on a satellite estimate of sunlight gives better forecasts than training it on a reanalysis estimate of sunlight. We trained one model on each, applied both to the same 51 weather forecasts, and compared their errors for the Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network). The model trained on the satellite estimate was better by only 0.035 points of capacity, far short of the 0.2 points we had predicted. A point of capacity is 1% of a series' effective capacity, roughly its usual maximum output.

This experiment is the second stage of P2 in the research plan. Experiment 00007 found that a fixed correction on CAMS irradiance removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual (the squared forecast error) of the ERA5-trained stage 1a (98.33% interval 38.4% to 53.1%), that a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%, and that one substation sets the pooled figure (18.2% without it). The result was inconclusive. This experiment trains stage 1a on CAMS at the training times and scores it on ENS.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: prediction sets and tables under this experiment's private folder. Nothing enters a Delta table.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Designs that would test the hypothesis defensibly: two. Replacing ERA5 shortwave by CAMS at the training times, planned here, is the simpler. Keeping ERA5 for training and quantile-mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS at application would also be defensible, and was not run here.
  • Callers that need searching for: none. The scripts copy the patterns of ml-experiments/00005-* and ml-experiments/00006-* and read their inputs.

The experiment is medium: it adds a data source to training and a method not yet run in this repository, and touches nothing stored for production. It gets a Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code, and one of the write-up. The earlier advice lists were read: this plan follows "Train a demand stage 1a from 2023-09" (00005), "Use the weather block, hour, weekday, and the COVID indicator" (00006), "Report a pooled share with and without the substation that has the largest residual" (00007), and "Compare irradiance read at the substation's own location, such as CAMS, with ERA5 shortwave" (00006). The plan departs from "Weight recent years more" (00006), so that the ERA5-trained arm matches 00005's r0_from2023. The residuals of experiment 00007 came from a forecast that used recency weights, so 00007's evidence transfers to this plan only approximately.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Two main arms differ in one input, which changes in three ways at once. Both are one XGBoost model per series, with 00005's settings (500 rounds, depth 6, learning rate 0.05, squared error, three seeds), trained on valid times from 2023-09-01 to before 2025-06-17. The columns are 00006's chosen set, as frozen in 00005: ERA5 shortwave, longwave, temperature, dew point, surface pressure, precipitation, and 10 m wind speed; solar zenith and azimuth; local hour and weekday; the COVID indicator; and the days to Christmas. The era5 arm reads ERA5 shortwave at the series' H3 cell. The cams arm reads CAMS irradiance at the series' own location instead (the download in PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations)). The CAMS column differs from the ERA5 column in the product (satellite-derived against reanalysis), the location (the series' own point against the mean of its H3 cell), and the time handling (hourly values held across two half-hours). At validation, both arms read the ENS member's shortwave. Every other weather column stays ERA5 in training and ENS in validation. A third arm, era5-hourly, is an exploratory control: ERA5 shortwave averaged over each hour and held across its two half-hours, so that contrast X1 (era5-hourly minus era5) shows how much of the difference comes from the time handling alone.

CAMS is hourly and the grid is half-hourly. A CAMS value is the mean over the hour ending at its stamp. Both half-hours of that hour take the value. Hourly holding differs from the half-hourly construction of ERA5 shortwave, and the Results section states the difference.

Each arm gives 9 quantiles from the 51 ENS members. The stage 1a XGBoost model is applied to every member and the quantiles are the empirical quantiles of the 51 forecasts, as in 00005's r0 arms. There is no calibrator, no stage 1b, and no lagged power, so no weather has to exist at lag times. CAMS is used in training only and is never needed at forecast time.

The scored rows are those of 00005. The rows are the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 for the 20 series, restricted to valid times with an observed power and before 2026-07-01. The 16 Primary series are the headline, and the substation that sets 00007's pooled figure (P2) is one of them. The 2 bulk supply point and 2 grid supply point series are reported separately and decide nothing. Intervals resample whole validation months and the three seeds. The climatology row is 00005's r2.

Two planned contrasts, both on Primary substations over all leads. C1 compares the arms (CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained). C2 repeats C1 without the substation that sets 00007's pooled figure. The 0.2-point threshold of the research plan is kept for C1. In 00005, a contrast between two stage 1a variants on Primary substations over all leads had a 95% interval about 0.2 points wide on each side (E11: +0.075, -0.060 to +0.265), so 0.2 is the size of the noise and not below it. C2 uses half that size because removing a substation removes much of the gain 00007 saw. The 97.5% level is a Bonferroni correction across the two.

The rule has limited power, and an inconclusive result is likely. The 95% interval of E11 reached 0.135 below and 0.19 above its estimate, so the 97.5% half-width of C1 will be near 0.2 points. A true gain of exactly 0.2 points would then clear "interval wholly below zero" about half the time, and refuting a gain of 0.2 needs an estimate near zero or worse. The write-up reports the interval half-width obtained.

Exploratory contrasts are read at 95%. They are: C1 by lead band and for daylight and night valid times separately (the gain should come in daylight); C1 for the bulk supply points and the grid supply points; C1 for each Primary series; C1 leaving out each Primary series in turn; and the quantile score of the ERA5-trained arm against the climatology. A deterministic diagnostic at the observed weather also compares the two arms at the validation hours, with the ERA5-trained arm reading ERA5 and the CAMS-trained arm reading CAMS, as in 00007's residuals. The diagnostic shows what training on CAMS gains when CAMS is also the input, which no forecast can supply. A table of the mean daylight shortwave of CAMS, ERA5, and the ENS members by month shows the scale mismatch the CAMS-trained arm meets at validation.

Leakage and calendar checks. Both arms train on valid times before 2025-06-17, 14 days before the first validation run, so no fit sees a validation hour. There is no early stopping. Both arms carry the same calendar columns, so a contrast between them cannot come from calendar memorisation.

Known limits. CAMS irradiance is estimated from satellite images and ERA5 shortwave comes from a reanalysis, so the two carry different cloud fields, and the CAMS-trained arm sees ENS shortwave, a forecast with its own bias and spread, which is the mismatch the experiment tests. Validation is one year (2025-07 to 2026-06), which is also 00006's confirmation year, so 12 months bound the interval's resolution. The 20 series and 73 runs are 00005's choice and were not re-selected.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The hypothesis is refuted: training stage 1a on CAMS irradiance lowers the Primary quantile score by 0.035 points, a sixth of the 0.2 points the plan required. The refutation is of a gain of the planned size. A small gain is present in daylight and at short range. C1 is -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), so the data exclude a gain of 0.2 points. C2, without the substation that set 00007's pooled figure (P2), is -0.043 (-0.081 to -0.004), so the small gain does not rest on that substation. In both contrasts the CAMS-trained arm is better in 10 of 12 months, and in 12 of the series (of 16 for C1, of 15 for C2). The refit of the ERA5-trained arm reproduces experiment 00005's r0_from2023 exactly (a mean absolute difference of 0.000 in all 9 quantiles over 2,898,789 rows), so the benchmark is the same forecast that experiment scored.

Arm Primary quantile score BSP GSP Primary error of the median ERA5-trained 7.88 (6.92 to 8.75) 8.60 21.08 9.49 CAMS-trained 7.84 (6.89 to 8.73) 8.56 20.98 9.46 ERA5 held hourly (control) 7.87 (6.92 to 8.75) 8.62 21.06 9.47 Climatology (00005's r2) 8.21 (7.45 to 8.97) 9.43 24.41 11.30

All scores are in points of capacity, over all leads, with 95% month-and-seed intervals for the Primary quantile score. The absolute intervals are wide because every arm's error rises and falls together from month to month, which pairing removes from a contrast.

The gain is small, its interval just reaches zero, and it is concentrated in daylight and in the first 6 days. In daylight the contrast is -0.089 (95% interval -0.149 to -0.034), and at night it is +0.001 (-0.041 to +0.031), which fits a gain that comes from the irradiance input. By lead band it is -0.072 up to 1 day, -0.080 for 1 to 2 days, -0.063 for 3 to 6 days, -0.021 for 7 to 10 days (-0.057 to +0.019), and -0.004 for 11 to 15 days. The gain is larger for the 2 grid supply points (-0.104, -0.211 to -0.006) than for the 2 bulk supply points (-0.044, -0.150 to +0.041), and the 4 series are too few to say more.

A mismatch at application is a likely reason for the small gain, and this experiment does not test it. At the observed weather, with each arm reading its own irradiance, the CAMS-trained arm's daylight error of the median is 10.46 points against 11.34 (-0.88, 95% interval -1.00 to -0.72). With ENS forecasts as input the same contrast is -0.17 up to 1 day (-0.31 to -0.03) and -0.04 over all leads (-0.13 to +0.04). The mean daylight shortwave of the 16 Primary series is 261 W/m² for both CAMS and ERA5 in the training period and 263 and 262 in the validation year, against 281 for the ENS members (7% higher). Neither arm saw that bias in training. The bias varies by month, and the ENS forecast's own cloud errors would also dilute a gain, so the shortwave comparison is a candidate cause only. A bias-corrected ENS shortwave would test it.

Hourly holding of the irradiance cannot be separated from the difference at this resolution. Holding ERA5 shortwave hourly changes the score by -0.012 (X1, -0.064 to +0.030). The CAMS-trained arm against the hourly-held ERA5 arm is -0.022 (X2, -0.075 to +0.038), so the remaining difference of the bundle cannot be split between product and location at this resolution.

Failures and limits. Series P2 scores worse with CAMS (+0.080, -0.001 to +0.178); the series P5, P15, and P12 gain the most (-0.125, -0.113, and -0.092). Series P9 and P14 have only 8 and 10 months of data, so their intervals are very wide. The plan guessed that the interval half-width of C1 would be near 0.2 points, and it came out at 0.035, so the 0.2-point threshold was far above the resolution of the data and a smaller gain could have been resolved. Intervals resample the initialisation months of the runs, which equal validation months except for runs near a month's end. Validation is one year (2025-07 to 2026-06), the confirmation year of experiment 00006. The experiment does not test quantile-mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS, which the shortwave comparison suggests.

Scripts: ml-experiments/00009-cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand/ (e00009_fit.py, e00009_score.py, e00009_charts.py).

docs.title: Does the lagged electricity price help the demand model at substations with batteries?
docs.text:
We asked whether the electricity price from 7 days earlier helps predict demand at substations that host a battery, whose charging may follow the price. We added that price to a weather-to-power demand model and compared its error with the same model without it, on the substation hosting the largest battery and on 16 other series, in a selection year and a confirmation year. The price lowered the error in the selection year, but the gain disappeared in the confirmation year, so the experiment cannot support the idea that batteries respond to the price.

Verdict: inconclusive. Adding the electricity price published by Elexon (the electricity market operator for Great Britain) from 7 days earlier did not lower the error of the stage 1a demand model at the substation hosting the largest battery (B2) with an interval that excludes zero, and the gain seen in the selection year disappeared in the confirmation year. The pre-registered mechanism test (C4) failed in the selection year and pointed the wrong way in the confirmation year, so the experiment cannot support a price response by batteries. Stage 1a is an XGBoost model per series that turns weather into power.

Absolute scores. The arms are BASE (the demand model without the price), PRICE (BASE plus the price from 7 days earlier), CONTROL (BASE plus three columns that contain no price), and SHUFFLED (BASE plus the price from a different week). The scores are the mean absolute error of the median in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity), averaged over 3 random seeds:

Scope and year BASE PRICE CONTROL SHUFFLED B2, selection 10.98 10.05 10.91 10.21 Other series (16), selection 9.79 9.40 9.78 9.47 Primary, selection 6.97 7.01 7.03 7.04 B2, confirmation 10.12 10.06 9.89 10.09 P4, confirmation 4.22 5.33 4.16 4.42 Other series (16), confirmation 9.35 9.41 9.13 9.29 Primary, confirmation 7.11 7.15 6.92 7.04

docs.title: What the contrasts say
docs.text:
• C1, price against base, B2: -0.92 (-2.10 to +0.07) in the selection year, so not material (the interval includes zero). In the confirmation year -0.06 (-0.38 to +0.23).
  • C2, price against demand and wind, B2: -0.86 (-2.10 to +0.21) in the selection year, so not material, and +0.18 (-0.08 to +0.41) in the confirmation year.
  • C3, price against shuffled price, B2: -0.16 (-0.53 to +0.17). The shuffled price reproduced about five sixths (0.77 of 0.92 points) of the selection-year gain at B2, and C1's own interval includes zero, so the gain is not evidence of a price effect. The CONTROL arm, with the same lag and column count, gained only 0.07 points at B2, so the experiment does not show why the shuffled price matched the real price.
  • Confirmation year, listed series pooled (B2 and P4): C1 is +0.53 (+0.14 to +1.27), C2 is +0.67 (+0.20 to +1.49), and C3 is +0.44 (-0.04 to +1.33). The pooled C1 interval excludes the selection-year estimate of -0.92, so the decision rule's confirmation clause makes the verdict inconclusive.
  • The prediction's second clause failed. The price lowered the selection-year error at the other series by 0.38 points (-0.77 to +0.07), against a predicted gain below 0.1.
  • C4, gain at the listed series minus gain at the others: -0.55 (-1.43 to +0.20) in the selection year, and +0.47 (+0.06 to +0.91) in the confirmation year, where the listed series got worse by more than the others.
  • The gain was concentrated at the series with the largest errors, not at the listed series. In the selection year the largest gains were at G1 (-4.89), P2 (-1.89), and G2 (-1.34). In the confirmation year G1 got worse by +1.34 while P2 still gained -2.35.

docs.title: Failures and deviations
docs.text:
• P4 could not be fitted in the selection year, because it has only 14,615 half-hours of training data before the purge, under the 17,520 the fit requires. The listed group in the selection year is B2 alone. P4 was fitted in the confirmation year, and the price made it worse by +1.11 (+0.23 to +2.85). Two further series have too little history in both years, so 17 series were fitted in the selection year and 18 in the confirmation year, not 20.
  • No month-by-half-hour climatology row was scored, which the ml-experiment skill asks for.
  • The refuted branch of the decision rule was unreachable, as the power check predicted.
  • No Opus review was run. Sonnet reviewed the plan, the code, and this write-up, as the brief asked. The code review found that the shuffled arm read prices from later weeks; that was fixed before any fit.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: A price taken from another week matched most of the selection-year gain at B2, and the gain did not repeat. The gain at B2 and the larger gains at G1 and P2 in the selection year are not evidence of a price effect, because intervals include zero and the confirmation year reversed G1. The advice list in the front matter carries the actions.

docs.title: Why the price, and why only a lag
docs.text: Future prices are hard to predict, so the inputs are prices already published. A battery that charges when the price is low and discharges when it is high moves a substation's demand by an amount the weather and the clock do not explain. The stage 1a demand model sees this only if it is given the price. The price at the same half-hour 7 days earlier is published well before any forecast issue time, so it exists at forecast time for every lead up to 7 days.

docs.title: Price source
docs.text:
The price is the APXMIDP provider's price in Elexon's Market Index Data. The data pull is in data/ml-experiments/00010-elexon-price-lags-stage1a-demand/prices/ and its README.md is the lineage note. Findings, all from e00010_fetch_prices.py:

  • Cost and licence: the Elexon Insights API needs no key and no payment. The script accepts no licence in anyone's name.
  • Coverage: 134,357 of 136,416 half-hours (98.5%) from 2019-01-01 to 2026-10-12. 36 whole days are empty, all between 2019-01-09 and 2021-04-28. 54 more days are partial, 45 of them before 2021-06. From 2024-04-14 the series is complete.
  • Product mix: the other provider, N2EXMIDP, reports volume 0 in all but 385 of its 134,249 rows, so only APXMIDP is usable. The API does not say which products feed the APXMIDP index. The plan therefore calls it the EPEX short-term half-hourly index, as studies/market_downloads does, and does not claim it is the day-ahead price.
  • Zero volume: 175 APXMIDP rows report volume 0 (64 in 2019, 50 in 2021, 18 in 2022, 15 in 2023, 11 in 2025, 12 in 2026, 5 in 2020). The experiment sets the price on those rows to missing.
  • Values: -102.92 to 1,983.66 GBP per MWh, the maximum on 2021-09-09. No nulls, and the longest run of an unchanged price is 30 half-hours.

The CONTROL columns need a second pull. The demand outturn and fuel-mix downloads already in data/studies/downloads/market/ cover only 2025-09 to 2026-09, so the same free Insights API pull was repeated for 2019 to 2026 with the same validation.

Training years with missing prices are not dropped. XGBoost handles a missing value natively. price_lag7d is missing when its half-hour is missing or has zero volume. The minimum and maximum are missing when fewer than 40 of the 48 half-hours are available. About 23 half-hours in the validation and confirmation years have a zero-volume price, so a few rows there carry missing price columns; the report counts them. No lead beyond 7 days is scored.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The base is experiment 00006's Primary input set: the weather block (ERA5, read at the series' nearest grid cell), hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, and the days to Christmas inside a 14-day window, trained with recency weights (half-life 2 years). Folds, XGBoost settings (no column subsampling), seeds, and the 7-day purge are those of 00006.

Arm Adds to BASE BASE nothing PRICE price_lag7d (price at the same half-hour 7 days earlier), price_min_lag7d and price_max_lag7d (the minimum and maximum over the 48 half-hours ending at the valid time minus 7 days, so nothing post-dates the valid time minus 7 days) CONTROL three columns with no price in them, matching PRICE's count: GB national demand outturn (Elexon INDO) at the same half-hour 7 days earlier, wind generation (Elexon FUELHH) at the same half-hour 7 days earlier, and the range of demand minus wind over the 48 half-hours ending 7 days earlier SHUFFLED the three PRICE columns, all taken from one other week of the same weekday and half-hour, drawn with a fixed seed from 1 to 4 weeks further back than the true lag (a negative control)

Weather and timing caveat. The weather block is ERA5 read at the valid time, as in 00006, so every score is a ceiling for the same reason 00005's was: ERA5 arrives about 5 days late. The columns this experiment adds are available at forecast time because they are at least 7 days old.

Calendar memorisation control. Hour and weekday are in BASE (as in 00006), so the price columns can stand in for the calendar. SHUFFLED keeps the calendar structure and removes the price's information, and it is the control for that.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
All are differences in mean absolute error of the median, in points of capacity, over the selection year (2024-07 to 2025-06) and then, once, the confirmation year (2025-07 to 2026-06), with a month-resampled interval at the 98.3% level that the decision rule sets.

  • C1: PRICE − BASE.
  • C2: PRICE − CONTROL (what the price adds beyond national demand and wind).
  • C3: PRICE − SHUFFLED (what the price adds beyond the calendar structure of the price columns).
  • C4: the gain PRICE − BASE at the two listed series minus the gain at the other fitted series (16 in each year), with the months resampled (a verdict contrast, as the decision rule says).

docs.title: The listed substations, chosen before any fit
docs.text:
The list comes from NGED's Embedded Capacity Register (August 2026 release), which is independent of the outcome. A series is listed if the register's connected storage rows under the series' name sum to a maximum export capacity of at least 5% of the series' effective capacity. The 5% threshold is a round number chosen before the sums were run; P4 passed it by 0.1 points, which is why the plan reports it only beside B2. The register has no commissioning dates, so a listed battery may have been absent for part of the training years or of the selection year, and batteries also earn from balancing and frequency response, not only the index price. A gain at B2 is therefore weak evidence of a battery response. The register names the primary, bulk supply point, and grid supply point each row connects to. The result for the 20 series 00006 scored:

  • Listed: B2, a bulk supply point, with 9.5 MW of connected storage against 47.6 MW of effective capacity (20%).
  • Listed: P4, a primary, with 0.37 MW of connected storage against 7.1 MW (5.1%, just over the threshold).
  • Not listed: the two grid supply points (10.5 MW of connected storage against 384 MW, and 7.4 against 171 MW, under 5%), the other bulk supply point (0.75 against 55 MW), and the other 15 primaries (at most 0.19 MW each, against 3 to 18 MW).

The listed group has two members, one of them with a 0.37 MW battery, so the mechanism cannot be tested well with this series set. C4 compares two listed series with the rest. The verdict therefore needs C4, and the register in the embedded-battery and unmetered-battery studies adds no further series: the unmetered-battery study's screen found no battery at any of its eight primaries, including the two the register lists with connected storage, so no other series can be named from data independent of the outcome. P4's battery is 0.37 MW. The advice for a later experiment is to repeat the test on a series set with more battery sites. No series is added after seeing results.

docs.title: Power check, run before any fit
docs.text: B2's 98.3% interval will be about 0.3 to 0.4 points wide on each side, so the refuted branch cannot be reached. The check resampled the 12 validation months of one seed of two close arms from experiment 00006's stored fits at B2 (the clock-only arm against the clock, COVID indicator, and days-to-Christmas arm), a difference of typical size. The half-width was 0.40 points, and 0.30 for a larger difference. The decision rule therefore applies: the refuted branch is dropped, and the verdict is supported or inconclusive. A gain at B2 needs to be about 0.4 points or more to be material.

docs.title: Resources and sizing
docs.text:
Sizing, one line per plan-issue trigger. Stores: only private predictions and a price parquet, no production table. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched, but a production port would need one (price missing means the columns go missing, which XGBoost handles). More than one defensible design: yes (which price, which lags), so the plan fixes them here. Code whose callers could not be named without searching: no. This is medium.

Resources. The fits ran on 8 CPU cores, one thread per fit, with no GPU: the 00006 per-series fits for four arms on two folds and three seeds. Sonnet reviewed the plan, the code, and the write-up.

Earlier advice. Follows the experiment 00006 advice to use its Primary set and recency weights. Departs from none of it.

docs.title: Do school-term and return-to-work columns lower the stage 1a demand error after Christmas, at Easter, and in school holidays?
docs.text:
We asked whether telling a demand model when people return to work after New Year and when Lincolnshire's schools are in term lowers its error in the weeks after Christmas, around Easter, and in school half-terms. We added those calendar columns to a weather-to-power model and compared its error with the same model without them, over 20 series that lie within Lincolnshire. The columns did not lower the error in the weeks after Christmas or at Easter, and the half-term change has an interval that includes zero. The rule we set before the run calls this refuted, but the rule was worded more loosely than intended, and the intended reading rules out a gain only in January.

Verdict: refuted, by the decision rule as pre-registered. For the Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), the return-to-work and school-term columns did not lower the error in the weeks after Christmas or at Easter. The half-term change of -0.29 points has an interval that includes zero.

The refutation clause of the rule is looser than intended, and the intended reading gives "inconclusive". The clause required the upper bounds of C1, C2, and C3 to exceed -0.25, -0.15, and -0.15, which every interval that includes zero satisfies, and so does an interval such as -1.4 to +0.2. Ruling out a gain of half the predicted size needs the lower bound above those values. Read that way, the data rule out a gain of 0.25 points in the January window (lower bound -0.17). They do not rule out a gain of 0.15 points at Easter (lower bound -0.19) or over the half terms (-0.68), so the intended reading is inconclusive for those two windows. The verdict field keeps the rule as written.

All 20 series lie in a box that is essentially Lincolnshire, so the term calendar is Lincolnshire County Council's recommended calendar. Primary substations are the headline, with 13, 13, and 14 series in the three validation years. Every score is the mean absolute error of the median, in points of capacity.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
None of C1 to C3 is a gain, and C5 and C6 fail. The whole-year point estimate of -0.02 is inside the predicted 0.1, but its interval is not. The table gives the change for the return and term columns together (Both) against the base arm, for Primary substations, with each year's change. The level is 99.2%, and each interval resamples 7-day blocks of days after averaging the three fitting seeds. The intervals understate the uncertainty, because neighbouring days share weather and each window has three occurrences.

Contrast Change Interval 2023-24 2024-25 2025-26 Base error Result C1: 2 to 20 January +0.06 -0.17 to +0.30 +0.14 +0.06 -0.03 8.44 Not a gain C2: Easter +0.20 -0.19 to +0.59 +0.37 +0.22 -0.01 7.17 Not a gain C3: half-term holidays -0.29 -0.68 to +0.07 -0.25 -0.12 -0.49 7.73 Not a gain (interval includes zero) C4: summer holiday (descriptive) -0.02 -0.25 to +0.21 -0.40 +0.09 +0.24 6.51 No harm detected for Primary C5: whole year -0.02 -0.11 to +0.07 7.18 Does not hold (lower bound -0.11 is outside -0.1) C6: against Placebo A, three windows -0.03 -0.25 to +0.19 +0.11 -0.05 -0.13 7.73 Fails C6: against Placebo B, three windows -0.04 -0.19 to +0.11 +0.12 -0.05 -0.18 7.74 Fails

Both is not 0.2 points better than either shifted calendar, so C6 fails. The shifted calendars score the same as the base arm (Placebo A +0.00, -0.13 to +0.12, and Placebo B +0.01, -0.18 to +0.20, pooled over the three windows), so for Primary substations the extra columns show no detectable effect.

docs.title: Which columns, and what else was measured
docs.text:
The return column shows no detectable effect in January, and the term columns' half-term effect cannot be separated from a smooth seasonal curve. The table gives descriptive contrasts against the base arm for Primary substations, and none was part of the decision. The return column is missing outside its window, so its zero effect at Easter and in half terms holds by construction.

Arm 2 to 20 January Easter Half-term holidays Return column only +0.02 (-0.20 to +0.23) +0.01 (-0.00 to +0.02) -0.00 (-0.03 to +0.04) Term columns only +0.04 (-0.25 to +0.25) +0.20 (-0.18 to +0.56) -0.28 (-0.66 to +0.06) One harmonic of time of year -0.05 (-0.32 to +0.15) +0.16 (-0.28 to +0.51) -0.46 (-1.02 to +0.05)

Primary error is higher in the weeks after Christmas than just before, and the arms differ only in single days. The lines are means of three days. The base arm's error is 6 to 8 points before Christmas and 7 to 10 from 8 to 26 days after it, averaging 8.4 from 2 to 20 January. Over the Christmas weeks (15 December to 7 January), Both is +0.12 points against the base arm (-0.21 to +0.61), and +0.64 in 2023-24, above the 0.1 tolerance the plan set. On the four days before Christmas Day, Both is 0.5 to 1.1 points worse than the base arm. The one harmonic of time of year tracks the base arm more closely.

The arm with the full history and the COVID indicator scored higher on the whole year than the base arm. The Reference arm (the base columns plus the COVID indicator, trained from 2019-09-01) scores 7.44 for Primary substations against 7.18 for the base arm: +0.26 (99.2% interval +0.12 to +0.43). The two arms differ in the start date and in the COVID indicator, so the gap cannot be assigned to either alone. For GSP the Reference arm scores lower (-0.48, -1.05 to +0.05), and for BSP higher (+0.17, 0.02 to 0.33). Over the three windows pooled, Both scores -0.21 (-0.50 to +0.04) against the Reference arm. Experiment 6 found a lower Primary error for a 2023-09 start on its confirmation year (-0.86) and no change on its selection year (-0.05). The arm was planned as a descriptive reference, so it does not belong to the decision.

Arm Primary BSP GSP Climatology (month, half-hour, weekend) 8.55 12.48 35.79 Reference (full history, COVID indicator) 7.44 9.06 27.82 Base 7.18 8.89 28.30 Return column 7.18 8.91 28.37 Term columns 7.16 9.11 28.96 Return and term columns 7.15 9.11 28.94 Placebo A (calendar from 17 days earlier) 7.22 9.12 28.87 Placebo B (calendar from 17 days later) 7.16 8.97 28.75 One harmonic of time of year 7.19 8.96 28.99

The columns do not help BSP and GSP either, and a shifted calendar raises the GSP error. The table gives whole-year error over the three validation years. In the 2 to 20 January window, Both is +0.35 (-0.50 to +1.48) for BSP and +1.30 (-0.99 to +3.84) for GSP. In the summer holiday, Both raises the BSP error by 1.31 (+0.47 to +2.80), so the Primary result for C4 does not carry to BSP. Placebo A raises the GSP error over the three windows by 1.29 (+0.19 to +2.43), from two series. The BSP group has one or two series per year and the GSP group two, so none of their intervals is decisive.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Few occurrences per window. The January, Easter, and summer windows have one occurrence per year, and the half-term window has three short holidays per year. A real effect of 0.3 points needs an interval narrower than the 0.5 to 0.8 points these windows give.
  • Midnight half-hours. hour_local and day_of_week_local describe the day that starts at valid_time, and the term and return columns describe the day the period ends in. The two differ only for the half-hour ending at 00:00.
  • Series set. A series needs a year of observed half-hours after 2021-09-01, so the three validation years score 13, 13, and 14 Primary series, and a Primary series that experiment 6 scored can be absent.
  • ERA5 weather. The stage 1a XGBoost model is fitted and scored on ERA5, so a gain here need not carry over to forecast weather. The term and return columns are known in advance.
  • Post hoc work. The intended reading of the refutation clause is post hoc. Every number above is from the pre-registered arms and windows, and e00011_report.py prints each of them.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• The return and term columns show no detectable gain on top of the Christmas column. The 2 to 20 January error averages 8.4 points for the base arm, and Both differs from it by +0.06.
  • A half-term effect needs more occurrences to test. The Easter and half-term windows gave intervals about 0.8 points wide.
  • A shorter training history, or the COVID indicator, deserves its own test. The arm with the full history and the COVID indicator scored 0.26 points higher on the whole year.

docs.title: Pre-registered plan
docs.text: This part of the page is the plan as committed before any fit. It fixes the arms, the windows, and the contrasts. It continues experiment 00006, which found that a windowed days-to-Christmas column lowers the Primary error by 1.8 points from 15 December to 7 January, and which left Easter and the school holidays without a column.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
The size is complex, because the experiment adds data and admits more than one defensible design.

  • What gets stored: one new committed file of hand-collected term dates, and private predictions. No schema in packages/contracts/ changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched. The columns are candidates for a later model release.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The window lengths, the encoding of a term boundary (a flag, signed day counts, or both), and the control all admit alternatives. This page fixes one.
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no. The fitting code is a copy of experiment 00006's, with new column groups.

docs.title: Which earlier advice this plan follows
docs.text:
• Followed: window the day counts and leave them missing elsewhere (00006, Christmas control); score a new calendar column on special-day windows as well as the whole year; add a control before crediting a signed or cyclic calendar column; split every score by substation type, and make Primary the headline.
  • Departed from: 00006's recommended set includes the COVID indicator and the full history. This experiment trains every arm from 2021-09-01, because school-term dates before the 2021-22 academic year are not collected. The indicator is then constant at zero and is dropped. One reference arm keeps the full history, to show what the shorter history costs.

docs.title: Data: Lincolnshire County Council's term dates
docs.text:
All 20 series lie in a box that is essentially Lincolnshire, so one calendar covers them. The latitude and longitude columns of the metadata place every Primary, BSP, and GSP series between 52.7 and 53.3 degrees north and -0.2 and 0.33 degrees east, in the East Midlands licence area. The box edge near 52.7 degrees north and 0.2 degrees east lies close to Norfolk, and no series was checked against the local authority boundary. The planned split "by nation and by local authority" therefore has one nation (England) and one local authority. The calendar is Lincolnshire County Council's recommended calendar, which binds community and voluntary-controlled schools. Academies and voluntary-aided schools set their own dates, often within a day or two of it. The columns are therefore a proxy for the calendar of the schools near a substation, not a count of pupils in school.

The dates are in the CSV file lincolnshire_term_dates.csv in the experiment's code folder, with sources and licence in the README beside it. The first and last day of 30 terms (2021-22 to 2025-26) were read by hand from the council's web pages and two school calendars. The 2024-25 year, which is the validation year of the second fold, rests on one school's copy of the council's calendar, confirmed against the amendment the council's page states. e00011_term_dates.py validates the file. The checks cover six terms per year, order and overlap, a weekday start, term length, holiday length, Christmas and Easter inside a holiday, and the 2025-26 dates against two other calendars. All 30 terms pass. Only 2025-26 has a second source to check against.

The 2024-25 calendar was amended after its first publication. An older copy gives term 5 starting on 22 April and term 6 on 3 June 2025. The file holds the amended dates, and a forecast made before the amendment would have seen the older ones. The difference is one day at each of two boundaries, so it is noted and not modelled.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Every column is computed from the local date alone and is known months ahead. The council publishes the current and the next school year, so each column exists at forecast time. The experiment uses no lagged weather or power.

Column Definition school_term_flag 1 from a term's first to last day (weekends inside a term included), else 0 days_from_term_start_w Signed days to the nearest term's first day, kept within 13 days either way, else missing days_from_term_end_w The same for a term's last day days_from_return_w Signed days from the first working day of the year (the first weekday that is not a bank holiday in England), kept from 7 days before to 14 days after, else missing placebo_a_* The same four columns read from the real calendar 17 days earlier placebo_b_* The same four columns read from the real calendar 17 days later

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
All arms train from 2021-09-01 except the reference arm, use three fitting seeds, and use reg:absoluteerror with the settings of experiment 00006. Folds are the three validation years of experiment 00006 (2023-07 to 2024-06, 2024-07 to 2025-06, and 2025-07 to 2026-06), each trained to a week before it starts.

Arm Columns Base W, hour, weekday, days_to_christmas_window Return Base plus days_from_return_w Term Base plus school_term_flag, days_from_term_start_w, days_from_term_end_w Both Base plus the Return and Term columns Placebo A Base plus the four placebo_a_ columns Placebo B Base plus the four placebo_b_ columns One harmonic Base plus one harmonic of the day of the year (a smooth-season control) Reference Base, trained from the full history with the COVID indicator, as in 00006 Climatology Month, half-hour, and weekend flag, trained on each fold's window

The placebo arms control for extra columns and for calendar memorisation. Each has the same number and shape of columns as Both. If its gain matches Both's, the gain comes from the tree having more calendar columns to split on and not from the real dates. A shifted calendar can also be worse than no calendar, because it marks working days as holidays, so Placebo A and Placebo B against Base are reported next to C6, and a placebo that is worse than Base weakens C6's support. The one-harmonic arm adds two columns, not four, so its comparison with Both is reported without a decision. It tests whether a smooth seasonal curve already explains a gain.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows are fixed by local date, and each has three occurrences, one per fold.

  • Return window: 2 to 20 January.
  • Easter window: from the first day of the Easter holiday (the day after term 4 ends) to the sixth day of term 5.
  • Half-term holidays: the autumn, February, and May half-term holidays, from the day after a term ends to the day before the next begins (nine holidays across the three folds).
  • Summer holiday: from the day after term 6 ends to 2 September.
  • Whole year: every day of the validation year.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
There are six planned contrasts, all for Primary substations, against the Base arm unless stated. The level is 99.2% (a Bonferroni correction of 95% across six). Each window interval first averages the three fitting seeds, then resamples 7-day blocks of local days. Neighbouring days share weather, so the interval still understates the uncertainty, and the rule that the sign must agree in all three folds is the stricter gate. C5 uses the month-resampling bootstrap of studies.bootstrap.

Contrast Arms Where Prediction C1 Both against Base Return window At most -0.5 C2 Both against Base Easter window At most -0.3 C3 Both against Base Half-term holidays At most -0.3 C4 Both against Base Summer holiday No prediction; reported as a check for harm C5 Both against Base Whole year Interval inside -0.1 to +0.1 C6 Both against Placebo A, and against Placebo B C1, C2, and C3 windows pooled At most -0.2 for each

The report also gives, without a decision attached: Return and Term separately; Both against One harmonic and against Reference; the Christmas weeks (15 December to 7 January), where Both should not be worse than Base by more than 0.1; the BSP and GSP series (two each); and absolute scores for every arm, with the climatology row repeated once per seed. Return and Term are close to collinear in the training years, because the first working day of the year and the first day of term 3 differ by 0 or 1 day until 2024, so their separate contrasts cannot be told apart in fold 1.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Fold 1 trains on 1.8 years, and one of its Januaries is unusual. It trains on 2021-09 to 2023-06, which holds two Januaries. January 2022 falls under the England Plan B guidance to work from home, which the COVID indicator (ending 2021-07-19) does not cover. Fold 1 is expected to show the weakest return-to-work effect, and the Reference arm, trained from the full history, shows whether the 2021 start is the cause.
  • The stage 1a model is fitted and scored on ERA5. ERA5 is an estimate of past weather, so a gain here need not carry over to forecast weather at serving time. The columns themselves are known in advance. The experiment uses no lagged weather or power.
  • The Christmas figure behind the Return-window prediction is not rechecked here. The research plan quotes 00006 errors of 9.3 to 10.3 points from 5 to 8 January, against a base of 9.8 to 10.5. Experiment 00006's page does not state those figures, so the report recomputes the Base error in the Return window and quotes that.
  • The row set is new. era5_val_3folds_2023_07_to_2026_06_v1 covers three years of valid times and does not match the row set of 00006's pilot (era5_val_2024_07_to_2025_06_v1).

docs.title: Resources and reporting
docs.text: The fits use the 10 cores of the experiment manager's slot B on the CPU. e00011_fit.py copies the structure of e00006_fit.py. Reading experiment 00006's private feature table is allowed, and the new columns join on the local date at fit time. The experiment scores no valid time on or after 2026-07-01. Predictions are written with experiment_store.write_predictions under row set era5_val_3folds_2023_07_to_2026_06_v1.

docs.title: Which inputs and which training start work best for the solar and wind stage 1a model?
docs.text:
We asked which inputs and which training start date give the most accurate weather-to-power model for solar and wind farms. We tried four changes, which were training on a satellite estimate of sunlight, a first step (stage 0) that maps forecast sunlight onto that estimate, predicting solar output as a share of the output the farm would give under a cloudless sky, and starting the wind model from the turbine power curve, together with later training start dates. None lowered the error by the 0.15 points of capacity that we counted as a gain. A point of capacity is 1% of a farm's effective capacity, roughly its usual maximum output.

Verdict: inconclusive. None of the four planned input changes (CAMS-trained stage 1a, the stage 0 model, the clear-sky-ratio target for solar, and the power-curve base margin for wind) lowered the error by the 0.15 points the plan counted as a gain, and the interval of the CAMS-trained arm (C1) did not rule a gain out. The training start moved the error by less than 0.3 points, and the weather block by less than 0.15 points for wind (C10) and unresolved for solar (C9). ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, ERA5 is its reanalysis of past weather, and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite irradiance estimate. Arm w reproduces experiment 00001's scores exactly (7.641 for solar and 15.386 for wind). The page is proposal P17 in the research plan. Stage 1a is an XGBoost model per series that turns weather into power.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute scores, all leads (points of capacity): solar w 7.64, cams 7.50, csr 7.59, start_2023 7.62, start_2024 7.62, small_block 7.64, cams_stage0 7.66, climatology 8.62, and a ceiling of 5.92 (the arm w given ERA5 weather, which is not a forecast). Wind w 15.39, base_margin 15.36, start_2023 15.37, start_2024 15.39, speed_block 15.39, climatology 19.15, and ceiling 7.90. Seed spread is at most 0.007 points.
  • C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained (solar): -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044). The interval lies below zero, but the estimate misses the -0.15 threshold, so the rule scores it unresolved. The gain is largest within 24 h (-0.35) and shrinks to -0.06 beyond day 7.
  • C2, stage 0 minus plain CAMS-trained (solar): +0.160 (-0.017 to +0.382). The stage 0 model lowers the error of the control member alone, from 8.34 to 7.82, and leaves the error of the 51-member average 0.16 points higher, from 7.50 to 7.66, with an interval that includes zero. For seed 0 and the control member, a fit that stops before the last 6 weeks maps ENS shortwave to CAMS with a mean absolute error of 120 W/m2, against 123 W/m2 for the raw ENS value, and the bias grows in size, from +19.5 to -27.6 W/m2.
  • C3 and C4: the clear-sky-ratio target changes solar by -0.048 (-0.093 to +0.024), and the power-curve base margin changes wind by -0.030 (-0.061 to -0.007). Both are equivalent to w within the 0.15-point band.
  • C5 to C8, training start: every estimate lies between -0.026 and +0.005, with intervals inside -0.19 to +0.10, so a start in 2023-09 or 2024-04 is equivalent to 2019-09 within 0.3 points.
  • C9 and C10, weather block: four solar columns against nine is -0.003 (-0.158 to +0.131), unresolved because the interval reaches slightly past the 0.15 band. Three wind columns against six is +0.008 (-0.147 to +0.138), equivalent.
  • Decision rule: supported needs a gain among C1 to C4. Refuted needs the lower bound of all four above -0.15, and C1's lower bound is -0.277. The verdict is therefore inconclusive.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• The first fit crashed after training on a missing lead_hours column in the validation frames and then on a mixed Float32 and Float64 stack. Both were fixed before any score was read.
  • The claims rest on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms in one validation year, and on one weather region each. The absolute-error intervals are 4 to 6 points wide. The paired contrasts have intervals 0.05 to 0.4 points wide, so a gain under 0.15 points is resolved only for the contrasts with the narrowest intervals.
  • No selection year exists for ENS-applied scores, so each contrast was scored once on fold A. The experiment did not combine winners.
  • The wind farms' ERA5 cells hold no temperature or pressure, so windchill and air density were not tested for wind.
  • The stage 0 model trains on the control member alone, so it cannot learn the spread of the other 50 members.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• Input changes to a stage 1a model that already reads the ERA5 weather block moved the solar and wind error by hundredths of a point, except CAMS training (-0.14) and stage 0 (+0.16). The differences between arms are far smaller than the gap to the ERA5 ceiling (1.7 points for solar, 7.5 for wind). The ceiling reads ERA5 weather at forecast time, so the gap mostly reflects the change of weather source, and the changes tested closed little of it.
  • A correction of ENS weather was worth scoring on the member average. The control member alone improved by 0.52 points under stage 0, and the 51-member average was 0.16 higher.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
The size is complex, because the experiment adds a new method (a stage 0 model, a clear-sky-ratio target, and a base margin) and admits more than one defensible design.

  • What gets stored: private predictions only. No schema in packages/contracts/ changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched. The winners are candidates for a later model release.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The definition of clear-sky power, the form of the power curve, and the inputs of the stage 0 model all admit alternatives. This page fixes one.
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no. The fitting code copies the patterns of studies/stage1_pilot/stage1_fit_stage1a.py and of experiment 00009.

docs.title: Which earlier advice this plan follows
docs.text:
• Followed: every arm gets the same columns unless the arm is the contrast (00001); the benchmark's absolute score and a climatology row are reported beside every contrast (00001); a CAMS-trained stage 1 is tested against ERA5-trained with irradiance applied from ENS (00006, 00007).
  • Departs from: 00006 selected on one year and confirmed on the next, using ERA5 weather as the input. This experiment scores once, on fold A applied to ENS members, because no earlier ENS year exists for the farms (the ENS-era data starts in 2024-04, and the pilot scored fold A only). The contrasts are pre-registered and each is scored once, so nothing is selected on the scoring year. The experiment does not combine winners, and so claims no effect of a combination.
  • Cannot follow: the production recipe's windchill needs temperature at the wind farms' ERA5 cells, which is not on disk, so windchill is not tested for wind. For solar, windchill is not a physical input.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Rows and series. The 6 solar farms (labels A to F) and 3 wind farms (W1 to W3) of fold_a_tuesdays_v1: 53 runs on Tuesdays, valid times from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30. Anonymised labels only appear in the write-up.

Training. One XGBoost model per series and seed (0, 1, 2) with 00005's hyperparameters, no calendar column and no power lag. Training uses cleaned power (the pilot's settling rule) at valid times before 2025-06-17, 14 days before the first run. Every arm starts in 2019-09 except the two start arms.

Weather at training and at forecast time. Training reads ERA5 at the farm's cell (and, for CAMS arms, CAMS irradiance at the farm). Application reads ENS members. CAMS is therefore needed only for training, and no weather source is read at lag times because no arm has a lag.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Arm Technology What differs from w w both Benchmark: solar 9 columns, wind 6 columns, from 2019-09 start_2023 both Training from 2023-09-01 start_2024 both Training from 2024-04-01, the ENS-era months small_block solar 4 columns: shortwave, temperature_2m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth speed_block wind wind_speed_100m and the two 100 m bearing columns only csr solar Target is power over clear-sky power, weighted by clear-sky power; the forecast is the predicted ratio times clear-sky power base_margin wind XGBoost base_margin from a monotone power curve of 100 m wind speed fitted on the arm's training rows cams solar CAMS irradiance replaces ERA5 shortwave in training; ENS shortwave is applied cams_stage0 solar cams, with each ENS member's shortwave first mapped to CAMS by the stage 0 model

Clear-sky power. Clear-sky irradiance comes from pvlib's simplified Solis model with its default aerosol and water-vapour settings, evaluated at the solar zenith. Clear-sky power is a farm-specific constant times that irradiance. The constant is the 99th percentile of power over clear-sky irradiance, over the arm's training rows with clear-sky irradiance of at least 300 W/m2. Training rows with clear-sky power below 1% of capacity are dropped, and the ratio is clipped to 0 to 2. The weight is the square of clear-sky power, because the power error is the clear-sky power times the ratio error, so a squared power error weights the squared ratio error by the square of clear-sky power.

Power curve. Mean power fraction in 0.5 m/s bins of 100 m wind speed, made non-decreasing by a running maximum, and interpolated linearly. The curve is fitted on ERA5 speeds and added, as the base_margin of the prediction matrix, to each ENS member's 100 m speed, so any bias between ERA5 and ENS speeds shifts the margin. The fit script checks that the margin changes the predictions.

Stage 0. A small XGBoost model (depth 4, 200 rounds, learning rate 0.05, pooled over the 6 solar farms, no farm identifier) maps ENS shortwave, longwave, 2 m temperature, 2 m dew point, solar zenith and azimuth, and lead hours to CAMS irradiance. It trains on the control member's rows from 2024-04-01 to before 2025-06-17, daylight rows only, and applies to every member. The control member alone trains it, because the ENS training frame holds that member only. The mapping is therefore conditional on the control run and learns nothing about the perturbed members' spread, so C2 mixes a bias correction with any distortion of the spread. C2 is also reported on the control member alone.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
