We asked whether a solar forecasting model built from the physics of a solar panel, with its parameters fitted by gradient descent, beats an XGBoost model for solar farms. We fitted the physics model and combinations of it with XGBoost for 6 solar farms, and compared their forecast accuracy. No combination beat XGBoost, and the physics model alone was worse by 0.079 points of capacity.

Verdict: refuted. No physics arm lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the XGBoost stage 1, and the PyTorch physics stage 1 alone scored 0.079 points of capacity worse (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135).

This page is proposal P31 in the research plan. ENS is the ECMWF ensemble, ERA5 is the ECMWF reanalysis, and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite irradiance estimate. Farms appear only under anonymous labels A to F.

docs.title: Survey of the earlier PV fits (step 1)
docs.text: The best fitted PV model in the earlier studies was a five-parameter physical model with free orientation, and it still trailed XGBoost. The beam-diffuse study fitted tilt, azimuth, capacity, an inverter limit, and a temperature coefficient per farm with a Powell optimiser. On CAMS irradiance it scored 6.28% of P99 output against 5.24% for XGBoost, and an XGBoost calibration that saw the weather closed most of the gap. The solar BMU study found that a free orientation held out better than a fixed or tracking plant, and recovered simulated plants' tilt with a +9.6 degree bias. Chosen: the SciPy free-orientation fit (studies.pv_fit) as the scipy arm, and for the PyTorch PV model the ideas the differentiable-physics page proposes: priors on tilt, azimuth, DC capacity, and the AC-to-DC ratio, a smooth clip, and a posterior for intervals. The SciPy model is the best fit in the two earlier studies we read, so it is the comparison for the new PyTorch PV model.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute CRPS, all leads (points of capacity): XGBoost stage 1 5.026 (95% interval 3.729 to 6.494), hybrid 5.026, PyTorch physics 5.105, SciPy physics 5.110, climatology 5.629. Seed spread is at most 0.001.
  • C1 PyTorch physics minus XGBoost: +0.079 (+0.029 to +0.135). C2 hybrid minus XGBoost: -0.000 (-0.015 to +0.018). C3 PyTorch minus SciPy: -0.005 (-0.020 to +0.010). C4 SciPy minus XGBoost: +0.084 (+0.029 to +0.148). The rule refutes the hypothesis when the lower bounds of C1 and C2 are both above -0.05, and they are (+0.029 and -0.015).
  • Stage 1 alone: the member-average physics power has a mean absolute error of 7.44 points (SciPy) and 7.53 (PyTorch), against 7.64 for experiment 00012's XGBoost stage 1a on the same rows. This comparison is descriptive: experiment 00012's CAMS-trained arm scored 7.50, level with the PyTorch physics, and the rows may differ. The cause of the CRPS gap was not isolated; a possible cause is the spread that the XGBoost layer builds from one physics column.
  • Coverage of the 5% to 95% band: SciPy 96.6%, PyTorch 96.5%, hybrid 94.8%, XGBoost 94.7%.
  • Fitted parameters: the table below gives every fitted parameter. Five of the six PyTorch tilts fall in the beam-diffuse study's 14 to 27 degrees, and farm E is higher; every azimuth is within 5 degrees of south, as in that study. SciPy values are within 3 degrees of tilt of the PyTorch values for five farms, and within 0.07 of capacity.

Fitted parameters, by anonymous farm label. The metadata holds no tilt or azimuth, so both are inferred. The fit works in fractions of each farm's effective capacity, the 99th percentile of its absolute power over the history, which is not the farm's registered capacity. The MW values are those fractions times the effective capacity in MW. Intervals are 90% posterior intervals from the PyTorch fit, and the SciPy fit gives point values only.

Comparison with NGED's Embedded Capacity Register (ECR), by anonymous farm label. We matched each farm to ECR rows only where the farm's name equals the ECR's customer name or customer site exactly (ignoring case and punctuation) and the licence area agrees, with no fuzzy matching. The PyTorch DC capacity is compared with the ECR's already connected registered capacity, and the PyTorch AC capacity with the ECR's maximum export capacity.

Farm ECR match ECR status ECR registered capacity (MW) ECR maximum export capacity (MW) Fitted DC over registered Fitted AC over export A no match B no match C no match D no match E one row Connected 18.7 17.9 0.88 (0.84 to 0.91) 0.82 (0.76 to 0.87) F no match

Only farm E matched, and its fitted capacities are 12% (DC) and 18% (AC) below the ECR. The fitted DC capacity interval (15.8 to 17.1 MW) excludes the registered 18.7 MW, so the interval does not cover the register. Farm E's effective capacity of 17.6 MW is about 98% of the export capacity, which means the metered peaks sit at the export limit. The fitted AC capacity of 14.7 MW is below that observed peak, so the physics model does not reach the metered peaks, which may explain the shortfall; we did not test this. The effective capacity therefore tracks the ECR export capacity and the fitted values do not. The other five farms are named differently in the ECR from the metadata, so their comparison is empty.

docs.title: Synthetic test (result)
docs.text:
• Same physics, 36 on-prior plants: tilt bias +0.11 degrees, azimuth -0.02, DC capacity -0.005, and 90% interval coverage of 92%, 100%, 97%. AC limit coverage 86%, DC:AC ratio 89%. This passes the pre-registered coverage rule (at least 80% for DC, AC, and ratio). Twelve off-prior plants (tilt 5 or 60, azimuth 110 or 250) give tilt bias -0.05 and azimuth bias +0.76 degrees.
  • Different chain (Hay-Davies sky): tilt bias +6.2 degrees (+3.8 off-prior), 0% tilt coverage, DC capacity bias +0.041 (8% coverage). The intervals reflect noise and not the mismatch of the physics, so they are overconfident under mismatch.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• 6 farms, one validation year: gains under about 0.1 points cannot be resolved.
  • The synthetic noise is additive and homoscedastic, and the different-chain version changes only the sky-diffuse term. The likelihood is a tempered pseudo-Huber and not a normalised likelihood, so posterior widths are approximate.
  • No post hoc tweak was run.
  • Predictions versus outcomes: C1 was predicted between +0.1 and +0.5 and came out at +0.079, just below that range. The hybrid within 0.05 of base and the different-chain tilt bias under 10 degrees were both met.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• Fitted PV physics is a competitive point forecast and a poor replacement for the XGBoost stage 1 in the quantile pipeline. The XGBoost stage 1 sees ENS irradiance, temperature, and cloud-related columns that the physics model does not.
  • The orientation and capacity the PyTorch PV model recovers are plausible and agree with the SciPy fit, so the physics is useful for interpretation and for checking a farm's metadata.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Arm Stage 1 Stage 2 base 00020's XGBoost quantile stage 1 on nine ERA5 weather columns Pooled mixture over 51 members scipy Fitted PV model from studies.pv_fit (free orientation, SciPy), run on each member's shortwave One XGBoost quantile model per farm on the physics power only, members pooled torch New PyTorch physics model with priors One XGBoost quantile model per farm on the physics power only, members pooled torch_hybrid The torch output XGBoost quantile model on the physics power plus the nine weather columns climatology None Month-by-half-hour climatology

Fitting. Physics parameters are fitted once per farm to metered power at rows before 2025-06-17, using CAMS shortwave and ERA5 temperature (CAMS exists for only part of the history, so rows without it are left out). Prior means and widths come from general knowledge about Great Britain's plants (studies.pv_fit.LOOSE_PRIORS), not from any fit to these farms. The stage 2 layer trains on physics power driven by ERA5 shortwave (base's weather source), and is applied to ENS members' shortwave. CAMS arrives about 1 day late and ERA5 about 5 days, but neither is read at forecast time (the arms read ENS shortwave and ENS temperature), because no arm uses a lag.

PyTorch PV model. The AC limit is the DC capacity times the AC-to-DC ratio (below 1). The model applies an Erbs split of global into beam and diffuse, isotropic-sky transposition onto a plane of fitted tilt and azimuth, a temperature derate, a DC capacity (a multiple of effective capacity), and a soft clip at DC capacity over an AC-to-DC ratio. Parameters have normal priors and a mean-field normal posterior fitted by stochastic variational inference (Adam, GPU).

docs.title: Synthetic test (step 2)
docs.text: Thirty-six synthetic plants (6 farm coordinates times 6 parameter draws: tilt 10 to 45 degrees, azimuth 150 to 210 degrees, DC capacity 0.9 to 1.3, AC-to-DC ratio 0.7 to 1.0) are driven by the real training irradiance and temperature of their coordinates, each with its own random two-year window and noise draw (autocorrelated noise, 4% of capacity). Two versions run: same physics (the PyTorch PV model's own chain), and different chain (the Hay-Davies sky from pvlib in place of the isotropic sky, so the fit cannot reproduce the data exactly). The write-up gives each parameter's bias and 90% interval coverage, each plant's clipping share, and the fit's mean absolute error.

docs.title: Checks before the contrasts are read
docs.text:
• Leakage. Every fit, including the physics parameters, stops before 2025-06-17. A reviewer reads the code for this.
  • No calendar columns in any stage 2 layer; the hybrid's nine columns are base's.
  • Reproduction. base is read from 00020's stored predictions, and its solar CRPS is checked against 5.05 within 0.05.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
Complex, because the experiment adds a new method and admits more than one defensible design.

  • What gets stored: private predictions only.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes (the transposition model, the prior widths, whether the stage 2 layer reads the weather).
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no; the code copies experiment 00020's patterns and calls studies.pv_physics, studies.pv_fit, and studies.experiment_store.

docs.title: Which earlier advice this plan follows
docs.text:
• Followed: base's absolute score and a climatology row sit beside every contrast (00012, 00020); no calendar columns (skill rule); a contrast is read against a threshold set by the cost of the change (00020).
  • Departs from: 00012's advice to test CAMS-trained solar on more farms; this experiment keeps the 6 farms, so it cannot resolve gains under about 0.1 points.

docs.title: Resolution limit
docs.text: 6 farms in one region and one validation year resolve gains of roughly 0.1 points of capacity.

docs.title: Which lagged power columns lower the error of Primary substation demand forecasts?
docs.text:
We asked which earlier readings of power, taken at the same time of day in previous weeks or years, lower the error of a demand forecast for Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network). We gave a single-step model 3 lags, the 6 weekly lags, the 7 annual lags, or all 13, and compared the quantile scores for 16 Primary substations. Adding all 13 changed nothing, the weekly lags alone helped a little, the annual lags hurt, and a 14-day error correction then removed the weekly gain. An arm added after the run, which gives the mean and median of the weekly values, scored lowest of all.

Verdict: inconclusive. Giving N1 all 13 lags of manual_heuristic as separate columns does not lower its quantile score: C3 is -0.01 points of capacity (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). The 6 weekly analogues alone lower the score by 0.30 (C1, -0.63 to -0.02), the 7 annual analogues raise it by 0.29 (C2), and the 14-day error correction then removes the weekly gain. A post hoc arm, N1 plus the mean and median of the weekly analogues, scores 0.05 below N1 with the correction (-0.08 to -0.02), the lowest score of any arm. A point is 1% of the series' effective capacity. N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model trained on the ensemble weather forecast (ENS) of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

docs.title: What the arms score
docs.text:
Every arm is scored on the same cases of the 16 Primary substations, on the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1. Intervals resample whole months and seeds.

Arm Quantile score With 14-day correction Median error With correction A0: N1, 3 lags 6.33 5.34 8.45 7.34 A1: plus 6 weekly lags 6.03 5.43 8.14 7.44 A3: 3 summaries of the 13 lags 6.48 5.31 8.64 7.27 A7 (post hoc): weekly mean and median 6.22 5.29 8.30 7.27 00019 stack 5.32 7.35 manual_heuristic 5.89 8.23 climatology 7.46 10.33

A2 (all 13 lags), A4 (recent values), and A5 (same-day-type analogues) were fitted for seed 0 only, and score 6.32, 6.30, and 6.25 without the correction and 5.53, 5.54, and 5.48 with it, against 6.33 and 5.34 for A0.

docs.title: Contrasts
docs.text:
The planned contrasts are read at 99.375%. Only C1 has 3 seeds; C2 to C8 use seed 0 only, so their intervals resample months and not seeds.

  • C1, A1 minus A0: -0.30 (-0.63 to -0.02). Gain without the correction; with it, A1 scores 0.09 above A0 (E2, +0.01 to +0.18).
  • C2, A2 minus A1: +0.29 (+0.13 to +0.49). The annual analogues lose.
  • C3, A2 minus A0 (primary): -0.01 (-0.45 to +0.43). Not a gain.
  • C4, A3 minus A2: +0.17 (-0.11 to +0.46). Summaries do no better than columns.
  • C5, A4 minus A2: -0.01 (-0.05 to +0.03). Recent values add nothing.
  • C6, A5 minus A2: -0.06 (-0.10 to -0.03). A gain, but small.
  • C7, A2 minus manual_heuristic: +0.43 (-0.00 to +0.93).
  • C8, A2 minus A0, both with the correction: +0.19 (+0.09 to +0.30). The annual and weekly columns hurt once the correction is applied.

Exploratory: A3 with the correction scores 0.03 below A0 with it (E12, -0.08 to +0.02); A7 with it scores 0.05 below (E15, -0.08 to -0.02) and 0.03 below the 00019 stack (E16, -0.06 to +0.00).

docs.title: Cuts, post hoc, and limits
docs.text:
• Cut for time: A2, A4, and A5 have seed 0 only; A6, the residual lag, was not run. The gain threshold for A6 therefore stays untested.
  • Post hoc: A7 was added after seeing that the annual columns hurt. Its contrasts (E14 to E17) are not pre-registered.
  • Untested explanation: the 7 annual columns are highly correlated and N1 trains on only 15 months, so the model may fit the year-ago level; no arm tested this.
  • One validation year and 16 series: every interval resamples the months of that one year.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets only, under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: more than one for the lag definitions; each is fixed below before a fit.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00013's and 00019's helpers, which the plan's author could name without searching.

Size: simple, because arms A1 to A5 permute the input columns of N1 with no new data and no new method. Arm A6 stores past forecasts as a model input, so it is exploratory. Review: one Sonnet reviewer reads the code for leakage and for the fit stopping at the training end, and one Sonnet reviewer checks the write-up against the printed report. The earlier advice that this plan follows: compare every Primary arm against manual_heuristic (00013); add lagged power measured from the forecast origin (00013); report the interval over validation months (00013). It departs from none.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
Each arm is N1 (00013: the 00006 columns, the lead in hours, recency half-life 2 years, 500 rounds, the 9-level quantile loss, trained on the ENS control member from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30) with a different lag block. colsample_bytree and colsample_bynode are 1.0 in every arm, so a wider arm has no subsampling advantage. Every lag is read from the observed power of the same series on the dense half-hourly grid and is null (NaN) when its grid index is later than the newest usable observation, 3.5 hours before the forecast origin (00021's and 00013's telemetry delay). No lag column looks past that index, in training or in validation.

Arm Lag columns A0 (N1, 00013's stored fits) 3: the newest usable value, and the latest earlier same-half-hour and same-weekday values A1 A0 plus the 6 weekly analogues: power at the valid time minus 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 weeks A2 A1 plus the 7 annual analogues: power at the valid time minus 49 to 55 weeks (the 13 lags of manual_heuristic plus A0's 3) A3 A0 plus 3 summaries of A2's 13 lags: the mean and the median of the usable weekly analogues, and the mean of the usable annual analogues A4 A2 plus 3 recent values: the mean of the 12 half-hours ending at the newest usable one, and the values 2 and 4 half-hours before it A5 A2 plus 3 same-day-type analogues: power at the same half-hour on the latest 3 earlier days of the valid time's day type (weekday against weekend or bank holiday, from the England holiday calendar) A6 (exploratory) A2 plus the mean residual of the last 14 days (actual minus the A2 median forecast of each half-hour, taken from cross-fitted fits of A2 over 3 blocks of training months)

A lag of a fixed number of weeks is null whenever the lead is long enough for it to fall after the newest usable observation, so the 1-week analogue is null beyond about 6.9 days of lead, which is also what the pipeline's _nullify_leaky_lags does. A0 already holds the latest day and the latest week analogue at any lead, so A4 and A5 test only what is added beyond them. Every arm is also scored with the 14-day error correction of 00019 (the mean error of the arm's median over the 14 days up to the newest usable observation, added to every quantile), and the report shows each arm with and without it. The 00019 stack is rebuilt from 00019's stored N1H fits. The arms are fitted for seeds 0, 1, and 2, and a climatology and the stored baselines are repeated per seed as in 00013.

docs.title: Plan: planned contrasts
docs.text: The eight contrasts in the decision rule are read over all leads at 99.375%. Every other contrast (each lead band, BSP and GSP, with and without the correction, A6, against the 00019 stack) is exploratory, read at 95%. BSP (2 series) and GSP (2 series) are descriptive and never averaged into the Primary figure.

docs.title: Plan: past weather
docs.text: No past weather is used at lag times; the lags are of power, observed before the origin.

docs.title: Experiment 31: do embedded-solar capacity features lower the error of Primary demand forecasts?
docs.text:
We asked whether telling a demand forecast for Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) how much solar generation capacity is installed behind each substation lowers its error. The capacity estimates came from the demand data and from a register. We added several versions of installed-capacity inputs to the best demand forecast, plus a control whose capacity values were shuffled between forecast dates within each series and calendar month, and scored 16 Primary substations over 73 forecast runs. None lowered the error. The reference forecast had a (smaller is better) quantile score of 5.32 points of capacity, and the best arms matched it to within 0.01 points. Two arms were worse: the one that added capacity statistics as columns and the one that added PV products built from the data alone.

Inconclusive: none of the capacity features lowers the all-lead quantile score of Primary demand forecasts, and the two arms that came closest cannot be separated from zero. B0 is the 00019 stack without its half-life: N1 with the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor. Scores are the quantile score over all leads, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity), on 16 Primary substations, 73 forecast runs every 5 days from July 2025 to June 2026, with ENS weather. B0 scores 5.32. A3 (PV products using the register) scores 5.32, A5 (the shaped correction) 5.33, A4 (the linear offset) 5.33, and the shuffled control A6 5.31. A1 (capacity statistics as columns) scores 5.49 and A2 (PV products from data alone) 5.35, which are losses. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better.

Arm Quantile score Median error Contrast with B0 (99.17% interval) B0, the 00019 stack 5.32 7.34 A1 capacity statistics 5.49 7.59 C1 +0.167 (+0.091 to +0.243) A2 PV products, data only 5.35 7.39 C2 +0.036 (+0.002 to +0.074) A3 PV products with the register 5.32 7.35 C3 +0.006 (-0.022 to +0.033) A4 linear offset 5.33 7.34 C4 +0.012 (-0.051 to +0.081) A5 shaped correction 5.33 7.35 C5 +0.016 (-0.069 to +0.100) A6 shuffled control of A3 5.31 7.33 C6, A3 minus A6: +0.018 (-0.002 to +0.033) manual_heuristic 5.89 8.23 climatology 7.46 10.33

The verdict follows the pre-registered rule. No arm reached "port" or "small gain". A1 and A2 are losses (intervals wholly above zero), A3 is a null with a half-width of 0.03, and A4 and A5 are nulls with half-widths of 0.07 and 0.08, wider than the 0.05 that would have excluded a gain of that size, so the verdict is inconclusive and not refuted.

The shaped correction trades gains in sunny hours for losses in cloudy ones. These are 95% breakdowns, which decide nothing. A5 lowers the score by 0.37 in daylight at a clear-sky index of 0.7 or more over the year (-0.51 to -0.25), and by 0.28 in April to September at that index (-0.43 to -0.15; B0 scores 5.63 there). It raises the score by 0.68 at a clear-sky index under 0.3 (+0.37 to +1.04) and by 0.41 between 0.3 and 0.7. Over April to September as a whole A5 is level with B0 (+0.004). At leads under 48 hours A5 lowers the score by 0.07 (-0.13 to -0.02), but the shuffled control A6 lowers it by 0.05 (-0.08 to -0.02), so that gain is not specific to the shaped correction. The slope of the 14-day residuals on PV output was fitted in 1,380 of 1,460 series-runs (20 series times 73 runs, including the BSPs and GSPs) and averaged -0.11 over all runs, so the substations hold PV that N1 under-allows for. One possible explanation of the cloudy-hour losses, untested here, is that the ENS irradiance forecast is biased against the CAMS irradiance the slope was fitted on, which would make the correction too large on cloudy forecasts.

The register adds little at Primaries. The median data estimate of PV capacity at a Primary was about 0.33 of effective capacity (0.35 data only, 0.33 with the register, on validation origins) against a register median of 0.08, so the weights favour the data estimate. A3 minus A2 is -0.030 (-0.061 to -0.007, 10 of 12 months negative), so the register improves on the data-only arm, but A3 is not distinguishable from the shuffled control (C6), so the gain is not evidence of capacity information. The estimator recovered an injected capacity ramp in the known-answer check (F1's error under 0.0011 share of capacity on 2 directional Primaries, measured after subtracting each series' un-injected F1, against a standard error of about 0.05).

At the 2 GSPs, true PV_Live generation lowers the score by 0.82. B0 scores 19.95 and the oracle A7 19.13 (A7 minus B0 -0.82, 95% interval -1.06 to -0.55; 12 of 12 months). The 2 BSPs and 2 GSPs are descriptive; A3 and A5 move them by less than 0.3 points, and no contrast is drawn.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One validation year gives 12 month blocks, so A4 and A5 cannot exclude a gain of 0.07 to 0.08 points.
  • A4 refits only the 8 directional Primaries, so C4 is pooled over 16 and diluted by half; the 8 non-directional Primaries reuse B0. Their folded readings (PV above demand) also enter F1 to F5, which no arm corrects.
  • CAMS publication delay was not measured. The features assume CAMS is available 48 hours before the origin, as the ECMWF notice of February 2026 says ("up to yesterday").
  • The register is a prior at Primaries by assumption: rows of 1 MW or more are treated as metered, because no larger solar farm is listed under a Primary in the metadata table.
  • Not run: the no-fit baseline (manual_heuristic on gross demand minus modelled PV), and the weekly lags of 00030 in every arm.
  • No tweak after the first run: the plan allowed one post hoc change; the sunny and cloudy split of A5 suggests calibrating ENS irradiance to CAMS first, which the next experiment can test.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets and a daily feature table under data/ml-experiments/.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: more than one (feature, offset, or correction; several estimators). The arms below test each family once.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00019's helpers and read its stored N1 fit, which the author could name without searching.

Size: complex, because more than one design defensibly tests the hypothesis and the experiment adds a data source (the ECR). Plan, code, and write-up each get one Sonnet review.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed: compare against N1 with the 14-day correction and the 00019 stack, not N1 alone (00030); keep colsample at 1.0; report absolute scores beside contrasts; guard against one substation setting the pooled figure (00007).
  • Departed from: 00030's weekly mean and median lags are not in B0, because 00030 has not merged; a follow-up can add them to every arm.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Capacity enters as a trailing estimate that changes over time, or as a linear offset. N1 fits one model per series, so a per-series constant gives the trees nothing. Every feature is computed at each forecast origin from power and irradiance observed up to 48 hours before the origin, so the same function serves training rows and validation rows.

  • Per-unit PV, p_unit: AC output of a generic fleet per MW of AC capacity (studies.pv_physics.plant_power_mw, tilt 35 degrees, azimuth 180 degrees, DC 1.15 MW, AC 1.0 MW, times a 0.86 system derate; untuned). Fitted constants (the shrinkage weights and prior variance) use training origins only, which are those before 2025-07-01; validation origins run from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30. At lag times the irradiance is CAMS GHI at the substation's location, which ECMWF publishes with a delay of at most 2 days (an ECMWF notice of February 2026 says "up to yesterday"; older pages say 2 days), so it exists before the 48-hour cut-off. The latency was not measured; if it exceeds 48 hours, the features would need the ENS analysis proxy, and the write-up says so. At valid times the irradiance is the ENS member's shortwave.
  • The ECR enters differently by series type (maintainer refinement, 2026-10-15). A Primary series is "Disaggregated Demand": NGED has already subtracted its metered generators, so the ECR rows with their own meter are not in the series. The ECR is therefore only a prior for a Primary, never a floor. The prior is the ECR solar capacity of the rows that have no meter of their own: every connected solar row on the Register Part 1 50kW - <1MW sheet. The rows of 1 MW or more are assumed to be metered, because the metadata table lists none of the larger solar farms under a Primary, and NGED's list of meters is not available to confirm it. The Primary name must match exactly after studies.name_matching.normalise (no fuzzy matching), and the prior is zero where no row matches. A BSP or GSP series is "Raw Flow": the metered generators below it are not subtracted, so the ECR solar capacity of every row below the substation (by bulk_supply_point or grid_supply_point name, using Substations.csv for the hierarchy) is a floor on the PV in the series. The decision per ECR row is printed by the script. The August 2026 snapshot is used at every date, a small look-ahead that can only inflate the ECR arms. BSP and GSP series are descriptive.
  • Features, 28-day windows ending at the origin minus 48 hours, daylight half-hours (sun above 15 degrees):
    • F1 cap_slope_28d: minus the slope of power on p_unit, with fixed effects for local hour by day type (weekday, or weekend or bank holiday). Null with fewer than 8 days.
    • F2 sunny_minus_cloudy_28d: mean power on sunny days (daily clear-sky index at least 0.7) minus cloudy days (at most 0.3), matched by hour and day type, over the matching difference in mean p_unit, sign flipped.
    • F3 cap_change_yoy: F1 minus F1 for the window 364 days earlier.
    • F4 unreg_cap: c - e, where e is the ECR capacity of the series (prior or floor, above) and c is the capacity estimate. For a Primary, c is c_fit (F1) pulled towards e by inverse-variance weights, with the prior variance fitted on training origins only, and clipped at zero; it may fall below e. For a BSP or GSP, c = max(c_fit, e).
    • F5 cap_total: c. In the data-only variant c = c_fit, clipped at zero, and e is unused.
    • F6 pv_hat: c * p_unit_ENS(valid). F7 lag_gross_2d: the power at the latest earlier time with the valid time's half-hour of day that is at least 48 hours before the origin, plus c * p_unit_CAMS(that time). F8 pv_ecr_hat: e * p_unit_ENS(valid).
  • Known-answer checks before real data: (a) inject -c(t) * p_unit_CAMS(t) with c rising linearly from 0 to 20% of capacity into two directional Primaries and check that F1, F2, and F4 recover c(t) within one standard error; (b) at the two GSPs compare c with PV_Live's installed capacity over the same months (trend only).

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Rows fold_a_every5d_v1, ENS weather, seeds 0 to 2, N1's 00013 configuration. Every arm carries the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor, as B0 does.

Arm Change from B0 Extra columns B0 The 00019 stack 0 A1 Capacity statistics F1, F2, F3 3 A2 Data-only PV products F6, F7 (c = c_fit) 2 A3 PV products with the ECR (prior or floor by series type): F6, F7, F8 3 A4 Linear offset: base_margin = -c * p_unit_ENS(valid), c with the ECR as above; directional Primaries only 0 A5 The flat 14-day mean replaced by a + b * p_unit fitted on the same residuals; b = 0 with fewer than 3 distinct sunny origin-run dates (daily clear-sky index at least 0.7) in the window, and b not sign-clipped; no refit 0 A6 Shuffled control of A3: c permuted across origin dates within series and calendar month, with F6 and F7 recomputed from the shuffled c; F8 keeps the true e 3 A7 Oracle at the 2 GSPs: B0 plus PV_Live at the valid time 1

A5 tests a sunshine-shaped correction of the median's remaining error, not capacity: the residuals come from runs whose forecasts already contain some PV signal. A4 reuses B0 on the 8 non-directional Primaries, which fold when PV exceeds demand.

Plus a no-fit baseline: manual_heuristic on gross demand minus c * p_unit_ENS(valid).

docs.title: Departures from the design
docs.text:
• No temperature covariate in F1. An archive of ENS analysis temperature at lag times would be daily for training runs and 5-daily for validation runs, so training and validation would differ. F3 cancels most of the seasonal confound instead.
  • No outcome-based half-hour selection on non-directional MVA series. Selecting half-hours by observed power biases the slope, so every daylight half-hour is used in A1 to A3 as well; the folded readings are a stated limit, not a result, and the write-up splits directional from non-directional series. The 99.17% interval's half-width is the one the refuted rule reads.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Primary first (16 series), absolute scores beside contrasts. BSP (2) and GSP (2) are descriptive and never averaged into the Primary figure. Breakdowns, all exploratory at 95%: clear-sky-index bins at the valid time (night, under 0.3, 0.3 to 0.7, at least 0.7); sunny against cloudy days; April to September against October to March; lead bands 0 to 48 h, 3 to 6 d, 7 to 15 d; per substation ordered by ECR capacity over effective capacity, split by directional MW and non-directional MVA; the pooled contrast without the series of largest B0 error and without D8, D12, and D22. The clear-sky index is used to bin only, never as an input.

docs.title: Limits to expect
docs.text: One validation year gives 12 month blocks, so a 0.05-point effect may be undetectable. The ECR prior is wrong in both directions at Primaries (an unmetered row may be missing or unregistered, and the snapshot includes future connections). The ENS forecast irradiance is biased against CAMS, so a capacity estimated on CAMS mis-scales when applied to ENS.

docs.title: Experiment 32: do substation fingerprints improve a pooled demand model?
docs.text:
We asked whether giving one shared demand model a short numerical description of each substation, such as its location or its recent power statistics, improves forecasts for substations of the same type. We added each description to the shared model of experiment 00024, scored 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) over 73 forecast runs, and also scored a substation held out of training. No description helped by more than 0.02 points of capacity, and the descriptions made the forecast worse for the held-out substation.

Inconclusive by the pre-registered rule, and no fingerprint helped: adding location, training-window statistics, or recent-window statistics to the by-type pooled model changed the Primary quantile score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and the fingerprints made a held-out substation worse. Scores are the quantile score over all leads in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity), after the 14-day error correction and spread factor 1.15, with ENS weather, on 73 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The by-type pool with the series identifier scores 5.47 on the 16 Primary substations (experiment 24; per-series models score 5.32). Adding the identifier's fingerprints leaves the score at 5.47 to 5.50 (C1 to C4). The rule needed C3 or C4 below -0.10 or both cold-start contrasts below zero, and none happened. The rule's "refuted" needs C1 to C4, C7, and C8 all at or above zero, and the lower limits of C1 to C4 are all below zero (-0.002, -0.008, -0.047, and -0.049). The verdict is therefore "inconclusive", even though the data exclude a gain above 0.01 points for C1 and C2 and above 0.05 points for C3 and C4. In this page ENS is the ECMWF ensemble, BSP and GSP are bulk supply points and grid supply points, and Primary substations meter in MW (megawatts) or MVA (megavolt-amperes).

Arm Primary (16) BSP and GSP (4) A0: no identifier, no fingerprint 6.29 14.84 A1: identifier 5.47 13.96 A2: identifier and location 5.47 13.97 A3: identifier and training-window statistics 5.47 13.97 A4: identifier and recent-window statistics 5.50 14.15 A5: identifier and both 5.49 14.16 A6: training-window statistics, no identifier 5.48 13.96 manual_heuristic 5.89 14.70 climatology 7.46 15.11

Training-window statistics can replace the identifier for series the pool saw in training. A6 scores 0.81 points better than no identifier and no fingerprint (C6, -1.21 to -0.46), and 0.01 points worse than the identifier (C5, +0.00 to +0.02), well inside the 0.15-point margin. The seven statistics identify a series as well as the identifier does.

Recent-window statistics did not help for series the pool saw in training. C3 is +0.02 (-0.05 to +0.10) and C4 is +0.02 (-0.05 to +0.10). A possible reason, not tested here, is that the 14-day error correction already follows the recent level. On the 4 BSP and GSP series A4 scores 14.15 against 13.96 for A1 (exploratory). The share of experiment 24's 0.15-point gap to per-series models closed by A4 or A5 is zero: both are 0.02 points worse than A1.

A fingerprint did not carry a substation held out of the pool. For 8 held-out Primary substations (one seed), the pool with no fingerprint and no identifier scores 6.08, against 5.07 for the pool with the identifier that had seen the substation (+1.01, 0.86 to 1.15, exploratory 95%). Training-window statistics make the held-out score worse by 1.39 (C7, +0.99 to +1.91), and training-window plus recent-window statistics by 0.49 (C8, +0.31 to +0.75). Location is worse by 0.14 (+0.02 to +0.28, exploratory). The uncorrected models are far worse: 21.3 with training-window statistics against 6.3 with none, with a bias of -23.7 points of capacity, so the correction removes most of the damage. Two causes are likely, and this experiment did not test either directly. A pool of 7 other series holds only 7 distinct training-window fingerprints, which the trees can use as 7 identifiers. The held-out substation's statistics also cover 28 days of summer against 15 months for the pool's, and the post hoc arm below suggests this mismatch accounts for most of the C7 damage.

Post hoc, recent-window statistics alone helped a held-out substation, and a fairer training-window fingerprint did not. These arms were added after the first run and decide nothing. Recent-window statistics without the training-window block score 5.86 against 6.08 with no fingerprint (-0.23, -0.29 to -0.16, 95%, 12 of 12 months). Taking the held-out substation's training-window statistics over the whole window instead of 28 days lowers the C7 arm from 7.47 to 6.54 and the C8 arm from 6.57 to 6.18, the first still above 6.08 with no fingerprint (+0.45, +0.30 to +0.64) and the second not distinguishable from it (+0.10, -0.00 to +0.21).

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Met: location (C1) and training-window statistics (C2) added nothing beyond the identifier (+0.00 for each).
  • Met: the training-window statistics without the identifier scored within 0.15 points of the identifier (C5, +0.01).
  • Missed: recent-window statistics were predicted to lower the score by 0.05 to 0.15 points (C3, +0.02).
  • Missed: training-window statistics were predicted to lower the held-out score by 0.2 to 0.5 points (C7, +1.39), and recent-window statistics to lower it by a further 0.05 to 0.2 (C8, worse than none by 0.49).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only 16 Primary series, and 7 other series in a held-out substation's pool. The intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so they say nothing about substations outside the sample. The cold-start result is specific to a pool this small.
  • The cold-start contrasts use one seed and 8 held-out substations. Their intervals resample months only.
  • The held-out substation's training-window statistics cover 28 days ending 2025-06-30, a summer window, while the pool's cover 15 months. The post hoc whole-window arms suggest this mismatch explains most of the C7 damage and some of the C8 damage.
  • Arms A0 and A1 are experiment 24's stored predictions, fitted in a different run with the same code and seeds, with a check that the series, runs, and valid times match.
  • The training-window statistics are fixed at 2025-06-30 for the whole validation year, so a deployed model that retrained would hold fresher values.
  • Latitude and longitude let a pool of 7 series look up its nearest neighbour, which is optimistic for location in a pool of 2,500.
  • The plan had one Sonnet review and the code one; the project's credit setting kept Opus for other work.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/ only.
  • Production serving path: not touched; the recent-window statistics would add a serving step if they win.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: more than one (which statistics, which window, which held-out series), so the columns and the held-out series are fixed below before any fit.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00024's fit and scoring, which the author can name without searching.

Size: complex. One Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code (leakage, the origin-minus-2-days bound, the fit stopping at 2025-06-30, the held-out series absent from training), and one of the write-up. The project's credit setting keeps Opus for work that is truly vital.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
Recipe. Every model is 00024's by-type pooled model (4 groups: BSP, GSP, Primary-MW, Primary-MVA): the 9-level quantile loss on the ENS control member, 00006's columns, the lead in hours, the three origin lags, recency half-life 0.5 years, training valid times up to 2025-06-30 23:30, 500 rounds, depth 6, colsample_bytree 1.0 in every arm (so the arms' different column counts cannot favour one arm), and the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15 after prediction. Experiment 30's lag columns are not added: its verdict was inconclusive, and keeping 00024's recipe lets A0 and A1 reuse 00024's stored predictions (same code, same seeds).

Fingerprint columns. All computed from power over effective capacity.

  • Static (S): latitude and longitude.
  • Training window (T): over valid times 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, the mean, standard deviation, 5th and 95th percentiles, the mean over the period-ending stamps 10:00 to 15:30 UTC minus the mean over the stamps 00:00 to 04:30 UTC, the weekend mean minus the weekday mean, and the half-hour of the daily peak of the mean daily profile. Seven columns, fixed at 2025-06-30 for the whole validation year, so their staleness is part of the test.
  • Recent window (R): over the 14 days ending at the forecast origin minus 2 days, the mean, the standard deviation, and the daytime-minus-night mean (as in T). Three columns, recomputed for every forecast origin in training and in validation; missing when fewer than 3 days hold observations. The 2-day gap is a safety margin on top of the 3.5-hour telemetry delay.

Arms (warm, 16 Primary and 4 BSP/GSP series, seeds 0 to 2).

Arm Columns added to the 00024 recipe A0 none, no identifier (00024 type_noid) A1 identifier (00024 type_id) A2 identifier and S A3 identifier and T A4 identifier and R A5 identifier, T, and R A6 T, no identifier

Cold start (seed 0). Eight Primary series are held out in turn, 4 from the Primary-MW pool and 4 from the Primary-MVA pool (Primary-MW sites 5, 10, 14, and 16; Primary-MVA sites 2, 4, 12, and 21). For each held-out series the by-type pool is refitted without it and forecasts it with no identifier. The held-out series' fingerprint comes from its own training-window and recent-window rows, which models a new substation with 4 weeks of telemetry: the held-out series' T uses only the 28 days ending 2025-06-30, and the pool never sees its target. The pool's other series keep the full-window T. Cold-start arms: K0 (no fingerprint), K1 (S), K2 (T), K3 (T and R).

Cost. Fit seconds are recorded per model; the work is capped near 2 hours of GPU time.

docs.title: Plan: leakage and scoring checks
docs.text:
• Training rows end at 2025-06-30 23:30 and use the control member only; asserted.
  • R uses power at grid indices below the origin minus 96 half-hours; a unit-style assertion in the fit script checks the window end for every row.
  • T is computed once from rows up to 2025-06-30 and is constant between retrains; it is not a function of any validation row.
  • A held-out series' rows are absent from its cold-start pool's training matrix; asserted.
  • The scoring script repeats 00024's correction-history assertions.
  • Validation rows are fold_a_every5d_v1, ENS weather, valid times before 2026-07-01. Past weather is not used at lag times.
  • A0 and A1 are 00024's stored predictions, copied unchanged, with an assertion that their keys match the new arms'. They were fitted by the same code but not in the same run, so GPU nondeterminism adds a small seed-sized difference.

docs.title: Plan: earlier advice
docs.text: Followed: the series identifier in every pooled model (00024), 00019's stack, 00006's columns, a climatology row, and colsample_bytree fixed across arms. Departure: none.

docs.title: Plan: limits stated in advance
docs.text:
• Only 16 Primary series. The intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so they say nothing about substations outside the sample; the cold-start contrasts rest on 8 held-out series and one seed.
  • With the identifier present, a static fingerprint is redundant for series seen in training; the warm arms measure what a fingerprint adds, and the cold-start arms measure what it carries.
  • Latitude and longitude in a pool of 7 other series let the model look up the nearest neighbour, which is optimistic for location in a pool of 2,500 series.
  • A cold-start substation with no telemetry at all (no T, no R, no lags) is not tested; every model here uses power lags.

docs.title: Experiment 33: does the best-guess architecture beat production, N1, and manual_heuristic?
docs.text:
We asked whether our best-guess forecasting design beats the design now in production (the stored xgboost_baseline), a single-step model (N1), and a simple baseline (manual_heuristic), for demand, solar, and wind. The best guess is N1 plus a 14-day correction for Primary substation demand, N1 alone for bulk supply point and grid supply point demand, and mixtures of models trained on ERA5 weather (an estimate of past weather) for solar and wind farms. We scored all of them on the same forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026, for 20 demand series, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms. The best guess lowered the error against production by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand, 3.81 for solar, and 6.27 for wind, and every interval lay wholly below its threshold.

Supported: the best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), and each interval lies wholly below its threshold. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, the estimate of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity). The best guess for the 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) is N1, an XGBoost model per series trained on the ensemble forecast of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ENS) with recent power as inputs, plus an additive correction by the mean error of the previous 14 days and a spread factor of 1.15 on the forecast band. For bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) substations the best guess is N1 alone. For solar and wind it is a mixture over the 51 ENS members of a model trained on ERA5 weather (the ERA5 reanalysis, an estimate of past weather), with a spread factor and, for wind, a power-curve margin. Production is the stored xgboost_baseline forecast. The rows are the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 for the 20 demand series and the 53 Tuesday runs of fold_a_tuesdays_v1 for the 6 solar and 3 wind farms, July 2025 to June 2026. The planned intervals use month-block resampling; the level is 98.33% for C1 to C3, and the other contrasts use their family's Bonferroni level (the Planned contrasts section and the appendix give each).

Production's forecast band is far too narrow. The band from its 5% quantile to its 95% quantile covers 10% of Primary cases and 20% of solar and wind cases, and its 0.95 quantile is exceeded in 49% of Primary cases, 39% of solar cases, and 33% of wind cases. The best guess exceeds its 0.95 quantile in 7%, 4%, and 7% of cases. The 14-day correction accounts for 1.38 of the 4.89-point Primary gap (99.44% interval -2.10 to -0.68; C8), and production still scores 8.59 with the correction and its band is still narrow (coverage 9%). No arm widened production's band, so the page does not say how much of the rest is calibration.

For Primary demand, the best guess beats manual_heuristic by 0.59 points (-0.94 to -0.29; C4), and the correction supplies nearly all of its gain over N1. N1 with the correction scores 5.34 against 6.33 for N1 (-1.45; C7), and the spread factor takes a further 0.02 off. climatology scores 7.46. On BSP and GSP demand, N1 beats production by 7.25 points (-8.46 to -6.18; C13) and manual_heuristic by 1.04 (-2.01 to -0.09; C14), and the correction does not help (+0.38, -0.12 to +0.92; C16), as experiment 21 found with the same 4 series. Production's correction raises its twCRPS at historical_p99 from 0.067 to 0.107.

Monthly retraining without the correction scored 5.12 on seed 0, against 5.32 for the best guess on the same seed. Against N1 on seed 0 (6.33) it lowers the score by 1.58 points (-2.18 to -0.86; C12). Adding the correction to monthly retraining raised the seed-0 score from 5.12 to 5.24, and monthly retraining with the correction scored 0.11 below N1 with the correction, an interval that includes zero (-0.24 to +0.03; C11). Monthly retraining also gives the model 12 months of newer data, so the page does not say whether the drift of a model frozen in June 2025 or the newer data explains the gain, and no arm separates them. The arm has one seed and one validation year, so it is a lead and not a ranking. The other notable demand ideas moved the score little: the weekly analogues by -0.05 (-0.10 to -0.01; C9) and one model per type by +0.13 (+0.02 to +0.23; C10).

For solar and wind, N1 trained on ENS scored within 0.1 and 0.3 points of the best guess over all leads. The best guess minus N1 is -0.08 for solar (-0.24 to +0.12; C17) and -0.32 for wind (-0.91 to +0.20; C20), both unresolved. For wind, N1 scores lower than the best guess at 0 to 24 hours (5.91 against 6.26) and 1 to 2 days (6.51 against 6.70), and the best guess wins only from 2 days ahead (9.02 against 9.56 at 2 to 6 days). The best guess beats manual_heuristic and climatology for solar and wind (C18, C19, C21, C22). No notable idea resolved a gain: CAMS-trained solar -0.02 (C23), the physics hybrid 0.00 (C25), physics alone +0.08 (+0.02 to +0.16, worse; C26), and wind with the power-over-wind-cubed column -0.05 (-0.11 to +0.02; C24).

Tail scores at historical_p99 separate the arms only where the data allow, and the exceedance counts show why. The best guess differs from production on twCRPS above historical_p99 by -0.003 for Primary demand (95% interval -0.013 to +0.006; C1), -0.004 for solar (-0.007 to -0.001; C2), and 0.000 for wind (C3). For BSP and GSP, N1 is better than production by 0.014 (-0.023 to -0.007; C13). For solar the best guess is worse than N1 by 0.005 (+0.001 to +0.016; C17), and for Primary demand its twCRPS and Brier score at historical_p99 (0.063 and 0.0083) are no better than N1's (0.058 and 0.0079) or manual_heuristic's (0.059 and 0.0081). At historical_p95 the best guess is better than production on twCRPS for all three families (-0.07, -0.24, and -0.04; C1 to C3), and for solar it is worse than N1 (+0.023, +0.003 to +0.057; C17). The wind threshold sits near capacity, and no arm in the event table scored a hit on wind at historical_p99. For Primary demand at 1 to 2 days ahead (seed 0), the best guess flagged 168 of 417 half-hours above historical_p99 with 164 false alarms, against 59 hits and 106 false alarms for production and 21 hits and 22 false alarms for manual_heuristic. The Brier score at historical_p99 mainly measures the scorer's tail assumption, an exponential decay of the exceedance probability beyond the 0.95 quantile.

Better weather would help wind most and Primary demand least. The ERA5 arms are ceilings for a weather product as accurate as ERA5, because ERA5 and CAMS are estimates of past weather and arrive days late. The ERA5 arms lowered the score by 0.11 points for Primary demand (-0.17 to -0.05; C27), 0.79 for BSP and GSP (C32), 1.05 for solar (C28), and 5.46 for wind (-6.91 to -3.90; C29). CAMS shortwave lowered the solar score by 2.09 (C28b) and the Primary demand score by 0.18, 0.07 more than ERA5 on all seven columns did (C31b). A demand model retrained on ERA5 and fed ERA5 lowered the score by 0.27 against N1 (C30). The demand and solar gain is zero or slightly negative at 0 to 24 hours (C27 +0.03, C28 +0.17), and for wind it grows from 0.71 at 0 to 24 hours to 7.68 at 10 days or more. Wind speed at 100 m alone supplies 4.24 of the 5.46 points.

docs.title: Example forecasts
docs.text: The fan charts show the first 72 hours of one forecast run, with the best guess above production. Shade shows the 5% to 95% and 25% to 75% bands, the coloured line is the median, and the black line is the observed power. Each window is chosen from the saved scores or weather and not by hand. Generators carry anonymised labels, and the axis counts days with no calendar date.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The monthly-retraining arm has one seed and one validation year. The arm's interval resamples months only. Its training rows after June 2025 are the control member of every daily run (364 runs, extracted as the stage 1 pilot did and checked to match it exactly on the run of 2025-07-01).
  • The correction was tested on runs 5 days apart. A daily service would build the history from forecasts at leads under 1 day.
  • The intervals resample months and seeds, not series. With 3 wind farms, 6 solar farms, and 4 BSP and GSP series, they understate the difference between farms and substations.
  • Production for the generators is the stored forecast of xgboost_baseline. The stored members give a very narrow band, and the appendix lists xgboost_baseline_retrain_638 and xgboost_baseline_retrain_790 as exploratory rows. Production has 124 of 282,916 solar and wind cases without a stored forecast, and manual_heuristic 195.
  • The generator thresholds sit near capacity. historical_p99 of power over capacity ranges from 0.59 to 1.01 across the 29 series, so a high threshold for solar and wind grades clipping.
  • Several contrasts were expected to be inconclusive and are. CAMS-trained solar, the physics hybrid, and the wind column lie within their intervals of zero.
  • The ceiling arms are not deployable. ERA5 and CAMS are estimates of past weather and not ground truth, so the gap bounds the headroom of a product with their accuracy at the site's grid cell.

docs.title: Checks and predictions that did not hold
docs.text:
• Reproduction: the rebuilt best guess matches experiment 19's stored set exactly (maximum difference 0), and the refitted N1 scores 6.328 against 6.329 for experiment 13's N1.
  • Cases: each family is scored on the cases every arm holds (Primary 768,073 of 805,410, with climatology the smallest arm); each contrast uses the cases of its own two arms. The fewest members of a stored arm are 51 for production and climatology, 1 for solar manual_heuristic, and 8 for wind manual_heuristic, so the exceedance rates of manual_heuristic carry finite-ensemble bias.
  • Predictions that failed: the twCRPS and the Brier score at historical_p99 did not rank the arms as the quantile score does, and the ERA5-trained generator models did not resolvably beat the ENS-trained N1 (C17, C20).

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
docs.text: One experiment compares, on one validation year, the architecture that experiments 1 to 32 recommend against the deployed recipe, three baselines, six notable ideas, and a perfect-weather ceiling. Units are points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity). The validation rows are the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 for the 20 demand series (16 Primary substations, 2 BSP, and 2 GSP) and the 53 Tuesday runs of fold_a_tuesdays_v1 for the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. No valid time on or after 2026-07-01 is scored.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
An arm whose recipe, rows, and seeds an earlier experiment already ran is read from that experiment's stored predictions, not refitted. experiment_store.read_predictions refuses sets on a different row set, and every reused set has three seeds. The table names the source of each reused arm. Every fit below is new code in this experiment's folder.

Family Arm Source Primary demand Best guess: N1 + 14-day correction + spread factor 1.15 reused: 00019 stack_minus_h Primary demand N1 (no correction), N1 + correction reused: 00013 n1, 00019 n1_c BSP, GSP demand Best guess: N1, no correction; N1 + correction and N1 + correction + spread as arms reused: 00013 n1; correction and spread computed here All demand Production (xgboost_baseline), manual_heuristic, climatology, each with and without the 14-day correction reused: 00013 production, manual_heuristic, climatology; the correction is computed here with 00019's code All demand Notable 1: weekly analogue mean and median, with and without correction reused: 00030 a7, a7_c All demand Notable 2: one model per substation type with the series identifier, with and without correction reused: 00024 type_id, type_id_stack; contrast bases own, own_stack Primary demand Notable 3: N1 retrained monthly with a 0.5-year half-life, plus correction new fit, below Solar Best guess: ERA5-trained mixture with spread factor reused: 00020 base-spread Wind Best guess: ERA5-trained mixture with power-curve margin and spread factor reused: 00020 full Solar, wind Production (xgboost_baseline), manual_heuristic, climatology stored forecasts; read for the Tuesday runs, quantiles of the stored members at the 9 levels Solar, wind N1 for generators new fit, below Solar Notable 4: CAMS-trained mixture with spread factor reused: 00020 full-no-s0 Solar Notable 6: PV physics, and the physics output as a column in the XGBoost model reused: 00029 scipy, torch-hybrid; contrast base 00020 base Wind Notable 5: margin plus top_decile_28d and power_to_wind3_q75_28d reused: 00026 a4, a0

Four substitutions are named here. The stored arms differ from the notable ideas in four ways.

  • Notable 4 is 00020 full-no-s0 (CAMS-trained plus the spread factor), so that it shares the best guess's spread factor.
  • Notable 5 is 00026's arm A4 (wind), which adds top_decile_28d as well as power_to_wind3_q75_28d and has the power-curve margin but no spread factor. Its contrast is A4 minus A0 within 00026, where A0 equals 00020 margin.
  • Notable 6 is the stored PyTorch-fitted hybrid torch-hybrid, because 00029 found the SciPy and PyTorch fits level on score (C3, -0.005, -0.020 to +0.010) and stored no SciPy hybrid. The hybrid has no spread factor, so its contrast is against 00020 base.
  • Notable 2's stored arms use a half-life of 0.5 years, and type_id_stack adds the correction and the spread factor. Its contrasts are against 00024's own per-series arms (own, own_stack).

Production for the generators is read, not refitted. The power_forecasts Delta table holds xgboost_baseline forecasts for all 31 series, including the 9 generators, on fold mid_2025_to_mid_2026. The arm uses experiment_name xgboost_baseline, the recipe experiment 13 scored as production for demand. The table also holds xgboost_baseline_retrain_638 and xgboost_baseline_retrain_790, reported as exploratory rows. Where a stored production forecast lacks a Tuesday run, the arm is scored on the cases all arms hold, and result.md states the count of dropped cases.

N1 for generators uses the 00013 recipe with no calendar columns. The recipe, applied to each generator, is one XGBoost model per farm with the nine-level quantile loss, trained on the ENS control member of every daily run with valid times from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, recency weights with a half-life of 2 years anchored at 2025-06-30, the technology's common columns (nine for solar, six for wind), lead_hours, and three power lags from the forecast origin (newest usable observation at origin minus 3.5 hours, latest earlier same half-hour, latest earlier same weekday and half-hour). The calendar columns are left out, because experiment 1 found calendar columns let an ENS-trained generator model memorise valid times (+3.40 wind, +1.13 solar). The 51 member forecasts are pooled as in 00013. No correction is applied to N1 for generators.

Monthly retraining refits each Primary substation's N1 model on the first day of each month. The refits run from 2025-07 to 2026-06 with a half-life of 0.5 years anchored at the refit date, on the ENS control member of every daily run (the NWP store holds a daily run from 2024-04-01) with valid times at least 3.5 hours before the refit. A run is forecast by the latest refit on or before its origin, so the refit is chosen by origin and not by valid time. The 2025-07-01 refit is close to the half-life-0.5-year fit trained to 2025-06-30 but stops 3 hours earlier. The 14-day correction history spans a change of model at each month boundary, and the page says so. The arm is reported with and without the correction. Building control-member features for the daily runs after 2025-06-30 is new code; if that costs more than about 2 hours, the arm falls back to the 73 validation runs' control members and the page says so. The arm uses seed 0 only (about 1 hour for 16 series by 12 refits), so it is contrasted with the seed-0 rows of the reference arms, and its interval resamples months only.

docs.title: Perfect-weather arms
docs.text:
The perfect-weather arms measure the headroom from better weather, not a deployable model. ERA5 and CAMS are estimates of past weather, not ground truth, so figures label the arms "ERA5-weather ceiling". ERA5 reaches us about 5 days late and CAMS is satellite-derived after the fact, so no serving system could use either at the target time. The page labels every perfect-weather result "ceiling".

  • Demand: the arms ens, era5_all, era5_shortwave, era5_temperature_2m, and era5_wind_speed_10m of 00022 are reused for all 20 series (N1H; 00019 C5 found the half-life neutral). Their contrasts are against 00022's own ens, never the 00019 set. Each is reported with and without the correction, and the correction and spread factor are applied here wherever 00022's stored set lacks them. Two variants are new fits: shortwave from CAMS at the series' own location with ERA5 for the other six columns, and the model retrained on ERA5 over the same 2024-04 to 2025-06 window and fed ERA5. For BSP and GSP the arms are N1 without correction. The contrasts use the forms with correction but without the spread factor, because the factor of 1.15 was tuned for 51-member mixtures and a single input has a narrower band; the forms with the spread factor are reported as exploratory.
  • Solar: the ERA5-trained model of the best guess is fed ERA5 at the valid time (one input per valid time, so the forecast is the model's 9 quantiles); a CAMS-trained variant is fed CAMS shortwave with ERA5 for the other eight columns. Single-variable swap: shortwave only.
  • Wind: ERA5 10 m and 100 m wind speed and direction at the valid time, with the power-curve margin reading ERA5 100 m speed; single-variable swap: 100 m wind speed alone.
  • Spread factor: for solar and wind, each perfect-weather arm is reported with and without the best guess's spread factor, refitted monthly on the arm's own earlier cases as 00020 did. A single-input band is narrower than a pooled mixture, so the unrefitted factor may mislead.
  • Lead bands: 0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 d, 2 to 6 d, 6 to 10 d, 10 days or more. For solar and wind the perfect-weather arm does not depend on lead, so the by-lead gap is the best guess's degradation.
  • Weather available at forecast time: neither ERA5 nor CAMS is available at forecast time. Lagged power uses the observation at least 3.5 hours old, as in 00013; no other lag-time weather enters any arm.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
All arms store 9 quantiles at 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9, and 0.95. For manual_heuristic, production, and climatology, the quantiles are those of the stored members at the 9 levels, as 00013 took them.

  • MAE of the median: the absolute error of q50.
  • Quantile score (the CRPS estimate): as in 00019.
  • twCRPS at historical_p99: replace every quantile and the observation by max(z, r) and take the quantile score. r is the 99th percentile of the series' power over capacity in the constraint direction (high positive power for demand and for generation) over the series' full history to 2026-06-30, as evaluation-metrics.md defines it. The threshold is a fixed scoring constant that no model sees. The page reports, per series, the count of half-hours and of distinct days above the threshold. For the generators the threshold sits near capacity (capacity is itself a P99), so historical_p95 is a co-primary line for solar and wind and an exploratory line for demand.
  • Brier score at the same threshold: the exceedance probability p(r) comes from the quantile function: linear interpolation of the level against the quantile between q05 and q95; above q95 the probability falls by half for every width q95 - q90 beyond q95, starting from 0.05 (an exponential tail), and is 0 beyond q95 when q95 = q90; below q05 the exceedance probability is 1 - 0.05 * 2^(-(q05 - r) / (q10 - q05)). The tails are approximations, and at historical_p99 most cases lie in the upper tail, so the Brier score there mainly measures the tail assumption. The page therefore also reports the Brier score at historical_p95, which is interpolated, and the hit rate and false-alarm count at the threshold for the 1-to-2-day and 2-to-6-day bands. The twCRPS ignores all mass above q95.
  • Exceedance rates of the 0.90 and 0.95 quantiles: the share of cases where the observation exceeds that quantile; the aim is 10% and 5%. The rates need no model of the tail, but they are calibration checks and not tail-skill rankings. The page reports each stored arm's member count; cases of manual_heuristic with fewer than 13 members are flagged, and its rates are read against a finite-ensemble reference.
  • Thresholds and the flexibility use case: NGED buys flexibility ahead of an expected constraint, so the exceedance metrics are also reported for leads of 1 to 2 days and 2 to 6 days, the horizons at which procurement decisions are made. Metrics are never ranked on half-hours chosen by the observed load.
  • Absolute scores for every arm are reported, not only contrasts. BSP, GSP, solar, and wind are reported per type and never averaged into Primary.
  • Intervals: month-block bootstrap, whole validation months and the three seeds resampled, with studies.bootstrap.bootstrap_difference_at_level and n_resamples raised for the Bonferroni level. Intervals resample months, not series, so with three wind farms they understate between-farm uncertainty.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
Only C1 to C3 decide the verdict, so only they carry the Bonferroni correction across the three (98.33%). The other contrasts are exploratory; each family below reads at 5% divided by its contrast count, so a reader sees which intervals survive a correction within the family.

  1. Decisive (3): C1 to C3, the best guess minus production for Primary demand, solar, and wind.
  2. Primary demand (9): C4 to C6, the best guess minus manual_heuristic, N1, and climatology; C7, N1 + correction minus N1; C8, production + correction minus production; C9 to C11, notable arms 1, 2, and 3 (with correction) minus N1 + correction, own_stack, and N1 + correction at seed 0; C12, monthly retraining without correction minus N1 at seed 0.
  3. BSP and GSP (4, pooled over 4 series): C13 to C15, N1 minus production, manual_heuristic, and climatology; C16, N1 + correction minus N1.
  4. Generators (10): for solar and wind separately, C17 to C22, the best guess minus N1, manual_heuristic, and climatology; C23, solar notable 4 minus the best guess; C24, wind notable 5 (A4) minus A0; C25, solar torch-hybrid minus 00020 base; C26, solar scipy minus 00020 base.
  5. Weather ceiling (8): all with correction where the arm is demand. C27, the all-variable ERA5 arm minus 00022 ens (both N1H) for Primary demand; C28, the ERA5 arm minus the best guess for solar, and C28b, the CAMS-shortwave arm minus the CAMS-trained arm; C29, the ERA5 arm minus the best guess for wind; C30, the demand arm retrained on ERA5 minus N1 refitted here on ENS; C31, the CAMS-shortwave demand arm minus 00022 ens, and C31b, the same arm minus 00022 era5_all, which isolates CAMS against ERA5 shortwave; C32, the BSP and GSP all-variable ERA5 arm minus 00022 ens, without correction.

Several contrasts are expected to be inconclusive. Notable 1 (-0.05 in 00030), notable 4 (-0.009, -0.127 to +0.072 in 00020), and notable 5 (-0.048 in 00026) will not resolve at a share of one tenth or less, and the BSP and GSP correction (+0.36, -0.19 to +0.98 in 00021) is unresolved with 4 series. Scores by lead band, by variable, at historical_p95, and for the exceedance rates are exploratory.

docs.title: Advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed: use ERA5-trained generator models with no calendar columns and no stage 2 or correction (00001, 00023); keep the demand correction at 14 days, additive (00019, 00021); leave the correction out of the best guess for BSP and GSP (00021).
  • Departed from: 00019 C5 shows a 0.5-year half-life on a frozen model changes nothing; notable 2 uses it because 00024 ran it, and notable 3 tests the half-life with monthly retraining, which 00019 never did.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
• Headline: quantile score of every arm per family with 98.33% intervals on the decisive contrasts, at the top of the page.
  • Metrics: twCRPS, Brier score, and exceedance rates of the 0.90 and 0.95 quantiles per arm.
  • By lead band: best guess, production, N1, manual_heuristic.
  • Perfect weather: gap to the best guess by lead band and by variable.
  • Fan charts (the 9 quantiles and the actual): several series per family on good and bad days, sunny and cloudy, windy and calm, a cold snap; the best guess beside production. Generators carry anonymised labels ("Solar farm A", "Wind farm B") from studies.anonymise, never a name or an identifier; substations may be named. Generator charts follow the dataviz skill: the axis shows days 1 to 7 and no calendar date, the text gives month and year only, aria is off, values are fractions of capacity and not megawatts, and no caption gives the date of a "windy" or "cold" day.

docs.title: Checks and compute
docs.text:
• Leakage checks. Every refit stops at its stated training end; lags and the correction use observations at least 3.5 hours before the origin; ERA5 and CAMS values are those of the valid time only and are used in the perfect-weather arms alone; the thresholds are fixed scoring constants from each series' history to 2026-06-30, which no model sees. A reviewer checks the monthly-retraining code for leakage.
  • Reproduction checks. The reused demand arms must reproduce 00019's stored scores to 3 decimal places on 00019's exact case set when rescored with this experiment's scorer; each family is then scored on its own case intersection and the page reports the dropped counts, and the refitted N1 must match 00013's n1 within 0.02 points.
  • Weather source at lag times. No arm uses weather at lag times; only the power lags read the past, and they read observed power available at the forecast origin.
  • Compute. About 3 hours in total on slots A and B (22 cores, one fit at a time on the GPU): generator N1 (9 series x 3 seeds, minutes); demand fits (N1 refit, 20 series x 3 seeds, about 20 minutes, and the ERA5-retrained variant, about 20 minutes); monthly retraining (about 1 hour, seed 0, plus the feature build); generator perfect-weather predictions (minutes). If the fits would run more than 5 hours in total, the plan proposes a reduction to the manager instead of cutting arms silently.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/00033-.../predictions/; no table.
  • Production serving path: not touched; the production arm is read from stored forecasts.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: more than one could compare the architectures (for example the choice of thresholds, the tail of the exceedance probability, and the reused-versus-refitted arms), so the plan is reviewed.
  • Callers: the scripts copy the helpers of experiments 13, 19, 20, and 22; the span of code is wide, so the size is complex.

docs.title: Experiment 34: how often should the demand model be retrained?
docs.text:
We asked how much a forecast of a substation's electricity demand improves when the forecasting model is refitted on newer data more often, and whether a cheaper stand-in for frequent refitting gives the same answers. For each of 16 Primary substations we refitted one gradient-boosted decision-tree model (XGBoost) on all the data available at the refit date, once a year, every 6 months, every quarter, every month, every week, or every day. We then scored its forecasts for 73 runs started 5 days apart between July 2025 and June 2026. The error is the quantile score, which rewards a forecast that is both close and honest about its uncertainty, in percentage points of the substation's capacity (lower is better). The best earlier setup we had tested was a model trained once, with a correction added from its own errors over the last 14 days; it scored 5.32. Refitting monthly with no correction scored 5.12, which is 0.20 points lower. The 95% interval for that difference excludes zero, but the stricter 99.375% interval that we fixed in advance does not. Refitting weekly scored a further 0.07 lower than monthly, and refitting daily (three months only) scored 0.01 lower than weekly. The 14-day correction stopped helping once the model was refitted often. We also tested four cheaper ways to imitate monthly refitting, and judged each by whether it changed three earlier experiments' results the way full monthly refitting changes them. Only refitting monthly on the latest 12 months of data, with 150 larger boosting steps in place of 500, agreed on all three.

Terms used below. N1 is the one-model-per-substation XGBoost recipe of experiment 13, trained on the control member of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather forecast. The stack is N1 trained once, then given the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 that widens its uncertainty. Frozen means trained once, up to 30 June 2025. BSP and GSP are the bulk supply point and grid supply point substations above the Primary substations. A GPU hour is one hour on the graphics card that fits the models.

Inconclusive at the planned level, with the direction established at 95%. The primary contrast C1 is monthly retraining minus the best-guess stack. It scores -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08), so by the pre-registered rule the verdict is inconclusive. The 95% interval is -0.38 to -0.01. Scores are the mean quantile score over all lead times on the 768,073 cases that every arm of experiment 33 holds, with a spread factor of 1.15 on every arm unless it says otherwise (_s), and the 14-day correction added where it says so (_cs). Weather is ENS forecast weather in every arm, so the numbers are deployable. The code is in ml-experiments/00034-*/, and e00034_report.py prints every number below.

Arm (refits in the year) No correction With correction Stack: frozen N1 with a 2-year half-life, correction, spread factor (3 seeds) 5.32 Frozen, trained to 30 June 2025 (1, 3 seeds) 6.29 5.32 Half-yearly (2) 5.43 5.28 Three a year (3) 5.46 5.32 Quarterly (4) 5.29 5.28 Monthly (12, 3 seeds) 5.12 5.22 Weekly (52) 5.04 5.27 Monthly, half-life 2 years (12) 5.14 5.21 manual_heuristic, climatology, production 5.89, 7.46, 9.52

Arms other than the stack, the frozen model, and monthly use seed 0. The 95% intervals on each score are about plus or minus 0.4 because they span months; the contrasts below are paired and much tighter.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
Each contrast is a difference in quantile score on the cases both arms hold, read at 99.375% (Bonferroni across eight). Negative favours the first arm.

Id Contrast Difference 99.375% interval 95% interval C1 monthly minus the stack -0.20 -0.44 to +0.08 -0.38 to -0.01 C2 monthly with correction minus monthly +0.11 -0.17 to +0.31 -0.09 to +0.27 C3 weekly minus monthly -0.07 -0.18 to -0.00 -0.15 to -0.02 C4 monthly minus frozen -1.17 -1.93 to -0.39 -1.72 to -0.60 C5 monthly minus three refits a year -0.35 -0.61 to -0.09 -0.54 to -0.16 C6 monthly, half-life 0.5 years, minus half-life 2 years -0.02 -0.05 to +0.02 -0.04 to +0.01 C7 weekly with correction minus weekly +0.23 +0.03 to +0.44 +0.09 to +0.38 C8 quarterly minus monthly +0.17 +0.03 to +0.38 +0.05 to +0.31

Retraining helps at every lead time, and most beyond two days. Monthly scores 4.39 against 4.51 for the stack in the first 24 hours and 5.26 against 5.46 at 6 to 10 days.

The gain per step shrinks as refits become more frequent. Against the frozen model, half-yearly retraining lowers the score by 0.86 (95% interval -1.37 to -0.35), quarterly by a further 0.14 (-0.28 to -0.03), monthly by a further 0.17 (C8), and weekly by 0.07 (C3). On the three months in which daily retraining ran (October 2025, January 2026, April 2026, 193,621 cases) daily scores 5.15, weekly 5.16, and monthly 5.22: daily minus weekly is -0.01 (-0.04 to +0.04) and daily minus monthly -0.06 (-0.12 to -0.02). The gain flattens at weekly cadence, not at monthly: weekly is still 0.07 below monthly, which is above the 0.05 band the plan set.

The correction stops helping once the model is retrained, and hurts at weekly and daily cadence. C2 is +0.11 and unresolved at monthly cadence. At weekly cadence it raises the score by 0.23 (C7), and on the daily months it costs +0.52 (+0.18 to +0.78). For the 2 BSP and 2 GSP series, monthly retraining lowers the score by 0.11 (-0.23 to +0.00) and 0.43 (-1.15 to +0.10) against the frozen model, and the correction costs +0.24 and +0.78; these intervals are wide on two series each.

A half-life of 0.5 years and 2 years score the same under monthly retraining (C6, -0.02).

docs.title: Cheap proxies for monthly retraining
docs.text:
Only the rolling 12-month window reproduced full monthly retraining on all three rank-test contrasts. The test compares each proxy's difference with full monthly retraining's, with a tolerance of 0.05 points; seeds differ by 0.0002 on R1, so the tolerance stands. R1 is the correction on versus off, R2 is the weekly-analogue columns of experiment 30 minus N1 (with the correction), and R3 is experiment 24's one-model-per-type minus one-model-per-series (with the correction). R2's difference under full monthly retraining is -0.007, below the 0.02 floor, so a proxy is not required to match its sign.

Regime Score (no correction) R1 correction R2 weekly analogues R3 pooled by type Frozen model (experiments 30, 24, and 33 values) 6.29 n/a -0.051 +0.149 Full monthly 5.12 +0.107 -0.007 +0.243 P-roll: 12-month window, 150 rounds 5.15 +0.117 -0.006 +0.231 P-anchor: three refits a year 5.46 -0.141 (fails) -0.019 +0.218 P-interp: blend of anchors (uses later data) 4.91 -0.105 (fails) not run not run P-warm, 20 rounds, monthly updates 5.41 -0.054 (fails) not run not run P-warm, 50 rounds, monthly updates 5.54 -0.006 (fails) not run not run

Three results change how later experiments should run. First, P-roll costs 0.03 points of score and about a third of the GPU time of a full monthly refit (about 3 s against 10 s per fit; 0.20 against 0.63 GPU hours for one seed); P-roll passes. Second, the weekly-analogue columns gained 0.05 on a frozen model but only 0.01 under monthly retraining (R2), so a frozen reference overstates a feature that follows recent demand level.
