Third, the P-warm chains get worse with more updates: 5.41 for monthly updates, 5.67 for weekly updates, and on the daily months 7.76 for daily updates against 6.21 for the weekly chain over the same rows (+1.55, +0.33 to +3.21). Adding rounds to a booster each update never forgets older rows, so warm starting cannot stand in for weekly or daily refitting. P-interp scores best of all arms (4.91) because its later anchor saw data after the forecast origin; it is a screening device only and is never a forecast score.

docs.title: Fitting time by retraining cadence
docs.text: N1 takes about 10 s per series for a refit on the GPU. For the 16 Primary series: a frozen arm is 16 fits (about 3 minutes); one seed of monthly retraining is 192 fits (0.63 GPU hours, 12 times as much); weekly is 832 fits (4.7 GPU hours on a GPU shared with another session, about 2.4 uncontended, 52 times as much); the rolling-window proxy is 192 cheaper fits (0.20 GPU hours, 4 times as much); daily over the three months is 288 fits (about 1 hour). The whole experiment used about 12 GPU hours, over the 8 hours the plan allowed, because another session shared the GPU and the manager approved the extra stage.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• No fit failed.
  • The correction history spans model changes. At each refit the 14-day correction reads forecasts from the previous model, which may understate the correction's value at weekly and daily cadence.
  • The validation rows are 5 days apart, not daily, so the correction reads forecasts 5 days apart (experiment 19 advised daily forecasts for this test).
  • C1 is not an independent test: experiment 33's seed 0 suggested it on the same rows. Seeds 1 and 2 changed C1 by under 0.01, because months, not seeds, set the interval.
  • R4 (experiment 32's fingerprints) and solar and wind were not run. The BSP and GSP part covers monthly retraining only (weekly was not run).
  • Daily retraining ran on three months only, and its warm-start version failed, so the daily result rests on 18 refits per series.
  • Experiments run after the plan (seeds 1 and 2, BSP and GSP monthly, daily warm start, full daily refits) are post hoc.

docs.title: Recommendation for the validation protocol (for the maintainer)
docs.text:
• Production: retrain demand models monthly, and consider weekly (0.07 points lower again, 10 s per series). Drop the 14-day correction for Primary substations once retraining is that frequent.
  • Screening experiments: use monthly refits on a 12-month window with 150 rounds and eta 0.15 (P-roll) on seed 0, because it agrees with full monthly retraining on all three tested contrasts at 0.2 GPU hours per arm.
  • Release experiments: use full monthly refits with an expanding window, testing each on the next month, at 0.63 GPU hours per seed.
  • Not as a protocol: a frozen model (it overstates level-following features), three refits a year, an anchor blend, or warm starting.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
Plan review (Opus), triaged. Accepted: gate the weekly and daily arms on the point estimate of C1, not its interval; set the porting threshold at zero; name the score form of every contrast; state when the correction counts as no longer helping; make daily descriptive; take the frozen arm from the monthly fits; calibrate the rank-test tolerance on seeds; say P-warm's weights are nearly flat and P-interp can never be the protocol; fix a money metaphor and the pooled-fit cost. Rejected: reusing experiment 33's monthly seed 0 instead of refitting (the half-yearly, quarterly, and three-a-year arms need the other refit dates, and the refit reproduced the stored scores to 0.001); reducing the Bonferroni family (kept at eight, as the house style sets it).

Code review (Opus), triaged. All accepted and fixed before any fit ran: weekly and monthly refits shared a folder (now separate), the assembler dropped arms whose seeds 1 and 2 were missing (now builds from the seeds present), BSP and GSP assembly overwrote the Primary tables (now one table per arm with every group), contrasts read three seeds where the plan said seed 0 (now seed 0 except C1 and C2), the daily arm needed the weekly arm built first, and warm-start writes were not atomic. No leakage was found.

Prose review (Sonnet): applied in this page; the triage is in the pull request.

docs.title: Experiment 35: does a lead-weighted blend of quantiles beat the best single model?
docs.text:
We asked whether averaging the forecast ranges of several stored models, with a different weight at each lead time, beats the best single model. We blended three stored models of demand at Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), and tested similar blends for solar and wind. For Primary demand the blend lowered the error by 0.10 points of capacity, which clears the threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve.

Primary demand gains 0.10 points of capacity from blending; solar and wind gain too little to resolve. The stack is N1 (the single-stage XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS, the ensemble weather forecast of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts) with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 (experiment 00019). The lead-band blend of the monthly-retrained N1, a7_cs, and the stack scores 5.025 points of capacity against 5.122 for the best member (difference -0.097, 98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026), so the outcome for Primary demand is "port" (threshold 0.05). Solar is -0.039 (-0.115 to +0.031) and wind is -0.074 (-0.194 to +0.055), both "null". The stop rule did not fire anywhere (corner cells: Primary 0 of 60, solar 6, wind 7), so the verdict is supported, on Primary demand alone. The prediction held for Primary demand's size but not its verdict (expected small gain, found "port"), and failed for wind, where the estimate was -0.074 against a predicted -0.10 to -0.30. Intervals resample whole months, and for Primary demand one seed, so they say nothing about other substations or about wind farms beyond the three scored.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
The quantile score (points of capacity, smaller is better) of every arm, over the cases that experiment 33's final shared case sets hold. Primary demand has 768,073 cases, solar 527,025, wind 321,138, and BSP and GSP 592,950. The in-sample arm chooses its weights on all 12 months and is an optimistic bound.

Technology Members Equal One weight Lead bands In sample Primary demand monthly 5.122, a7_cs 5.268, stack 5.318 5.059 5.020 5.025 5.008 Solar N1 5.113, best guess 5.035 4.978 4.986 4.996 4.973 Wind N1 11.359, best guess 11.042 10.965 10.941 10.969 10.907 BSP and GSP (descriptive) N1 13.665, a7 13.658 13.621 13.643 13.644 13.621

docs.title: Contrasts
docs.text:
• Weights per lead band are no better than one weight. The lead-band blend minus the one-weight blend is +0.005 (-0.008 to +0.023) for Primary demand, +0.009 (-0.005 to +0.028) for solar, and +0.028 (-0.019 to +0.082) for wind. The equal-weights blend beats the best member by -0.063 for Primary demand (-0.279 to +0.091), so equal weights are not resolved.
  • Primary demand gains at every lead band; wind's short-lead gains are unresolved. The lead-band blend minus the best member for Primary demand is -0.17 at 0 to 24 h (-0.35 to -0.03) and -0.08 at 10 days or more (-0.20 to -0.002). Wind is -0.37 at 0 to 24 h (-0.81 to +0.02) and +0.05 at 2 to 6 days (-0.12 to +0.25).
  • Correct each member before blending, not the blend afterwards. The blend with the correction applied afterwards scores 5.208 against 5.160 for the same blend with every member corrected first (+0.048, 95% interval +0.008 to +0.101; the contrast favours the corrected-first arm, because that arm's weights were chosen on it). Correcting the monthly-retrained N1 as well still scores 0.135 points worse than the headline blend, whose monthly-retrained N1 is uncorrected.
  • Against the stack of experiment 19, the Primary blend is -0.293 (-0.447 to -0.140, 95%). The monthly-retrained N1 alone is 0.196 below the stack on the same cases (5.122 against 5.318).

docs.title: Chosen weights
docs.text: The weights favour the member with the lower score in that band, and for wind and solar they vary from band to band. Mean chosen weights over the 11 months with history, by lead band from 0 to 24 h to 10 days or more: Primary demand gives the monthly-retrained N1 0.59 to 0.70, a7_cs 0.30 to 0.39, and the stack 0.00 to 0.05. Wind gives N1 0.68 and 0.61 under 2 days and 0.20 to 0.30 beyond. Solar gives N1 between 0.30 and 0.57. Weights lie on a 0.25 grid. The stop rule counts corner cells over all 60 cells: Primary 0, solar 6, wind 7 (BSP and GSP 13).

docs.title: Porting cost
docs.text: A blend serves one more model per technology, and for Primary demand two more. Wind and solar would serve N1 beside the ERA5-trained mixture, which is a second training source and a second feature pipeline. Primary demand would serve the monthly-retrained N1 (a refit each month for 16 series), a7_cs (seven weekly-analogue columns), and the stack, and a fixed weight vector of three numbers suffices. The experiment does not decide a port; a release plan does.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• One validation year and one seed for Primary demand. The retrained N1 has seed 0 only.
  • Selection history is short. Months 2 to 12 choose weights on 1 to 11 months, July 2025 uses equal weights, and the long-lead bands start with few cases.
  • The Primary member scores come from experiment 33's stored tables, which that experiment may still be re-scoring; the case sets read here carry that experiment's shared_keys as of 2026-10-15.
  • BSP and GSP are 4 series and the result is descriptive.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text: See advice in the front matter. In short: blend with one fixed weight vector, correct inside the members, and test wind on more farms.

docs.title: Experiment 36: do forecasts of the series beneath a BSP or GSP lower its error?
docs.text:
We asked whether forecasts of the substations beneath a bulk supply point help forecast the demand of that point, and whether adding wind and solar generation helps at a grid supply point. We added those forecasts to a single-step model and scored 4 series: 2 bulk supply points and 2 grid supply points. Neither addition lowered the error. A model trained on estimates of past weather lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40 points of capacity, but its intervals span -1.8 to +1.0 points.

Verdict: inconclusive. Adding forecasts of the series beneath a bulk supply point (BSP) to N1 (the single-stage XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS, the ECMWF ensemble weather forecast) did not lower its quantile score, and adding wind and solar columns to a grid supply point (GSP) did not either. The N1 trained on ERA5 (a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) lowered the GSP scores by 0.36 and 0.40 points of capacity, but its 99.17% intervals span -1.8 to +1.0 points. Scores are in points of capacity (1% of a series' effective capacity) on 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days, July 2025 to June 2026, with ENS weather, for four series: the BSPs Boston and Skegness and the GSPs Walpole and Bicker Fen. The intervals describe these four series only. Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The arms. B0 is N1. B1 adds the summed median forecasts of the Primary substations and metered generators beneath a BSP (the generators only at a GSP). B2 regresses the BSP on its children's median forecasts. B3 trains N1 on ERA5 and applies it to the ENS members. B4 adds a generic wind power curve and a PV_Live solar forecast as columns at the GSPs. O is B1 with the observed values of the children. C1 to C6 are the six planned contrasts, in the order below.

Per family, by the pre-registered rule: the BSP family is refuted, the GSP wind and solar family is refuted, and the GSP ERA5-trained family is inconclusive. All three families are not supported, so the experiment is inconclusive. The oracle gave a gain of more than 0.5 at both BSPs, so the stop rule did not apply and B1 and B2 were fitted.

Series B0 N1 B1 child columns B2 bottom-up sum B3 ERA5-trained N1 B4 wind, solar columns O oracle Climatology Boston (BSP) 9.72 9.76 9.97 9.31 4.13 11.32 Skegness (BSP) 6.39 6.58 6.68 6.29 2.97 7.26 Walpole (GSP) 18.41 18.36 18.05 18.39 19.97 Bicker Fen (GSP) 20.74 20.70 20.34 20.70 22.51

The table shows the quantile score over all leads. The refit B0 matches experiment 13's stored N1 within 0.003 points at every series.

  • C1 and C2, B1 minus B0 (BSPs): +0.04 (99.17% interval -0.18 to +0.25) at Boston and +0.19 (-0.10 to +0.73) at Skegness. Both lower bounds exceed -0.5, so the BSP family is refuted.
  • C3 and C4, B3 minus B0 (GSPs): -0.36 (-1.60 to +0.43) at Walpole and -0.40 (-1.84 to +0.97) at Bicker Fen. The point estimates are smaller than the predicted 0.5 to 1.5, and the intervals are too wide to exclude zero or the -0.5 bar. By lead band the estimates are +0.37 (0 to 24 hours), then -0.53, -0.51, -0.54, and -0.21 at Walpole, and +0.61, -0.31, -0.54, -0.58, and -0.36 at Bicker Fen, every interval including zero (exploratory).
  • C5 and C6, B4 minus B0 (GSPs): -0.02 (-0.06 to +0.03) at Walpole and -0.04 (-0.13 to +0.07) at Bicker Fen. Both lower bounds exceed -0.5, so the family is refuted.
  • The oracle (exploratory, 95%): O minus B0 is -5.58 (-6.56 to -4.55) at Boston and -3.42 (-4.30 to -2.62) at Skegness, and O minus B1 is -5.62 and -3.61. The share of oracle child values filled from forecasts is 9.8% at Boston and 9.5% at Skegness in the validation rows (11.6% and 1.5% in the training rows), printed by e00036_fit.py.
  • B1 at the GSPs (exploratory, generator column only): -0.05 (-0.14 to +0.02) at Walpole and -0.04 (-0.12 to +0.05) at Bicker Fen over all leads. At Bicker Fen the 0 to 24 hour band is -0.30 (-0.44 to -0.15), which excludes zero.
  • B2 (exploratory): B2 minus B1 is +0.21 (-0.15 to +0.59) at Boston and +0.10 (-0.68 to +0.63) at Skegness, inside the predicted 0.5. B2 minus B0 is +0.25 (-0.11 to +0.63) and +0.29 (-0.16 to +0.67).
  • B3 at the BSPs (exploratory, 95%): -0.41 (-0.66 to -0.15) at Boston and -0.10 (-0.28 to +0.07) at Skegness. At Boston the gain is -0.70 (0 to 24 hours), -0.88 (1 to 2 days), and -0.66 (3 to 6 days), and shrinks beyond day 6.

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Missed: B1 minus B0 was predicted at -0.5 to -1.5 and was +0.04 and +0.19.
  • Met: B2 within 0.5 of B1, and O below B1 at both BSPs.
  • Not resolved: B3 minus B0 at the GSPs was predicted at -0.5 to -1.5, largest beyond day 2. The estimates, -0.36 and -0.40, fall short of the range, are worse than N1 at 0 to 24 hours, and have intervals that include zero, so the lead pattern is untested.
  • Missed: B4 minus B0 was predicted at -0.2 to -0.8 and was -0.02 and -0.04.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: The forecast columns added nothing although the oracle's observed children added a great deal. One reading is that the observed children tell N1 what is happening now, and a forecast of a child carries no more than N1 already derives from the same ENS weather and the power lags. The experiment did not test this reading.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Four series. Two BSPs and two GSPs cannot support a release decision, and the intervals resample months and seeds, not series.
  • Training columns come from the control member and validation columns from each member, so the ensemble spread of the children reaches the model at validation and not in training.
  • The training columns are cross-fitted by time block, not out of time. A block's child model sees months both before and after the block.
  • Unforecast flows. Four series beneath Boston have no forecast, and the GSPs carry flows from outside the trial area.
  • B4's bias correction was dropped, and experiment 28 found the PV_Live member mean 1.8 to 3.0 points of PV_Live capacity too high.
  • The 14-day correction was not applied, because experiment 21 found it unproven at BSP and GSP.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
docs.text: Units are points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity). The rows are the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 (one run every 5 days, valid times 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30) for four series, each fitted with seeds 0, 1, and 2. No valid time on or after 2026-07-01 is scored.

docs.title: Why the question is worth asking
docs.text: A bulk supply point (BSP) flow is almost exactly a linear sum of the series beneath it, and N1 does not use that. On the validation year, a least-squares fit of each BSP on the Primary substations and metered generators beneath it gives R² 0.994 at Boston and 0.992 at Skegness, with a residual standard deviation of 1.2 to 1.3 MW against 14 to 15 MW for the BSP itself. The two grid supply points (GSPs) carry flows from outside the trial area (R² 0.16 at Walpole and 0.74 at Bicker Fen against their BSP and generators), so a sum of children cannot reproduce them, but the metered wind and solar generation beneath them is a large share of their variance. Experiment 33's interim ceiling arms (not yet published) suggest that an N1 trained on ERA5 and fed ERA5 removes about a fifth of the error at BSPs and GSPs, three times the gain of an ENS-trained N1 given the same ERA5 inputs. This experiment asks how much of that headroom a deployable forecast can capture.

docs.title: Series and hierarchy
docs.text:
NGED's hierarchy file (private, never committed) assigns each Primary substation and metered generator to a BSP and a GSP. The series are:

Type Series Beneath it BSP Boston 9 Primary substations; 3 solar farms and 1 wind farm BSP Skegness 7 Primary substations; 2 solar farms and 2 wind farms GSP Walpole Boston and the series beneath Boston GSP Bicker Fen Skegness and the series beneath Skegness

The 16 Primary substations of the earlier demand experiments are exactly the Primaries beneath these two BSPs. Solar farm C does not appear in the hierarchy file and is left out. Four series beneath Boston have no forecast (a biofuel generator, a battery, a solar site, and a generator of another type), so their flows stay in the residual. Every generator beneath Skegness has a forecast. Generator names and identifiers never appear on the published page.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
All arms are N1 per series, with experiment 13's recipe: a nine-level quantile XGBoost model (500 rounds, eta 0.05, depth 6) trained on the ENS control member of every daily run, valid times 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, recency weights with a 2-year half-life anchored at 2025-06-30, the Primary column set, lead_hours, and the three power lags from the forecast origin. The 51 ENS members are pooled into nine quantiles as in experiment 13. No 14-day correction is applied to a BSP or a GSP, because experiment 21 found it unproven there.

  • B0: N1 refitted by this experiment's code. The fit is checked against experiment 13's stored n1, and the check is printed.
  • B1, bottom-up columns: B0 plus two columns in MW at the valid time. The Primary column is the sum over the Primary substations beneath of the median of experiment 13's N1 (no correction, no spread factor). The generator column is the sum over the metered generators beneath of the median of experiment 20's best-guess recipe (ERA5-trained, with the power-curve margin for wind). The spread factor leaves a median unchanged, so it is not applied. Each ENS member's row of the BSP or GSP XGBoost model receives the medians of the same member's child forecasts, so the pooled forecast keeps N1's member-by-member structure. At a GSP, B1 holds the generator column only, as the proposal for this experiment specifies.
  • B2, bottom-up sum (BSPs only): a least-squares regression of the observed BSP power on an intercept and the median forecast of each child, fitted on the training rows. The regression is applied to each member's child medians, and the member forecasts are pooled as in B0. Each member's quantiles are its regression value plus the empirical residual quantiles of the training rows, taken per lead band. Nothing else enters B2.
  • B3, perfect prognosis: N1 trained on ERA5 at the valid times of the same training rows (same window, half-life, lags, and lead_hours), applied to each of the 51 ENS members and pooled. All four series.
  • B4, regional proxies (GSPs only): B0 plus two columns computed from the GSP's own ENS cell. The wind column is a generic wind power curve (0 below 3 m/s, a cubic ramp to 1 at 12 m/s, 1 to 25 m/s, 0 above) applied to the ENS 100 m wind speed of each member. The solar column is experiment 28's PV_Live solar share (an ERA5-trained XGBoost model of PV_Live's share of its own capacity), computed for each member's own weather. Training rows use experiment 28's five forward-chain models, whose quarters match the five blocks below and which never saw the quarter they score, applied to the control member of every daily run. Validation rows use the final model. The bias correction the proposal named is dropped: with the training column and the validation column both computed per member, a constant offset only shifts tree splits. Experiment 28 found the member mean 1.8 to 3.0 points of PV_Live capacity too high, and the page reports this as a limit. Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0.
  • O, oracle (BSPs only): B1 with the observed values of the children at the valid time, and the same member's child forecast median where the observation is missing (in training rows, the cross- fitted column). The page prints the share of filled children per BSP before the stop rule is read.

A month-by-half-hour climatology row (ClimatologyForecaster) is scored for reference, repeated once per seed.

docs.title: How the child columns are built without leakage
docs.text:
A child's forecast in the training rows must not come from a model that saw those rows. An XGBoost model with 500 rounds and depth 6 reproduces its own training rows closely, so an in-sample column would look far better in training than at validation, and B1 would learn to trust it too much. The experiment cross-fits the training columns in time instead:

  • Blocks. The training window is split into five blocks by valid time: 2024-04 to 2024-06, 2024-07 to 2024-09, 2024-10 to 2024-12, 2025-01 to 2025-03, and 2025-04 to 2025-06. The column for a training row in block k comes from a child model trained without block k and without the 15 days either side of it.
  • Primary substations. Each Primary's N1 is refitted five times per seed with a block left out, on the same recipe as above (ENS control member, 2-year half-life).
  • Generators. Each generator's ERA5-trained model of experiment 20 is refitted five times per seed with the block left out, and applied to the control-member ENS rows of the block. The validation columns use the full models (training to 2025-06-17), pooled over the 51 members.
  • Validation columns for Primaries come from a sixth, full-window N1 fit per Primary and seed, applied member by member (experiment 13's stored n1 holds pooled quantiles only, so it serves as a check). The validation columns for generators need ENS rows at the generator cells for the 73 runs, which are not stored (the pilot stored Tuesday runs only). This experiment extracts them from the ENS archive with the same upsampling that demand_build_ens.py uses, and checks the refitted models against experiment 20's stored predictions on the runs the two row sets share. The generator full models train to 2025-06-17 and N1 to 2025-06-30, a difference inherited from experiments 20 and 13.
  • Same child sets everywhere. B2's coefficients, B1's columns, and the oracle all use the same children.

Training columns come from the control member and validation columns from each member. The BSP or GSP XGBoost model trains on one child forecast per row (the control member's) and receives one per ENS member at validation, so it sees the same kind of column in both. The ensemble spread of the children is therefore part of what the model receives at validation and not in training, and the page reports it as a limit.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text: Quantile score and MAE of the median, per series, over all leads and in the five lead bands (0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 days, 3 to 6 days, 7 to 10 days, 11 to 15 days). Contrasts use experiment_store.losses_for_bootstrap and studies.bootstrap.bootstrap_difference_at_level, resampling the 12 validation months and the three seeds, with n_resamples raised for the 99.17% level. The page reports the absolute score of every arm, per series. Intervals describe these four series and say nothing about other BSPs or GSPs. B3 minus B0 at the BSPs, B1 minus B0 at the GSPs, B2 minus B1, O minus B0, and the lead-band contrasts are exploratory.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets and cross-fitted columns under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched. Porting B1 would add a dependency of the BSP model on the Primary and generator models in the Dagster asset graph.
  • Degradation rule: not touched. A missing child forecast would need a degradation rule at porting time, and that rule is outside this experiment.
  • Defensible designs: more than one (the child columns, the cross-fitting scheme, the regression in B2, and the filling rule of the oracle). Each is fixed above.
  • Callers: the scripts copy experiment 13's N1 fit, experiment 20's generator fit, experiment 28's PV_Live loader and solar model, and experiment 33's ENS extraction. The author could name each without searching.

Size: complex. Sonnet writes the plan, Opus reviews it, Sonnet implements, Opus reviews the code, Sonnet runs the code and writes up, and Sonnet reviews the write-up.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed: treat BSP and GSP findings as provisional with four series (experiments 6, 21, 24); report intervals over validation months (13); keep the 14-day correction off BSP and GSP (21); pool ERA5-trained quantiles over ENS members (2); add a climatology row (10); report the absolute score of every arm.
  • Departed from: the experiment adds no calendar-placebo or shuffled-input control. The columns are forecasts of real series, and the oracle already bounds what a perfect column gives.

docs.title: Past weather
docs.text: B3, B1, B2, B4, and every child forecast use ENS weather only, so all are deployable as far as weather goes (ERA5 arrives about 5 days late and is used only at training times). The lag features use observed power from the forecast origin, as in experiment 13. B4's PV_Live model trains on ERA5 weather and PV_Live's revised values, both of which exist at training time.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Four series. Two BSPs and two GSPs cannot support a release decision alone.
  • Unforecast flows. Four series beneath Boston are not forecast, and the GSPs carry flows from outside the trial area.
  • Cross-fitted training columns are out-of-sample, not out-of-time. A block's child model sees months both before and after it.

docs.title: Experiment 37: does a neighbour-balance detector find logged switching in the telemetry?
docs.text:
We asked whether comparing a substation with its neighbours can find the moments when load was switched from one substation to another, which NGED's logs of closures record. We built a detector based on the balance between neighbouring substations and a simpler detector that looks at one series, and measured how much of the switched power each found, against how many alarms had no logged cause. The neighbour-based detector found 0.326 of the switched power in the validation months (the even-numbered months, kept apart from the months used to set its threshold) and beat the single-series detector. The 18 visible switching events were too few to show whether it meets the bar we set.

Inconclusive: the neighbour-balance detector D1 (which flags a step in a substation that its neighbours' steps do not balance) recovers a third of the MW of the 18 visible validation transfers, and beats the single-series detector D0 by about +0.14 at equal alarm rates, but the small reference set leaves the verdict between the two pre-registered bars. D1 with a 4-hour window and a threshold of 4 reaches a size-weighted recall (the share of switched megawatts found) of 0.326 (95% interval 0.093 to 0.579) at 0.38 unexplained alarms (alarms with no logged closure) per series-month. D0 reaches 0.036 (0.000 to 0.131) at 0.14, and the difference is +0.290 (+0.034 to +0.557). The two thresholds sit at different alarm rates, so the fairer comparison is at about 0.5 alarms per series-month, where D0 reaches 0.224 and D1 0.362. Shifted logs give 0.004 for D1. D1 misses the 0.35 bar for supported and clears the 0.20 bar for refuted, so the rule gives inconclusive. Of 612 logged closures of 2 hours to 60 days, 37 are confirmed, and about 6 of those are expected by chance (shifted logs give 6.2). Eighteen of the 37 are in the validation months, above the stop-rule minimum of 15 but not by much. Recall on all logged closures of 2 hours or more is 0.086. All figures are on the residual of the monthly- retrained XGBoost model with ERA5 weather and no power lags (experiment 00017's H0.5). ERA5 arrives about 5 days after the event, so the detector is retrospective and cannot yet run live.

docs.title: Purposes the results speak to
docs.text:
1. Lagged power in the forecast. Not tested here. The confirmed transfers give the intervals in which a lag would sit inside a switching event, but no forecast uses them yet.
  2. Cleaner targets in the first model version. Untested: no mask was applied to any training target. D1 at its budget finds about a third of the MW of the visible transfers, so a mask built from it would leave most visible events in place.
  3. A report back to NGED. The 18 validation transfers and the 37 in total are a list of inferred events that NGED could check against its own logs. At 0.38 unexplained alarms per series-month, a reader would get about 6 candidate events a month across the 16 substations.

docs.title: Raw data first
docs.text: Where load visibly moves, the two substations step in opposite directions for the whole closure and the steps are close in size. The first figure shows the six validation closures in which both residuals have a step. The second figure shows missed closures, closures with no visible step, and the detector's alarms. The third shows quiet periods.

docs.title: Q1: which logged closures move load
docs.text:
6.0% of logged closures of 2 hours to 60 days are confirmed, against 1.0% on shifted logs; the prediction of 8% to 20% was too high. Of 612 closures since 2022-01, 37 are confirmed: 13 have both sides and 24 have one side. On the shifted logs, 6.2 of 608 closures are confirmed per seed. The confirmations by duration (real against the mean of five placebo seeds, two-sided and one-sided together) are 9 against 5.8 for 2 to 6 hours, 11 against 0.2 for 6 to 24 hours, 5 against 0.0 for 1 to 3 days, 8 against 0.0 for 3 to 14 days, and 4 against 0.2 for over 14 days. The one-sided confirmations of 2 to 6 hour closures are mostly chance, because 5.6 of the 9 appear on shifted logs.

  • The steps are conserved where both sides show one. For the 13 two-sided confirmations the second step over the first step has a median of 1.09 (quartiles 0.75 and 1.30).
  • Pairs with only MW series confirm more often than pairs with an MVA series. The rates are 3 of 16 (19%) against 10 of 140 (7%), on small counts.
  • Large transfers are common among the confirmed, and small ones are absent. 17 of 37 (46%) are 25% or more of the receiving substation's load, against the predicted third at most. No confirmed transfer is under 10% of that load, so the small-event tail cannot be measured here, and the headline recall describes only transfers of 10% or more.

The step is not constant within an event. For 26 of the 28 confirmed closures of 6 hours or more (two lack a usable half), the relative step (step divided by the substation's expected power) keeps its sign between the first and second half in 25. The second-half step is within a factor of 2 of the first-half step in 18, and the median ratio is 1.14. In 8 closures the step changes by more than a factor of 2. Both detectors still look for a constant-MW level shift in the residual, so they would misjudge the shape of those closures, though they only need the shift to be large enough to alarm.

Load that splits across several receivers is hard to check with this telemetry. Of 849 logged operations since 2022, 67 have a substation on two or more sheets of the same operation. Only 9 of those have telemetry on that substation and on a receiver, and none is confirmed. In those 9, the hub's step against the sum of the receivers' steps gives a ratio from -59 to 23, and only 4 fall in the detector's accepted range of 0.4 to 2.5. In 7 of the 9, only one receiver has a step, so no split was estimated. The detector reports splits for its own alarms (114 of D1's 347 alarms at the headline threshold name two or more neighbours), but no logged operation checks them.

docs.title: Q2: does switching matter to the stack's errors
docs.text: Confirmed-transfer half-hours hold 0.9% of the stack's cases and 39.7% of its threshold-weighted score at the 99th percentile, but 99.9% of that share lies on series 17 and 18, almost all in one 370-hour closure. That closure is sheet 17-18 from 2025-12-30. It has a step on series 18 only, and the step shrinks to about zero by the second half. The stack is experiment 19's N1 with the 14-day correction. The cases are July 2025 to 2026-03-25. The quantile score share of confirmed half-hours is 2.7%. Per case, the threshold-weighted score of a confirmed half-hour is 40 times that of a logged-but-unconfirmed half-hour and 75 times that of all non-confirmed half-hours (83 times that of half-hours with no logged closure). The prediction that confirmed half-hours hold at least twice the score per case of unconfirmed ones therefore holds, and the prediction that all logged half-hours hold under 44% of the score fails (confirmed plus unconfirmed: 51%). The confirmed share on the other substations rounds to 0.0000.

docs.title: Q3: the detectors
docs.text:
At the budget fixed on odd months, D1 beats D0 at the 4-hour window on even-month transfers, and the gain shrinks when the two are compared at equal alarm rates. Weighted recall is the share of the transfers' MW that the detector flags, with an alarm on either substation, or any substation of the same operation, within 2 hours of the onset.

Detector, window Threshold Alarms per series-month, tuning / validation Size-weighted recall (95%) Unweighted All logged closures of 2 h or more Shifted logs D0, 4 hours 7 0.23 / 0.14 0.036 (0.000 to 0.131) 0.056 0.013 0.003 D1, 4 hours 4 0.32 / 0.38 0.326 (0.093 to 0.579) 0.278 0.086 0.004 D0, 24 hours 4 0.35 / 0.28 0.276 (0.098 to 0.524) 0.389 0.056 0.002 D1, 24 hours 2.5 0.11 / 0.07 0.171 (0.026 to 0.383) 0.222 0.033 0.004
  • Contrast. D1 minus D0 at 4 hours is +0.290 (+0.034 to +0.557). The largest transfer holds 12% of the weight, and D1's recall without it is 0.373.
  • The pre-registered grid does not match the two detectors' alarm rates. The next D0 threshold down (6) has 0.54 alarms per series-month on tuning, just over the budget, and a validation recall of 0.224 at 0.49 alarms per series-month.
  • Post hoc, a finer grid (steps of 0.25) moves both budgets. D0 at 6.25 reaches 0.074 (0.000 to 0.206) and D1 at 3.75 reaches 0.362 (0.127 to 0.621) at 0.50 validation alarms per series-month, with a difference of +0.288 (+0.030 to +0.558). At the same validation alarm rate of about 0.5, D0 at 6 gives 0.224 and D1 at 3.75 gives 0.362, a gap of about +0.14 that has no interval. The verdict stays as pre-registered.
  • By size band, D1 finds more of the largest transfers. Unweighted recall for transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load is 0.43 for D1 and 0.00 for D0, and for 10% to 25% it is 0.18 and 0.09. Recall weighted by share of the receiving load, and precision by size band, are not reported: precision needs a reference set of every real event, which the logs do not give.
  • Detection delay. The median offset of the alarm from the first affected stamp is 0 for D1 and 1 half-hour for D0.
  • The month-boundary check is clean. 2.3% to 2.6% of the 4-hour alarms fall on the first day of a month (chance 3.3%), and none of the 24-hour alarms do.

docs.title: Predictions against results
docs.text:
• Q1 missed: 6.0% confirmed against 8% to 20%, and 46% of the confirmed at 25% or more against a third at most. The MW pairs confirm more often, as predicted.
  • Q2 held for the ratio and failed for the share (51% against under 44%).
  • Q3 partly held. D0 recall at 4 hours (0.036) was below the predicted 0.20 to 0.40. D1 (0.326) fell inside the predicted 0.30 to 0.55, near its lower edge. D1 minus D0 was at least +0.10, the placebo recall was under 0.08, and recall on all logged closures was under 0.10. The prediction that D1 reaches 0.5 or more on transfers of 25% or more of the load missed: 0.43.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The confirmation label uses the same residual as the detectors, so recall on confirmed transfers is an upper bound for load the residual can see at all.
  • Unexplained alarms are an upper bound on false alarms, because real unlogged steps exist.
  • The reference set has 18 validation transfers, 12 of them one-sided. The intervals are wide and a rerun with different odd and even months would move the headline.
  • Series 12 and 13 have residuals only from 2026-02, so closures on their sheets are mostly one- sided.
  • The substation pair 14-25 is missing from the interconnection list, so the detector cannot attribute those closures.
  • Two planned figures are not drawn: the distribution of the oracle's step statistic against the placebo, and the alarm share by day of month. The Q1 and Q3 text gives the numbers they would show.

docs.title: Proposed next experiment
docs.text:
Run F4 next: whiten the residual and score the detectors on injected transfers. The design's rule names no follow-up for inconclusive, so each candidate's own condition decides. F1 needs supported, and the 40% confirmed share of the stack's threshold-weighted score sits on series 17 and 18, almost all of it in one 15-day closure from 2025-12-30. F3 needs more than a third of the missed transfers to be grouped operations, and 2 of the 13 missed validation transfers are. F4's condition holds: D1 misses 4 of the 7 validation transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load. D0 with a 24-hour window reaching 0.276 also points at residual noise, not missing topology, as the cap on recall. Injected transfers remove both causes of the inconclusive verdict: only 18 validation transfers, and a confirmation label built from the detectors' own residual. Choosing F4 is a judgement, because the rule has no branch for inconclusive.

  • Hypothesis. An AR(1) model per series and hour of day, fitted on odd months, whitens the H0.5 residual enough that D1 finds more of the injected load at the 0.5 budget.
  • Prediction. On injected validation transfers of 10% or more of the receiving load, D1 on the whitened residual reaches a size-weighted recall at least 0.10 above D1 on the raw residual, and at least 0.35, with a placebo recall of 0.08 or less. The prediction fails if the gain is under 0.10 or its 95% interval includes 0.
  • Decision rule. supported when both bars hold, refuted when the gain's interval includes 0, and inconclusive otherwise. The +0.10 bar matches experiment 37's D1-minus-D0 bar. About 600 injected validation transfers should give an interval of roughly plus or minus 0.04 on a recall, a binomial estimate rather than a measurement. If supported, rerun experiment 37's verdict on its 18 real transfers with the whitened D1, and move to F1 if that verdict is supported.
  • Contrasts. Raw against whitened residual, for D0 and D1, at windows of 4 and 24 hours, each re-tuned on odd months to 0.5 unexplained alarms per series-month. The primary contrast is whitened D1 minus raw D1 at 4 hours. The other contrasts are reported and decide nothing.
  • Injection. Transfers go into quiet periods with no logged interval within 7 days. Each moves a fraction of the donor's expected power, so the moved load keeps the donor's daily shape, to one or two interconnected neighbours with drawn split fractions. Durations are drawn from the 37 confirmed closures, and sizes span the under 10%, 10% to 25%, and 25% or more bands. Recall is weighted by MW and by share of the receiving load, and the under-10% band decides nothing.
  • Stored. Scratch tables only, under data/ml-experiments/<id>-switching-whitened-residual/: the whitened panel, the injected-event table with true split fractions, the alarm tables, and the recall curves.
  • Compute. CPU only, at most 2 cores, under 1 hour.
  • Size: medium. What gets stored: scratch tables only. Production serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one defensible design: yes, the whitening model and the injection shape, both fixed above. Callers nameable without searching: yes, only the experiment's own folder.
  • First steps. Copy e00037_grid.py, e00037_detect.py, and e00037_score.py into the new folder, then write a whitening script (AR(1) fit on odd months, whitened panel) and an injection script (quiet-period finder, shaped injection, event table), each checked on a synthetic panel before any real run.

docs.title: Experiment 38: is detecting a switching event worth anything to the forecast?
docs.text:
We asked whether a switching detector improves a demand forecast when the half-hours it flags are left out of the correction that uses recent forecast errors. We compared the forecast error with and without that exclusion, and against an exclusion built from the logs of real switching and a random exclusion of the same size. Excluding the detector's half-hours made the error 57.1% larger (95% interval +0.4% to +133.5%), where we had asked for a reduction of 5%, so the idea is refuted.

Refuted: leaving the half-hours that the neighbour-balance detector D1 flags out of the stack's error correction made the forecast worse, not better, on half-hours outside logged switching. The pre-registered primary contrast, d1_mask7 against plain7 (the threshold-weighted absolute error, which counts errors only where the load exceeds each series' P99, on the proxy stack of experiment 00017 plus a correction, at leads of 4 to 48 hours, on half-hours outside logged closures), is +57.1% (95% interval +0.4% to +133.5%, from resampling whole calendar months), against the bar of -5% or better. The oracle mask built from the logs lowers the same error by 8.9% for the 14-day window (-21.8% to +0.0%), so the ceiling is small, and 95% of it is one month. A random mask of equal volume changes the error by +0.1% (-0.7% to +0.5%). P99 is the power that a series exceeds 1% of the time. The d1_mask7 arm leaves D1's flagged half-hours out of the 7-day correction, and plain7 is the same correction with nothing left out. All numbers are from e00038_report.py and are in points of capacity unless stated.

docs.title: What the arms scored
docs.text:
Every pre-registered arm built on the detector fails; the oracle and the placebo behave as the plan expected. Tier A is experiment 00017's H0.5 (ERA5 weather, out of sample) plus a correction, daily 09:00 UTC origins from 2022-01-15 to 2026-03-25. ERA5 arrives about 5 days after the event, so the weather is not available at forecast time and the numbers are a ceiling for the correction rule. Lead 4 to 48 hours is counted from the newest usable observation, 4 hours before the origin. The rows are the 1,648,578 half-hours outside logged closures (plus 2 hours either side), the same for every arm.

Arm Threshold-weighted error at P99 Change (95% interval) Mean absolute error plain14 (experiment 00019's rule) 0.0292 reference 5.603 plain7 (the detector-free bar) 0.0277 -5.2% against plain14 (-10.8% to +0.0%) 5.478 d1_mask7 (primary, against plain7) 0.0435 +57.1% (+0.4% to +133.5%) 5.614 d1_mask14 0.0445 +52.4% (+0.3% to +125.1%) 5.719 d0w48_mask14 0.0479 +63.8% (+21.9% to +136.3%) 5.958 oracle_conf14 (logs, confirmed transfers) 0.0266 -8.9% (-21.8% to +0.0%) 5.573 oracle_logged14 (logs, all 612 closures) 0.0261 -10.6% (-26.1% to +0.8%) 5.561 random14 (placebo) 0.0292 +0.1% (-0.7% to +0.5%) 5.626
  • The ceiling is concentrated. January 2026, which holds the 2025-12-30 closure of Primary substations 17 and 18, supplies 95% of the oracle_conf14 gain. Without it the oracle change is -0.5%. Odd and even months give -13.0% and -1.2% for the oracle, and +39.3% and +89.9% for d1_mask7.
  • The detector found the dominant closure, and the interval rule then lost it. D1 raised an alarm on the 17-18 closure under both builders. As specified, the interval for series 18 ended on the first failing 24-hour block and the closure's return step then started an interval that ran the 60-day cap, so the correction held its pre-closure level for 60 days. On that closure, d1_mask7 raised the error from 3,011 to 11,657 (sum over the closure window and 16 days after).
  • Per event, nothing improved under the as-specified builder. Of the 17 confirmed closures of 24 hours or more, d1_mask7 improved 1, worsened 3, and left 13 unchanged (binomial p 0.94 with ties dropped; the plan's condition was 12 improved). The oracle improved 6 and worsened none. Of the 17 windows, 6 have zero threshold-weighted error in every arm, because the load never exceeded the series' P99 outside the closure.
  • The cost of false alarms is large. On the 417,213 quiet rows, more than 16 days from any logged closure or D1 alarm on that series, d1_mask7 raises the mean absolute error by 0.125 points (the plan's bar was within +/-0.01) and the threshold-weighted error by 60.6%. A detected interval that overlaps no logged closure still removes real history: 75% of the 498 D1 intervals overlap no logged closure, and 1.0% reached the 60-day cap.
  • In the proxy stack, the 7-day window beats the 14-day window, as the exploratory pilot suggested. plain7 against plain14 is -5.2% (-10.8% to +0.0%) in tail error and -0.12 points in mean absolute error; the real stack disagrees (Tier B below). The lead 144 to 192 hour band agrees on sign for the primary (+49.8%) and oracle (-11.4%) contrasts.

docs.title: Post hoc: a revised interval builder
docs.text:
Labelled post hoc, and not part of the verdict. The diagnosis above led to four changes to the builder, all made after seeing the first scores: the onset step comes from the first 24-hour block (not the first 4 hours), an event ends only after two consecutive failing blocks, an alarm inside an earlier interval of the same series or within one block after its end is skipped (it is the return step), and known_from no longer moves earlier across empty blocks. The arms keep their names with fx and are scored on the same rows.

  • The tail error falls, within the noise. d1fx_mask7 against plain7 is -5.4% (-15.1% to +1.5%); d1fx_mask14 against plain14 is -8.9% (-22.2% to +1.3%), which equals the oracle's -8.9%. Without January 2026, the 7-day change is +0.3%. Per event, 3 improve, none worsen, and 14 are unchanged (p 0.125). randomfx14 changes the error by +1.9% (-0.6% to +6.8%).
  • The mean absolute error still rises. d1fx_mask7 raises it by 0.254 points (+4.6%) outside logged closures and by 0.164 points on quiet rows. The tail gain and the typical-error cost come from the same mechanism: a masked history cannot follow the level shifts that the logs never recorded.
  • D0 with a 24-hour window is worse than D1 under both builders (+63.8% as specified, +48.6% revised, both against plain14).

docs.title: The two views of the target
docs.text: The maintainer has to settle whether NGED wants the normal running arrangement (NRA) or the metered load; this experiment cannot. The NRA view scores half-hours outside logged closures, as above. The metered view scores every half-hour. Under the metered view (all rows, lead 4 to 48 hours), the persistence arm, which follows the recent residual while a D1 interval is open, changes the threshold-weighted error against plain14 by -4.6% (-12.3% to +3.1%) as specified and -8.5% (-18.9% to +1.3%) revised. The plain 7-day window alone gives -7.1% (-13.1% to -0.4%), so persistence adds nothing the shorter window does not already give. At lead 144 to 192 hours the three are -4.8%, -6.8%, and -4.6%.

docs.title: Tier B: the real stack
docs.text: The real stack agrees in sign with the proxy on the masking contrasts, and disagrees on the 7-day window. Experiment 00019's n1h arms (three seeds, runs every 5 days from July 2025, 1,397,181 half-hours outside logged closures) give +68.4% (+0.1% to +221.5%) for d1_mask7 against plain7, -21.2% (-34.6% to +5.1%) for the oracle against plain14, +0.4% (-0.3% to +1.4%) for the placebo, and -22.7% (-35.1% to +0.0%) for the revised d1fx_mask7. The nine-level quantile score moves by +4.3% (+0.1% to +8.7%) for d1_mask7 and +0.03% for d1fx_mask7. For the 7-day window, the real stack gives plain7 against plain14 of +8.5% (+2.4% to +10.7%) in threshold-weighted score and +2.8% in quantile score, the opposite sign to the proxy's -5.2%. Only 3 to 4 closures sit in the runs, so Tier B decides nothing alone.

docs.title: Q2: injected transfers
docs.text: The detector finds a transfer only when the moved load is about 30% of the donor's own power, and it does not recover the split. Six hundred synthetic transfers (1 to 3 receivers, durations drawn from the 28 confirmed closures of 6 hours or more) were injected into quiet periods. D1's recall by moved share is 0.5% at 5%, 8.6% at 15% (as specified), and 45.6% at 30%; it does not rise with the number of receivers (43%, 52%, and 47% at 30% for 1, 2, and 3). Of the 39 found transfers of 2 days or more, 85% (as specified) and 87% (revised) have the end within 24 hours. The median absolute end error is 6 hours at 30%. The pooled split fraction has a mean error of 0.64 to 0.70 because only 11% to 15% of the receivers are matched to a detected partner. Within-day variation of the split was found for too few events to say (3 found events with a true range of 0.3 or more).

docs.title: Q3: the detected-interval table for NGED
docs.text: The tables are written but unvalidated. D1 produced 347 alarms and 498 intervals under the as-specified builder (alarm and partner series), and 198 alarms with 374 intervals revised. Only 25% (as specified) and 31% (revised) overlap a logged closure. The median interval is 24 and 48 hours. At 0.38 unexplained alarms per series-month in experiment 00037, the list is about 6 candidates a month across the 16 substations, mostly unexplained by the logs. The tables are q3_table_d1.parquet, q3_table_d1fx.parquet, and split_fractions_*.parquet in the private data folder.

docs.title: Process and deviations
docs.text:
• Code review (Opus, one round). Nine findings; the code was changed for seven and the rest are recorded here.
    • Fixed: the monthly-gain table was written with the wrong arm labels (figure 4 read it); the day 6 to 7 band was actually day 3 to 4 (now offsets 136 to 183, lead 144 to 192 hours); the persistence arm opened partner intervals before they exist; alarms were released at onset + window + 2 when the peak test needs onset + 2 * window + 2; an empty block made an interval's end known early; ties counted as losses in the per-event test; the plain arms carried a correction forward when under 3 days remained, where experiment 00019 uses zero. The causality check now covers D0, both builders, and the open-interval start at 11 origins. The reruns moved no headline number by more than 0.5 points.
    • Not changed: the random mask wraps from 2026 into 2022 (it keeps volume exactly, which the plan asked for), and the quiet rows exclude 16 days around D1 alarm stamps only, as the plan words it, so rows inside a long false-alarm interval count as quiet, which is the cost of false alarms the quiet rows exist to show.
  • Deviations. The lead bands count from the newest observation (lead 4 to 48 hours is 0 to 87 half-hours from the origin). The post hoc builder and every fx arm are labelled as such. The injection split estimate pools the four clock blocks (changed after seeing 0.7 errors from block ratios). Tier B's quantile score uses 00037's scorer, copied.
  • Sizing, as registered: medium. Stored: scratch tables only. Production serving path and degradation rule: not touched. Compute: 2 cores, under 5 minutes per script.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Masking detected switching does not help the correction, and the detector is not the reason. The dominant closure was found in every variant. What failed is the interval's end, and then the cost of masking half-hours that the logs never recorded as switching.
  • The gain a mask could deliver is one closure. January 2026 holds 95% to 105% of every gain, and removing it leaves between -0.5% and +0.3%. The write-up of any further switching experiment should report the result without that closure first.
  • The 7-day window is a separate question, and the two stacks disagree. The 7-day window beat the 14-day window in the proxy stack and lost to it in experiment 00019's real stack, so it belongs in its own stack experiment and is not a finding of this one.

docs.title: Proposed next experiment
docs.text:
Proposed: stop the switching line's forecasting purposes here, and run no SW1b-3 masking experiment. The verdict is refuted, and the plan's stop rule says that ends purposes 1 and 2 (lags in the forecasting model, and a normal-running-arrangement forecast in v1). The post hoc builder does not reopen the question. Its -5.4% (-15.1% to +1.5%) has an interval that includes zero, and becomes +0.3% once January 2026 is removed. The same mask raises the mean absolute error by 0.25 points outside logged closures. A further masking experiment would therefore be testing one closure of Primary substations 17 and 18, which no amount of tuning the interval builder can turn into a general result.

Proposed for purpose 3: offer NGED the detected-interval table as an unvalidated list. The table is q3_table_d1.parquet, about 6 candidates a month across the 16 substations, and 75% of its intervals overlap no logged closure. The cheapest way to learn whether those unexplained intervals are real switching is to ask NGED to check a sample of them against their own records. That request is a decision for the maintainer to agree with NGED, not an experiment.

Proposed separately, outside this line: test the 7-day correction window on the real stack. The proxy stack favours plain7 over plain14 (-5.2%, -10.8% to +0.0%), but the real stack in tier B disagrees: plain7 raises the threshold-weighted error by 8.5% (+2.4% to +10.7%) and the quantile score by 2.8% outside logged closures. A stack experiment on the 7-day window should therefore be scored on experiment 00019's runs, not on the proxy alone.

docs.title: Experiment 39: can a CAMS-driven fit separate embedded solar from Primary substation demand?
docs.text:
We asked whether the output of solar farms embedded in the distribution network can be separated from the demand at a Primary substation (a substation that steps power down to the local distribution network) by fitting a model to the demand and a satellite estimate of sunlight. We added the recorded output of real solar farms to the demand of the 8 Primary substations that meter power in one direction, and checked how much of the added capacity the fit found again. The fit found a median of 77% of the added capacity, and its daily version found 85%, over 218 units (every Primary, solar farm, and season-year). We then ran the same fit on the real series with four further checks. Our rule needed 6 of the 8 substations to pass all four checks and the first check, which fits a placebo sky, to pass at all 8. Six of the 8 passed all four, but the placebo-sky check failed at one substation (Wrangle T1).

Verdict recovers-but-confounded: injected solar-farm output is recovered to within 25%, but the real series pass the four checks at 6 of 8 Primaries, and the pre-registered rule needs K1 to pass at all 8. A fit of a calendar-plus-temperature demand term minus one CAMS-driven PV shape recovers a median 0.773 of the capacity of real solar-farm output injected into the demand of the 8 directional Primary substations (95% interval 0.740 to 0.818). The daily version of the fit recovers 0.854 (0.815 to 0.866) and passes the recovery rule. The aim is explanation and capacity estimation, not forecast skill. Neither CAMS irradiance nor ERA5 temperature arrives in time to drive a live forecast, so the fit describes past data only. CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite estimate of sunlight.

Contrast (medians over 218 units, 95% two-way bootstrap interval) Prediction Result C1: M1, CAMS at the substation 0.77 (0.70 to 0.83) 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818) C2: M1d minus M1, substation +0.08 +0.081 (+0.040 to +0.100) C3: M1 at the farm minus M1 at the substation +0.08 +0.078 (+0.041 to +0.102) C4: M1L (cloud term) minus M1, substation -0.04 -0.042 (-0.078 to -0.021) Half-hourly nMAE, M1, substation 0.12 0.119 (0.104 to 0.131) nMAE, M1d, substation 0.105 (0.092 to 0.113)

The decision rule picks M1d. C2 is above the +0.05 threshold and its interval is above zero, so M1d is the model the rule scores. Its median ratio, 0.854, lies in [0.75, 1.25], its interval lies in [0.65, 1.35], and its nMAE, 0.105, is below 0.15, so recovery passes. The 10th to 90th percentile spread of the units is 0.763 to 0.902. The ratio does not depend on the injected size, because the fit is linear. The known-answer self-tests passed, and the timestamp scan peaked at a shift of zero (median ratio 0.850 at zero, 0.81 at plus or minus one half-hour, 0.73 at plus or minus two).

docs.title: Real series: 6 of 8 pass, K1 fails at Wrangle T1
docs.text:
K1 to K4 are the checks that a demand confound would fail. Injection cannot test them, because a linear fit gives the same increment whatever demand it sits on. The expectations come from the injected units: summer and winter fits differ by +0.011 of the capacity (K2), and adding the cloud term multiplies the capacity by 0.937 (K3). The table shows each Primary in 2025/26.

Primary Capacity (MW) K1 placebo sky K2 season K3 cloud term K4 day type All pass Kirton 2.81 pass fail (+0.54) fail (0.41) pass no Trusthorpe 2.04 pass pass pass pass yes Spilsby 2.22 pass pass pass pass yes Horncastle 2.98 pass pass pass pass yes Mount Bridge Boston 3.24 pass pass pass pass yes Wrangle T1 0.89 fail pass fail (0.48) fail (-0.58) no Donington 3.16 pass pass pass pass yes Wrangle T2 1.87 pass pass pass pass yes

In 2025/26 two Primaries account for the failures. Over all 41 Primary-years, K1 passes in 38, K2 in 30, K3 in 34, K4 in 40, and all four in 27; Mount Bridge Boston, Spilsby, and Horncastle also fail K2 or K3 in single earlier years. Kirton fails K2 in 5 of 7 years (winter capacity 29% to 54% above summer) and K3 in 4 of 7 (the cloud term cuts its capacity by 20% to 60%). Wrangle T1 has 2 season-years and a fitted 0.89 MW. It passes the first half of K1 (its capacity is above the 95th percentile of the placebo fits, 0.163 MW) and fails the second by a hair: the median absolute placebo capacity, 0.099 MW, is just above one tenth of 0.886 MW. Its weekend capacity differs from its weekday capacity by 58%. This page does not decide which of these failures is a demand confound and which is noise from two years of data.

The fitted capacity is 0.9 to 3.2 MW per Primary in 2025/26 and rose at 4 of the 5 Primaries with 4 or more years. Dividing by the M1 recovery ratio, 0.77, gives about 1.2 to 4.2 MW of solar. Kirton is flat. Only 2 of 33 year-to-year changes are falls larger than 2 combined standard errors (Donington 2021, Kirton 2022). The detection limit is about 2.5% of capacity per season-year: the median day-clustered standard error is 1.2% of the Primary's effective capacity (figure 11).

docs.title: What else the injection showed
docs.text:
• Summer and winter recover alike. Injected PV gives 0.766 in April to September and 0.770 in October to March at the substation (figure 12), so K2 expects no seasonal gap.
  • Farm E is the worst case. The median ratio by farm runs from 0.70 (Solar farm E) to 0.84 (Solar farm D) at the substation (figure 10). Farms lie 16 to 24 km from the Primaries on average.
  • Detail is lost at the peaks. The recovered half-hourly output has a correlation of 0.88 with the injected output at the substation point and 0.92 at the farm point (figure 9), and the energy recovered is 0.80 and 0.87 of the injected energy.
  • The 8 non-directional (MVA) Primaries fold. Stickney fits a negative capacity every year, and the MVA Primaries' winter and summer fits differ widely (figures 15 and 18). They are left out of the verdict.
  • The bulk supply points are descriptive. The fitted capacity at Boston and Skegness lies above the sum of the directional Primaries and metered farms below it, as it should (figure 19).
  • The Embedded Capacity Register comparison was not run. The register code lives in experiment 00031's folder, which a script may not import.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The design's rule for recovers-but-confounded is PVDIS-2B: does a richer demand model bring K3 to pass without lowering the recovery below 0.75? Add demand shapes (a flat cloud term, a dawn and dusk term, temperature by hour) and the orientation menu in studies.pv_separation.separate, inject a known dull-day demand term into the real series to measure its bias, and report K1 to K4 at Kirton and Wrangle T1 first. The failures sit at two Primaries, so a result of the 2B kind could move the count of Primaries that pass from 6 to 8, which the arc's stop rule counts as a move of 2.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text: The first figure is above. Figures 2 to 5 show the raw data, 6 to 8 the method, 9 to 12 the recovery of injected PV, and 13 to 19 the real series.

docs.title: Method and files
docs.text:
• Data. Power is the cleaned half-hourly series of each Primary and of the 6 solar farms. CAMS irradiance at hours with reliability 0.9 or more is spread to half-hours by the cosine of the zenith. Temperature is ERA5 at each Primary. Season-years run September to August, 2019/20 to 2025/26, and a window needs 3,000 daylight half-hours.
  • Injection. The 218 units are every Primary, farm, and season-year with enough shared rows. The injected output is minus the farm's output scaled so that its 99th percentile over daylight half-hours is 20% (also 5%, 10%, and 40%) of the Primary's effective capacity.
  • Code. ml-experiments/00039-pv-disaggregation-cams-injection/, run in the order e00039_inputs, e00039_inject, e00039_real, e00039_report, e00039_charts. e00039_report prints every number on this page.
  • Differences from the plan. The farm's 99th percentile is taken over its daylight half-hours, the convention that matches the unit PV shape's, and not over all half-hours.

docs.title: Experiment 40: how far can the capacity fitted to embedded solar be trusted?
docs.text:
We asked how far the solar capacity fitted to the demand at a Primary substation (a substation that steps power down to the local distribution network) can be trusted. We built a test that compares the capacity found by six fits of the same series. The six fits differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows. We checked the test on solar-farm output added to demand and on extra demand shaped like a response to cloud. The test raised a false alarm in 5.5% of the simulated trials in which the added load was pure solar-farm output. It detected four of five cloud-shaped loads at 25% of the true capacity. It detected a day-long cloud-shaped load in only 35% of simulated trials, so it failed our rule that the test must detect such loads in at least 80% of trials.

Verdict underpowered: the misfit test is calibrated and detects four of five cloud-driven loads at 25% of the true capacity, but it detects a day-long cloud load in only 0.35 of simulated trials, so the pre-registered rule that the test must detect such loads in at least 80% of trials fails. The test compares the capacity that six least-squares fits assign to the same series. Pure injected solar-farm output gives a median capacity over truth of 0.992 (95% interval 0.951 to 1.032) with a false-positive rate of 0.055. Kirton is the one directional Primary substation flagged in 2025/26, and the other seven are unflagged. The capacity at those seven carries a bound B of 0.18 to 0.71, and the test has almost no power at Wrangle T1, so the bound is wider than the 0.10 predicted. The aim is explanation and capacity estimation, not forecast skill. CAMS irradiance is the only weather input at the lag times and it arrives too late to drive a live forecast, so the fits describe past data. CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite estimate of sunlight.

docs.title: Results against the plan
docs.text:
Quantity Prediction Result Median capacity over truth on pure injected PV (V1) 1.00 (0.97 to 1.03) 0.992 (0.951 to 1.032) False-positive rate 0.05 to 0.10 0.055 (0.024 to 0.108) Power at amplitude 0.25, lowsun at least 0.8 at 7 of 8 Primaries 1.00 (median), at 7 of 8 Power at amplitude 0.25, evening same 1.00, at 7 of 8 Power at amplitude 0.25, mixture same 1.00, at 7 of 8 Power at amplitude 0.25, threshold same 1.00, at 6 of 8 Power at amplitude 0.25, dayL same 0.35, at 0 of 8 Kirton flagged 2022/23 to 2025/26 2019/20 and 2021/22 to 2025/26 Other seven unflagged in 2025/26 at most 3 flagged Primary-years elsewhere 0 flagged Primary-years elsewhere Bound B at an unflagged Primary at most 0.10 0.18 to 0.23 at five, 0.47 at Trusthorpe, 0.71 at Wrangle T1

The test is calibrated. The false-positive interval (0.024 to 0.108) comes from resampling Primaries and farms independently, and the 218 units are the (Primary, farm, season-year) triples of experiment 39. The ratios of one solar farm do not transfer to the others, which is a finding about the ratio vector and not about the test. Solar farm E's ratios leave the capacity at 0.825 of truth and its false-positive rate at 0.230, and the other five farms give a median between 0.955 and 1.046 with a false-positive rate of at most 0.087.

The test finds a load with a within-day shape and misses a load that is the same all day. Four shapes are flagged at 25% of capacity in at least 0.997 of draws at the median Primary: low sun, evening, a cloud threshold, and a half-and-half mixture. The shape dayL, the day's mean cloud on every daylight half-hour, reaches median power 0.904 only at amplitude 0.5. The post hoc detection limit, the smallest grid amplitude with median power at least 0.8, is 0.1 for low sun and evening, 0.25 for the threshold and the mixture, and 0.5 for dayL.

A load that rises with sunshine escapes the test by construction. Its shape is the solar shape, so every fit assigns it the same negative capacity. Its median power over units is 0.055 at amplitude 0.1, 0.175 at 0.25, and 0.74 at 0.5, and the capacity it leaves undetected is 14%, 33%, and 64% too low.

docs.title: The real series
docs.text:
Kirton is flagged in 6 of 7 season-years, and no other Primary is flagged in any. Kirton's misfit is 0.075 and 0.098 in the two early flagged years and 0.20 to 0.31 from 2022/23, against thresholds of 0.07 to 0.12. The capacity of 2025/26 ranges from 1.2 to 4.4 MW across the library of confound shapes. The test cannot flag Wrangle T1, whose threshold is 1.23 against a misfit of 0.25, so "unflagged" at Wrangle T1 means that the test has no power, and not that no load is present.

Primary, 2025/26 Capacity (MW) 95% interval Bound B Status Kirton 3.35 3.02 to 4.01 0.41 flagged, library range 1.2 to 4.4 MW Trusthorpe 2.48 2.23 to 2.88 0.47 unflagged Spilsby 2.57 2.16 to 3.01 0.21 unflagged Horncastle 3.43 3.04 to 3.98 0.21 unflagged Mount Bridge Boston 3.86 3.37 to 4.55 0.19 unflagged Wrangle T1 1.41 0.62 to 2.07 0.71 unflagged, no power Donington 3.69 3.20 to 4.22 0.18 unflagged Wrangle T2 2.29 2.10 to 2.61 0.23 unflagged

The capacity is the daily fit divided by its recovery ratio. The bound is the median error of the no-confound capacity at the largest grid amplitude whose power is under 0.8, taken as the largest over the five shapes no fit contains. At every Primary the day-long load sets the bound. At Wrangle T1 the other four shapes are also undetected at amplitude 0.25. The bound moves in steps of the amplitude grid and is an approximation of the error, not an interval.

On the continuity checks of experiment 39 the count does not move. With the checks defined as in experiment 39, K1 to K4 pass at 7, 7, 6, and 7 of 8 Primaries in 2025/26 and all four pass at 6. With K1's second clause replaced by a capacity over standard error above 4, K1 passes at 8 of 8 and all four checks still pass at 6.

docs.title: Raw data and the method
docs.text:
The raw data show a cloud response that solar generation cannot explain. Overcast days raise Kirton's power more than Donington's in every half-hour, in winter too (figure 2). Kirton's midday power falls with irradiance in winter as well as summer (figure 4). Evening demand, after dark, rises with the day's cloud at some Primaries (figure 3).

The six fits differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows, so a cloud load leaks into them unequally. The arms are M1 (calendar cells and temperature), M1L (plus a flat cloud term), M2 (cloud term by season half), M2h (cloud term by season half and three local-hour bands), and M1 and M2h on April to September rows only. Every arm is linear, so the capacity fitted to a series plus a load is the sum of the two fitted alone. A unit's injected solar output and each of eight loads are therefore fitted once and added as vectors. The heat map shows each load's leakage per MW into each fit. The daily fit cannot carry a cloud term, because after the cell means are removed the daily sums of the solar shape and of the cloud response correlate at -0.986 to -0.977.

The detector is a misfit of the six capacities to a multiple of the recovery ratios. For a unit of injected solar output of true capacity 1 MW, fit a returns R_a, the median over the Primary's units of the other farms (leave-one-farm-out). For an arm vector c, the capacity under no confound is C = (R . c) / (R . R) and the misfit is T = sqrt(mean((c - R * C)^2)) / C. The noise is 200 resamples of whole 7-day blocks of each real Primary-year, minus their mean. The threshold of a Primary-year is the 95th percentile of T over the units of the other farms scaled to the real capacity, each with its own farm also left out of R. The real Primary-years use the ratios of all six farms. The injected loads are flat, lowsun, winter, dayL, evening, threshold, mixture, and sunload. The first and third are contained in some fits and are reported, not scored. The self-tests of linearity, exact recovery, a contained shape, the sign of sunload, and the false-positive rate of the threshold all passed, and the farm-point timestamp scan of experiment 39 peaks at a shift of zero.

The orientation menu is not identified. The east, south, and west capacities swap from one season-year to the next at the same Primary (figure 14), so the menu decides nothing.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The real Primary-years use the ratios of all six farms. Every injected unit leaves its own farm out of the ratios, the threshold, and the real capacity it is scaled to.
  • Solar farms are not rooftop fleets. The ratio vector comes from six metered farms with one orientation each, and a fleet of mixed orientations may have a different ratio vector. Only the comparison with an external capacity register can test that.
  • The write-up quotes a bound with a step of the grid. The grid is 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
  • The unflagged Primary-years include Wrangle T1. The clean count of 7 includes a Primary where the power is under 0.3 for every shape.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should ask whether the evening cloud response measures the daylight load that the six fits cannot detect. The two loads that set the bound, a day-long cloud load and a load that rises with sunshine, are the loads the misfit test cannot see. Evening demand after dark responds to cloud at some Primaries (figure 3), and solar generation cannot cause that response. An experiment could inject a known day-long load into the real series, estimate its amplitude from the evening rows alone, and test whether that amplitude predicts the bias of the capacity. The test is whether such a covariate narrows the bound at Spilsby, Horncastle, Mount Bridge Boston, Donington, and Wrangle T2 below 0.1. The fitting code lives in this experiment's folder and a later experiment, or the deliverable, could move it to packages/studies, which needs the maintainer's review.

docs.title: Experiment 41, part 2 (SW2-0b): which logged switching jobs show up in the power readings?
docs.text: We asked which of the electricity network's logged switching jobs since January 2022 really moved load from one substation to a neighbour, so that later experiments have a list of real events to test detectors against. We turned each job into a card that summarises the power readings around it. Two separate runs of an AI language model (Sonnet) read every card. Each run said whether load visibly moved, and when the move started and ended. A stronger model (Opus) settled the 66 cards where the two runs disagreed or were unsure. To measure how often the labellers see a transfer we know is there, and how often they see one that is not there, we hid 200 cards with known answers among the real ones. Of 537 logged jobs lasting 2 hours to 60 days, 66 (12%) show load moving between substations. The method cannot see small or short transfers, so few of the other jobs are proven quiet, and we cannot tell which.

docs.title: What was labelled
docs.text: The set holds 1,017 cards: 817 real and 200 hidden known-answer cards. The real cards are 537 logged operations of 2 hours to 60 days (jobs that overlap in time and share a substation count as one operation), 42 edge cards for the first and last 72 hours of 21 closures over 60 days, 50 closures under 2 hours, 148 alarms that experiment 37's detectors raised where no closure was logged, and 40 quiet windows with no alarm. An alarm card puts the alarm's time where the log time would be and draws a duration from the real operations. The hidden cards are 100 placebo cards (a real job's log time moved to a quiet period, with no transfer), 80 cards with a transfer we added to a quiet period, and 20 more with an added transfer and a log time that is wrong by 1 to 3 hours. They are built as in experiment 41's gate. Each card's "excess" is the power above the usual level for that weekday and clock time.

docs.title: The hidden cards look like the real ones, except in missing data
docs.text: A two-sample test found no difference between hidden and real cards on six card-text fields, but the hidden cards have fewer unavailable values. The fields are the minute of the log time, whether side B of the switching sheet is unmetered, the clock hour, the duration, the number of neighbour rows, and the card length. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test gives p of 0.24 or more on each. The mean duration differs (53 hours on real cards, 36 on hidden ones), and the test cannot rule out a difference of that size. The hidden cards were drawn to match the real cards' missing data, but real cards still show 1.6 unavailable values per hourly row against 0.9 on hidden cards, because real jobs sit among more gaps in the telemetry.

docs.title: The first labeller found 0.60 of the added transfers and no placebos
docs.text:
The first Sonnet run called none of the 100 placebo cards visible and found 0.60 of the 80 added transfers. It found 19 of 21 large, long transfers (25% or more of the receiving load, lasting 6 hours or more). The table splits recall by unavailable values per row.

Unavailable values per row Added transfers found Placebo cards called visible Share of real operations under 1 26 of 42 0 of 62 0.49 1 to 2 13 of 22 0 of 27 0.23 2 to 3 9 of 13 0 of 5 0.14 3 or more 0 of 3 0 of 6 0.14

Recall does not fall steadily with missing data, but only 3 hidden cards sit in the group with the most missing data, so weighting by the real mix is unreliable. Weighted to the real operations' mix, recall is 0.53 against 0.60 unweighted, and the placebo rate stays 0 of 100.

docs.title: Of 537 logged operations, 66 show a transfer
docs.text:
The labellers found 35 conserved and 31 one-sided transfers among the 537 operations. A conserved transfer is one where two substations step in opposite directions, so the load moved rather than vanished. A one-sided transfer is one where only one substation steps. The other 471 operations are 440 not visible and 31 that cannot be assessed because power readings are missing.

  • Missing readings: for 13 of the 35 conserved operations, one of the two substations has readings for under half of the event's half-hours (the substation is likely switched off or its meter was off), so the pair was not seen stepping together. Treat those 13 as one-sided at best. The figure above shows only conserved operations with readings from both substations.
  • Size: the median transfer is 1.0 MW (10th to 90th percentile 0.55 to 2.5 MW) and 0.30 of the donor's usual range (its 99th minus its 1st percentile over the previous year).
  • Length: of the 66 visible operations, 16 last 2 to 6 hours, 15 last 6 to 24 hours, and 35 last over 1 day.
  • Share of receiving load (known defect): the stored moved_share_of_receiver column is missing for most events, because the labeller wrote series ids as text (such as "13") and the share calculation compares them with whole numbers. Of the 35 visible operations lasting over 1 day, recomputing the share as in experiment 44 gives 14 of 25% or more of the receiving load, 11 under 25%, and 10 with no named metered receiver. Use experiment 44's load_events for any share.
  • Edge cards: 5 of 42 are visible (1 at the start of a long closure, 4 at the end), and 16 cannot be assessed.
  • Short closures: 2 of 50 closures under 2 hours are visible and 10 cannot be assessed. The gate treats closures under 2 hours as outside the bands it scores.

docs.title: Of 148 unexplained alarms, 9 show a transfer
docs.text: Of 148 alarms with no logged closure, 9 (6%) show a transfer, and 0 of 40 quiet windows do. The 9 are 4 conserved and 5 one-sided, with a median transfer of 1.9 MW. The logs miss real switching, so 6% is a lower bound on the share of alarms that are real, across all four detector settings. Each setting raised 37 alarms that were labelled. The detector D0 with an 8-half-hour window gives 4 of 37, D1 with an 8-half-hour window gives 2 of 37, D1 with a 48-half-hour window gives 3 of 37, and D0 with a 48-half-hour window gives 0 of 37. By the duration drawn for the card, 4 of 56 alarms lasting 2 to 6 hours, 2 of 40 lasting 6 to 24 hours, and 3 of 52 lasting over 1 day are visible.
