Experiment 34 scored 73 forecast runs, 5 days apart, and found weekly retraining 0.28 below the best-guess stack with no correction; this experiment asks whether the gain holds on the other 292 daily runs of the same year. The 292 runs share their months and weather with the 73, so the test guards against the choice of origins and seeds, not against an unusual year. Experiment 34 also left three gaps: its correction read forecasts 5 days apart, retraining was not tried for BSP, GSP, solar, and wind beyond monthly BSP and GSP, and the 7-day correction was not tried on a retrained model.

Rows. The row set fold_a_daily_gap_v1 holds the daily 00:00 UTC ENS runs from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30 that fold_a_every5d_v1 does not. All 365 daily runs exist in the ENS archive, so the set holds 292 runs, and the 73 of fold_a_every5d_v1 are forecast again from the same refits as a reproduction check. Each run spans about 14.6 days, so the 73 runs already cover every valid time of the year: the 292 runs score the same observed demand at other origins and leads, and guard against the choice of origins, not against the outcome data. The demand frames use the same builder as studies/stage1_pilot/demand_build_ens.py (production's half-hourly upsampling, all 51 members, lags from the observed power). No experiment scores a valid time on or after 2026-07-01. The generators need frames for their 9 series over all 365 runs and 51 members, built the same way for the generators' H3 cells and the technology's columns (experiment 33 holds only the 53 Tuesday runs).

Arms.

  • Primary (16 series): the stack; weekly and monthly full refits with a half-life of 0.5 years and an expanding window, no correction, spread factor 1.15, using experiment 34's n1h recipe and its refit times (52 weekly, 12 monthly); P-roll (12-month window, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, monthly); and the weekly arm with the 7-day and the 14-day correction, built from the 365 daily forecasts as issued: each past half-hour's forecast comes from the refit that served that run, never from a re-forecast by the current refit, and no correction reads a run before 2025-07-01. The stack's frozen model is refit with experiment 33's recipe (half-life 2 years, anchored at 2025-06-30, 500 rounds) because it was stored only for the 73 runs, and forecasts all 365 runs.
  • BSP and GSP (2 each): frozen (with the correction as the deployable reference, and without), monthly, and weekly, with and without the correction.
  • Solar (6) and wind (3): the ERA5-trained stage 1a (solar base, with no CAMS and no stage 0; wind margin, with the power-curve margin), refitted monthly on ERA5 up to 5 days before each refit date (when ERA5 arrives), against the frozen model trained to 2025-06-17, both applied to the ENS members and pooled as in experiment 33. Both arms take the spread factor the same way as experiment 33's apply_spread, fitted only on cases whose valid time precedes the origin. The prediction of no change rests on experiment 12's training-start result, not on a retraining measurement.
  • Baselines: manual_heuristic and climatology on the same 292 runs.

Resources. About 5 to 7 GPU hours inside slot A (10 cores, at most 24 GB): weekly Primaries 2.4, monthly 0.6, BSP and GSP weekly 0.6, generators 1 to 2, P-roll 0.2. The 292 new demand frames add about 8 GB of disk, and the generator frames some more; each worker loads the runs of one refit at a time, so memory stays inside 24 GB, and the fits run as parallel workers, one output file per refit written atomically, so a run resumes. The GPU is shared with other sessions, so the timings are not reproducible; the numbers are, because seeds are fixed per job.

Sizing, by the five triggers. Stored: predictions under data/, private, nothing in production. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one defensible design: no, the approved ranking fixes arms and refit dates. Callers not nameable without searching: no, the scripts are copies of experiment 33's and 34's. The experiment is complex only because it builds new frames and a new solar and wind refit, so it gets the full review set: one plan review (Opus), one code review (Sonnet), one write-up check (Sonnet), one prose review (Sonnet), and one result review (Opus).

Earlier advice followed. Retrain monthly in the Primary stage 1 model and drop the correction (00034); screen on P-roll (00034, used here only as a descriptive arm); read the contrasts with a Bonferroni-level interval, because months set the width (00034). Departures: none.

Plan review (Opus), triaged. Accepted: state that the correction reads forecasts as issued and nothing before 2025-07-01; predict a smaller Primary gap because the daily stack's correction is fresher; set C3's threshold to zero; split C8 into solar and wind and make "no change" conditional on the interval; name which frozen reference C7 uses; report each series; limit the reproduction check to arms without a correction; add the generator frame builder, the disk and memory budget, and the spread-factor rule. Rejected: none.

Code review (Sonnet), triaged. No leakage found. Accepted: run --check on the frames, cap threads through environment variables, split the frozen fit across workers, and note the correction's July warm-up and the generator spread factor's first months. Rejected: relabelling C6 and C7 in the report script, because the page states the rule for each.

Write-up check and prose review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the absolute scores now use the cases the contrasts use (the baselines had shrunk the shared case set, so the table and C1 had disagreed), the prediction list, the lead-band claim, the reproduction counts, and the opening's undefined terms. Rejected: moving this section to the pull request, because the plan review is a record of what changed the design.

Result review (Opus), triaged. No leakage and no scoring mismatch; the verdict stands. Accepted: the limits on the interval method and on D8, D12, and D5, the 99.44% level, and the upper bound of C1 (-0.035). Rejected: none.

docs.title: Experiment 49: which Primary demand components still improve the score under monthly retraining?
docs.text:
We asked which parts of the Primary substation demand forecast still lower the forecast error once its XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data. A Primary substation steps power down to the local distribution network. Only averaging the forecasts of five XGBoost models clearly helped: the average's quantile score (an error that rewards forecasts that are both close and honest about their uncertainty, in points, where 1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity) was 0.08 below the best single model's. Four other changes each moved the score by under 0.05 points, and the experiment could not tell any of them from zero, meaning that each interval included zero. Those changes were re-choosing the spread factor that widens the uncertainty band (the factor is 1.15 in the forecast we use now), adding recent-window statistics of each substation (its "fingerprint") to a pooled model trained on many substations at once, dropping the column that marks the 14 days around 25 December, and giving older training rows a half-life of 2 years instead of 0.5 years. One more change could not be tested: the indicator for the 2020 to 2021 lockdowns is always 0 inside a 12-month training window. The next experiments could test the blend with weekly refits, and the Christmas column on a second winter.

Supported, on the blend alone. Scores are the quantile score over all leads, in points of capacity, for 16 Primary substations, 73 runs started 5 days apart from July 2025 to June 2026, with weather from ENS (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble), seed 0, with the spread factor 1.15 applied and without the 14-day error correction. P-roll is a cheaper approximation to the full monthly refitting of experiment 34: refit monthly on the latest 12 months, 150 rounds, eta 0.15. Stage 0 re-used predictions that experiments 33 and 34 stored, and stage 1 refitted P-roll. The screening reference stays monthly P-roll, and a weekly result from experiment 48 would not change the stage 0 findings. B1's stack member is the frozen N1 with the 14-day correction, so B1 is not a blend of retrained models alone. The code is in ml- experiments/00049-*/, and e00049_stage0.py and e00049_stage1.py print every number below.

Id Contrast Difference 99.17% interval State D0 spread factor chosen on earlier months minus fixed 1.15, monthly refits -0.0001 -0.012 to +0.018 null; no gain B1 five-model blend minus best single model -0.076 -0.135 to -0.023 port (threshold -0.05) C1 P-roll without the Christmas column minus P-roll -0.017 -0.058 to +0.007 unresolved C2 P-roll without the COVID indicator minus P-roll +0.0002 -0.003 to +0.003 rule says removable; untestable (indicator constant) C3 P-roll with a half-life of 2 years minus 0.5 years -0.003 -0.034 to +0.027 unresolved F1 pooled P-roll with fingerprints minus without +0.009 -0.037 to +0.050 not worth porting

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Arm Score 95% interval (months resampled) Blend of five models, one weight vector per month 4.968 4.634 to 5.329 Weekly refits, all history (best single model) 5.044 4.688 to 5.430 Weekly-analogue model, monthly refits 5.084 4.715 to 5.503 Monthly refits, all history 5.118 4.724 to 5.575 P-roll, no Christmas column 5.134 4.742 to 5.588 P-roll, half-life 2 years 5.148 4.751 to 5.602 P-roll (the screening reference) 5.150 4.760 to 5.604 P-roll, no COVID indicator 5.151 4.760 to 5.604 Pooled by type, monthly refits, all history 5.288 4.933 to 5.678 Pooled P-roll 5.307 4.955 to 5.690 Pooled P-roll with fingerprints 5.316 4.973 to 5.695 Stack (frozen N1, 14-day correction, spread 1.15) 5.318 4.943 to 5.686 manual_heuristic 5.888 5.392 to 6.389 climatology 7.462 6.556 to 8.341

The intervals on each score come from resampling the 12 validation months, and are about plus or minus 0.4 points for the XGBoost models and wider for the baselines. The P-roll rows use this experiment's refits, which differ from experiment 34's stored scores (5.151 and 5.308) by under 0.001. The contrasts are paired and much tighter. Refitting P-roll with this experiment's code reproduced experiment 34's stored scores to within 0.0007 points for both reference arms (P-roll and pooled P-roll), so the drop-one contrasts are not noise from the refit.

docs.title: Stage 0: stored predictions
docs.text:
The spread factor needs no re-tuning for a retrained model. The score is flat from 1.05 to 1.15: monthly refits score 5.113 at their best factors, 1.075 and 1.10, and 5.118 at 1.15. The factor chosen on earlier months ranged from 1.025 to 1.125 from August 2025 (July uses 1.15). It moved further from 1.15 than the prediction of at most 0.10, but moved the score by only -0.0001 (D0). Weekly refits gave -0.002 and P-roll +0.0004. The factors chosen from August 2025 all sat below 1.15, and the in-sample best is 1.075 to 1.10, so 1.15 is indistinguishable from the best factor, not preferred to it. The factor 1.15 was chosen in experiment 19 on validation months that overlap these, so D0 is not fully out of sample.

Blending still helps after retraining, by almost as much as in experiment 35 (-0.097). B1 averages the quantiles of five XGBoost models: weekly refits, monthly refits, the weekly-analogue model, the pooled model, and the stack. In 10 of the 11 months with history the weights were 0.5 for weekly refits, 0.25 for the weekly-analogue model, and 0.25 for the stack, with zero for monthly refits and the pooled model; in October 2025 the weekly-analogue model took 0.5 and weekly refits 0.25. The gain, -0.076, is smaller than experiment 35's -0.097. The three-member blend of experiment 35's design (monthly refits, the weekly-analogue model, the stack) scores -0.096 against its best member, so the gain is unchanged for that design. The smaller figure appears only against the stronger reference, weekly refits. The prediction's reason, that retrained members differ less, is therefore not supported.

Neither the weight rule nor the two extra models adds a resolvable gain. Descriptive contrasts at 95%: weights per lead band -0.062 (-0.100 to -0.025) against the weekly refits, equal weights -0.060 (-0.115 to -0.012), and experiment 35's three members with a retrained N1 (monthly refits, the weekly-analogue model, the stack) -0.096 (-0.139 to -0.058) against its best member, the weekly- analogue model. The five-model blend minus the three-model blend is -0.021 (-0.051 to +0.005), so the two extra models add nothing resolvable. Weekly minus monthly refits is -0.074 (-0.146 to -0.018), and monthly refits minus the stack -0.201 (-0.379 to -0.004), the same contrasts as in experiment 34, recomputed on this row set.

docs.title: Stage 1: P-roll drop-one arms and fingerprints
docs.text:
P-roll could not resolve whether the Christmas column or the longer half-life matters. Dropping the Christmas column lowered the score by 0.017 points (-0.058 to +0.007). The prediction was that the column stays worth keeping; the estimate points the other way. The column is set only within 14 days of 25 December, and the validation year holds one winter. A half-life of 2 years changed the score by -0.003 (-0.034 to +0.027). Neither interval fits inside the plus or minus 0.03 margin set in advance, so both are unresolved.

The COVID indicator cannot be tested under P-roll. The 12-month training window holds no lockdown days, so the indicator is 0 in every training row and in every forecast, and C2 is +0.0002 by construction. The finding says nothing about full-history models that still train on 2020 and 2021.

Substation fingerprints did not help the pooled model. The 7 training-window statistics are constant for each series within a refit, so they duplicate the series identifier, and F1 tests the 3 recent-window statistics in effect. F1 is +0.009 points (-0.037 to +0.050), in line with experiment 32's frozen-model result (changes of at most 0.02 points) and far from the -0.10 needed to port a recent-window statistic. Experiment 34's fourth rank-test contrast (R4, fingerprints in the pool) was not run with full monthly refits, so whether P-roll matches full refits on fingerprints is untested.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• No fit failed. The two reference refits reproduced the stored scores.
  • One validation year with 12 months sets every interval, and the seed is 0 for every arm.
  • B1's best member is chosen with hindsight, which makes the contrast stricter, never looser. The blend's weights are chosen on earlier months only.
  • D0 is not fully out of sample, because the factor 1.15 came from experiment 19's validation months, which overlap these.
  • The stage 1 arms are P-roll, not full monthly refits, so a contrast that experiment 34's rank test did not cover (the COVID indicator, the half-life under a 12-month window) may differ under full refits.
  • Five members at weights in steps of a quarter give 70 weight vectors per month.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Test the blend in its serving form: weekly-retrained N1, the weekly-analogue model refitted weekly, and the stack, with fixed weights 0.5, 0.25, and 0.25. The weights settled there in 10 of 11 months, and the weekly-analogue model has only been refitted monthly so far. Separately, test the Christmas column on a second winter, using the second validation year that the ENS backfill allows (experiment R11, the second validation year). Experiments that screen a level-following input take P-roll (5.150 here) as their reference row.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
Plan review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: take every drop-one contrast against a fresh refit of P-roll and add a pooled reference refit; state the fingerprint cutoffs; name the stored files and the 768,073 shared cases; one weight vector per month throughout, and the first-month weights; remove the unreachable "small gain" for the spread factor and the unusable "refuted" verdict; fix prose faults. Rejected: none.

Number check (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the reproduction tolerance is 0.0007, the factor range, grading prediction (a), the like-for-like comparison with experiment 35, the advice that credited a three-model blend nobody scored, the F1 advice limited to P-roll, the interval widths, and the research-log wording. Rejected: none.

Result review (Opus), triaged. No leakage found, and the verdict follows the rule. Accepted: the stack member of B1 carries the correction (stated on the page), the lessons line about adding gains, the fingerprint block that duplicates the series identifier, and the weak reason in the D0 advice. Not run: a sensitivity check of B1 with an uncorrected stack, because no uncorrected stack arm is stored.

Prose review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: a plain opening paragraph that defines every term, the split of the blend paragraph, and the rewording of unclear referents. Rejected: none.

docs.title: Experiment 50: does a second weather forecast give a better forecast of the solar anomaly than ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether a second weather forecast, the American Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), predicts how much sunnier or cloudier than usual a day will be better than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS) that the demand forecast uses today. Experiment 46 had found that a correction for embedded solar panels lowered the demand forecast's error by about 20% when it used the true sunshine (taken from the satellite- based Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) data), and by almost nothing when it used the ENS forecast of sunshine. We scored three forecasts of the sunshine anomaly (ENS, GEFS, and a weighted blend of the two) against the CAMS sunshine, at five substations that meter in MW, and planned to lay the best one into experiment 46's correction only if it beat ENS. Neither GEFS nor the blend did. In cross-validation on 9 held-out months, GEFS made 10.9% more squared error than ENS and the blend made 0.2% more. On the 6 validation months (July to September 2025 and April to June 2026), GEFS correlated with the true sunshine anomaly less well than ENS in every lead band, and the blend matched ENS. The experiment therefore stopped before the demand forecast was tested.

The verdict is refuted: no tested forecast beats ENS by the 1% the gate requires, so the demand contrasts C7 and C7s (the change in the demand forecast's score from using the selected anomaly in place of ENS's, on all leads and on leads of 0 to 48 hours) were not run. The rule is in the front matter. Each calibration is a slope (or a pair of weights) fitted per substation and lead band on the training window, and the gate scores April-to-September daylight half-hours at leads of 0 to 240 hours.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Stage 1 gate, training window only. Fifteen month-block folds fit every calibration on the other months and predict the held-out month. Nine folds hold April-to-September rows. The pooled mean squared error against the CAMS anomaly is 0.03194 for ENS, 0.03542 for GEFS (1.109 times ENS's), 0.03201 for the blend (1.002 times), and 0.04422 for a zero anomaly. GEFS is worse than ENS in all 9 months, and the blend beats ENS in 4 of 9 months by at most 0.1%. The gate needs the blend or GEFS at 0.99 or lower.

Absolute skill on the validation year (exploratory; the gate decided the verdict). The correlation of each calibrated anomaly with the CAMS anomaly, pooled over the five verdict series, with 68,903 scored rows in total (the printed report gives the rows in each band):

Lead band ENS GEFS Fitted blend GEFS minus ENS (95% interval) Blend minus ENS (95% interval) 0 to 24 h 0.822 0.749 0.824 -0.072 (-0.100 to -0.039) +0.002 (-0.001 to +0.006) 1 to 2 d 0.747 0.685 0.754 -0.062 (-0.141 to -0.003) +0.007 (+0.000 to +0.010) 2 to 6 d 0.628 0.518 0.627 -0.109 (-0.204 to -0.031) -0.001 (-0.001 to +0.000) 6 to 10 d 0.337 0.328 0.336 -0.009 (-0.077 to +0.050) -0.001 (-0.001 to +0.000) 10+ d 0.247 0.182 0.181 -0.064 (-0.201 to +0.098) -0.065 (-0.201 to +0.097)

The intervals resample the 7 months in which runs were started (July to September 2025 and March to June 2026; the March 2026 runs reach into April), so they are wide. The calibration slope of the CAMS anomaly on each calibrated anomaly (1 is ideal) is 0.98 for ENS and 1.09 for GEFS at 0 to 24 hours, and 1.21 for ENS and 2.01 for GEFS at 6 to 10 days. The mean-squared-error skill against a zero anomaly for ENS is 0.676, 0.555, 0.400, and 0.118 in the first four bands. Averaged to 3-hour windows (exploratory), the correlations are higher for all three arms and keep the same order: at 0 to 24 hours ENS 0.883, GEFS 0.810, blend 0.886.

The raw data. In bins of each forecast's raw anomaly, the mean CAMS anomaly rises with both. The slope of the CAMS anomaly on the raw GEFS anomaly is 0.87 at 0 to 48 hours, so GEFS's raw anomaly is about 15% too large, while the slope for ENS is 0.98 to 1.07.

The blend learns to ignore GEFS. Over the five verdict series, the mean fitted weight on GEFS is 0.107 at 0 to 24 hours, 0.080 at 1 to 2 days, -0.012 at 2 to 6 days, and -0.005 at 6 to 10 days (3 of the 5 weights negative), where the blend is ENS alone. At 10+ days the weights (0.24 on GEFS, 0.01 on ENS) are fitted on little skill. Across all bands, 8 of the verdict series' 25 weight pairs have a negative weight (10 of 30 over all six sites, and -0.008 for the 6 to 10 day mean over all six); they were kept and flagged. An equal-weight average of the two calibrated anomalies (exploratory) correlates 0.814 at 0 to 24 hours, below ENS, and 0.357 at 6 to 10 days, above it (0.337); neither difference was tested.

Predictions against results. The plan predicted GEFS correlations of 0.68, 0.63, 0.50, and 0.20 in the first four bands against ENS's 0.79, 0.75, 0.58, and 0.27. The results are GEFS 0.749, 0.685, 0.518, and 0.328 against ENS's 0.822, 0.747, 0.628, and 0.337, so the ordering held. GEFS was more skilful than predicted in every band, and ENS in three of the four (at 1 to 2 days ENS was 0.747 against 0.75 predicted). The plan predicted blend gains of +0.01 to +0.03 at 0 to 6 days, and the results are +0.002, +0.007, and -0.001.

docs.title: Data validation, and what is unverified
docs.text:
The GEFS archive and the conversion passed seven checks (e00050_validate_gefs.py).

  • All 821 00 UTC runs from 2024-04-01 to 2026-06-30 are complete (31 members, 9 grid cells, no duplicate keys, no NaN after lead 0).
  • De-accumulation: 2.55% of the 3-hour means are below -1 W/m² (lowest -20.0), and clipping them at zero removes 0.057% of the positive energy.
  • The half-hours of each native window average to the native mean.
  • The daily profile's centre of mass lies within 0.10 half-hours of CAMS's.
  • The true cell weights beat the latitude-mirrored mapping at the five sites that mirroring changes.
  • The chain test gives 0.999 on window means at every site and 0.91 to 0.93 on half-hours (planned bound 0.95; see the implementation notes).
  • The 99th percentile of the clear-sky index is 1.081, and GEFS irradiance is 6% to 22% above CAMS's by month, which the anomaly removes. The monthly ratio stepped by 19.4% into November 2025, a warning that did not persist as a lasting change.

The latency check is unverified. The check needs observations between 07:00 and 09:00 UTC on three dates. The session ran at 15:00 UTC, so results/latency_decision.json records the same-day 00 UTC run as an assumption. The same-day run is the optimistic case for GEFS, so the verdict also holds for the previous day's run. Today's run was present in the store at 14:59 UTC. For D16 the crop covers 0.898 of the cell, and the weights were renormalised.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: ENS stays the source of the solar anomaly. GEFS adds under 1% over 0 to 48 hours: the blend's correlation gain is +0.002 at 0 to 24 hours and +0.007 at 1 to 2 days (interval +0.000 to +0.010), and its cross-validated squared error is 1.002 times ENS's. The first 2 days hold nearly all of the skill (correlation 0.75 to 0.82), and there GEFS is worse and the blend adds at most 0.007. GEFS's raw anomaly needs a calibration slope of about 0.87 where ENS's slope is 0.98 to 1.07.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Does a product of a different kind than a global ensemble, such as a high-resolution regional model at the substations' own points or a satellite-based nowcast of the next few hours, raise the correlation with the CAMS anomaly above ENS's 0.82 at 0 to 24 hours? This experiment found that GEFS adds under 1% there, so the next test should use a source with independent errors at short range, calibrated in-fold as here and scored first without any demand fit. The live UKV differs statistically from the CEDA UKV archive, so the product must be the same in training and serving. Beyond 6 days, none of the products on disk that we considered is likely to beat ECMWF, so a gain there is unlikely, and the equal-weight blend, untested, is the one hint otherwise (0.357 against ENS's 0.337 at 6 to 10 days).

Suggestions for that experiment (not commitments). First, add noise to the CAMS anomaly to reach correlations of 0.85 and 0.90, and push those anomalies through e00050_predict.py, to map anomaly correlation to demand score and show how much a better anomaly could be worth. Second, blend ENS with the CAMS anomaly at the forecast origin, to bound what a nowcast could add. GFS is not worth testing, because it shares GEFS's model physics.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: The demand contrasts C7 and C7s, and the repeats of experiment 46's contrasts, C3b and C6b, did not run, because the stage 1 gate stopped the experiment. e00050_predict.py and e00050_stats.py are written, are tested against experiment 46's stored arm (a rebuild matches to 1.2e-7), and stay unrun. No prediction set was written, since no demand arm exists.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Sizing. Each of the five triggers gets one line.

  • What gets stored: private intermediate tables and about five prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • The production serving path: not touched. Adoption would add an ingest, which a later production issue would own.
  • A degradation rule: not touched. Adoption would need a rule for a late or missing GEFS run, which a later issue would own.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The choices are the product, the blend form, same-day or previous-day runs, the climatology window, and how the member spread is handled. This plan fixes each.
  • Code whose callers could not be named without searching: no. The scripts copy named experiment 46 helpers, call _upsample_nwp_to_half_hourly as experiment 46 does, and call geo.h3.compute_h3_grid_weights.

The size is complex. The process is a plan review, a code review for leakage (training-window cut-offs, the selection running before the predictions, and the choice of GEFS run), a run and write-up with a prose review, and a review of the result.

Earlier advice followed. Experiment 46's advice is followed in four places: fit the solar coefficient by lead band instead of fixing it at 1; limit any gain test to leads of 0 to 48 hours (C7s); check the sign of a contrast in every valid month before reading its pooled interval; and compare arms that share one fitted booster. The experiment departs from none of it.

The second product is GEFS, with GFS as the one fallback. GEFS (31 members, 00 UTC runs, 0.25 degrees) is on disk for 2020-10 onward, comes from Dynamical.org like the ENS ingest, and was the same operational GEFS v12 product throughout. NOAA's deterministic GFS is the fallback if GEFS fails the latency check or a data-validation check; its radiation windows run from 1 to 6 hours and need a running-mean de-accumulation, which this plan does not implement unless the fallback is used. ECMWF's AIFS model is ruled out: its shortwave field is missing before 2025-02-24, and two model versions fall inside the validation year. The CEDA UKV archive and the Open-Meteo archives are ruled out for different reasons: the CEDA UKV differs from the live UKV, and the Open-Meteo archives are held at the generator meter points and reach at most 5 days. No download is needed.

GEFS radiation is a 6-hour mean at 00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC and a 3-hour mean at 03, 09, 15, and 21 UTC, so the means are de-accumulated before use. The 3-hour mean ending at a 6-hourly label L is 2 * v(L) - v(L - 3 h). Means below zero are clipped to zero and counted (the first look found 5.2% of 3-hour means below -1 W/m², and the full sample 2.55%). Beyond a lead of 144 hours pairs of 3-hour means are averaged into 6-hour means, which gives the same schedule as ENS's native radiation windows, so the conversion passes the production resampler's schedule check. Each Primary's H3 cell is area-weighted over the GEFS grid cells; for D16 only 0.898 of the cell lies inside the downloaded crop, so its weights are renormalised, and the write-up says so.

The run used depends on a latency check made before any score. Production's forecast origin is the 00 UTC run plus 9 hours. e00050_latency.py records, on three or more dates between 07:00 and 09:00 UTC, whether the store already holds that day's 00 UTC GEFS run. If it always does, the arms use the same-day run. Otherwise they use the previous day's run, and lead bands stay measured from the forecast origin. The decision is written to results/latency_decision.json before any GEFS input is built.

docs.title: Stage 1: the anomaly
docs.text:
Three calibrated anomalies are scored against the CAMS anomaly. The anomaly of a source is its unit PV shape u minus its own month-by-half-hour climatology over the training window. The ens arm is slope times the ENS ensemble-mean anomaly (experiment 46's). The gefs arm is slope times the GEFS ensemble-mean anomaly. The blend arm regresses the CAMS anomaly on both ensemble-mean anomalies with two weights and no intercept. Slopes and weights are fitted per site and lead band; a negative weight is kept and flagged. An equal-weight average of the two calibrated anomalies is an exploratory fourth arm and takes no part in the selection.

The gate and the scores use different data. The selection gate is the cross-validation of the decision rule and uses the training window only. The validation-year scores fit once on the whole training window and report, by lead band and pooled over the five verdict series: the correlation (A1), the calibration slope (A2), and the mean-squared-error skill against a zero anomaly (A3). The difference in correlation between each arm and ENS has a 95% interval from resampling the 7 initialisation months of the runs. These reads are exploratory and decide nothing. A second exploratory read repeats A1 on 3-hour mean anomalies, free of any difference in resampling shape.

docs.title: Stage 2: the demand contrasts
docs.text:
Every demand arm is a shift of experiment 46's saved d1l boosters (its demand models without radiation inputs; d0 is the same models with them), so nothing is refitted. The shift of ENS member m is -K(site, band) * C * (central + (a_m - mean(a))) / capacity, where C is experiment 40's 2023/24 capacity, K is experiment 46's fitted lead-band coefficient (1 in bands where none was fitted), central is the arm's calibrated anomaly, and a_m - mean(a) is the raw ENS member's deviation from the ENS mean. The arms differ only in central. The 14-day correction and the spread factor 1.15 are applied to each arm as in experiment 46.

Id Contrast Read Predicted C7 selected arm's shift minus ENS shift, all scored rows decides, 97.5% -0.02 (-0.06 to +0.01) C7s the same, scored rows at leads of 0 to 48 hours decides, 97.5% -0.04 (-0.10 to 0.00) C3b selected arm's shift minus d1l exploratory, 95% (experiment 46's fitted C3 was -0.143) -0.16 C6b selected arm's shift minus d0, all leads and 0 to 48 hours exploratory, 95% +0.02, and -0.05 at 0 to 48 hours

C7 compares two shifts of one booster, so it has no GPU fit noise but also little contrast. The difference between the two central anomalies is expected to have about a third of the standard deviation of the ENS shift. Scaling experiment 46's C3 intervals by that third gives an expected 97.5% half-width of 0.03 to 0.05 points for C7 and 0.05 to 0.10 for C7s. C7s can therefore clear -0.1 only if the true gain is about 0.15 to 0.2, roughly three times the predicted gain. The statistics script prints the realised half-widths. PVDIS-5's test is a gain test at 0 to 48 hours only if C6b is wholly below zero there.

Exploratory reads (95%, labelled so): C7 by lead band, by valid month (the sign must match in every month before a pooled read is believed), by series, and without D9; the other arms' shifts, including the equal-weight blend; the coverage of the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles in sunny and cloudy rows; and a week-block bootstrap.

docs.title: Checks before any read
docs.text:
Data validation of GEFS (e00050_validate_gefs.py, with each number printed):

  1. Every 00 UTC run from 2024-04-01 to 2026-06-30 is present with 31 members, the expected lead times, and 9 grid cells, with no duplicate keys; every NaN shortwave value after lead 0 is listed.
  2. De-accumulation: clipping removes under 1% of the positive energy, windows that are dark throughout hold under 10 W/m² at each of the six sites (a post hoc bound, see the implementation notes), and twice a 6-hour mean equals the sum of its two 3-hour halves.
  3. Each native window's mean equals the mean of its half-hours to within the 13-bit quantisation step.
  4. The centre of mass of the hour-of-day profile of GEFS irradiance in the first 48 hours lies within one half-hour of CAMS's, which would fail if windows were labelled by their start.
  5. The true cell weights give a higher cloud-driven correlation with CAMS than the latitude-mirrored mapping at every site whose mapping the mirroring changes.
  6. CAMS irradiance, presented as GEFS windows and passed through the GEFS chain, reproduces the window means of the CAMS anomaly at leads up to 360 hours (3-hour windows to 144 hours, 6-hour windows after; correlation 0.99 or more), and the half-hour correlation is printed against the planned 0.95 and against CAMS smoothed to the same windows.
  7. The 99th percentile of the clear-sky index is at most 1.3. The monthly ratio of mean GEFS to mean CAMS irradiance, over every run, is printed with a warning, not a gate, for a step over 15% between neighbouring months.

Experiment checks: (1) the rebuilt d1l_ens_shift_fitted matches experiment 46's stored arm to within 1e-5 on every quantile and key; (2) a blend with weights (ENS slope, 0) reproduces the ens central anomaly bit for bit; (3) all arms hold the same scored keys; (4) every climatology, slope, weight, and fold uses valid times up to 2025-06-30 23:30 only, which the code asserts; (5) the latency decision is recorded before stage 1 runs; (6) stage 1's selection is written before any script reads an anomaly for the demand stage.

Stop rule. The experiment stops without a verdict if experiment check 1, 2, 5, or 6 fails and one revision does not fix it. Nothing is tuned after the scores or any contrast is read: the bands, the folds, the 1% selection margin, K, C, and the threshold are fixed here.

docs.title: Compute and amendments
docs.text:
The run fits in 4 cores, and the GPU is optional. Reading and converting GEFS takes minutes (four worker processes, one Polars thread each). Prediction from the boosters runs on the CPU, one thread per worker, at about 1.5 to 3 minutes per series-and-seed job; the shifts and the bootstrap take minutes.

Amendments from the plan review, accepted: clip the de-accumulated means at zero and state the clip; add "neither wholly below zero" to refuted, so that small gain and refuted cannot both hold; fit the ENS calibration, each climatology, and the blend weights inside each fold; check the publication time of the GEFS run; and verify the D16 crop coverage in the private store. Changes at code review, made before the run. The gate scores April-to-September rows only, like the validation scoring, and drops training rows of runs initialised in the held-out month. Scored on all months, the gate gives GEFS 1.141 and the blend 1.002 times ENS's error, so neither change decides the verdict.

Rejected: skipping the demand stage, because the brief requires repeating experiment 46's C3 and C6, and a fixed 50/50 blend as the only blend, because the fitted blend is one of the three pre-registered arms (the fixed blend is added as an exploratory arm). Open: the Bonferroni correction across C7 and C7s widens both intervals; both stay at 97.5% unless the maintainer rules otherwise.

Implementation notes (post hoc, labelled so). Check 6 gates on window means because averaging CAMS to 3-hour or 6-hour windows discards its within-window cloud detail, which caps the half-hour correlation near 0.91 to 0.95 whatever the chain does; a smoke run gave 0.98 or more on window means and 0.91 to 0.93 on half-hours. The dark-window bound of check 2 is 10 W/m², set after a smoke run found up to 8.0 W/m² across the six sites, because the archive's 3-hour and 6-hour windows are not exactly consistent near dusk, and the PV model returns 0 when the sun is below the horizon. The monthly-ratio step of check 7 reached 19.4% (into November 2025, in low winter irradiance) over every run, which is why that read is a warning. The calibration of the 10+ d lead band uses every training lead to 351 hours, and the cross-validation gate uses leads to 240 hours. Rows without a GEFS value are dropped from the stage 1 scores and counted, so that no arm is scored on a fallback to ENS.

docs.title: Experiment 51: why does the solar term lose at sunny summer middays?
docs.text:
We asked why a correction for rooftop solar panels made a forecast of a Primary substation's power worse around midday in summer. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation in the electricity distribution network. Experiment 46 lowered each forecast by the panels' estimated capacity times how much sunnier the day was than the average for that month and half-hour. At 09:00 to 15:00 UTC in June to August, 2 days ahead, the corrected forecast had a quantile score (our probabilistic forecast error score, in points where 1 point is 1% of the substation's capacity) 0.48 points worse than the baseline forecast (d0) that kept its own radiation inputs and had no correction. We tested three explanations on the forecasts experiment 46 had stored, without fitting a new weather-to-power model: (a) the panels' inverters, which convert direct current to alternating current, cap their output on sunny days, (b) the correction is too large, or (c) the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble forecast (ENS) add noise. The correction built from the sunshine that actually occurred (the oracle shift) is too large: the actual power fell by only 0.4 to 0.7 of the amount the correction removed, in every month and time of day. A cap on inverter output could not be told apart from a too-large correction, and the ensemble members accounted for 0.13 points of the loss.

The verdict is partly supported: one leg of the hypothesis survives, and the other two do not. The hypothesis said the loss comes mainly from a coefficient that is too large for the sunniest rows, which an inverter clips, and not from noisy ENS members. The coefficient is too large (cause b met). A clipping knee is not distinguished from a straight line (cause a not met). The members' noise adds to the loss (cause c met), so the "not noise" leg fails. The decision rule is in the front matter of this page, and the plan, which stated it, was committed before any result was read. The rule does not say why the coefficient is too large, and the page does not claim to know.

Prediction made in the plan Result Knee between 0.6 and 0.9 at 3 or more of the 5 series Not met: 2 of 5 (D14 at 0.60 and D16 at 0.65) A clip lowers the median's error by 0.05 to 0.15 points Not met: the hinge lowers it by 1.02 points, almost all through its intercept The ensemble-mean shift removes under a third of the ENS shift's excess over d1l Not met: it removes 0.129 points, more than the whole 0.057-point excess

All figures are for 5 Primary substations (anonymised as D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, as in experiment 46), June to August, valid 09:00 to 15:00 UTC, 1 to 3 days after the forecast origin. There are 3,575 forecast cases: each one is a Primary, a valid half-hour, and a forecast run, with its quantiles averaged over the 3 random seeds of the XGBoost fit. The cases come from 13 weeks of forecast start. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals from resampling whole weeks of forecast start. With so few weeks the intervals are probably somewhat narrow.

docs.title: Raw data: the error left after the oracle shift
docs.text: The oracle shift is too large on cloudy rows as well as sunny ones, in every lead day, hour, and Primary. Let e be the actual power minus the forecast after the oracle shift, in points of capacity. A value of 0 means the shift was exactly right, and a positive value means the shift lowered the forecast too far. The mean of e is negative on cloudy rows (about -3 to -4 points, where the shift raised the forecast too far), crosses 0 near a clear-sky index (irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, CAMS, over clear-sky irradiance) of 0.7, and reaches +5 to +7 points between 0.9 and 1.0. A negative value on cloudy rows points to a scale error, because a cap on output would not act there. The grey dots are a sample of the cases, and the line is the mean of all of them.

docs.title: The correction's coefficient is too large (cause b)
docs.text:
In every month and hour bin the actual power falls by 0.4 to 0.7 of what the oracle shift removes, so a coefficient of 1 over-corrects. A coefficient of 1 would give a slope of -1 of the d1l residual (the actual power minus the forecast before any solar correction) on the shift. The slope is between -0.42 and -0.69 in each of the 6 cells of month by hour bin (09-12 then 12-15 UTC: June -0.42 and -0.51, July -0.69 and -0.65, August -0.69 and -0.60), by lead day -0.61, -0.54, and -0.61, and by Primary -0.52 to -0.81. In 4 of the 6 cells the interval lies wholly above -0.85, which meets the rule's count; the 2 August cells have lower ends of -1.03 and -1.12. Each cell holds only about 4 to 5 weeks of forecast start, so these intervals are the least reliable in the page. A coefficient fitted per series and hour bin on half the weeks lowers the median's mean absolute error on the other half by 0.991 points (-1.473 to -0.495), against the oracle shift with coefficient 1.

The slope below 1 has several possible causes that these data cannot separate. The panels' estimated capacity may be too large. Error in the CAMS sunshine pulls the slope towards 0. The d1l forecast already absorbs part of the sunshine through its temperature and lagged-power inputs. Clipping flattens the response on sunny rows. Demand that rises with sunshine, such as cooling, offsets the panels' output. Panel temperature lowers the output on hot days. A coefficient fitted on CAMS is also not the coefficient used in service, where the shift comes from ENS and is attenuated more at longer leads.

docs.title: A clipping knee is not distinguished from a straight line (cause a)
docs.text:
A hinge that is flat below a knee and rises above it fits no better than a straight line out of fold, and adds nothing after the coefficient repair. The hinge lowers the median's error against the unrepaired oracle shift by 1.023 points (-1.526 to -0.521), but a straight line in the clear-sky index lowers it by 0.920 (-1.382 to -0.437). The hinge is lower than the line by 0.103 points (-0.233 to +0.030), and the rule needed an interval wholly below 0. Both repairs lower the error mostly through a free intercept, so the 1.023 alone is not evidence of clipping. The comparison also could not separate the causes: the shift is itself S-shaped in the clear-sky index, so a hinge traces it even when the only fault is a scale error. A post hoc test is sharper: a hinge fitted to what the coefficient repair leaves behind changes the out-of-fold error by +0.003 points (-0.071 to +0.084), so no knee remains once the scale is fixed.

The fitted knees do not look like clipping. The slope above the knee is positive at all 5 series, with intervals above 0, but the knees lie between a clear-sky index of 0.40 and 0.65 with wide intervals (0.40 to 0.78), and the knee of D9 sits at the lowest value the search allowed. The CAMS shape gives the panels' output as a fraction of their direct-current capacity, and the inverter caps output near that fraction at the knee, so the knee implies a ratio of direct-current to alternating-current (DC:AC) capacity of 1.8 to 3.2. We expect rooftop inverters to sit well below that, which is a judgement this page did not check against a source. The page therefore reports no per-Primary knee for PVDIS-6 (the planned test of panel orientations, which a knee would feed). The test could also not have found the effect the plan predicted: the interval on hinge minus line has a half-width of about 0.13 points, so an effect of 0.19 points would be needed for 80% power, and the plan predicted 0.05 to 0.15.

Series Knee (clear-sky index) Slope above the knee (points per unit index, 95% interval) Implied DC:AC D9 0.40 24.1 (19.6 to 32.9) 3.2 D10 0.575 32.2 (18.7 to 55.1) 2.1 D11 0.55 20.7 (15.6 to 33.2) 2.2 D14 0.60 24.1 (17.4 to 45.7) 2.0 D16 0.65 15.3 (9.8 to 24.4) 1.8

docs.title: Splits for sunshine-dependent demand, and the temperature read
docs.text:
The splits do not show that the knee comes from demand that rises with sunshine, or that it does not. Demand such as cooling or visitor load at coastal resorts rises with sunshine and would mimic a clipping knee. Of the 5 Primaries, 2 are within 10 km of the open coast, so the coastal split compares 2 series with 3. The slope above each series' own knee is 24.1 at the 2 coastal series and 22.7 at the other 3. It is 25.2 on term-time weekdays and 17.3 on school-holiday weeks and weekends; these are point estimates with no intervals. The hinge is lower than the line by 0.161 points (-0.282 to -0.038, 10 weekly blocks) in holiday-and-weekend rows, and by 0.081 points (-0.253 to +0.097) on term-time weekdays. Of the 7 scopes read (all rows, day+2 and day+3, sunny, coastal, inland, term-time weekdays, and holiday-and-weekend), this is the only one whose interval excludes 0. Chance alone would produce about 1 such interval in 7. The holiday period (22 July to 31 August) also covers most of August, so the split confounds holiday demand with the month.

At fixed clear-sky index, the sunniest rows' error rises with 2 m temperature, and demand is only one explanation. The rise is 0.67 points per kelvin (0.21 to 1.15), from the mean of e in three temperature bands within each series and 0.1-wide index bin (-2.27, -0.17, and +2.49 points in the coolest, middle, and warmest band). Demand that rises with heat could cause it. So could panel temperature: output of crystalline-silicon panels falls by roughly 0.4% per kelvin, so a shift that ignores cell temperature over-states the panels' output on hot days. This page did not check whether the CAMS unit output models cell temperature. Hot rows also cluster in few weeks (8 weekly blocks in the warmest sunny band), and d1l already takes temperature as an input.

docs.title: Noisy ENS members add to the loss (cause c)
docs.text:
The member spread adds 0.129 points to the ENS shift's score at day+2 and day+3, which is under half of the 0.324-point loss of the ENS shift against d0. The table gives the quantile score of the first arm minus the second, at day+2 and day+3 pooled (2,340 cases), with its interval. Cause c is met as the rule is written, because the interval of the ENS-shift-minus-ensemble-mean-shift row lies wholly above 0 and 0.129 exceeds half of the ENS-shift-minus-d1l difference (0.057). The rule compares with d1l, and the lead above compares with d0. The test is weak: the interval of the ENS-shift-minus-d1l row spans 0, so almost any positive spread effect would pass it.

Contrast (negative favours the first arm) Difference (95% interval) ENS shift minus d0 (experiment 46's C6) +0.324 (-0.144 to +0.761) ENS shift minus d1l (experiment 46's C3) +0.057 (-0.495 to +0.570) ENS shift minus ensemble-mean shift (cause c) +0.129 (+0.057 to +0.212) Ensemble-mean shift minus d1l -0.072 (-0.625 to +0.441) Fitted-coefficient ENS shift minus ENS shift (post hoc) -0.435 (-0.689 to -0.139) Fitted-coefficient ENS shift minus d0 (post hoc) -0.111 (-0.348 to +0.110)

The loss that prompted the experiment reproduces: experiment 46's C6 is +0.477 (+0.057 to +0.842) at day+2 and +0.172 (-0.580 to +0.807) at day+3. Over the two days pooled, the interval of C6 includes 0 when 13 weeks are resampled, so the loss is small and uncertain here. The fitted-coefficient shift of experiment 46, fitted on its training window, removes the loss: it scores +0.004 (-0.255 to +0.241) against d0 at day+2 (post hoc, with a wide interval). The oracle shift puts too few sunny actuals below the 0.05 quantile as well (0.002 to 0.015, against 0.05; the ENS shift puts 0.010 to 0.027 there), so member noise cannot be the only source of a lower tail that is too wide.

docs.title: What it could not show
docs.text:
• The hinge test has little power. Its half-width is 0.13 points, as set out under cause a.
  • The folds are weeks of the valid time. One forecast run spans up to 3 valid middays and can fall into both folds, which mildly favours every repair. The intervals resample fixed fits and are somewhat narrow. The free intercept of the hinge and the line favours both against the coefficient repair.
  • Hour of day and month are untested as causes. The 2 hour bins differ by at most 0.09 within a month, and the month differences come from one summer.
  • The coastal flag rests on a coarse coastline (7 coastline points and a 10 km threshold), and 2 of 5 Primaries qualify.
  • The experiment cannot say which of the six causes of a slope below 1 is at work. Several can act together.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: A design for PVDIS-5 (the planned retest of the solar term with weekly capacity estimates) could fit the solar coefficient per lead band and season on the ENS shift, test non-inferiority against d0, and report no clipping knee. The margin of 0.10 points of capacity was set in the plan: it is about 2% of d0's mean quantile score of 4.62 points, and close to the 0.104 points by which d0's radiation inputs improved on d1l over April to September. A margin as large as the whole effect of the radiation inputs is generous. On these summer-midday rows the gap between d1l and d0 is about 0.27 points. The PVDIS-5 plan could confirm 0.10 or halve it to 0.05 after a power calculation. Non-inferiority means the upper end of the 95% interval of (solar term minus d0) lies below the margin. The fitted shift's upper end here is +0.110 over 13 weeks at day+2 and day+3 (post hoc), and the half-width of about 0.23 would fall to about 0.16 with 25 weeks, so a pass at 0.10 needs a true difference below about -0.06. Resampling at least 25 weeks of forecast start (April to September) and repeating the test for 0 to 48 hours separately would be sensible. A per-Primary clipping knee would need a different design: rows at or near the inverters' rated output, such as the clearest days at midday, a hinge fitted after the coefficient repair, and more than two coastal series.

docs.title: Experiment 52: do more weather forecasts lower the wind farms' error at 1 to 2 days ahead?
docs.text:
Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts did not resolve any gain at 1 to 2 days ahead. The best guess is the quantile forecast of wind-farm power from experiment 33. It is built from the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast (ENS) and a wind-power model trained on ERA5, the ECMWF estimate of past weather. We fed that wind-power model the 100 m wind forecast of ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional weather model) and of the ECMWF high-resolution forecast (IFS, on a 0.25 degree grid). We then averaged each quantile with the best guess's, using weights chosen only on earlier months. Over the three metered wind farms, the average scored 0.055 points of capacity better (a lower quantile score is better) than the best guess at lead days 1 and 2. The 95% interval, -0.200 to +0.072, includes zero, so the experiment cannot say whether the extra forecasts help.

Inconclusive: at lead days 1 and 2, the primary blend (the best guess averaged with ICON-EU and IFS) scores 0.055 points of capacity better, with a 95% interval of -0.200 to +0.072. A lead day counts calendar days from the date of the ENS run, so lead days 1 and 2 are the two days after the run's date. This decisive contrast (C1) must lie wholly below -0.15 for the verdict supported. The same contrast over all leads (C2) is +0.018 (-0.020 to +0.054) and does not change the verdict. The intervals resample whole months and the three seeds, so they describe these three farms and cannot speak for other farms. The prediction (-0.2 to -0.4 at days 1 and 2) was too large.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
The blend scores 0.055 points better at lead days 1 and 2, 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6 (because of the spread factor), and the same from day 7, where no product exists. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better). Coverage is the share of cases inside the 5% to 95% band, which is nominally 0.90. At lead days 1 and 2 the share of cases above the 0.95 quantile is 0.053 for the best guess and 0.056 for the blend. The cases are three farms, three seeds, and the 53 Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026.

Scope Best guess Primary blend Cases Coverage, best guess Coverage, blend Lead day 0 6.722 6.525 13,695 0.902 0.903 Lead days 1 and 2 6.701 6.646 44,328 0.909 0.901 Lead days 3 to 6 9.702 9.824 88,716 0.909 0.917 Lead days 7 and later 13.154 13.154 174,624 0.916 0.916 All leads 11.037 11.054 321,363 0.912 0.914

Per farm, the two arms differ by at most 0.07 points over all leads. The best guess scores 10.67, 12.38, and 10.06 at W1, W2, and W3, and the primary blend 10.68, 12.36, and 10.13.

docs.title: What else the numbers show
docs.text:
All reads in this section are exploratory.

  • The farms disagree at lead days 1 and 2. The primary blend minus the best guess is -0.087 (-0.330 to +0.156) at W1, -0.233 (-0.447 to -0.035) at W2, and +0.151 (+0.028 to +0.287) at W3.

  • The blend scores worse at lead days 3 to 6 only because of the spread factor. The primary blend minus the best guess is +0.122 (+0.028 to +0.221) at days 3 to 6, and +0.005 (0.000 to +0.016) without the spread factor. From August the chosen weights there are 1, 0, and 0, so the blend equals the best guess, but the spread factor (1.65 in August, 1.35 in September, 1.2 in October) was fitted on earlier months blended under other weights. At day 0 the contrast is -0.197 (-0.460 to +0.051).
  • At day 0, 8 of the 16 blend contrasts exclude zero. They are all four with GFS, the two one-weight arms with ICON-EU alone, and the two one-weight arms with ICON-EU and IFS. The best guess averaged with the US Global Forecast System (GFS), also from the Open-Meteo archive, scores -0.229 (-0.371 to -0.090). These reads are many, correlated, and chosen after the fact.
  • No single extra product resolves a gain at lead days 1 and 2. The best guess averaged with ICON-EU only gives -0.053 (-0.199 to +0.079), with IFS only +0.071 (-0.034 to +0.185), and with GFS only -0.069 (-0.172 to +0.034). The IFS arm with one weight is worse, +0.101 (+0.036 to +0.194).
  • Each product's own forecast is far worse than the best guess at lead days 1 and 2. With a spread factor (a multiplier that widens each quantile band about its median), ICON-EU's own forecast scores 2.469 points worse, IFS's 1.264, and GFS's 1.853. The wind-power model receives raw product winds with no bias correction, so the gap may reflect that mismatch and not only the ensemble's advantage; the experiment does not test which.

Over the first 6 months, the plan's stop rule (drop any product more than 1.0 points worse) fired for all three products. The exploratory arms ran for all three products anyway, and the primary arm was fixed before the run. - At lead days 1 and 2, the chosen weights stayed mostly on the best guess. Averaged over the scored months, days 1 and 2 gave 0.72 to the best guess, 0.24 to ICON-EU, and 0.05 to IFS. Day 0 gave 0.51, 0.34, and 0.15. Days 3 to 6 gave 0.94, 0.03, and 0.03, which is 1, 0, and 0 in every month from August; July, with no history, used equal weights. One weight for all leads (-0.060, -0.200 to +0.065, at days 1 and 2) scored about the same as weights per lead band (-0.055). - Widening the quantile bands with a spread factor did not help. Without it, the primary blend minus the best guess is -0.080 (-0.217 to +0.039) at lead days 1 and 2 and -0.018 (-0.043 to +0.005) over all leads. The factors ranged 1.0 to 1.25 for days 0 to 2 and 1.0 to 1.65 for days 3 and later. - The placebo passes: weight selection rejected the shuffled forecasts, and its positive score comes from two other steps. The placebo shuffles the product forecasts among cases of the same farm, month, lead day, and time of day. In every month after July the chosen weights are 1, 0, and 0, so the placebo equals the best guess apart from July (equal weights, no history) and the spread step. It scores +0.343 (+0.061 to +0.762) at lead days 1 and 2.

docs.title: How the experiment was run, and where it departs from the plan
docs.text:
• Cases and benchmark: the 53 Tuesday runs of experiment 33's wind best guess (bg_full), three farms and three seeds, scored on its stored half-hourly cases. The farms are labelled W1 to W3.
  • Product age: previous_day(d+1) selects runs about half a day older than the ENS run (0 to 24 hours older, depending on the hour of day). The service reads at 09:00 UTC, so the 00 UTC runs of ICON-EU and IFS from the ENS run's own date would be available. The experiment therefore tests deliberately aged products, which rules out lookahead and handicaps the products.
  • July: July 2025 has no earlier months, so it uses equal weights and no spread factor. At lead days 1 and 2 the primary blend minus the best guess is +0.188 in July, against a mean of -0.070 over the other eleven monthly differences, and July's cases shape the factors of August onwards.
  • Product forecast: experiment 33's ERA5-trained wind-power model, refitted per seed on valid times before 2025-06-17, fed each product's wind at the farm's grid point from Open-Meteo's Previous Runs archive. A case at lead day d reads previous_day(d+1), which the archive defines as a run initialised at least that many days before the hour, so the run was initialised no later than 00 UTC on the ENS run's date. The experiment did not check that definition against the archive itself; the matched-lead study checked it on GFS for 2 days. A case beyond a product's horizon (ICON-EU after lead day 3) or with a missing value keeps the best guess.
  • Blend: the average of each quantile level, with weights on a grid of quarters chosen per lead band on earlier months only, then a spread factor fitted on earlier cases. The spread factor is fitted for lead days 0 to 2 pooled and days 3 and later pooled, so that each fit has enough cases; the plan said per lead band. A half-hour valid time takes its speed and direction from the averaged east-west and north-south wind components of the two hours either side.
  • Not run: the solar arm (the matched-lead study found no solar gain at this lead), AIFS (the ECMWF machine-learning forecast, which needs its own rows because its weather-model version changes over time), and the climatology row.
  • ICON-EU's mean 100 m wind speed is highest (8.90 m/s) and IFS's lowest (7.56), against 8.18 for ERA5. GFS is 8.00. Each product's mean covers only the cases it covers, so the comparison flags a bias without measuring it. ICON-EU's 100 m wind is Open-Meteo's rescaling of its 120 m level.
  • The plan and code reviews found no leakage. The Sonnet code review noted that the availability check in e00052_fit.py cannot fire, because the lead rule already guarantees availability. Code: ml-experiments/00052-more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms/.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Whether the products help when read at the service's own time. The next experiment should feed the 00 UTC runs of ICON-EU and IFS from the ENS run's own date, correct each product's wind speed for bias, and fit the spread factor on blends made under the same weights. A day 0 test needs more wind farms than the three metered ones can supply, and the day 0 reads here (GFS in particular) were generated after the fact, so a confirmation must name them in advance.

docs.title: Experiment 53: does the UKV forecast the solar anomaly better than ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether the Met Office UKV (a 2 km weather model of the United Kingdom that runs to 2 to 5 days ahead) predicts how sunny each half-hour will be better than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble forecast (ENS) that the forecast uses today. We converted each forecast's sunshine into the output of a generic solar fleet, subtracted that forecast's own monthly average for each half-hour of the day (the "anomaly"), and compared the result with the anomaly of satellite-based sunshine estimates from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) at 5 Primary substations, on 72 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The UKV alone was worse than ENS at every lead time. A mix of ENS and UKV, with weights fitted on the earlier 15 months, had a squared error 4% to 14% lower than ENS within 2 days in a cross-validation on those 15 months. In the validation year its correlation with CAMS was higher than ENS's by only 0.02 to 0.03 within 24 hours, and several of those gains are within the range that chance alone could produce. The mix was no better beyond 54 hours. The one UKV we found with a long matching history is the CEDA archive, which differs from the live UKV and is licensed for non-commercial use, so any gain is an upper bound. This experiment was run post hoc and was not pre-registered, as explained below.

The verdict is small gain for the blend, and no gain for the UKV alone. The blend clears the 1% cross-validation margin of the stage 1 gate in every lead band within 54 hours, and the UKV alone clears it in none (relative mean squared error +12% to +31% against ENS). The gate therefore does not stop the experiment as refuted, and the verdict follows the pre-stated all-months gate. The correlation evidence from the validation year is weaker than the gate: the blend-minus-ENS interval touches zero at 0 to 6 hours (+0.019, -0.000 to +0.038) and includes zero over 0 to 54 hours (+0.011, -0.006 to +0.027), and at 48 to 54 hours the blend's validation mean squared error (0.0382) is worse than ENS's (0.0337), although the cross-validation says the blend is 3.8% better there. As the brief says, the experiment stops at the gate: the demand contrasts were not run, and the manager decides whether to run them (see "The demand step was not run").

What was fixed beforehand and what was chosen after seeing results. The brief for PVDIS-8b and the PVDIS-8 plan fixed the three arms (ENS, UKV alone, a fitted blend), the lead bands, the 1% margin, and the 15-fold month-block cross-validation before any score existed. No prediction was written down. The ukv3w control and the t54_late variant were added after the first scores were seen, so they are post hoc, and neither changes the verdict.

All figures are for 5 Primary substations (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, anonymised as in experiment 46), daylight half-hours of April to September, valid from July 2025 to June 2026, on 72 forecast runs (one every 5 days). The 1,000 to 4,714 half-hour rows per lead band come from only 6 or 7 calendar months of forecast origin (July to September 2025 and March to June 2026), so every interval below, which resamples those months, understates the true uncertainty.

docs.title: What was compared, and when each forecast would have been available
docs.text:
Lead is counted from the forecast origin that the production service has, which is the 00 UTC ENS run plus 9 hours, 09:00 UTC. Each arm uses the freshest forecast available at that origin.

  • ENS is the daily 00 UTC run, as in experiment 46.
  • UKV, t54 is the 06 UTC run of the same day (leads to 54 hours from the run, so to 51 hours from the origin), assuming a run is available 3 hours after its initialisation.
  • UKV, t120 is the 03 UTC run of the same day, whose T120 files reach 120 hours from the run (114 hours from the origin, since the run starts 6 hours before the origin).
  • UKV, t54_late is the 00 UTC run of the same day, a sensitivity check that assumes the 06 UTC run is not yet available (leads to 45 hours from the origin).
  • CAMS is the reference: experiment 39's half-hour irradiance for the substation, kept where CAMS reliability is at least 0.9.

The five arms are ENS alone, the UKV alone (native steps), the blend, and two controls that separate the time resolution of the UKV from its skill. Control ukv3h subsamples the UKV to ENS's 3-hourly steps and passes the instantaneous values through the production ENS resampler, labelled as if they were ENS's 3-hour window means, as the maintainer asked. Control ukv3w first forms 3-hour window means from the UKV (the trapezoid mean of the instantaneous values inside each window) and then uses the same resampler. The second control was added after the first scores because the first has a half-window timing error built in: in the hour-of-day figure below, the mean fleet output u of ukv3h peaks at 10 UTC, while CAMS, ENS, the UKV, and ukv3w all peak at 12 UTC.

The calibration is a slope through the origin of the CAMS anomaly on a forecast's anomaly, fitted per series and lead band on the training window (valid times to 2025-06-30), leaving out site-band cells with fewer than 50 fitting rows. The blend regresses the CAMS anomaly on the ENS and UKV anomalies, with two coefficients and no intercept, and its weights are fitted rather than equal. Fitted on the whole training window, the ENS weight is 0.57 to 0.83 per series and band and the UKV weight is 0.17 to 0.46, with no negative weight (t54).

Each source's climatology keeps, for every valid time, the run with the shortest lead. The same rule applies to ENS, the UKV, and the controls, so they have the same lead mix. Experiment 46 averages its ENS climatology over all leads instead. The two ENS climatologies correlate at 0.998, and the rebuilt ENS anomaly correlates with experiment 46's calibrated ENS anomaly at 0.986 to 0.989 (t120, t54, t54_late). That difference follows from the lead rule and is not a defect, so the script requires only a correlation above 0.98.

The cross-validation removes the held-out month from the climatology. The fitted climatology therefore uses the neighbouring months only for a held-out month other than April to June, which has two neighbours inside the window, while the validation scores use the full 15-month climatology. This affects every arm alike.

The latency of the 06 UTC run is assumed, not measured. The t54 arm assumes that the 06 UTC run is available 3 hours after its initialisation, so just in time for the 09:00 UTC origin, with no slack. No source for the real delivery time of the live UKV was checked. The t54_late and t120 arms are the cautious readings. The latency at which the blend's gain would disappear was not measured: even when the 06 UTC run is replaced by the 00 UTC run (a delay of more than 3 hours), the blend's cross-validated error is still 3.6% to 7.7% lower in every band.

docs.title: Shortwave conventions and how each was aligned with CAMS
docs.text:
CAMS and ENS are half-hour or window means labelled at the period end, and the UKV and MOGREPS-UK are instantaneous values, so only the UKV and MOGREPS-UK need the interpolation.

Source Shortwave convention Valid-time stamp Alignment with CAMS CAMS (experiment 39) Half-hour mean irradiance End of the half-hour None needed ENS Mean over the native window (3 hours to 144 hours, 6 hours after) End of the window The production resampler _upsample_nwp_to_half_hourly shapes each window by the clear-sky index and conserves its energy, giving half-hour means ending at the stamp CEDA UKV, shortwave_down Instantaneous flux, not a mean The instant, init time plus step; hourly steps to 48 hours, then 3-hourly The clear-sky index (flux over the Haurwitz clear-sky flux at the same instant) at each step is interpolated linearly in time to the midpoint of each half-hour, then multiplied by the clear-sky flux at that midpoint MOGREPS-UK, shortwave_total Instantaneous, as the archive notes (no cell methods or time bounds in the files) The instant; hourly steps The same as the UKV

The same fleet chain then turns each half-hour irradiance into u. A clear-sky index is only formed where the clear-sky flux is at least 20 W/m2, and a midpoint more than 3 hours from a usable step takes the nearest step's index, so nothing is interpolated across a night. Beyond 48 hours the native UKV steps are 3-hourly, so the interpolation there spans 3 hours. The index is capped at 1.5. Each site's UKV value is the cell whose centre is nearest (the largest distance is 1.09 km).

docs.title: Raw data first
docs.text:
The UKV anomaly follows the CAMS anomaly, with a wider scatter than ENS. The panels show the calibrated forecast anomaly against the CAMS anomaly at leads under 24 hours. The ukv3h control is visibly the worst, with a flat top.

All sources peak at 12 UTC, as CAMS does, so no label is shifted, except the ukv3h control, whose mean u peaks at 10 UTC. The UKV's mean u is 0.875 of CAMS's at leads under 24 hours and ENS's mean u is 1.023 of CAMS's. A multiplicative bias of the UKV does not affect its anomaly, which is taken against its own climatology.

The number of blocks with a higher correlation is 5, 6, 5, 5, 3, 3, and 5 of 7 in the same bands.

Time resolution is not what limits the UKV. The ukv3w control, which forms 3-hour window means from the hourly UKV as ENS delivers its flux, scores 0.019 higher in correlation than the native steps over 0 to 54 hours (0.011 to 0.027) and has a lower mean squared error by 4.2% (2.3% to 6.2%). The literal ukv3h control scores 0.122 lower than the native steps over 0 to 54 hours (-0.150 to -0.093), because the instantaneous values stand in for window means, which moves the peak of its mean u from 12 UTC to 10 UTC.

The next table gives the calibration slope (ideal 1) and the mean squared error of the calibrated anomaly, on the same rows as the correlations:

docs.title: The stage 1 gate on the training window
docs.text:
The blend clears the 1% margin in every band within 54 hours and the UKV alone in none. The table gives the cross-validated mean squared error relative to ENS, pooled over the five verdict series (t54). The last column restricts the same cross-validation to the folds of local months April to September, the months the validation year scores. The verdict follows the all-months column, as the decision rule states.

Lead ENS (mean squared error) UKV alone Blend ukv3w control Blend, April to September folds only 0-6 h 0.0257 +13.8% -13.8% +7.7% -14.1% 6-12 h 0.0083 +12.5% -11.5% +3.8% -11.9% 12-24 h 0.0078 +12.3% -5.6% +9.8% -5.0% 24-48 h 0.0198 +30.5% -5.4% +23.1% -5.8% 48-54 h 0.0365 +20.8% -3.8% +22.2% -2.1% 0-54 h pooled 0.0208 +22.3% -7.6% +17.4% -7.4%

The April to September column shows the same gain as the all-months column (-7.4% against -7.6% pooled), and the UKV alone is worse by 22.8% in those months, so the winter months do not drive the result.

For t120 the blend is 3.4% lower pooled over 0 to 120 hours and 1.1% lower at 54 to 120 hours, just over the 1% margin, while the validation correlation gain at 54 to 120 hours is +0.004 (-0.020 to +0.025). If the 06 UTC run were not available at the origin (t54_late), the UKV alone is worse by 18.2% to 41.5% in the bands to 48 hours, and the blend is still lower by 3.6% to 7.7% in every band.

docs.title: The check on MOGREPS-UK
docs.text:
MOGREPS-UK, the live ensemble of the Met Office, is no better than ENS on 14 days of overlap with CAMS. Its point estimates are above ENS's in some bands, but an equal-weight blend is not distinguishable from ENS. MOGREPS-UK has 3 members and about 7 weeks of archive (27 August to 16 October 2026), so nothing was calibrated or fitted. The blend here averages the two anomalies with equal weight. The check starts after the holdout date of 2026-07-01, so it uses holdout-period data that no calibration touched, outside the validation year. MOGREPS-UK is anomalised against the CAMS climatology of experiment 46, while ENS is anomalised against ENS's own climatology, so MOGREPS-UK's bias is not removed. The mean squared error of MOGREPS-UK is therefore unfavourable, and its correlation is not affected. CAMS ends on 11 September 2026, so the reference covers only 14 forecast origin days (27 August to 10 September). Correlation with the CAMS anomaly, 95% interval from resampling whole origin days:

At 6 to 12 hours, 12 to 24 hours, and 48 to 54 hours, the point estimates of MOGREPS-UK and of the blend are above ENS's, but every interval overlaps ENS's widely, on 12 to 14 days. Over all 49 origin days from 27 August 2026, the MOGREPS-UK anomaly correlates with the ENS anomaly at 0.768 within 24 hours, 0.699 at 24 to 54 hours, and 0.545 at 54 to 120 hours. That correlation between the two anomalies is not a skill score, because neither anomaly is the reference. MOGREPS-UK's mean u is 0.303 against ENS's 0.373 and CAMS's 0.378 on those rows.

docs.title: The demand step was not run
docs.text: Experiment 46's contrasts C3 and C6 (the demand forecast with the solar term, at 0 to 48 hours) were not run with the blend. The blend's gain is a ceiling from a product that is not the live one (the CEDA UKV) and whose licence is non-commercial. The interval of the blend's gain over ENS across 0 to 54 hours includes zero (+0.011, -0.006 to +0.027). The scores here predict a change in the demand contrast of the order of a 0.02 gain in correlation, which experiment 46's intervals (half-widths of 0.13 to 0.32 points of capacity at 0 to 48 hours) could not resolve. A non-live product with a licence that forbids production is a weak case for the spend, so the manager decides whether to run the contrasts.

docs.title: What these data could not show
docs.text:
• The live UKV is not the CEDA UKV. The CEDA archive differs statistically from the live feed, the CEDA licence is non-commercial, and the live product has no history at the Primaries, so the blend's gain is a ceiling.
  • The delivery delay of the 06 UTC run is assumed. See "What was compared" above: it was not measured, and the blend's gain survived the t54_late reading, so no latency at which it disappears was found.
  • The demand-forecast effect is untested. A 0.02 gain in correlation of the anomaly need not carry through experiment 46's solar term, whose coefficient the residual fitted below 1.
  • The 48 to 54 hour band is thin. It holds 1,225 rows from leads of 48 to 51 hours and its intervals are wide.
  • Calibration and the blend use 15 months. Each source's climatology is fitted on the same 15 months, with neighbouring local months pooled as in experiment 46.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The manager decides whether to run experiment 46's C3 and C6 contrasts at 0 to 48 hours with the blend's anomaly. See "The demand step was not run" for why the case is weak.

docs.title: Experiment 54: does UKV, learned from its own history, help the wind-farm forecast?
docs.text:
Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to a wind-farm forecast that already uses the European Centre's ensemble (ENS) lowered the error by about 0.2 points of the farms' capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead, a small but real gain, so the verdict is small gain. The error is the quantile score, a measure of how well a forecast's range of likely power fits what happened, and 1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity. The 95% interval is 0.07 to 0.32 points, so the 0.15-point gain we decided in advance would justify a new weather feed lies inside it. UKV, the Met Office's 2 km weather forecast, adds information and does not replace ENS: UKV alone scores 0.88 points worse than ENS alone. The UKV data come from a research archive (CEDA), not the live feed, so even this is an upper limit on what a service could get. We tested it by training XGBoost models, each on its own forecast history, for three metered wind farms, with the same training window and settings, at 24 to 54 hours after the ENS run's 00 UTC start (UKV's forecasts stop at 54 hours). The next step is to find or build a live UKV history for the farms, or to test UKV at lead day 0, the first 24 hours, where a live history exists.

UKV helps as an addition to ENS, and the gain is not an artefact of extra columns. The placebo (the UKV values shuffled among similar rows) differs from ENS alone by no more than 0.04 points (+0.013, -0.012 to +0.040). At W1 the gain is clear (-0.413), at W2 it probably exists (-0.198, with the end of its interval nearest zero at -0.000), and at W3 there is none (+0.018). The 95% interval excludes a gain larger than 0.32 points at these three farms. The ENS-only model scored 0.218 points better than experiment 33's ERA5-trained best guess at these leads, but the interval (-0.472 to +0.069) includes zero, so that comparison is unresolved.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The primary contrast C1 is the ENS-plus-UKV arm minus the ENS-only arm, for cases 24 to 54 hours after the 00 UTC start of the ENS run's date. UKV's leads stop at 54 hours, so these cases are lead day 1 and the first 6 hours of lead day 2. C1 is -0.198 (95% interval -0.316 to -0.069; 28,230 cases, three farms, three seeds, whole months re-drawn), and the pre-registered threshold was -0.15 for the end of the interval nearest zero (-0.069 here). The CEDA archive is not the live product: its licence is non-commercial (from the archive's catalogue) and the UKV-CEDA blends study found it statistically different from the live feed. The page therefore reports the result as a ceiling: a gain a matched UKV might add, not one a service could now deliver. The prediction was -0.2 to -0.5, and -0.198 is at the weak end of that range.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Arm B scores best at 24 to 54 hours (5.921), and arm C, UKV alone, scores worst (7.000). The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better). Coverage is the share of cases inside the 5% to 95% band (nominally 0.90), and the 0.95 column is the share above the 0.95 quantile. Arm A is the ENS-only XGBoost model, B adds UKV, C is UKV alone, and the placebo is B with the UKV values shuffled.
