  • The offset adds to the analogues. A3E minus A3, the offset's gain on top of the analogues, is -0.121 (-0.157 to -0.086).
  • The offset carries solar information. C5 (planned) shows the offset beats its twin by 0.246 (0.173 to 0.322), and experiment 64 found the same direction (0.300).
  • At night the analogues are close to random days. At night rows of April to September, A3 minus A3S is -0.020 (-0.042 to +0.002), A3 minus R0 is -0.006 (-0.030 to +0.017), and E minus R0 is +0.004 (-0.001 to +0.009).
  • Radiation inputs help the reference too. R0_rad minus R0 is -0.120 (-0.151 to -0.090), a context read that no contrast uses.
  • Coverage. The 0.05 quantile lies above the actual power on 13.5% to 15.0% of sunny rows in every arm, and the 0.95 quantile lies above it on 80.6% to 82.9% of cloudy rows.
  • No analogue exists for 8.7% of rows (a bank holiday, or no day of the same type with observed power and CAMS data in the window), and 89.4% of rows have all 3.

Seeds 1 and 2 changed no planned contrast by more than 0.003 points. The widths of the intervals come from the weeks of forecast start, not from fit noise. The verdict from seeds 0 to 2 together is also inconclusive (C3 lower end -0.048, C4 upper end +0.016). The seed check is post hoc.

docs.title: Which predictions held
docs.text: Prediction made in the plan Result C1 at -0.10 to -0.25 Held: -0.149 C2 at -0.02 to -0.10 Held, at the end of the range: -0.095 E beats A3 by 0.03 to 0.20 Held in the point estimate (+0.054); the interval includes zero C4 within -0.03 to +0.02 Not met: -0.066, with an interval from -0.149 to +0.015 E_twin worse than E by 0.15 to 0.35 Held: 0.246 A3S worse than A3 by 0.01 to 0.06 Not met: 0.081, slightly beyond the range A3 and A3S within 0.02 at night Not met, at the edge: -0.020 (-0.042 to +0.002)

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
The experiment departed from its plan in four ways, none of which changes the hypothesis, the prediction, or the decision rule.

  1. A ninth arm, R0_rad, was fitted as context. It enters no contrast.
  2. Seeds 1 and 2 were fitted after the verdict, as a post hoc check.
  3. The prediction sets are stored under lower-case names, r0, e, a3, and so on, for seed 0, and with the suffix -s012 for seeds 0 to 2, because a stored set cannot be overwritten.
  4. The common starting level is the median of the training labels, not zero. Experiments 76 and 78 found that starting from XGBoost's estimated base score raises the score by 0.07 to 0.10 points against a start at zero in the same pipeline. The plan gave every arm one common level so that the contrasts do not carry that effect. Whether a start at zero would change R0, or the ranking of the arms, is not tested.

Limits that the plan stated hold. The capacity table is experiment 64's and is 5% to 19% below experiment 45's 2025/26 values, which experiment 78 found worsens am by about 0.02 points. The weights and the sunshine calibration are fixed on data to 2025-06-30. The analogues are matched in training to the ensemble-mean sunshine and at inference to each member's own, which widens the pooled spread of the analogue arms. The candidates share a half-hour of the day in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), so a window that straddles a clock change shifts a local-time profile by an hour. The placebo twin of E is a cyclic shift over the whole window's rows. A donor for a row from the early window may therefore be a forecast issued after that refit. Only a sunshine anomaly crosses that boundary. No power or label does.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test the analogue columns on top of the offset with more forecast weeks, one analogue, and a variant matched on the day type alone. A second validation year with as many weeks (experiment R11, which needs the ENS backfill) would cut the half-width of C4 from 0.08 to about 0.06, because the half-width falls with the square root of the number of weeks. That is still above 0.05, so the plan should either set the threshold near 0.06 or ask for a third year. The plan should also read sunny and cloudy rows separately and add the day-type-only variant, because C6 does not separate the sunshine from the day type. The decision whether to port either way belongs to the maintainer and the roadmap. The offset costs a table of capacities and weights. The analogue columns cost the last 3 to 16 days of telemetry, a CAMS-like sunshine record, and a bank-holiday calendar at every forecast.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
Plan review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: give every arm one starting level, state the rule that separates small gain from supported, rebuild the training inputs for the whole P-roll window, state how E_twin is trained, note the column-count difference between arms, one definition of day type, and the prose faults. Rejected: none.

Code review (Sonnet), triaged. No leakage and no wrong join. Accepted: add the ninth arm to the plan, make the guard in known_rows check the origin as well as the valid time, and state the mismatch between the training and inference sunshine shape. Rejected: a check of an A3 variant matched to the ensemble-mean shape at inference, because the arm of experiment 64 shares the same design and the experiment answers the plan's question without it.

Number check (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: the September value, the context scores copied from experiment 74's own printout, the night prediction row, the half-width range, the exploratory labels, the claim that the monthly figures have no interval, and the unsupported statement that a second year would resolve a 0.05-point gain. Rejected: none.

Prose review (Sonnet), triaged. Accepted: an opening that defines every term before use, a legend of the arms, the four verdicts, the pronoun and bare-noun fixes, the money-metaphor fixes, and the research-log rewrites. Rejected: moving all the legend ahead of the take-home paragraph, which would bury the conclusion.

docs.title: Experiment 76: does experiment 64's gain beyond 10 days come from a leak?
docs.text:
Take-home message: we found no route for a leak, and a refit with no solar term at all reproduces the gain of experiment 64's best arm at 10 days and beyond. The gain therefore matches the XGBoost model starting its fit at zero, which happens whenever a base margin is supplied, and not the solar offset. A caveat limits that reading: the reference model d1l was fitted in experiment 46's pipeline, so a refit of d1l in this pipeline would show whether the start-at-zero effect is real.

We asked whether the lower error of experiment 64's arm am at forecast leads of 10 days and beyond could come from information that was not available at forecast time. In am, the XGBoost model starts from a base margin: a starting prediction, added to each row, equal to the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be, times a weight fitted on the training years. The weight, and so the margin, is zero from 10 days. Yet am still scored 0.082 points below the best guess d0 there. The score is the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a Primary substation's capacity. A Primary substation feeds 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network. d0 is experiment 33's best-guess recipe, and d1l is the same recipe without the radiation inputs, from experiment 46.

We read the code and checked the margin at every training row and at the validation rows at 10 days and beyond in the first 8 forecast runs of each series. We also made two new sets of forecasts. am0 is am refitted with a margin of zero in every row, so that it starts from zero like am and carries no solar term. am_train_only is the stored am model predicted with the margin set to zero at every lead.

The verdict is supported. The prediction of no leak held. The prediction that am0 scores 0.03 to 0.08 points above am at 10 days and beyond held after the 14-day correction in size (0.035) but its interval reaches zero, and without the correction the difference is +0.004.

docs.title: The audit found no route for a leak
docs.text:
All 20 checks of e00076_audit.py pass, 4 for each of the 5 Primary substations.

  • The margin is zero from 10 days. Of the training rows, 98,965 to 98,973 per series have a lead of 10 days or more, and the largest margin among them is exactly 0. In the first 8 forecast runs, 1,784 validation rows per series have a lead of 10 days or more, and zeroing the margin changes none of their predictions. The weight is set to zero for those leads by construction, so this confirms that the lead bands agree and that the margin reaches the model as zero. At shorter leads, zeroing the margin changes the quantiles by up to 0.086 points.
  • Every training row is at or before 2025-06-30 23:30 UTC. The weights are cross-fitted on those rows, the capacity fit leaves out the week of 2025-06-30, and the calibration of the ensemble forecast of sunshine stops with an error if a row is outside the training window. The audit checks the training rows themselves. The weights, capacity, and calibration were checked by reading the code of experiments 46 and 64.
  • Prediction applies the margin once. Rebuilding am's predictions from its stored models with the margin that the validation code supplies reproduces experiment 64's stored quantiles exactly for seed 0 (largest difference 0).

Across all 5 series and 3 seeds, the 244,185 prediction rows at 10 days and beyond have raw quantiles that are identical between am_train_only and am (largest difference 0). At shorter leads they differ by up to 0.17 points of capacity.

docs.title: The gain matches a start-at-zero effect
docs.text:
Mean quantile score at 10 days and beyond, in points of capacity, after the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor: am 4.904, am0 4.939, am_train_only 4.941, d0 4.986, and d1l 5.025. Without the correction (the spread factor kept), am scores 4.739, am0 4.735, and d1l 4.837.

Contrast at 10 days and beyond Difference Interval am minus am0, corrected (offset in training) -0.035 -0.074 to +0.003 (98.33%) am0 minus d1l, corrected (start at zero) -0.086 -0.135 to -0.040 (98.33%) am minus d1l, corrected (whole effect) -0.121 -0.176 to -0.064 (98.33%) am minus am0, uncorrected +0.004 -0.012 to +0.021 (95%, exploratory) am0 minus d1l, uncorrected -0.102 -0.158 to -0.047 (95%, exploratory) am minus d1l, uncorrected -0.098 -0.150 to -0.048 (95%, exploratory) am minus d0, corrected (experiment 64) -0.082 -0.126 to -0.038 (95%, exploratory) d1l minus d0, corrected +0.039 +0.006 to +0.074 (95%, exploratory) am_train_only minus am, corrected +0.037 +0.001 to +0.072 (95%, exploratory)

A negative difference means that the first arm has the lower error. The three corrected decision contrasts are read at 98.33%, which is a 95% interval split across three contrasts (a Bonferroni correction). Every other row is exploratory, meaning that it is not in the decision rule, and is read at 95%. All intervals come from 50,000 resamples that draw whole ISO weeks of forecast start (26 weeks at 10 days and beyond) and the 3 seeds, on 21,658 scored rows per seed.

The decision rule, as written before any code ran, names the effect a start-point effect. The rule applies when am0 minus d1l has an upper end below zero and am minus am0 does not, and the corrected rows meet both conditions. The uncorrected rows agree: the offset in training adds +0.004 (-0.012 to +0.021), and the refit with no solar term accounts for all of the gap to d1l.

The 14-day correction moves the corrected contrasts by about 0.03 points, because it uses each arm's own recent errors. am_train_only scores 0.037 points worse than am at 10 days and beyond although its raw quantiles are identical. We infer that the correction, which adds the mean of an arm's own recent median errors, carries the margin's effect from shorter leads into the longer ones. The uncorrected rows remove that route, and the corrected am minus am0 of -0.035 shrinks to +0.004.

The XGBoost model am0 scores worse than d0 at leads under 10 days (+0.051, interval +0.002 to +0.099, exploratory). Starting at zero therefore does not help at every lead. The mean scores at those leads are 4.267 for am and 4.502 for am0, so the solar offset lowers the error there by about 0.24 points, which agrees with experiment 64 (no interval computed here).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The start-at-zero reading is not isolated. d1l is experiment 46's stored model, and am0 is fitted in experiment 64's pipeline, so any difference between the two pipelines is in the contrast. The mechanism, that an XGBoost model given a base margin starts from zero instead of from its estimated base score, is the documented behaviour of XGBoost and is not tested here.
  • The validation rows are experiment 64's. They are daylight half-hours at five Primary substations from July to September 2025 and from April to June 2026, and the result is measured on 26 weeks of forecast start at 10 days and beyond.

docs.title: What a next experiment could answer
docs.text: A refit of d1l in this pipeline, with the same seeds, compared with am0, would show whether the start-at-zero gain is real. If the two matched, the gain beyond 10 days would be an artefact of the pipelines. If am0 stayed lower, the base score of the production XGBoost model would merit a test of its own.

docs.title: Experiment 77: does the fitted solar shape lower the error of arm am? (PVDIS-6b)
docs.text:
Take-home message: the shape of the solar panels in the solar term does not limit experiment 64's best forecast. Experiment 64 forecast a substation's power with an XGBoost model (a gradient- boosted tree model) that starts from an explicit solar term: the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be. We call that forecast arm am. Replacing its south-facing panel shape with a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing shapes, fitted to each substation's own power, left the error unchanged, and so did using another substation's blend. What did matter was the forecast of the sunshine itself: giving the same arm the sunshine of another date worsened the score by 0.32 points (the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better). The next work on the solar term should go into the sunshine forecast and the capacity table, not into the panel shape. The verdict is refuted, which here means that the fitted shape does not lower the error by 0.5% or more.

We asked whether a forecast of the power drawn at a Primary substation improves when its solar term is built from a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing panel output instead of south-facing panels only. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation in the electricity distribution network. Experiment 73 (PVDIS-6) found that the blend fits the half-hourly power of Primary substations 1.3% better than south-facing panels do, although the shares of the blend (the fraction of capacity assigned to each orientation) are not identified. We fitted one set of shares per substation on rows up to 30 June 2025, rebuilt the solar term of arm am with the blend, and scored the forecasts on the same rows as experiment 64: 5 Primaries, 68,903 daylight half-hours per seed in April to September, and 3 seeds (repeated fits with different random numbers). One point of the score is 1% of a substation's capacity. The blend scored 4.466 points and am 4.467.

The verdict is refuted, read by the rule written before any arm was scored. The rule uses three contrasts, each an arm's score minus another arm's, at a 98.33% interval from 50,000 resamples of whole weeks of forecast start. C1 is the fitted shape minus am. C2 is the fitted shape minus all-south panels at the fitted shape's tilt of 25 degrees, which separates mixing from the tilt change. C3 is the fitted shape minus its placebo twin, the same arm given the forecast sunshine of another date. The threshold is 0.5% of am's score, which is 0.022 points. The rule says refuted when the lower end of C1 is above -0.022 and the upper end is at most +0.022, so that a gain of 0.5% is excluded and a loss of 0.5% is not shown.

Contrast Difference 98.33% interval C1: fitted shape minus am -0.001 -0.018 to +0.014 C2: fitted shape minus all-south at tilt 25 -0.001 -0.014 to +0.011 C3: fitted shape minus its placebo twin -0.323 -0.441 to -0.212

The differences are in points of capacity, and negative favours the fitted shape. The interval of C1 has a half-width of 0.016 points, below the 0.022-point threshold, so the design could have seen a gain of 0.5% and did not.

docs.title: Every arm scores the same, except the placebo twin
docs.text:
The fitted shape, the all-south shape at either tilt, and another Primary's shape are not distinguishable. Absolute scores, in points of capacity, with 95% intervals from the same resampling:

Arm Quantile score d0, the best guess (experiment 33) 4.620 (4.294 to 4.946) am0, am without the solar term (experiment 76) 4.640 (4.295 to 4.977) am, all-south shape at tilt 35 (experiment 64) 4.467 (4.143 to 4.785) am_s25, all-south shape at tilt 25 4.467 (4.142 to 4.783) am_blend, the fitted shape 4.466 (4.144 to 4.781) am_shuffled, another Primary's fitted shape 4.465 (4.143 to 4.781) am_blend_twin, fitted shape with the sunshine of another date 4.789 (4.430 to 5.157)

The fitted shape minus the shuffled shape is +0.001 points (95% interval -0.006 to +0.007, exploratory). If the shares carried information about a Primary's panels, the shape fitted to the Primary's own power would score below the shape fitted to another Primary's. This agrees with experiment 73's finding that the shares are not identified, and the same holds for the forecast.

The forecast sunshine carries the gain. The fitted shape scores 0.173 points (95% interval -0.227 to -0.121) below am0, the same arm without a solar term, and 0.323 points below the same arm given the sunshine of another date. The fitted shape scores 0.153 points (-0.193 to -0.116) below d0, as am does in experiment 64. A season-year capacity vintage does more than the fitted shape: the fitted shape scores 0.017 points (+0.002 to +0.033) above experiment 78's am_sy.

docs.title: Lead time, series, and month show no gain either
docs.text: The fitted shape minus am has an interval that includes zero in every lead band, at each of the five series, and over leads under 48 hours (+0.006, -0.031 to +0.044). Beyond 10 days, where the weight of the solar term is zero, the difference is -0.010 points (-0.023 to +0.002), and experiment 76 found no route for a leak there. By local valid month the difference runs from -0.022 points in April to +0.019 in August with no pattern, on 29,715 to 39,663 rows per month over the three seeds.

docs.title: The fitted shapes, and the evening-west check
docs.text:
The five fitted shapes differ little from all-south panels at a tilt of 25 degrees. As Figure 2 shows, the five fitted shapes have a lower midday peak and a larger afternoon and evening share, by amounts small beside the error of the sunshine forecast. The shares behind them are a flexible shape and not a measurement of panel orientation: the south share is 0.06 to 0.15 at three of the five Primaries and 0.34 to 0.57 at the other two.

The evening-west check does not settle whether the west share is evening demand. For each Primary we removed the mean of each calendar cell (month, half-hour, and weekday or holiday) and the heating degree-days from the after-dark half-hours of April to September (18:00 to 23:30 local time) and regressed the remainder on that day's mean daytime cloud. The change from a clear to a fully cloudy day is +0.29 MW at D9 (95% interval +0.04 to +0.59), which has the largest fitted west capacity (3.04 MW), and between +0.01 and +0.10 MW at the other four, with intervals that include zero. Five Primaries give too few points to show a relation, and D9 is a low-power Primary with two training years. The check is descriptive and no verdict reads it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text: • Weights differ by arm only through the shape. Each arm refits the weight w on its own cross-fit of the same XGBoost model without a solar term. GPU fits are not exactly repeatable, so w carries a small amount of noise that differs between arms. The mean weights are -0.32 to -0.48 (blend) and -0.38 to -0.52 (all-south at tilt 25). - The capacity of the Primary D14 is scaled, not fitted. D14 has no 2024/25 weeks, so its capacity is experiment 64's capacity times the median ratio of the shape's capacity to experiment 64's at the other four series. - The capacity keeps the recovery ratio of the all-south shape. Each shape's capacity is divided by experiment 45's recovery ratio, which was measured with the all-south fleet shape and not with the blend. The weight w is refitted per arm and absorbs a constant scale error, so the effect is expected to be small, but it was not tested. - The shares of the Primary D9 rest on two training years. The other four Primaries have five or six. - The result is for ensemble-forecast sunshine at five Primaries in one trial area. A different weather forecast with less error could make the panel shape matter more.

docs.title: Candidate next experiments
docs.text:
The solar term of arm am is limited by its inputs, not its panel shape. The candidates that the evidence supports are a better sunshine forecast (experiment 50 and experiment 53 compared other weather forecasts) and a capacity table that is current (experiment 78 found a gain of 0.018 points from a season-year vintage).

The sections from here to the end are the plan as committed before any code ran. The last section lists the changes made after the plan and before any arm was scored.

docs.title: What is held fixed and what changes
docs.text:
One set of shares per Primary, fitted on the training window only, replaces the all-south shape. Experiment 73's pooled fit (one set of east, south, and west shares per Primary, shared by every season-year) is refitted on summer half-hours up to 2025-06-30 only, on experiment 73's plane-of-array shapes at a tilt of 25 degrees and a DC to AC ratio of 1.15. Experiment 73's own shares used rows up to 2026 and are not reused. The shares are held fixed across training years, which removes the median swing of 0.24 in the shares between consecutive season-years that experiment 73 found.

The blend replaces the all-south shape everywhere that the solar term is built. The CAMS shape, the CAMS and ENS climatologies, the ENS anomaly and its calibration slope per lead band, the capacity, and the weight w fitted on the training window are all rebuilt for the blend, by the code of experiments 46 and 64 with the plant output replaced by the blend of the three orientations' output. The per-member ENS anomaly is computed from the shortwave radiation of each of the 51 members, as in experiment 46. The weight w absorbs a scale error in the capacity, so the capacity keeps experiment 45's recovery ratio of the fleet shape; the Caveats section says what that choice does to the comparison.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• am_blend: arm am with the fitted shape.
  • am_s25: arm am with all-south panels at a tilt of 25 degrees, the control for the tilt change. The script prints the AC capacity of am_s25 and of am_blend for each series, and the weights w, so that a difference in level between the arms is visible.
  • am_blend_twin: am_blend with the forecast sunshine taken from another date, by experiment 64's permutation of runs within series, month, half-hour, and lead band. The donor run is the same for the east, south, and west anomalies, so the twin keeps their mutual timing.
  • am_shuffled: am with the shares of another Primary (a fixed cyclic permutation of the 5 series), refitted capacity and weight. This is exploratory.
  • Reference rows, read from experiment 64's stored predictions: am, am_twin, d0, d1l, climatology, and manual_heuristic.

Each XGBoost arm has 5 series and 3 seeds, 15 fits, with experiment 64's settings and column list. Each XGBoost model is trained on its own history.

docs.title: No fitted quantity sees the validation period
docs.text: Every fitted quantity is read with a valid time up to 2025-06-30 23:30 UTC, and the scripts assert it. The quantities are the shares, the AC capacity, the CAMS and ENS climatologies, the calibration slope per lead band, the weight w, and the 14-day correction and spread factor, which are refitted per arm on training rows only. Each script prints the latest timestamp of every table it fits. The shares are fitted on rows of shapes.parquet and the frame up to that time. The ENS members' half-hour irradiance is read from the archive and passed through the plane-of-array calculation for the east, south, and west orientations at 25 degrees, since the stored ENS tables hold only the fleet shape. The reliable-hour mask of the CAMS shapes must give the same scored rows as experiment 64's; where it does not, all arms are restricted to the intersection, and am is rescored on it.

docs.title: The evening-west check
docs.text: A west-leaning share at some Primaries may be evening demand and not solar. Experiment 73's advice recommends a check before the west share is read as solar. For each Primary, using training rows only, we remove the calendar cell and heating degree-days from the half-hours after dark (solar zenith above 90 degrees, 18:00 to 23:30 local time), and regress the remainder on that evening's mean cloud cover and on its mean temperature. If evening demand were the source of a west share, the after-dark residual would rise in dull weather, so a positive cloud slope is the expected sign. We tabulate, for each of the 5 Primaries, the slope as a share of the Primary's capacity beside its west share. With 5 Primaries, no rank correlation has power, so the table is descriptive, and no verdict uses it.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: prediction sets under data/ml-experiments/ (private, uncommitted); nothing in production.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes, in how the shares are fitted (fixed, or under a year-to-year penalty) and at which tilt. The plan fixes the shares across years because that choice removes the instability experiment 73 found, and uses am_s25 to separate tilt from mix.
  • Callers not nameable without searching: the code is copied from experiments 46 and 64, so the callers are known.
  • Size: medium. One Sonnet plan review, one Sonnet code review, one Sonnet write-up review, and one Sonnet prose review.

docs.title: Changes made after the plan was committed and before any arm was scored
docs.text: • The flat-timing control am_blend_flat is dropped. A reviewer of the code showed that a single scale on the south shape cancels: the calibration slope, the capacity, and the weight w absorb it, so the arm would equal am_s25. A per-cell version was not built. - The evening-west check regresses on the day's mean daytime cloud and heating degree-days. The frame holds no cloud measure after dark, because irradiance is zero then, so the cloud variable of the plan's "that evening" is the same day's daylight cloud. - The fallback capacity of the series with no 2024/25 constant (D14) is scaled by the shape. It is experiment 64's capacity times the median ratio of the shape's capacity to experiment 64's at the other four series. - Exploratory contrasts against am0 and am_sy are added, at the request of the experiment-manager session, because experiment 78 found that a zero base margin alone lowers d0's score. am0 is experiment 76's am without the solar term, and am_sy is experiment 78's am with a season-year capacity vintage.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed and departed from
docs.text:
• Followed: use am (a starting offset) and not an input column or a shift after the fit (experiment 64); describe the blend as a fitted solar shape and not as a measurement of orientation, and do not publish shares (experiment 73); hold the shares fixed across training years (experiment 73); check the west lean against after-dark demand (experiment 73).
  • Departed from: none.

docs.title: Experiment 78: does a re-estimated solar capacity lower the error? (PVDIS-5, check 2)
docs.text:
Take-home message: re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowers the quantile score of am, the best-scoring forecast of experiment 64, by only 0.018 points, so a capacity table refreshed about once a season-year is enough. The quantile score is an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity. A larger finding sits beside this one. XGBoost starts each model from an estimated starting prediction (its base score). Starting from zero instead lowered the score of the reference model d0 by 0.07 points, and by about 0.10 points for the model that carries no solar term, so part of the gain that experiment 64 reported over d0 was a start-at-zero effect. The solar term still lowers the score by 0.100 points against a d0 that starts from zero. The next experiment should test the starting point, which needs no extra production work to change.

We asked whether a better estimate of how much solar capacity sits behind each Primary substation improves a forecast of the substation's power. A Primary substation steps electricity down from 33 kV or 66 kV to 11 kV. Experiment 64 forecast power with an XGBoost model that starts from a solar term: the substation's solar capacity times a forecast of how sunny the day will be, added as a base margin (a fixed starting prediction supplied for each row). That experiment fixed the capacity at the value estimated from data before July 2025. Here we re-estimated the capacity before every forecast run from only the data available then, and predicted again with the same fitted XGBoost models. The score fell by 0.018 points. We also refitted two reference models, d1l and d0, to find out whether the start-at-zero effect that experiment 76 suspected is real. The start-at-zero effect is real.

The verdict is small gain. The pre-registered rule is in the front matter and was committed before any code ran. The headline contrast C1 is the quantile score of am_sy (am with the season-year vintage of the capacity) minus that of am (experiment 64's held capacity), over all leads. The upper end of C1 is -0.004, below zero but not below the threshold of -0.05. The threshold is a third of experiment 64's gain over d0, because a weekly refit of the capacity table is a production step that a fixed table does not need. C3 and C4 in the table confirm that the solar term carries solar information.

Contrast Difference in quantile score 98.75% interval C1: am_sy minus am, all leads -0.018 -0.036 to -0.004 C2: am_sy minus am, leads under 48 hours -0.033 -0.086 to +0.012 C3: am_sy minus am0, all leads (the solar term) -0.190 -0.267 to -0.118 C4: am_sy minus am_sy_twin, all leads (a wrong-date sunshine forecast) -0.357 -0.496 to -0.227

The values are in points of capacity and come from 50,000 resamples of whole ISO weeks of forecast start (29 weeks) and of 3 seeds, on experiment 64's 68,903 scored rows per seed: daylight half-hours of April to September at the five Primary substations D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, in July to September 2025 and April to June 2026. am0 is the XGBoost model with a base margin of zero and no solar term (experiment 76). C2 does not meet the rule for a gain at short leads, because its interval includes zero.

docs.title: The arms
docs.text:
• am, am_twin, d0, d1l: experiment 64's stored forecasts. am has a base margin of the weight times the held capacity times the forecast sunshine anomaly. d0 is the best-guess recipe, and d1l is d0 without the two radiation inputs.
  • am0: experiment 76's stored forecasts: am's recipe with a margin of zero in every row.
  • am_sy, am_sy_twin, am_wk: experiment 64's fitted am and am_twin models, predicted with the capacity of the season-year vintage (am_sy, am_sy_twin) or the weekly vintage (am_wk). Nothing is refitted, so the weights and the capacity in the training margin stay experiment 64's.
  • d1l_r, d0_r, d0_m0: d1l and d0 refitted here with experiment 64's recipe and seeds, and d0 refitted with a zero base margin.

The season-year vintage re-fits experiment 45's season-year constant before each forecast run. The fit uses the usable half-hours of the weeks up to two weeks before the Monday of the run's week, and divides by experiment 45's recovery ratio. The recovery ratio is experiment 45's measured fraction of injected solar capacity that the fit recovers, and a usable half-hour is one with an observed power and a CAMS solar estimate. A run takes the capacity from the first of three steps that applies. Step 1 is the vintage's constant for the run's season-year (September to August), once that season-year has 8 observed weeks. Step 2 is the previous season-year's constant. Step 3 is experiment 64's held capacity. Step 1 supplied 84% of runs at D9, D10, and D16, 47% at D11, and 29% at D14. D14's weeks from 2023-09-04 to 2025-08-25 are unobserved, so step 3 supplies the other 71% of its runs. The weekly vintage averages the 4 latest observed weeks of experiment 45's frozen weekly fit (a free capacity per week with a fixed penalty on changes), from the vintage with the latest origin up to a week before the run.

docs.title: The estimated capacity rose 13% to 31% above the held value by May 2026
docs.text: The vintages move away from the held capacity in November 2025 and sit 13% to 31% above it in May 2026. D9's vintage falls 14% below the held value in November, and D10's and D16's rise 9% and 10% above it. The season-year vintage in June 2026 is 3.0 MW at D9 (held 2.751 MW), 2.9 at D10 (2.356), 4.3 at D11 (3.457), 4.8 at D14 (3.705), and 4.6 at D16 (3.578), against experiment 45's final 2025/26 constants of 2.9, 2.9, 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4. The weekly vintage is higher and noisier. In November 2025 the new season-year's own constant takes over at D9, which is why the vintage there falls (2.37 MW against 2.75). Experiment 45 found that the latest weeks of a real-time fit are the least accurate.

docs.title: The gain is small and sits mostly in May 2026
docs.text:
The point estimate is negative at every lead, but only the 2-to-6-day and 10-days-and-beyond intervals exclude zero. The effect is almost zero at 10 days and beyond. The point estimates of am_sy minus am are -0.039 (-0.097 to +0.014) at 0 to 24 hours, -0.027 (-0.061 to +0.003) at 1 to 2 days, -0.029 (-0.053 to -0.009) at 2 to 6 days, -0.013 (-0.032 to +0.003) at 6 to 10 days, and -0.006 (-0.012 to -0.001) at 10 days and beyond. By valid month, the read is about zero from July to September 2025 (the vintage is within 4% of the held capacity there), -0.035 (-0.097 to +0.002) in April 2026, -0.058 (-0.100 to -0.028) in May, and -0.008 (-0.021 to +0.015) in June. At D16 the read is -0.045 (-0.073 to -0.020), at D14 -0.022 (-0.044 to -0.002), at D10 -0.018 (-0.034 to -0.003), at D11 -0.012 (-0.032 to +0.005), and at D9 +0.006 (-0.003 to +0.018). These reads are exploratory, at 95%.

The weekly vintage does no better than the season-year vintage. am_wk minus am_sy is -0.005 (-0.013 to +0.003), and am_wk minus am is -0.023 (-0.042 to -0.007) over all leads and -0.054 (-0.116 to +0.004) under 48 hours. A weekly refresh would lower the score by a further 0.005 points at most, which the intervals do not separate from zero. Restricted to runs where step 1 supplied the capacity, am_sy minus am is -0.022 (-0.037 to -0.008), so the fallback to the held value dilutes the effect slightly.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Mean quantile score in points of capacity, after the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor.

Arm All leads Under 48 hours 10 days and beyond am_wk 4.444 3.717 4.896 am_sy 4.449 3.739 4.898 am 4.467 3.772 4.904 d0_m0 4.550 3.966 4.916 d0 4.620 4.044 4.986 d0_r 4.620 4.044 4.987 am0 4.640 4.237 4.939 d1l_r 4.723 4.342 5.025 d1l 4.724 4.343 5.025 am_twin 4.767 4.478 4.975 am_sy_twin 4.807 4.570 4.982

The climatology scores 5.272 on the 68,863 rows it holds (a month-by-half-hour mean, experiment 64). The wrong-date twin gets worse when the capacity grows: am_sy_twin minus am_twin is +0.040 (+0.022 to +0.058), as expected for a solar term that carries no timing information.

docs.title: XGBoost's estimated starting point raises the score by 0.07 to 0.10 points
docs.text:
A refit of d1l in this pipeline scores the same as experiment 46's stored d1l, so the gap that experiment 76 saw is not a difference between pipelines. d1l_r minus d1l is -0.0004 (-0.0020 to +0.0013), and d0_r minus d0 is +0.0004 (-0.0018 to +0.0025).

Contrast Difference 98.33% interval D1: d1l_r minus am0, 10 days and beyond, no 14-day correction +0.102 +0.035 to +0.169 D2: d0_r minus d0_m0, 10 days and beyond, no 14-day correction +0.089 +0.028 to +0.153 D3: d1l_r minus am0, all leads +0.084 +0.053 to +0.121

The pre-registered rule reads D1 as a real starting-point effect: the lower end of D1 is above zero and its point estimate is above 0.05. D2 gives the same reading for d0. Over all leads, d0_m0 minus d0_r is -0.071 (-0.099 to -0.047, exploratory), and under 48 hours -0.078 (-0.118 to -0.036).

XGBoost estimates one base score per quantile level, and the score rises with the level. For d0_r at D9 it runs from 0.403 at the 0.05 level to 0.899 at the 0.95 level (power over capacity), and it is identical across seeds and for d1l_r. The recipe trains a fixed 500 rounds at a learning rate of 0.05, with no early stopping, so no interaction with early stopping exists. The reason a start at zero scores better is not tested here.

The solar term survives the correction for the starting point. am_sy is 0.100 points (-0.142 to -0.061) below d0_m0 over all leads and 0.227 (-0.361 to -0.103) under 48 hours (post hoc, exploratory), against 0.171 and 0.305 below d0. Experiment 64's gain of am over d0, 0.152, is 0.082 (-0.113 to -0.052) over d0_m0.

docs.title: Which predictions held
docs.text: Prediction made in the plan Result C1 at -0.02 (-0.04 to 0.00) Held: -0.018 (-0.036 to -0.004) C2 at -0.04 (-0.09 to 0.00) Held in size: -0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012) am_wk the same as am_sy or 0.00 to 0.05 higher Held for "the same": -0.005 (-0.013 to +0.003) d1l_r 0.00 to 0.10 above am0 at 10 days and beyond, uncorrected Just above the range: +0.102 (+0.035 to +0.169) Verdict small gain or inconclusive small gain

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
1. The weekly vintage drops weeks older than 8 weeks before the run's Monday. The code review found that D14's weekly vintage would otherwise average weeks from 2023, from before the gap in its record. The change was made before any arm was scored.
  2. The first run of the statistics script grouped the bootstrap by month, not by week. A column name was wrong, so the intervals rested on 7 blocks. The corrected run uses 29 weeks. The verdict changed from refuted to small gain, so every number on this page comes from the corrected run.
  3. Six exploratory reads were added after the results were seen, and are labelled post hoc: d0_m0 against d0_r under 48 hours, am_sy and am against d0_m0 (each over all leads and under 48 hours), and am0 against d0_m0. The reads against d0_m0 carry the claim that the solar term survives a zero start.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The training margin keeps the held capacity. The weights, and the capacity inside every training row, are experiment 64's, so the contrast measures the capacity at prediction only. A refit with a vintage capacity in the training rows is a larger design that this experiment does not test.
  • The recovery ratio is the full-record value. Each vintage divides by one number per series, from experiment 45's injection test on the full record, so the vintages carry a small look-ahead that am and the vintage arms share.
  • One validation year and 29 weeks of forecast start. July to September 2025 and April to June 2026 are two seasons of one year, and the 2026 months hold the gain.
  • D14 keeps its held capacity for 71% of runs. The vintage for D14 matters only from March 2026.
  • The reason a zero start helps is not tested. The experiment shows the size, not the mechanism.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does a zero base margin help every XGBoost model in the production recipe, and at which leads? The effect is 0.07 to 0.10 points on the Primary demand models of this experiment, larger than the effect of the capacity, and it costs nothing in production. A test across the series and model types that the best guess d0 covers (BSP and GSP demand, solar, and wind) would settle whether the base score belongs to the production recipe. If the capacity matters for a later model release, the evidence here is consistent with refreshing the capacity table once a season-year.

docs.title: Experiment 79: can the direction of flow be recovered at Primaries metered only in MVA?
docs.text:
Hiding the sign of a Primary's power and recovering it works for the solar capacity, and finds the direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78 (0.5 is a guess), but the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA show almost no reverse flow to recover, and the one that might (Stickney) cannot be checked. A Primary is a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. At 7 of the 8 Primaries metered only in megavolt-amperes (MVA), the MVA reading can stand in for megawatts (MW) from April to September, so no fit is needed there. Stickney is the exception, and the next step is a few weeks of signed power from NGED for Stickney. The verdict is partly supported: the capacity part passed the pre-registered rule and the direction part did not.

We asked whether the direction of the power flowing through a Primary, and the capacity of the solar panels behind it, can be found from a meter that records only the size of the flow, not its direction. First we tested the method where the answer is known. We took the 8 Primaries whose meters record signed power in MW. We subtracted the recorded output of a real solar farm, scaled to the Primary's typical midday power (level 1.0) or to 1.5 times that (level 1.5), so that the flow reversed on sunny middays. Then we threw the sign away and asked the fit to recover the capacity and the direction. Last, we ran the same fit on the real readings of the 8 other Primaries, which are metered only in MVA. The median error of the fitted capacity was 0.09 to 0.11 of the capacity found by fitting the unhidden signed power. A fit that treated the magnitude as if it were signed (the naive fit) had median errors of 0.29 to 1.00. The fit gave the right direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78 to 0.81 (the mean of the share of reverse-flow half-hours and the share of forward-flow half-hours labelled correctly), or 0.82 to 0.86 after leaving out one Primary where reverse flow is the usual state. The balanced accuracy fell to 0.67 when the reading also held reactive power equal to 20% of midday power, which the fit does not know about. At 7 of the 8 real Primaries metered only in MVA, the fit found no reverse flow.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Capacity is identified, and direction is not, by the rule fixed before the run. In this rule, capacity needed a median relative error of at most 0.25 and an upper interval end below zero for the difference from the naive fit (contrast C1). Direction needed a balanced accuracy of at least 0.80 and a lower interval end of at least 0.25 above the all-positive guess of 0.5 (contrast C2). A window is one Primary in one April-to-September season, and the years run from September to August as in experiment 00073. Intervals are 99% from a bootstrap that resamples Primaries and then windows. The unfolding fit is the method under test: it alternates between choosing a sign for each half-hour and fitting the signed model to the signed series.

Injected solar Capacity error, unfolding fit Capacity error, naive fit C1: unfolding minus naive Balanced accuracy C2: accuracy minus 0.5 Level 1.0 (227 windows) 0.092 0.290 -0.198 (-0.409 to -0.068) 0.779 +0.279 (+0.157 to +0.337) Level 1.5 (227 windows) 0.113 1.000 -0.887 (-0.920 to -0.754) 0.811 +0.311 (+0.184 to +0.372)

Median relative capacity error against the signed fit, and balanced accuracy of the fitted flow direction, 8 MW Primaries and 6 farms. Four windows at level 1.0 and one at level 1.5 had too few reverse-flow half-hours to score for sign.

Against the capacity of the injected farm alone, the median error is 0.151 at level 1.0 and 0.073 at level 1.5, where against the signed fit it is 0.092 and 0.113, so the signed fit's own error is part of every figure in the table. Level 0.5 has little reverse flow at 7 of the 8 Primaries and is a no-signal check. The median relative capacity error is 0.004 for the unfolding fit and 0.001 for the naive fit, and the median fitted negative share is 0 (single windows reach 0.21). On the 30 windows of the 5 Primaries that almost never go negative, with no injection, the median fitted negative share is 0.0000, so the fit does not invent reverse flow. The no-injection check passes trivially for a fit that never finds reverse flow.

A reactive-power floor the fit cannot see lowers both parts quickly. The reading was sqrt(power² + q²) with q equal to 10%, 20%, or 40% of midday power (level 1.0). The unfolding fit's capacity error is 0.130, 0.309, and 0.529 against the naive fit's 0.331, 0.404, and 0.539, and its balanced accuracy is 0.756, 0.666, and 0.561. At 20%, three Primaries (Horncastle, Trusthorpe, and Donington) fall to a recall of reverse flow of 0.01 to 0.23. The reactive-power result is descriptive and did not change the verdict. A power factor of 1 is therefore a strong assumption for the direction, and nothing in this experiment measures the real reactive power at any Primary.

docs.title: Post hoc: Wrangle T1 and Stickney
docs.text:
One MW Primary, Wrangle T1, drags the direction score below its limit, and the same weakness may hide Stickney. Wrangle T1 is net generation on 59% to 94% of April-to-September daylight half-hours in its two seasons. With level 1.0 injected, the fit returns capacity 0 and no negative flow there, against a signed capacity of 1.73 MW, so its balanced accuracy is 0.5. Without it, the balanced accuracy is 0.819 (0.791 to 0.843) at level 1.0 and 0.856 (0.831 to 0.874) at level 1.5, with 0.69 and 0.77 of reverse-flow half-hours found and 0.95 and 0.94 of forward-flow half-hours kept. The split between Wrangle T1 and the other Primaries was chosen after seeing the result and does not change the verdict.

Stickney's reading rises on sunny middays, which is what reverse flow would look like, and the registered fit does not find reverse flow there. Stickney's median midday reading is about 2.4 times its typical reading on sunny days and about 0.8 times on cloudy days (figure 1). Ingoldmells is flat, and the other six MVA-only Primaries fall on sunny days by 1% to 38% of their typical reading. Experiment 00039 found a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. With extra starting sign patterns that flip every half-hour above a solar-output threshold (a post hoc change, not tried on the known answers) the fit reaches a capacity of 1.3 to 7.2 MW with a negative flow in 75% to 87% of daylight half-hours from 2021, and lowers the loss by 9% to 18% in 4 of 5 windows. Because the same fit fails at Wrangle T1, where the answer is known, the Stickney capacity from the post hoc starts is not evidence.

docs.title: The real series
docs.text: At 7 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries the fit finds no reverse flow, and its capacity equals the naive fit's (figure 4). The median fitted negative share is 0.0% at all of them except Stickney, where the registered fit gives 0.7% and a capacity of 0. The fitted capacities are 6.0 MW at Warth Lane Skegness, 2.5 at Sleaford Road Boston, 1.4 at Langrick, 1.1 at Alford, Chapel St Leonards, and Marsh Lane, and 0.7 at Ingoldmells. These capacities come from a fit that cannot be checked against signed power, and a load that tracks sunshine would give the same numbers. The 95th percentile of the negative share over resampled weeks is 0.095 at Ingoldmells, 0.054 at Stickney, and under 0.001 at the others. The 5th to 95th percentile of the fitted capacity runs from 0 to 3.4 MW at Ingoldmells and from 0 to 2.4 MW at Marsh Lane. The lowest midday readings are 0.017 MW at Stickney, 0.026 MW at Marsh Lane, and 0.099 MW at Langrick; the other five stay above 0.87 MW.

docs.title: Failures and caveats
docs.text:
• All 6 solar farms (A to F) are used for the injection, because the fit has no tuning parameter that could be chosen to favour a farm. The 8 MW Primaries are 8 independent clusters in the bootstrap, so every conclusion about direction rests on 8 Primaries, one of them an outlier.
  • The capacity truth is the signed fit, so a capacity error here measures the unfolding step and not the real solar capacity. Real capacity at the MVA-only Primaries has no truth.
  • Natural reverse flow, with no injection, gave only 5 eligible windows (Spilsby in three season-years and Wrangle T1 in two), so known answer (4) of the plan says little. Spilsby's recall of reverse flow is 0.35.
  • The unfolding fit's starting sign patterns are sized from the magnitude reading alone, and not from the scale that sizes the injection, so the fit never begins at the answer.
  • The fit's capacity at the MVA-only Primaries uses the fleet shape (0.2 east, 0.6 south, 0.2 west at a DC:AC ratio of 1.15) and the nuisance terms of experiment 00073. The capacity is not corrected for the 0.77 recovery that experiment 00039 found.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text: The sign can be recovered where reverse flow is sometimes present, and the capacity follows, but the fit has no validated answer for a Primary that exports power on most sunny days. Wrangle T1 is the known answer where the fit fails, and Stickney is the real Primary that looks like Wrangle T1. The registered starts and the post hoc starts both need a known answer in that regime before any Stickney value is quoted.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does a starting pattern that flips every daylight half-hour of the clearest days recover the capacity and direction at Wrangle T1, and, if so, does the pattern give a consistent answer at Stickney? The threshold-flip starts of the post hoc section already return capacity 0 at Wrangle T1 in both seasons. The test should use injection at levels where reverse flow is the usual state (level 2.0 and above), keep the 50-row sign rule, and add the post hoc starts to the self-tests. The test should also check that the other seven MVA-only Primaries, which show no reverse flow, still return the naive fit. Signed power from NGED for Stickney on even a few days would settle the question without a fit.

docs.title: The plan as registered
docs.text:
Question. Eight of the 16 trial-area Primaries have a meter that records only the magnitude of apparent power (MVA). When embedded solar pushes net flow through zero, that reading bounces off zero and shows no direction. NGED cannot supply real and reactive power at these 8, so the only route to MW is the model. The fit assumes a power factor of 1.

Method. Each window's model is as in experiment 00073: power equals a calendar cell (month, half-hour, day type) plus heating degree-days and cloud terms, minus a capacity c >= 0 times a solar shape (the fleet orientation mix of 0.2 east, 0.6 south, and 0.2 west at 25° tilt, clipped at a DC:AC ratio of 1.15). The unfolding fit sees only |power|. It starts from a set of sign patterns (all positive, and the patterns implied by capacities of 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 times the window's median absolute midday power), alternates between fitting the model to sign x |power| and resetting each sign to the sign of the fitted value, and keeps the start with the lowest squared error. The naive fit is the first pass of the all-positive start.

Known answers. (1) Injected: the output of each metered solar farm (A to F, normalised to a 99th percentile of 1) is scaled and subtracted from each of the 8 MW Primaries' power, at levels 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 times the window's median absolute midday power, then the sign is hidden. The truth is the signed fit to the same series. (2) Reactive floor: the same at level 1.0, with sqrt(power^2 + q^2) taken as the reading, where q is 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 times the window's median absolute midday power, unknown to the fit. Only 0.2 enters a contrast (C3). (3) No injection: the sign of the five MW Primaries that almost never go negative is hidden, and the share of half-hours where the fitted flow is negative counts false reverse flow. (4) Natural reverse flow: Wrangle T1 and T2 and Spilsby go negative in the real data; the sign is hidden and recovered with no injection, where a window has at least 20 reverse-flow half-hours.

Self-tests. On a synthetic series with a known capacity and no noise, the fit recovers it to 1%. On series with capacity 0 and a small capacity that never nears zero, the unfolding fit returns an all-positive sign pattern. A start that flips the signs wins only if it lowers the loss by more than 0.5% of the all-positive start's loss. The run records, per window, the number of distinct capacities the starts reach and the loss gap between the best and second-best start. Before any fit runs, a script tabulates the reverse-flow rows per window and level, and the midday minimum of the magnitude at each MVA-only Primary, to show whether level 1.0 resembles the real series.

Size. Medium. What gets stored: private tables only. Serving path: untouched. Degradation rule: untouched. More than one defensible design: yes (alternating signs, a grid over capacity, or a mixture fit), so the plan is reviewed once. Callers: the experiment copies experiment 00073's fitting code, and nothing imports it.

Earlier advice followed. Experiments 00039 and 00056: leave the MVA Primaries out of a signed capacity estimate (here they are fitted with the unfolding fit and reported apart), and report the share of near-zero half-hours. Experiment 00039: injection into a linear fit tests the shape only; the magnitude link is non-linear, so injection tests the fit here. Experiment 00045: use the season-year constant capacity, which this experiment does. No earlier advice item is departed from.

docs.title: Experiment 82: do two improvements to the load-transfer detector add up?
docs.text:
Yes: the two improvements find different missed load transfers, so using both finds about twice as much extra moved power as either alone. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor's) onto neighbouring substations (the receivers) for hours or days. A Primary substation steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. On injected transfers, the combined detector (XL) found a share of 0.770 of the megawatts (MW) moved, and the benchmark detector (PF14) found 0.656. The misses that remain are mostly (by count) transfers with a small donor step and no metered receiver, so the next experiment could test a stronger detection signal for those transfers. The verdict is supported.

We asked whether two earlier improvements to a detector for load transfers combine. The detector subtracts an XGBoost forecast, which uses no past power, from a substation's measured power, and raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of that residual steps by 4.0 noise units or more. One noise unit is the usual size of that step on odd-numbered months. The XGBoost model is refitted on the 1st of every month, and PF14 ignores every alarm within 24 hours of a refit. Experiment 71 removed that blind spot by adding a second XGBoost model refitted on the 16th (the refit offset). Experiment 70 scored each alarm candidate partly by the number of neighbouring substations stepping the same way as the donor (the same-sign neighbour count).

We added synthetic transfers to the real power history of 16 Primary substations, combined the two improvements, and counted the share of the moved MW that each detector found. Each detector was held to 80 alarms on odd months that no closure in the switching log (the log of real switching operations) explains. Odd months set the thresholds and fitted the scores. Recall was read on transfers that start in even months.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. PF14: alarm when the 24-hour residual step reaches 4.0 noise units, end at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step. X: PF14 with the step taken from whichever of two residual models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours. LOGIT_SAME: PF14's candidates scored by a logistic regression that includes the same-sign neighbour count. XL: the same logistic score fitted on X's candidates.
  • Row set. 611 fresh headline-band transfers per injection shape (25% or more of the receiving load, over 1 day) starting in even months, shapes S2, S3, and S4 pooled (S2 a constant MW, S3 a share of the receiver's profile, S4 a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers); 214 long transfers (15.6 to 60 days). Fresh seeds, not those of experiments 69 to 71.
  • MW-weighted recall (98.33% interval, resampling whole calendar months): PF14 0.656 (0.530 to 0.727); X 0.713 (0.596 to 0.803); LOGIT_SAME 0.706 (0.591 to 0.776); XL 0.770 (0.665 to 0.857). The sanity arms X and LOGIT_SAME reproduce their experiments' gains: +0.056 and +0.050 over PF14.
  • Planned contrasts: C1 XL minus PF14 +0.114 (+0.074 to +0.182); C2 XL minus X +0.058 (+0.034 to +0.096); C3 XL minus LOGIT_SAME +0.064 (+0.028 to +0.127). All three lower ends are above zero, C1 is above the threshold of +0.02. The sum of the single gains (+0.106) is slightly below C1, so the gains add and do not overlap; C1, C2, and C3 all landed above the ranges predicted in the plan, which expected a combined gain smaller than the sum.
  • Share of the moved MW missed: PF14 0.344, X 0.287, LOGIT_SAME 0.294, XL 0.230. For XL, 0.195 is transfers with no alarm at the start and 0.035 is transfers with a wrong end.
  • Shapes: XL minus PF14 is +0.107 to +0.116 for S1, S2, S3, and S4, and +0.096 for S5; all lower ends are above zero.
  • By donor step, transfers found (S2 to S4 summed): with a metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4 noise units, XL 109 of 151, PF14 81. With no metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4, XL 149 of 550, PF14 42. With no metered receiver and a step of 4 to 6, XL 175 of 255, PF14 131.
  • Long transfers (descriptive): XL minus PF14 +0.000 (-0.026 to +0.026).
  • Labelled real transfers of more than 1 day (35): found XL 12, X 10, PF14 8, LOGIT_SAME 7; an alarm started within 2 hours of the labelled start for XL 15, X 12, LOGIT_SAME 12, PF14 11. The 35 are too few to rank the arms; MW-weighted recall on them is XL 0.357, X 0.350, PF14 0.156, and LOGIT_SAME 0.144, so X alone nearly matches XL there.
  • Alarms: unexplained alarms on even months were PF14 80, X 80, LOGIT_SAME 61, XL 67, against at most 80 on odd months for all arms (X 75, at its grid threshold of 4.1).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The alarm ends use up to 14 days of hindsight, so the detector serves training-time masks and the NGED event table, not live forecast inputs.
  • The logistic score is fitted on odd-month injections, so the odd-month contrast (+0.141) is in-sample and decides nothing.
  • A check on experiment 71's draw (850 rows per arm) reproduced the found flags of PF14, X, and LOGIT_SAME exactly; there is no earlier reference for XL.
  • The 35 real transfers give a weak signal only (12 against 8 found).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: By count, 401 of the 725 transfers XL misses have a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units and no metered receiver (149 of 550 found). Options to test include a longer averaging window and a check that the receivers' combined step balances the donor's.

docs.title: Experiment 83: tail calibration, on experiment 48
docs.text: Every stored forecast of experiment 48 is too narrow in both tails, and weekly retraining has the lowest pinball loss at both levels. We built a tail-calibration table for the studies code and ran it on the stored demand forecasts of experiment 48. The stack is the demand model fitted once, with a correction from its own recent errors. This experiment first also built a single-series curtailment-cost metric. We withdrew that metric, because curtailment binds at a substation, so a metric that scores each meter alone against its own history does not measure it.

docs.title: Results (exploratory, 20 demand series pooled, every lead and run from 2025-07-02)
docs.text:
• Coverage: coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927, so every forecast is too narrow in both tails. The target coverage is the level itself.
  • Pinball loss: weekly retraining has the lowest pinball loss at both levels.
  • Levels not delivered: the 0.01 and 0.99 rows read "not delivered", because the stored sets hold nine quantiles from 0.05 to 0.95.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Not scored: experiment 64's stored sets carry no actual column, so they were not scored here.
  • Next: write the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles in new experiments.

Reproduce with uv run python ml-experiments/00083-*/e00083_report.py. The printed report is in data/ml-experiments/00083-curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-worked-example/report.md.

docs.title: Experiment 84: the substation-limit curtailment metric on the pilot, a worked example
docs.text:
Two substations hold too few half-hours beyond a limit to rank forecasts: at 0.9 times each substation's earlier maximum export there are 19. We asked what it would have cost if the electricity network operator had capped nearby generators whenever a forecast said a substation would export more than a limit. We scored the stored demand and generator forecasts of experiment 48 (an earlier experiment that stored them) for Boston and Skegness, two bulk supply points (132 kV to 33 kV substations), over the year to 30 June 2026.

Most of the cost is breach, not unneeded cuts. For the best guess at 0.9 times the maximum, 81% of the avoidable cost is breach: export that stayed over the limit because the forecast did not order enough cuts. The next step is the January 2027 delivery of about 2,500 series, which the same code can score unchanged.

Verdict: inconclusive (no registered contrast). Every cost below is a calibration to history, not a saving. The best guess has the lowest avoidable cost at all three limits, but at 0.9 the order of the arms cannot be separated statistically: no difference is significant at the 5% level. The published thermal limits are NGED's, Supported by NGED Open Data. Questions for NGED are collected in issue #1318 (Questions to ask NGED about curtailment).

docs.title: Which limit, and why a scaled one
docs.text: The published thermal limit is a ceiling, and the maintainer understands that NGED does not operate to it. The understanding, unconfirmed, is that NGED curtails early so that one more fault still leaves headroom. Boston's metered export reached its published limit once, so the ceiling is not unreachable. The limit we score against therefore stands in for operating headroom: 0.9, 0.75, or 0.5 times each substation's maximum export before 2025-07-02 (the scaled limit). Boston's earlier maximum is about 39 MW, so 0.9 times it is 35.2 MW. History's maximum can be exceeded in the scored year: the highest export in all history, 45.08 MW at Boston, came inside it.

docs.title: The event census comes first
docs.text:
The counts are too small to rank forecasts at the headline limit. Counts below are half-hours of metered flow beyond the limit in the scored year, from cleaned unflagged power. The published thermal limits (NGED's, Supported by NGED Open Data) are the smaller of each substation's two transformer limits. A Technical Limit is the single figure NGED publishes for a grid supply point.

Node Published thermal limit (reference) 0.9 x maximum 0.75 x maximum 0.5 x maximum Boston 1 (45.0 MW) 17 36 215 Skegness 0 (29.8 MW) 2 10 108 Bicker Fen (sign unconfirmed, not scored) 0 0 84 734
  • Scored nodes: Boston and Skegness together have 19 half-hours at 0.9 times the maximum, 46 at 0.75, and 323 at 0.5. Only at 0.5, half the observed peak, are there more than 100 per node.
  • Scoring coverage: the census counts all 34,942 metered half-hours of the two nodes. Scoring uses the 27,936 that have a stored forecast in the 12 to 36 hour lead window. All 19 events at 0.9 are scored, 41 of 46 at 0.75, and 268 of 323 at 0.5. The unscored half-hours hold 4% of the excess energy at 0.75 and 14% at 0.5.
  • Import: the scaled import counts are in figure 1. No published import limit is used, and curtailing generators cannot relieve an import limit, so import is counted and not priced.
  • Signs: Boston and Skegness are -1 (a positive reading is import), inferred from the sign of the metered net flow in our power table. Bicker Fen is +1 and unconfirmed. Walpole's sign is unknown, so the metric excludes it.
  • Seasons: each limit is the same in all four NGED seasons (Winter December to February, Intermediate Cool March, April and November, Intermediate Warm May, September and October, Summer June to August).

docs.title: Does the code reproduce a hand-worked answer?
docs.text: Yes: all eight quantities agree exactly. The example is made up (a 45.0 MW limit and two generators of 10 MW and 20 MW). One generator's share is cut to its own forecast energy, and some export is left over as breach. e00084_known_answer.py fails if the code and the hand answer disagree.

docs.title: What the cost contains
docs.text:
Each arm forecasts a substation's export and its generators' output, and the cost counts cuts and breach. An arm is one pair of forecasts. When an arm's 95th-percentile forecast of export (tau 0.95) exceeds the limit, the metric orders the generators beneath the substation to cut that excess, sharing it by capacity. The energy proxy is the price times (MWh of generator output cut + 20 x MWh still over the limit after the cuts). The 20 is the breach ratio, so a MWh left over costs 20 times a MWh cut. Curtailment Limit 0 means no hours of curtailment are free. The six arms are:

  • Best guess (weekly retrained): the substation forecast retrained every week, with each generator's forecast retrained monthly.
  • Best-guess stack: the substation forecast fitted once, corrected from its own recent errors, with a generator forecast fitted once.
  • Climatology: the typical value for that month, half-hour and weekday or weekend.
  • NGED baseline (unconfirmed): the manual heuristic's substation forecast, with every generator assumed to run at full capacity. This is the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of NGED's practice, and the name always means that.
  • Best-guess nodes with actual generation: the best guess's substation forecast, with each generator's metered output known exactly (a diagnostic).
  • Perfect forecast: every quantile equal to the metered value, so the arm is charged only what cannot be avoided.

For the best guess at 0.9 times the maximum, the avoidable cost of GBP 571,823 splits into three parts. Avoidable cost is the arm's cost minus the perfect forecast's GBP 87,460.

Part GBP Unneeded cuts: output cut in half-hours where metered export was within the limit 114,496 Energy lost on the 19 event half-hours, more than the perfect forecast loses -7,791 Breach: MWh still over the limit on event half-hours, at 20 times the price 465,118

The forecast ordered 13.6 MWh of cuts on event half-hours against 35.1 MWh needed, so most of the excess was left as breach. Climatology orders no cuts at 0.9, so its whole avoidable cost is breach. The perfect forecast still costs GBP 87,460 because it cuts a little more than needed: some generators produce more than their estimated capacity, and the cap removes that extra output.

At the published thermal limit, both figures are absolute costs. The one scored half-hour is 0.038 MWh over the limit. Every arm except the perfect forecast costs GBP 1,540 (0.038 MWh x 20 x GBP 2,000, because none ordered a cut) and the perfect forecast costs GBP 1,225. The avoidable cost is GBP 315.

docs.title: Cost per arm
docs.text:
Absolute cost of the perfect forecast, and avoidable cost of each other arm, in GBP over the scored year at GBP 2,000 per MWh, Curtailment Limit 0. All figures are a calibration to history, not a saving.

Arm Avoidable GBP at 0.9 x maximum at 0.75 x at 0.5 x Perfect forecast (absolute cost) 87,460 252,428 1,341,908 Best guess (weekly retrained) 571,823 2,449,203 9,385,270 Best-guess stack 1,572,512 4,889,923 13,161,772 Climatology 1,318,078 4,638,378 20,187,791 NGED baseline (unconfirmed) 1,323,425 4,136,392 18,073,166 Best-guess nodes with actual generation 779,645 2,718,739 11,574,478

Figure 4 also shows the avoidable cost at three other prices, GBP 100, 380 and 11,100 per MWh. The last three are the ends and the geometric middle of a GBP 380 to 11,100 range reconstructed from April 2025 contracts, and GBP 100 is an illustrative balancing price. The energy proxy scales with price, so the order of the arms does not change. The DCUSA form follows the payment rule of the Distribution Connection and Use of System Agreement (Metric 2 of the cost-savings roadmap). It charges each instructed generator its whole headroom, so it ranks arms differently. Its avoidable cost is negative for climatology because the perfect forecast instructs generators and is charged for their headroom, while climatology instructs none.

  • 0.9 times the maximum: no difference is statistically significant at the 5% level. The best guess minus the NGED baseline is -GBP 751,603 (95% interval -2,293,480 to +14,988), and minus climatology is -GBP 746,255 (-2,288,392 to +30,815). The stack minus the best guess is +GBP 1,000,690 (0 to 2,865,606).
  • 0.75 times the maximum: the stack costs GBP 2,440,720 more than the best guess (96,371 to 6,686,043), which is significant. The best guess minus climatology is -GBP 2,189,175 (-6,255,250 to 0) and minus the NGED baseline is -GBP 1,687,189 (-5,138,390 to +38,991), neither significant.
  • 0.5 times the maximum: the best guess is GBP 10,802,520 cheaper than climatology (-20,880,964 to -3,342,553), which is significant. Against the NGED baseline it is GBP 8,687,896 cheaper (-26,251,726 to +2,339,946), not significant. We have no evidence that NGED operates at this limit, so it is a rehearsal.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
• Generators without a forecast: summed over the six arms, 100,632 of 754,272 generator-half-hours (13%) on the scored rows had no finite forecast. Those generators were not capped, gave no relief, and so add to the breach. None had a forecast with no metered output.
  • Forecast capped at capacity: a generator forecast above its effective capacity is capped at the capacity, as node_curtailment requires. All arms are capped alike.
  • Thermal limits: Boston's highest export in all history, 45.08 MW, sits on the published 45.0 MW limit, so 45.0 MW may be an operating ceiling or a clipped meter.
  • Anonymisation: no generator appears singly. Every generator figure is a sum over at least 4 generators, in GBP or MWh, and the table joining generators to substations stays in the private data folder.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Whether a ranking appears once the January 2027 delivery gives about 2,500 series. The same function scores any number of nodes from longer tables.

Reproduce with uv run python ml-experiments/00084-*/e00084_report.py, then e00084_split.py, e00084_known_answer.py and e00084_charts.py. The printed reports are in data/ml-experiments/00084-substation-limit-curtailment-cost-worked-example/.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
This roadmap outlines the planned order of development toward the v1.0 live forecast release (January 2027) and beyond. This page was last substantially revised July 2026, following a full codebase review and a reprioritisation (decided 2026-07-01) that made getting any forecast running on AWS the top priority over scientific-improvement work. That shipped as v0.1 in July 2026; the live service is now on v0.2 (deployed 13 August 2026), and work continues on the milestones below toward v1.0. Technical plans change as we learn more — treat this as a best-estimate, not a guarantee.

For how this page relates to GitHub issues, docs/architecture/, and the rest of the docs — and which place to put new planning content — see the Documentation Guide.

Status legend (used throughout these design docs): ✅ Implemented — exists in code today · 🚧 Planned — designed, not yet built · 🔬 Research — exploratory / v2.

docs.title: Design documents
docs.text:
• Delivery tables — the five Delta Lake tables OCF delivers to NGED (power_forecast, power_forecast_warnings, asset_health_history, effective_capacity, substation_switching), with full field-level schemas.
  • Forecast building blocks — "normal" vs. "prevailing conditions" forecasts, sign conventions, and worked examples.
  • Metrics & leaderboard — cross-fold validation protocol, evaluation metrics, horizon time-slices, and leaderboard grouping tags.
  • Estimating the money a better forecast saves — the two £ leaderboard metrics (flexibility procurement and curtailment), the equal-risk method that avoids needing a price for a network breach, their limitations, and the open questions for NGED.
  • Data sources — NGED power data + supporting files, network topology, and the weather datasets (ECMWF ENS, CAMS, ERA5, and the CEDA UKV archive that version 1 does not ingest), with the dated list of upgrades to each weather model.
  • Live service — the AWS deployment: the live_forecasts inference asset, the champion-model container, the costed AWS architecture options, production monitoring, and the handling of NWP model upgrades.
  • Handover to NGED — the operating model after the Network Innovation Allowance (NIA) project ends (the working assumption is that NGED runs the service on its own AWS account): the operator-contract design constraint, and the handover workstreams (runbooks, alert-on-absence, infra-as-code, confirming NGED's cloud and security standards, and game days).
  • XGBoost improvements — the v0.5 experiment backlog: four effort tiers, ordered best bang-for-the-buck within each tier, targeting the 3–10 day user band.
  • Extending the training history — using estimates of past weather, CAMS for irradiance and ERA5 for other variables, to train on the power data that predates the ECMWF ENS archive: the era-confounding hazard that dictates the ingest's scope, the reconciliation and pooling variants, how a weather product with a few months of history could enter the forecast, the COVID covariate, and why scoring against estimates of past weather is a diagnostic rather than a promotion criterion.
  • A staged probabilistic forecast — 🔬 a design under test: a stage 1 that turns weather into power, a stage 2 that calibrates, uses lagged power, and blends weather products, and coupling that restores coherent ensemble members. The experiments that test it are in the research log.
  • Experiments run by an LLM agent — a large language model (LLM) agent searching for improvements to the XGBoost forecasting model in two phases: experiments run overnight from a plan agreed the day before, then a careful search in which the agent runs as a separate Unix user that never sees the leaderboard's validation window. The page also summarises what published research agents found. A person re-implements every idea that survives either phase.
  • Engineering health — scientific-rigor tests and cleanup.
  • Capacity estimation — the v0.7 head-to-head between candidate estimators of the time-varying effective capacity of metered generators: a convex (CVXPY) censored quantile-envelope estimator, a differentiable-physics variational estimator, and cheap baselines — the winner ships in v1.
  • Net-demand disaggregation — the canonical v2 research arc: graph-structured disaggregation of net substation power into latent demand and DER generation, the convex dictionary baseline, MVA metering, prior art, and the novelty claims.
  • Switching events — the canonical treatment of switching events and estimating latent demand under the normal running arrangement: the v0.6 unsupervised statistical detector and the v2 mixture models (the graph is a data structure).

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text: The milestone sections below show the order in which this work is planned. Each maps 1:1 to a GitHub epic issue.

docs.title: v0.1 — "Naive" MVP (internal only)
docs.text:
Epic: #137 — deploy the naive forecast on AWS. ✅ Shipped July 2026 (v0.1.0), superseded on AWS by v0.2 on 13 August 2026.

Goal: A simple XGBoost forecast that lets us test infrastructure end-to-end and establish a baseline. Intentionally does not detect switching events or estimate effective capacity — hence "naive" (assumes the grid is always in perfect health). The data pipeline, per-series XGBoost models, and CV leaderboard were already built; the remaining work was deployment, now running on AWS — see Live service.

docs.title: v0.2 — Code Quality & Documentation
docs.text:
Epic: #138 — code quality, reproducibility, and observability hardening. ✅ Shipped 13 August 2026 (v0.2.0) — running on AWS.

  • More unit tests, including feature-level lag-leakage and forecaster-level determinism tests ✅ (#62; exercised by test_nullify_leaky_lags, test_engineer_features_weather_lag_leakage_prevention and test_random_seed_makes_training_deterministic, alongside new package coverage for dynamical_data (#163) and geo (#164)). The CV-windowing no-lookahead, leaderboard-fairness and fold-level determinism guardrail tests remain unwritten — see Engineering health
  • CI on GitHub (ruff + ty + pytest on every PR) ✅ (per-PR gate + nightly network tests; see Testing → Continuous integration)
  • Improve documentation ✅ (#139)
  • Verify daylight savings time handling is correct ✅ (#84; test_apply_local_time_features_dst_transitions covers both the spring-forward and fall-back transition instants)
  • Reproducibility stamping: git SHA + Delta table versions on every MLflow run ✅ (implemented in ml_core.repro; every MLflow run carries the stamp)
  • Drop Hydra in favour of plain YAML + importlib + pydantic ✅ (contracts.config_schemas owns the _target_ round-trip; dropping the two dependencies also unpinned antlr4-python3-runtime, which had been breaking Dagster's asset-selection strings)
  • Asset check on live_forecasts reporting missed NWP runs at forecast time (#424) ✅ (live_forecasts_are_healthy: it also reads the slot's rows back off disk, so every production asset now has a check — including the one NGED consume)
  • Start the intervention log ✅ (started with the v0.1 AWS period; its measurement window opens at v1.0, but it cannot be reconstructed retrospectively, which is why it exists now)

docs.title: v0.3 — Leaderboard / Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Epic: #6

  • Implement the ML energy forecasting "leaderboard" (cross-fold validation metrics in MLflow), ready for systematic cross-validation runs ✓ (CV assets added)
  • Metrics: MBE, MAE, NMAE, RMSE, Pinball loss, PICP, interval width, CRPS, Spread-Skill Ratio — all ✅ (definitions in the evaluation-metrics reference; plan and remaining 🚧 items in Metrics & leaderboard)
