Build the inflation as a wrapper forecaster rather than as a step inside predict, so that the calibrated manual heuristic and the later degradation-conditional conformal calibration share one implementation and one metric path — once we settle how a wrapper derives its class-level MODEL_NAME from the model it wraps. The product calibrator under research in A new weather product with a few months of history would be the wrapper's third consumer.

Spread inflation widens the fan but cannot reshape it (the inflated ensemble is still 51 point forecasts, just pushed apart). It is the stopgap the full fix below must beat to earn the effort of building it. [Issue

docs.title: 1156](https://github.com/openclimatefix/nged-substation-forecast/issues/1156)
docs.text: plans EMOS and conformal variants of spread calibration, scored on the same rows as the quick-wins study.

docs.title: Phase D — ensemble of quantile forecasts (Representation 3 → pooled Representation 2)
docs.text:
The full fix from the probabilistic-forecasting explainer: have the model emit a conditional distribution per ensemble member (per-member quantiles — Representation 3 in the delivery tables), then recombine the 51 members with the linear-pool mixture into one set of delivered percentiles (Representation 2). Three steps, one PR each:

  1. Percentile representations in PowerForecast (#262) — extend the contract (and the Delta write/read paths) with the Rep 2 and Rep 3 percentile columns, alongside the existing deterministic-ensemble representation.
  2. Quantile XGBoost model family (#263) — objective: reg:quantileerror with several quantile_alphas, as a separate model family emitting Rep 3. Sort each member's quantiles at predict time (monotonic rearrangement fixes quantile crossing). The lead-time feature and training on multiple members (xgboost-improvements — the lead-time feature and ensemble-member training) are the double-counting mitigations discussed in the explainer — land them first or measure without them consciously.
  3. Linear-pool combining step (#264) — pool the per-member quantiles into delivered Rep 2 percentiles (the pseudo-sample recipe in the explainer), with a per-horizon affine recalibration hook (fit on train) applied only if the pooled spread-skill/PICP numbers demand it. Scored with pinball/PICP/CRPS head-to-head against the Phase-C inflated deterministic champion. The quick-wins study found that crossing the quantile model's output with the 51 members left the 10% to 90% band covering 57% of outcomes, against a nominal 80%, and issue #1156 plans the follow-up checks on how to score and recombine the quantiles.

docs.title: Grouping the results
docs.text:
Each CV run is tagged with metadata so we can group CV runs and compute average performance per group (e.g. "does lagged power always help, regardless of model sophistication?", or "how robust is each model to weather-forecast uncertainty — estimates of past weather vs. operational NWP?"). Example tags:

Tag Example values time_series_type PV, Wind, disaggregated demand (primaries) model_family manual_heuristic, baseline_persistence, xgboost, pytorch_mlp, pytorch_graph_dp weather_source none, ecmwf_control, full_ecmwf_ensemble, cams_ceda_ukv, era5 input_features datetime, power_lag_24h, power_lag_7d, temperature training_strategy direct_multistep, horizon_as_feature, end_to_end generator_capacity_estimation none, simple_p99, convex_envelope, differentiable_physics switching_event_detection none, simple_statistical pre_training none, CAMS + ERA5, ERA5 alone

Accuracy is published separately for each class of asset — grid supply points, bulk supply points, primary substations, and metered generators — each against its own stated naive baseline, for the reason given under Publishing results that others can compare against. The unweighted mae__all aggregate is dominated by the grid supply points for exactly that reason. The time_series_type tag above is what carries the split.

The battery, the gas generator, and the biofuel plant are reported separately from the wind and solar sites, for the reason given under Publishing results that others can compare against — pooling them with weather-driven generators would hide how well either group is forecast.

Every leaderboard row also carries two cost savings (£) figures — one for flexibility procurement, one for curtailment — designed in Estimating the money a better forecast saves. They are deliberately rough proxies, not a cost analysis.

docs.title: A staged probabilistic forecast
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Research. The design on this page is a best guess under test. The research log holds the experiments that test it, and the research plan lists the experiments to run next. No production code implements it.

The page describes a probabilistic power forecast in three parts with fixed roles. Stage 1 turns weather into power, stage 2 calibrates the result, uses lagged power, and blends weather products, and coupling restores coherent ensemble members. Each part always runs. The page states the aims, the design, the evidence so far, the alternatives, and the open questions.

Terms used below. NWP means numerical weather prediction. ENS is the ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts) ensemble, with 51 members per run, served by Dynamical.org from 2024-04-01. UKV is the Met Office's deterministic regional model, and MOGREPS-UK is the Met Office's regional ensemble. ERA5 is ECMWF's reanalysis and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite-derived solar irradiance; the docs call these "estimates of past weather". A series is one half-hourly power time series (a substation, a solar farm, or a wind farm), and version 2 targets 2,500 of them. A quantile model is trained with pinball loss. PIT is the probability integral transform, a histogram that shows calibration. EMOS is ensemble model output statistics. ECC is ensemble copula coupling, which turns a calibrated marginal distribution back into ensemble members that keep their dependence across time and series, and ECC-Q does it by sorting quantiles against member ranks. Clear-sky power is the power a site would produce under a cloudless sky. ERA5T is the preliminary release of ERA5, which lands about 5 days late. GEFS is the Global Ensemble Forecast System of the United States' National Centers for Environmental Prediction. CEDA is the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis, which hosts a UKV archive. MIDAS is the Met Office Integrated Data Archive System. A GPU is a graphics processing unit.

docs.title: Aims
docs.text:
The aim is not only a skilful forecast on day one. A design that wins today's leaderboard but cannot take a second weather model is the wrong design. The aims, in priority order:

  1. A skilful, calibrated probabilistic power forecast at 2,500 series, judged by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the mean absolute error (MAE).
  2. Easy addition of new NWP products, including products with very short histories. Blending many NWP products is a strong hunch for improving the forecast. Some of the best products have too little history to train a full forecasting model on (MOGREPS-UK, a few months). Some are deterministic (UKV). Some have different step widths (hourly beyond day 5, against ENS's 3-hourly then 6-hourly) or different variable conventions (a mean over the previous period, an instantaneous value, or a change between the two inside one product's life).
  3. Reuse of the weather-to-power model ("stage 1") elsewhere in the system: switching-event detection, effective-capacity estimation, data cleaning (metering-fault detection), and the lag-anomaly features (how unusual was each lagged power value, given the weather then).
  4. Coherent ensemble members. The grid physics must be coherent within each ensemble member (a member that is very windy for one wind farm is windy for all of them). Coherence matters most beyond day 7, where ENS members disagree sharply about wind speed and irradiance.
  5. Explainability. An engineer should be able to say which stage produced an error.
  6. Inherent stability. Each stage always runs. No conditional skips a stage. A missing input is a null that XGBoost routes, never a raised exception.
  7. Research first. Experiments test every idea before production code changes.

Aims 2 and 5 are the reason the forecast chain has more than one learned stage. Each stage has one job: stage 1 turns weather into power, stage 2 calibrates and blends the products, and the coupling step restores coherent members. One model doing several of those jobs is harder to explain, to test, and to extend with a new product. Aim 3 needs stage 1 only as an offline artefact that runs on analysis weather, so aim 3 does not by itself justify serving the chain. Stage 1 also runs at serving time on analysis weather, or on the analysis proxy, to compute the lag anomalies.

Design principles traded away. The staged design departs from three of the design principles. Principle 2 (complexity belongs offline, not in the serving path) is met for training but not for serving, where the adapter, stage 1, stage 2, and coupling all run on every forecast. Principle 3 (one execution path from research to production) is strained because stage 1 has no lead time and so does not fit the BaseForecaster interface. Principle 6 (the whole system runs on one laptop) requires three chained trained artefacts (stage 1, the stage 2 calibrator, and the blend) to run on one machine. In return the design buys aims 2 and 5. The experiments keep the stage count to what they prove: a stage that does not earn its place is removed.

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
The best-guess design has three parts with fixed roles: stage 1 turns weather into power, stage 2 calibrates, uses lagged power, and blends the products, and coupling restores coherent members. Every part always runs, and each has one job. The experiments so far support a stage 1 trained on analysis weather, and support lagged power in stage 2. They do not support stage 2 for a single product without lags, so stage 2 must earn its place under the two conditions it exists for: several weather products and lagged power. The main challenger is a single-stage quantile XGBoost model on ENS statistics with a small correction per additional product. A learned weather-correction stage ("stage 0") and a learned persistence stage ("stage 1b") are not in the first design; see the alternatives.

NWP n, member m ─▶ adapter ─▶ canonical weather ─▶ Stage 1 ─▶ power(n,m,s,t)
                                                                          │
        per-product statistics across members, lead, lag anomalies ◀──────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
             Stage 2a: shared per-product calibrator ─▶ calibrated quantiles per product
                                    │
                                    ▼
             Stage 2b: learned blend over the products present ─▶ calibrated quantiles(s,t)
                                    │
                                    ▼
                                   ECC ─▶ 51 coherent members

Notation: n is the NWP product, m the ensemble member, s the series, t the valid time.

Stage Input Output Per NWP Per member Lead input Adapter (code, not learned) One member's raw fields; a per-NWP, per-variable, per-date convention table Fields on the common half-hourly grid in the canonical convention Yes Yes No Stage 1 (learned) Canonical weather, calendar, site static fields Conditional quantiles of power for one series (9 levels), with the median used as the member's point value No Yes No Stage 2a, calibrator (learned) One product's stage 1 statistics across its members (mean, spread, percentiles), lead, lagged power, lag anomalies Calibrated quantiles of power at 19 levels for that product One shared function fitted per series, with a spread factor per product No Yes Stage 2b, blend (learned) The calibrated quantiles of the products that are present, lead Calibrated quantiles of power per series and valid time Combines the products No Yes ECC (code) Calibrated quantiles, stage 1 member medians 51 coherent members (the ENS member count) No Output No

The adapter handles known facts as code. Each NWP has a table of step width, accumulation or instantaneous convention, and the date each convention applies from. The adapter resamples every NWP (and ERA5 and CAMS) to the same half-hourly grid in the same convention. Two parts exist: short-wave radiation conserves each native window's mean and long-wave radiation uses a shape-preserving cubic interpolant (PR #1166 (Resample short-wave and long-wave radiation over native intervals)), and wind travels as eastward and northward components, with speed and bearing derived afterwards (PR #1167 (Retain wind components through interpolation)). Learning conventions from data would waste a short history and could not be unit-tested. A validation check (diurnal profile against solar geometry) catches an undeclared convention change and raises a WARN asset check, not an exception.

Stage 1 is NWP-agnostic and lead-agnostic. The experiments call stage 1 "stage 1a" when it has no lags and no lead. It trains on analysis weather (ERA5 and CAMS) to power. Most trial-area power series go back to late 2019 and the ERA5 ingest starts in 2020, so it could use up to roughly 7 years against the roughly 2 years of ENS. Experiments 00001 and 00003 found that the extra years do not help generators and hurt demand, so the training start is a setting for each technology. Stage 1 outputs conditional quantiles of power given the weather, which cover what remains uncertain when the weather is known (cloud flicker, unmetered load, site variation). The forecast chain uses the per-member median as the member's point value and, as a baseline, the mixture of the quantiles over members. CAMS on disk covers the six solar farms and the 22 demand series of the experiments: hourly point downloads from 2019-09-01 in data/studies/downloads/reanalysis/CAMS, fetched for issue #784 (Throwaway experiment: does the beam/diffuse split help an XGBoost PV forecast?) and PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations). Stage 1 for 2,500 series needs CAMS at every series' location, and the service is a point API (see the data-sources note on using the point API), so CAMS at every series is a fetch of its own. The experiments so far run stage 1 on the 31-series row set.

Stage 1 is a perfect-prognosis model, and that is a risk. Trained on analysis weather, it learns the sharp relationship that satellite irradiance supports (CAMS 5.09% MAE against ERA5's 9.08% on the solar studies' row set), and analysis cloud carries about twice the gain forecast cloud does. It will lean on variables that are much less informative in a forecast. A variance-preserving stage 0 does not close that gap. The repo's explainer on why a power model trained on past weather does not hedge names the same trade-off as perfect prognosis against model output statistics, and cites Marzban, Sandgathe and Kalnay (2006) for model output statistics beating perfect prognosis on mean squared error. Experiment 00001 found a gain over an ENS-trained model up to day 6 and none beyond, which is consistent with that risk. The deciding contrast stays the full chain against a single-stage model trained directly on ENS, by lead band, and a stage 1 trained on ENS early leads remains an arm.

Lagged power enters stage 2, as lagged power and as lag anomalies. A lag anomaly is the observed power at a lag time minus stage 1's expectation at that time, given the weather then. It tells stage 2 how far recent power sat from what the weather explains, which is the "delta" that stage 2 needs to read the lags. Experiment 00005 supports this placement over a separate persistence stage that predicts the residual from the lags, as the 00005 bullet under "What the experiments show" gives. The roadmap already has a related idea (weather-delta compensation for power lags). Three risks apply. The lag anomalies of 00005 are ceilings, because serving has ERA5T about 5 days late and CAMS about 1 day late. Flagged or stuck-meter lags enter as nulls. A lag no longer than the lead is nullified, so the lead decides which lags exist. Stage 1 alone stays lag-free and lead-free, and reusable for aim 3.

Stage 2 is one calibrator shared by all products, followed by a learned blend. The calibrator is one function with identical feature names for every product: that product's mean, spread, and percentiles of stage 1 power across its members, the lead, and the product-independent lagged power and lag anomalies. It is fitted on the pooled rows of all products, per series (experiment 00005 fitted one per series), with a multiplicative spread factor per product, and it outputs a location plus a positive scale times a fixed quantile shape. The blend combines the calibrated distributions of the products that are present. A product that is absent gets no weight and the other weights renormalise, so the stage always runs and a missing product is a degradation, not an exception. A deterministic product has zero spread, so its scale term needs a lead-dependent intercept. A product with a short horizon fades its weight to zero towards its last lead. ENS alone is the one-component case. Stage 1's values on the ENS-era months are forward-chained out-of-fold, or stage 2 would see stage 1 predictions that are too good. Experiment 00005 trained the calibrator as one multi-quantile XGBoost model per series at 9 levels, on every third daily ENS run.

A new product joins stage 2 as extra rows in the pooled fit plus a spread factor and a blend weight, not as new columns. An XGBoost model given an NWP identifier splits on it freely, so the identifier cannot act as a scale adjustment only. Separate feature columns per product also do not transfer what the model learned: splits learned on the ENS spread column do not apply to a UKV spread column. Null versus non-null also acts as a date flag, because the new product's columns are non-null only in the most recent months, so the trees can split on "recent month" and absorb any drift in that period. A 3-month overlap is millions of rows but only about 30 to 45 independent weather episodes (the estimate in the training-history roadmap). The experiments keep one model with per-product columns as a control arm (the "per-product-columns control"), which a new product retrains in full. The shared calibrator above is the alternative the experiments test against it.

Challenger: a single-stage ENS champion with a per-product correction. The champion is a quantile XGBoost model trained on ENS only, with stage 1 statistics, lead, lagged power, and lag anomalies as inputs. Each additional product adds a correction and the champion is never retrained. The correction shifts the champion's location by a × Δ and its log-scale by b × |Δ| + c × (the product's spread), where Δ is the product's stage 1 median minus the ENS stage 1 median, and a, b, and c vary smoothly with lead, are pooled per technology, and shrink towards zero. A missing product gives zero correction, so a product enters with zero correction by construction, and the safe-entry check of the second-product experiment tests that claim. The correction cannot learn interactions between a product and the lags, which is probably a small loss (the lead column gained only 0.05 points in quick-wins) but is unmeasured. The long ENS record supports this design for generators, although the project's own demand results (00003, 00006) found that a long history hurts demand: in the study of Lang et al. (2020), on 2 m temperature at central-European stations, training on several years beat a sliding window of recent days, including across an ECMWF model change. This design is also the baseline that stage 2 must beat or tie before stage 2 earns its place.

The blend is learned, with few parameters, because a fixed blend is not calibrated by construction. An equal-weight mixture of individually calibrated distributions is generally over-dispersed (Ranjan and Gneiting (2010) show that a weighted average of distinct calibrated forecasts is uncalibrated, in a case study of binary probability-of-precipitation forecasts), and averaging quantiles re-creates under-dispersion (see the explainer). The beta-transformed linear pool fixes this with two shape parameters and nests the plain linear pool (when both equal 1); Gneiting and Ranjan (2013) extend it to full predictive distributions. We have read abstracts and secondary summaries of both papers, not the full texts. Stage 2b has two learned parts, fitted on held-out months: one weight per product, smooth in lead and shrunk towards equal weights when the overlap is short, and the two shape parameters, smooth in lead. A mixture already widens when the product medians disagree, so a separate disagreement input is added only if an experiment shows the beta-transformed pool is still under-dispersed when products disagree. The control arm is a fixed equal-weight mixture. The studies score both with the PIT histogram and coverage by lead band.

Width must be monotone in spread, and XGBoost does not guarantee it. XGBoost monotone constraints bound a prediction against a feature, not the difference between two quantiles (both bounds can rise while the gap shrinks). The experiments therefore parameterise the calibrated distribution as a location plus a positive scale times a fixed quantile shape, with the scale monotone in spread, and test the width property directly on held-out data.

Pooling stage 1 quantiles over members is a valid baseline, not double counting. If stage 1 estimates the distribution of power given the weather and the members are draws of the weather, the mixture over members follows from the law of total probability. The quick-wins study's 57% coverage of a nominal 80% band is not explained, and experiment 00006 used out-of-fold stage 1 on analysis weather and still covered only 83% to 85% of a nominal 90% band. Stage 2 must beat the mixture baseline (with and without a simple spread rescaling) to earn its place. The repo's double-counting caveat applies to models trained on forecast weather, whose learned spread already includes some forecast error. Stage 1 trains on analysis weather, so its spread does not. The mixture itself is the pooling recipe in that explainer.

One coherent distribution comes out of stage 2 and ECC. The marginal distribution per series and valid time is stage 2's quantiles. ECC-Q needs one quantile per member, so the coupling step interpolates the 19 stage 2 quantile levels to the levels i/52 for i = 1 to 51, with a stated tail rule beyond the outermost levels, and assigns them to members by the rank of each member's stage 1 median. Ties at night-time solar, where every member is zero, need no rule because every assigned quantile is also zero. Other ties (for example when weather is missing and the medians coincide) would, if broken by member identifier, give perfect rank correlation across the affected series and times and distort aggregate uncertainty, so they break by a dependence template instead: the ranks of the members' stage 1 medians at neighbouring times, or a template taken from history (the Schaake shuffle). The experiments test the template with the coherence scores. At short leads members are nearly identical and ranks are mostly noise, so the experiments score coupling by lead band with the variogram score and include the Schaake shuffle there. The output is always the 51 ENS members. Other NWPs enter stage 2 as pooled rows and a blend component and do not add members, which removes the question of how to pool members of different NWPs.

Models are specific to each site for substations and pooled for solar and wind, as a decision of the maintainer. For Primary substations, experiment 00006 found one model per substation slightly better than one model per type with a series identifier (7.11 against 7.34 points of capacity), by a small unpaired margin whose intervals overlap. For bulk supply points and grid supply points the pooled model was marginally lower (8.93 against 9.06, and 23.91 against 23.97), and 00006 says the margin is not established. The quick-wins study found the pooled model with a site identifier its best arm. The evidence is mixed, so a later experiment may revisit the choice. Solar and wind farms share a model, because their output follows the weather and a farm has too little history to carry a model of its own. The pooled choice for solar and wind has no experiment behind it.

Targets for solar and wind power. Stage 1 could predict a ratio for solar: power divided by clear-sky PV power, multiplied back by the known half-hourly clear-sky curve, so the output stays in megawatts (roadmap section). Quantile loss in ratio space needs weights equal to the clear-sky power so that it equals the megawatt loss. Rows with zero clear-sky power are dropped. The per-site clear-sky scale is unknown for embedded PV, so it comes from a trailing (not centred) rolling quantile of clear-sky-normalised output, or from a physics model for solar farms. For wind, the analogue is a base_margin from a power curve of forecast wind speed, with stage 1 learning the residual. The ratio target is tested once, as a stage 1 arm. Multiplying quantiles by a positive clear-sky value preserves their order, so the coupling step is unaffected.

Lead time. Stage 0 (if built) sees all leads and takes the lead as an input. Stage 1 takes no lead. Stage 2 takes the lead, and the lead also decides which lag features exist: a lag shorter than or equal to the lead is nullified. Lead buckets (for example day 0 to 1, 1 to 6, 6 to 15) are one arm in a later experiment. In quick-wins the lead column gained 0.05 points, so a bucketed design must clear a low bar. The risks are thin data per bucket and quantile jumps at bucket boundaries.

Training scenarios and cadence.

  • From scratch: take the cleaned power history from clean_nged_power_data. Fit stage 1 on ERA5 and CAMS, from the training start chosen for the technology, with forward-chained out-of-fold predictions: each block is predicted by a model trained only on earlier blocks, with a purge gap of at least one week. Run the adapter then stage 1 per ENS member over the NWP era, using the out-of-fold stage 1. Fit stage 2 on the per-product statistics. Score end-to-end CRPS on held-out months.
  • Monthly retrain: keep stage 1 frozen, because its predictions for the new month are out of sample. Choose between the candidate and the incumbent stage 2 by rolling-origin evaluation: fit each on months up to a cut-off and score both on the following months, which neither saw. Only after the promotion decision, refit the winner on all months. Scoring the newest month after fitting on it would favour the candidate. Stage 1 retrains yearly, or when cleaning rules change or sites are added.
  • A new NWP with short history: add an adapter table. Stage 1 is untouched. Stage 2's calibrator keeps its form: the new product's rows join the pooled fit with one new spread factor, and the blend gains the product's weight, shrunk towards equal weights. The second-product experiments in the research plan measure how few months of history this needs. The single-stage challenger instead adds a correction (a few numbers per technology) to a frozen champion, and the per-product-columns control retrains in full.

Leakage rules. Stage 1 must not train on months that stage 2 or the end-to-end score uses for validation, and ERA5 overlaps the ENS era. Forward-chained out-of-fold predictions replace a two-sided cross-fit, because a two-sided fit would let stage 1 see later capacity, later embedded PV, and later cleaning outcomes, giving residuals smaller than those it meets when serving. Lag anomalies are built from the source and latency serving will have: ERA5T lands about 5 days late and CAMS about 1 day late, so short lags use the analysis proxy (the early leads of the latest ENS run), whose errors exceed ERA5's. Experiment 00005 did not do this, so its lag results are ceilings.

Regime changes in the long history, including the COVID lockdowns. Stage 1 could train on power from late 2019 to 2026, which includes the COVID lockdowns (about 2020-03 to 2021-07, roughly 1.3 of about 7 winters). The lockdowns distort the occupancy and calendar response of demand far more than the weather-to-power response of wind and solar farms, so the question applies to demand series and net-load substations, not to generation. The docs already contain ideas for how to represent the lockdowns and for which datasets to ingest, but nothing is decided and nothing is ingested. The era covariates section of the training-history roadmap lists the candidate ways to represent the lockdown: a scalar in [0, 1] sourced from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker (a daily UK stringency index) or from Google's COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports (closer to the causal driver, thinly supported by one national preprint); recency sample weights; and excluding the period. Both candidate series ended in 2022, so whether they are still downloadable is unchecked, and nothing has been downloaded. The section also records three cautions: the evidence is national or building-level and none of it is a distribution substation; a scalar that returns to 0 cannot say that the post-lockdown world differs from the pre-lockdown world; and the scalar breaks under a global model unless a customer-mix covariate exists. The design consequences are:

  • Stage 2 is unaffected by construction. It trains on the ENS era (2024-04 onward), which has no lockdown.
  • Stage 1 is where the choice lives. For a technology whose training starts in 2019, the forward-chained out-of-fold run predicts the 2020-21 blocks with models that never saw a lockdown, so those blocks carry large residuals. For demand, where the experiments point to a start in 2023-09, the lockdown lies outside the window, and the first forward-chained blocks train on fewer than 12 months, so a block starts only when a full year of training data exists. Those residuals matter only for the reuse cases (the roadmap already names the lockdown as the largest phantom event for the switching baseline, and as a free labelled test case) and not for stage 2.
  • The cheap arms have run for Primary substations (experiment 00006). A 0/1 indicator for 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, set to 0 in all forecast data, lowered the selection-fold error by 0.26 points, and it helped grid supply points most. Recency weights helped more, and a 2023-09 training start helped most on the confirmation year only. No Oxford or Google series has been downloaded, and the results give no reason to download one yet.

Alternatives considered.

  • A learned weather-correction stage ("stage 0") that maps each NWP towards ERA5 and CAMS, member by member, before stage 1. It is a further learned artefact, a variance-preserving correction cannot close the perfect-prognosis gap, and a climatological quantile map has known defects (it does not fade with skill, it injects incoherent variance from coarse steps, and it breaks consistency between variables). Built only if the second-NWP experiment shows stage 2 failing. If built: fit at the NWP's own step width, correct wind speed and clear-sky index and not their components, smooth over lead, exclude the validation months, and include an identity arm.
  • Merge stages 0 and 1 (pretrain on ERA5 and CAMS, fine-tune per NWP with power): needs power data per NWP, which is the short-history problem, and suits a neural network better than XGBoost (an XGBoost warm start can only add trees). Studied only if stage 2 fails on a second NWP.
  • Pool the products as exchangeable members of one ensemble: a deterministic UKV would get a weight of 1/52. Hagedorn et al. (2012) found that a nine-system multi-model ensemble did not beat the ECMWF ensemble alone on extratropical temperature, and that calibrated ECMWF often matched the multi-model ensemble. The gain from blending products may therefore be smaller than hoped for solar, while the project's matched-lead study found a wind gain of 0.184 points of capacity.
  • Weather-space correction fitted on power error through the frozen stage 1, as the training-history roadmap proposes, instead of towards ERA5 and CAMS. The correction keeps each member's rank. The weather-space correction is an arm if stage 0 is built.
  • A persistence stage ("stage 1b") that predicts the residual of power against stage 1 from the residuals at the forecast origin and earlier, trained on ERA5 and CAMS with simulated origins and leads. Experiment 00005 found that lagged power in stage 2 beat it by 0.84 points, and that adding it on top of stage 2 gained 0.06 (both ceiling results). Revisit only if serving-latency lag anomalies weaken stage 2.
  • The single-stage ENS champion with a per-product correction: the challenger above. It drops a stage and is the baseline that stage 2 must beat or tie.
  • A physics stage 1 (differentiable physics, version 2): drops into the same slot with the same interface and has few parameters, so it suits new sites. Not studied now.
  • An NWP better than ERA5 (UKV at short leads, for local wind and cloud): the canonical past-weather estimate becomes a per-variable choice or blend, settled by the ceiling test.
  • Station observations (MIDAS Open): an offline referee and a candidate component of the past-weather blend. No live feed exists.
  • Direct CRPS training: a guess, not a sourced figure, puts its gain below 0.2 points over pinball loss at many levels. Runs only if the PIT histogram stays U-shaped.

Interaction with switching detection, effective capacity, and metering faults. All three want "expected power from analysis weather and calendar", and all three share one risk, a loop between detection and training. The guard is the same each time: a robust fit, out-of-fold expectations, one versioned stage 1 artefact, and a rule-based detector first.

  • Switching-event detection: the roadmap's approach 1, the two-stage forecaster, is nearly this design. Stage 1 is the baseline and its residual is the switching signal. The residuals feed stage 2 as lag-anomaly features (the existing idea of residual lag features from the switching-detector baseline), and a recent detected event could widen stage 2's interval. Live detection runs on the analysis proxy.
  • Effective capacity: the PV ratio target needs a per-site clear-sky scale, which is an effective-capacity estimate, so capacity estimation feeds stage 1 and stage 1 feeds the cheap capacity baselines. The scale must be causal. A physics stage 1 would make capacity a fitted parameter.
  • Metering faults: large residuals against stage 1 could flag stuck meters and spikes, as a layer after the existing rule-based cleaning. Stage 1 would otherwise learn the faults it should detect, and multi-month faults span the blocks, so cleaning recall is tested on the known faults from PR #1159 before any reuse.

docs.title: What the experiments show
docs.text:
Seven experiments and one closed study give the evidence so far. The research log holds each experiment's question, verdict, and figures; the bullets give the headline of each. Pull request numbers for 00005 and 00006 are PR #1195 (Experiment 5: where lagged power enters a two-stage demand forecast) and PR #1202 (Experiment 6: which input features work best for the ERA5-trained demand model).

  • 00001, solar and wind, ENS only: stage 1 trained on ERA5 and applied to the 51 ENS members and averaged had a lower mean absolute error than the same columns trained on ENS weather, by 0.57 points of capacity for solar (interval −0.83 to −0.32) and 1.70 for wind (−2.33 to −1.08), up to day 6 and not beyond. The gain follows the training weather and not the training length.
  • 00002, solar and wind, ENS only, quantiles: pooling the ERA5-trained quantiles over the members beat an ENS-trained quantile model (CRPS −0.62 for wind, −0.24 for solar). A stage 2 calibrator with a learned blend, given one product and no lags, did not improve on the pooled mixture (wind +0.26) and was materially worse for solar (+0.40, interval +0.26 to +0.61); the learned blend changed CRPS by +0.00 to +0.08.
  • 00003, 22 series that are not wind or solar farms (16 demand series, 4 grid flows, and 2 others): with weather only, the ERA5-trained model was worse than the ENS-trained model by 1.37 points (+0.68 to +2.17), and with calendar columns and lags the two were equal (+0.10, −0.26 to +0.50). The error fell steadily as the training start moved later, which points to drift, with the customer mix, embedded generation, network changes, and the pandemic as candidate causes.
  • 00005, 16 Primary substations, ceiling arms (verdict: refuted, because the experiment predicted that a separate persistence stage would win): lagged power in the stage 2 calibrator beat a lag-free calibrated stage 1 by 1.80 points of quantile score (12 of 12 months, 16 of 16 series), and beat lagged power through a separate persistence stage ("stage 1b") plus a calibrator by 0.84 (99% interval +0.28 to +1.50). Lagged power through the persistence stage was the better placement in 8 of the 16 series, so the 0.84 is an average over mixed series. The experiment assumed no telemetry delay at the forecast origin, which is a second ceiling. Adding the persistence stage on top of lags in stage 2 gained 0.06 (−0.15 to +0.03). The advantage of stage 2 persisted at 3 to 15 days, and 9 of 12 months favoured lags in stage 2.
  • 00006, Primary substations, confirmation year: hour and weekday were the largest non-lag input (−0.46, 99.4% interval −0.61 to −0.30). A COVID indicator, a 14-day Christmas window, and recency weights helped, and a 2023-09 training start helped most (confirmation-year evidence only). Time of year added nothing, because the weather block already carries the season, and trailing temperature means and windchill showed no detectable gain.
  • 00007, Primary substations: a static correction of the stage 1 daytime residual with CAMS irradiance was inconclusive. CAMS added to ERA5 shortwave had a partial R² of 0.110, and the result rests largely on one substation, so it does not separate an irradiance error from a change in embedded solar capacity.
  • 00008, Primary substations: summaries of recent power (the minimum, mean, and maximum of the latest 24 hours and of the latest day on the same weekday) in the stage 2 calibrator added -0.02 points to raw lags up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.14 to +0.13). The interval is too wide to resolve 0.15 points, so the verdict is inconclusive.
  • Indicative inputs from a closed study (PR #1175 (Study XGBoost pipeline fixes, lean inputs and calibration diagnostics)): the radiation correction lowers solar pinball loss by about 0.34 points, and the pooled quantile forecasts under-cover for wind. No human reviewed those numbers.

All lagged arms of 00005 are ceilings: the lag anomalies use ERA5 weather at past times, which serving does not have. The ceiling is the main open risk of the lag design, and the next experiments build the lag anomalies from the sources serving will have.

docs.title: Cost at version 2 scale
docs.text:
Basis. The quick-wins study measured, for 31 series on one GPU, 37 s (squared error) and 5 min (9 quantile levels) for one model per series, 9.76 million training rows (production trains on the control member, about 315,000 rows per series), 8 GB peak memory, and a feature frame of 5 min 19 s and 5.3 GB, extrapolating to about 7 hours and 430 GB for 2,500 series in one process. That is about 9.7 s per series at 9 levels. The rates below assume cost grows linearly with series, rows, and quantile levels. The last assumption is unverified. Read everything as an order of magnitude.

Stage Training at 2,500 series Inference per daily run Adapter Not trained Seconds to minutes, dominated by reading the NWP Stage 0 (if built) Not yet sized; depends on the form chosen About 1,000 cells (unverified) × 51 members × 720 half-hours × about 10 variables, about 370 million values Stage 1 About 105,000 rows per series at 9 levels: about 3 s per series, so about 2 GPU-hours per fit; about 6 fits for the forward-chained run plus the final fit, so about 12 GPU-hours, yearly About 92 million rows (51 members × 2,500 series × 720 half-hours): minutes on GPU, tens of minutes on 8 CPU cores Stage 2 One row per (init time, valid time), the production layout, with 2 to 3 years of ENS: about 15 to 25 s per series at 9 levels, so about 10 to 17 GPU-hours monthly if fitted per series; a per-type model would be cheaper but does not fit GPU memory at 2,500 series About 1.8 million rows: seconds ECC None Seconds

Stage 2 is the stage whose cost scales worst. A monthly refit of 10 to 17 GPU-hours is a design constraint. Options for the experiments: fit stage 2 per series type with row subsampling, or on fewer lead steps. Each NWP added adds rows to the pooled fit and raises the cost. The feature frame and input/output still probably dominate wall-clock time and need chunking by series.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which uses need coherence across time, across series, or both, and does feeder-to-substation hierarchy data exist for scoring it?
  • Is the target overall CRPS or exceedance at the 95th percentile? The answer decides between the location-and-scale form and a free quantile calibrator, which the research plan tests.
  • The final 51-member output fits PowerForecast, whose ensemble_member already has a different meaning for each forecaster (for climatology it is the rank of a quantile level). Should a docstring line say what the index means for the staged forecaster? The 19-level quantile table and the stage 1 tables need their own schema in the experiment store, and the contract is not changed without asking.
  • Stage 1 for the demand series now has ERA5 and CAMS at their locations. For the 2,500-series scale, is CAMS fetched at every series' location, given that the experiments found CAMS explains more of a Primary substation's residual than ERA5 shortwave (a post hoc result)?
  • The closed study of pipeline fixes found that pooled wind quantiles under-cover, and no merged experiment has measured wind coverage. Should a wind-specific calibration experiment come ahead of the multi-product work?
  • Which second NWP is tested first? The experiments can use a product already on disk, such as UKV from CEDA or a product downloaded from Open-Meteo, before any ingest into the production pipeline. The CEDA UKV archive differs statistically from the live feed, so a result on it may not carry over. Is a long-history ensemble such as GEFS obtainable?

docs.title: Work still to do
docs.text:
The research plan lists the experiments to run next, and two pieces of infrastructure are tracked as GitHub issues because they change production-facing code. The research plan is a page next to the research log. The two pieces of infrastructure are:

  • The conventions adapter. The radiation and wind rules have shipped. Remaining: step widths for hourly-stepped NWPs, the same adapter for ERA5 and CAMS, the per-NWP convention table, and the validation check, all with unit tests on synthetic input.
  • The scoring harness and coverage test. One scorer for every output: pinball loss at 19 levels from 0.05 to 0.95 plus a stated treatment of the tails beyond them, and the same estimator for ECC-coupled members (the fair-CRPS factor, which depends on the member count, can flip a comparison). PIT; coverage by lead band and series type; a synthetic spread-factor positive control; the in-sample against out-of-sample coverage test on the saved e1_quantile samples; one coherence score (CRPS of summed solar farms in a weather cell), with the energy and variogram scores added once coupled members exist.

The ingest of a second NWP into the production pipeline also needs an issue, but only after the experiments on products already on disk show which product to ingest.

docs.title: Switching events — Approach & Implementation Roadmap
docs.text:
Scope. How to make each NGED primary substation's forecast robust to switching events — and, further out, how to reconstruct its latent demand under the normal running arrangement (NRA) (the demand that would be metered if the electricity network were never reconfigured) — given that the electricity network is in fact reconfigured roughly 10% of the time by switching events. The nearest-term approach is a switching-robust forecaster; the latent-demand reconstruction is later research. Background on what switching events are and why they are hard is at Switching Events. This document defines the ordered set of approaches, from the v0.6 forecaster and detector to the later v2-scale mixture models.

Status: 🔬 Research / 🚧 Planned. Epic: #151 (the v0.6 switching work). None of the switching-events work described on this page is implemented yet. The nearest-term piece is the two-stage forecaster (approach 1), which makes the production forecast robust to switching by consuming continuous switching-state features, and ships no discrete event table. It is an open question, governed by the decision point, whether the explicit staged detector is then built on top of the two-stage forecaster — feeding the substation_switching table and the training-data mask. The two v2-scale mixture models are later research. The post-v2.0 roadmap is not yet fully specified, so read those two as "some time after v2.0". See the roadmap index for status conventions and where this fits the overall plan. This is the canonical treatment of switching events; the "switching state-space model" formulation is rejected in its favour (see the note in Net-demand disaggregation).

See also A staged probabilistic forecast, which reuses the stage 1 weather-to-power baseline for switching detection.

docs.title: The approaches
docs.text: The work is organised as a set of named approaches, tried in the order set out just below. The three v0.6 approaches all build on one shared baseline. "Baseline" here means a fitted model of expected power whose residual every approach consumes. The baseline's purpose is to remove seasonality to help make the switching events visible. A substation's metered power moves for ordinary reasons — a cold snap, a sunny afternoon, a Sunday — and a change in the electricity network's topology is buried under that variation. Subtract the power the weather and the clock explain, and — we hope — switching events surface in the residual as a sustained level shift. Escalation from a simpler approach to a heavier approach must be justified by measured residual structure the simpler approach leaves behind.

docs.title: Overview and ordering
docs.text:
Everything in v0.6 rests on one shared baseline: a per-substation model of expected power from weather and calendar covariates alone (no power lags). The baseline's per-series-normalised residual is the raw material every approach below consumes. Before building that baseline, though, there is an easier first look: a multiple seasonal-trend decomposition (MSTL) needs no weather input and no training run, and answers the question that decides whether any of the rest is worth building — are the switching events visible above the noise at all? Work on v0.6 is starting there. On top of the baseline we could then try, in order:

  1. The two-stage forecaster. Its two stages are:

    1. The shared baseline. Fit expected power per substation from weather and calendar covariates alone, using no power lags, then take the residual (observed power minus expected power) and normalise it by that series' own spread. That procedure is the same shared baseline named above, and the two-stage forecaster's first stage is that baseline — nothing extra.
    2. The same XGBoost forecaster used elsewhere in v1, but with more features that help explain switching events:. Plain lagged power features don't carry any information about whether that lagged power features was in a switching event or not. The idea here is simple: Give XGBoost enough information to allow it to infer which lagged features are in a switching event. Feed the lagged normalised residual, together with event-age and neighbour features, into a gradient-boosted model that forecasts metered power robustly to switching. Switching is handled implicitly: the model is never told an event happened, and instead learns from features that make switching events visible.

    But this approach has a major disadvantage: It never explicitly identifies switching events. So it cannot supply the switching event table, or the abnormal running arrangement (ARA) mask, or a sensitivity floor.

  2. The staged statistical detector — changepoint detection, balance attribution across neighbours, and a composition read-off, run on the same residual, producing an explicit event table, an ARA mask for the training data, and a quantified detection sensitivity floor.

  3. The joint edge-flow estimator — a single convex solve that replaces the detector's detect-then-match logic with one certified-optimal fit, adopted where it beats the staged version head-to-head.

The decision point below governs how far down that list we go. The v1 priority is forecast skill.

Two further approaches sit further out as later research, built at v2 scale once v2.0 is operational, and numbered to continue the ordering. Approach 4 is the magnitude-only mixture model, the workhorse: it models each substation's observed power as a time-varying blend of its own normal demand and its neighbours', so it estimates how much power moved between substations without saying what kind of demand or generation moved — magnitude only. Approach 5 is the type-resolved mixture, which splits each substation into physically-typed components — demand, solar photovoltaic (PV), and wind — and lets each type move with its own weights, so a switching event can shift proportionally more PV than load. (We haven't fully specified the roadmap after v2, so read anything "at v2 scale" as just meaning "some time after v2 is operational".)

v0.6 scale ── First look: MSTL decomposition — are the events visible above the noise?
  │            Then - if necessary - one shared baseline (weather/calendar expected power), and in order:
  │            1. The two-stage forecaster — switching-robust forecasting; handles switching
  │               implicitly. No event table.
  │            2. The staged statistical detector — explicit events, ARA mask, sensitivity floor.
  │            3. The joint edge-flow estimator — detection + attribution in one convex solve.
  │            How far past (1) we build is set by the decision point, not fixed in advance.
  │
v2 scale   ── Reconstruct latent NRA demand per substation, after v2.0 is operational:
  │            4. Magnitude-only mixture model. The workhorse. Fully unsupervised.
  │            5. Type-resolved mixture with differentiable PV/wind/demand modules —
                  lets a switching event move proportionally more PV than load.

Approaches 2 and 3 may never be built, and it is worth knowing that before reading their designs. The decision point below weighs the explicit detector against a feature-based mainline in which the discrete layer is deferred behind forecast skill. NGED's top priority is probabilistic normal-running-arrangement forecasts, and handling switching implicitly inside the forecaster is an acceptable way to deliver them. An explicit switching record is still genuinely wanted — the substation_switching table was specified in our most recent formal report to NGED — but that record sits further down NGED's continuum of priorities. Approaches 4 and 5 are v2-scale and start only once v2.0 is operational.

docs.title: v0.6 — switching-robust forecasting, and switching detection
docs.text: Everything below builds on the shared baseline. The two-stage forecaster (approach 1) is the nearest-term deliverable and needs nothing but that baseline. The staged detector (approach 2) and the joint edge-flow estimator (approach 3) add the explicit event machinery. Past approach 1, the decision point sets how far we go.

docs.title: The baseline (shared foundation)
docs.text:
For each substation, form an expected-power baseline that is a function of exogenous, switching-independent covariates only — temperature, solar irradiance, recent weather, time-of-day, day-of-week, holidays — fitted across a long history (e.g. an XGBoost or generalised additive model (GAM) regression). Take the residual (observed − expected): a switching event shows up in it as a sustained level shift — not a spike, not a slope. This residual, normalised by each series' own spread, is the raw material both the two-stage forecaster and the staged detector consume.

Why the baseline must be weather/calendar-based and not a lagged-power baseline. A tempting simple baseline is "same half-hour last week." But, if last week sat in a switching event and this week is normal (or vice versa), the residual shows a step of the same magnitude and shape as a real event — but with the sign reversed, because the contamination is in the reference, not the observation. Approach 2's balance-attribution stage would then hunt for donor rises coincident with a source drop that is a baseline artifact. The hunt manufactures phantom events and mis-attributes them. Worse, because switching events can persist for days to months, a lag can land inside the same ongoing event. There is then no step at all, and a real event is masked entirely. Weather and clock time are unaffected by the electricity network's topology, so a baseline built only from them cannot be contaminated by switching state. The residual then isolates "power the weather and clock don't explain," which is exactly where a topology change appears, with no comparison period to poison.

The first approach to try is a classical multiple seasonal-trend decomposition (MSTL). MSTL splits each substation's series into a trend, one seasonal component per period — daily and weekly, plus annual where the history is long enough — and a remainder. The remainder plays the same role as the model residual above: a switching event appears in it as a sustained level shift. MSTL has no features to engineer. MSTL is therefore the simplest way to answer the question that decides whether the rest is worth building — are the level shifts visible above the noise at all?

Two limits keep MSTL a first look rather than the baseline. MSTL carries no weather covariate, so a cold snap or a still week lands in the remainder alongside the switching events. And MSTL also estimates the trend and the seasonal components from the series' own history, so a months-long event can be partly absorbed into the trend it ought to be standing out against. Absorbing an event into the trend is a milder form of the lagged-power contamination described above. A published detector, Kim (2025) described under stage 1 below, is built on a robust seasonal-trend decomposition used in exactly this role.

Baseline implementation: reuse the existing XGBoost forecaster with no lag features. The production forecaster already consumes most of the covariates the baseline needs — weather from numerical weather prediction (NWP), time-of-day, day-of-week (holiday flags are a planned quick win) — through the existing feature pipeline. Configuring the production forecaster with no power-lag features yields the switching-independent baseline (a lag feature would smuggle the lagged-power contamination above back in through the side door). Fit with a robust (median) objective, which doubles as the robust loss required below. A median (absolute-error) fit is a config-only change to the existing forecaster today. The per-series, per-time spread estimate used by the normalisation step below can come from either of two sources: additional quantile heads (e.g. 10%/90%) once the quantile-objective model family lands — the tidiest option — or an interim rolling median absolute deviation (MAD) of the residuals. The baseline is therefore not hard-blocked on that model family.

What "normal" means for demand-driven series — the behavioural calendar. For weather-driven series (solar photovoltaic (PV), wind), "normal for this weather at this time of day" is well-defined and the covariates above capture it. For demand-driven series, "normal" also depends on human behaviour, and the baseline is only as good as its calendar features. The saving grace is that the baseline is a supervised model, not an empirical climatology. The baseline pools across days whose feature vectors look alike (all Mondays in May borrow strength from each other automatically), so the fiddly question "which days count as similar?" reduces to "is the calendar encoding rich enough?" (see background: GB demand's calendar-driven quirks).

A calendar event the baseline does not know about looks like a switching event, so the calendar features decide how many phantom events the detector reports. An unmodelled calendar event surfaces as a coherent residual excursion that approach 2's changepoint detector may flag, erroneously, as a switching event. Two safeguards keep the phantom-event risk manageable. First, the failure has a distinctive shape: a holiday miss hits many demand-driven series simultaneously and with the same sign, whereas a real switching event is localised and balance-conserving. Approach 2's balance-attribution stage therefore discriminates a holiday miss from a switching event, because its neighbourhood sum does not balance for a holiday miss. Second, the fix must come from the feature side — richer holiday encodings (the planned quick win) and, at V2 scale, cross-series pooling (a global model sees dozens of Easters where a per-series model sees about three) — and never from trailing same-weekday power averages. Trailing averages would smuggle the lagged-power contamination above back in through the side door, absorbing a persistent switching event into "expected" within a few weeks and blinding the detector to exactly the events it exists to find.

Fitting the baseline has three traps, all of them caused by the switching events sitting in its own training history.

  • Fit robustly, because the training history itself contains switching events. Fitted straight, the baseline is biased toward the contaminated periods. Fit with a robust loss (quantile or Huber), or iteratively: fit → flag large residuals as candidate events → refit excluding them. Because events occupy only ~10% of the time, a robust fit recovers the NRA relationship and the events fall out as residuals. That robust-fit recovery closes a virtuous loop with the detector itself — detected events feed back to clean the baseline's training data.

    Use v1's logged events to measure, once, the contamination penalty the robust fit leaves behind. In v1 we also hold NGED's logged switching events, which enables the cleanest of the three options: train the baseline with labelled event periods excluded. Labels will not exist beyond the trial area, so v1 should run labelled-event exclusion as a small experiment family: the shared baseline trained with and without labelled-event exclusion, plus a third arm that excludes the same volume of randomly chosen non-event periods. The random-exclusion control separates the effect of removing contamination from the effect of simply training on less data. Score all arms on out-of-event periods only: during a logged event the metered target is precisely what a label-clean model is supposed to disagree with. In-event scoring would penalise the cleaner model for being right. The gap between the labelled-exclusion arm and the random-exclusion control measures the contamination penalty that the robust fit fails to absorb, i.e. the accuracy the label-free V2 fleet will lose — quick to measure now, impossible to measure later.

  • Keep the baseline static, so that a months-long event stays visible. A months-long ARA appears as a residual level shift that stays shifted. The changepoint detector handles a sustained shift, because it catches the onset step. What breaks the detector is a baseline that slowly adapts and comes to treat the new level as normal. Drive the baseline from weather and calendar alone over the detection window, and a sustained ARA stays visible as a sustained residual offset.

  • Keep the seasonal terms low-flexibility, because outages cluster in maintenance seasons. Planned switching is not uniform through the year. A flexible time-of-year covariate fitted on contaminated history can therefore absorb systematic ARA effects into "seasonality", and the robust loss does not fix that absorption, because the contamination is locally dense within the season even though it is only ~10% overall. So prefer multiple years of history, and make sure the fit → flag → refit loop removes flagged periods from the seasonal fit too.

docs.title: Approach 1 — the two-stage forecaster
docs.text: The two-stage forecaster is a good candidate for the first approach to try, and the current v0.6.0 target. Stage 1 is the shared baseline above. Stage 2 is a booster that replaces (or augments) the forecaster's raw power-lag features with residual lags — the normalised "actual − expected" delta at each lag time, for the target substation and, optionally, its neighbours. The intuition: a raw power lag conflates "what the weather was doing" with "what is anomalous". Handing the model the anomaly component directly tells it how normal each recent observation is. The two-stage forecaster needs nothing beyond the baseline, so it can run as soon as normalised residuals exist — ahead of any detector machinery.

docs.title: What the two-stage forecaster improves
docs.text:
The two-stage forecaster is plausibly the largest forecast-accuracy win available from switching-awareness, because:

  • A cleaner lag representation in general. Separating the expected part from the anomalous part of each lagged observation is plausibly useful everywhere, not only during switching events.
  • Learned event persistence. During an ongoing switching event the residual is a sustained level shift, so the model can learn "sustained recent residual → carry the offset forward". That learned persistence is the model-learned version of the zeroth-order patch, applied at forecast time instead of to the training data. For pure forecast accuracy, "the current shift will persist" is most of the value switching-handling can deliver, since event onsets are unpredictable from power data by definition.
  • Neighbour context. Neighbour residuals (e.g. the signed neighbourhood-sum feature designed below) expose the conservation fingerprint — my residual dropped while my neighbours' rises sum to the same amount. The fingerprint distinguishes "a transfer that will persist and eventually revert" from "a permanent change such as load growth or a meter re-base".

docs.title: What the two-stage forecaster does and does not produce
docs.text: This approach makes the forecaster robust to switching. The approach produces none of the detector's discrete deliverables. There is no event list or donor attribution (so no substation_switching table), no ARA mask, no sensitivity floor, and no latent-NRA reconstruction. A good forecast of metered power is a different product from an estimate of what demand would have been under NRA. How much each of those absences matters is a requirements question as much as a technical question, and is taken up at the decision point below. The two paths still compose rather than compete: if the staged detector is built, its outputs (an in-event flag, event age, attributed magnitude) are themselves natural features for this model.

docs.title: Caveats to build in from the start
docs.text:
• A residual is not only switching. It is also NWP error — autocorrelated and heteroscedastic, exactly the stage-1 problem. Feed normalised residuals (divide by the baseline's spread estimate, which stage 1 fits anyway) rather than raw MW deltas for the self-series features, and include a neighbourhood-sum residual — whose unit convention is different, and set out in the design note below — so the model can separate a regional NWP bust (the sum steps too) from a genuine transfer (the sum stays flat).
  • Fold hygiene, in both directions. The baseline is a hindcast fitted on history. In cross-validation, each fold's residual features must come from a baseline trained only on that fold's training period, otherwise the test period leaks into the features. Less obviously, the training-row residuals need protecting too: a baseline evaluated on its own training period produces in-sample residuals — shrunken and shaped by overfit — while at serving time the residuals near forecast time are out-of-sample for the deployed baseline. A booster whose split thresholds were calibrated on in-sample residuals therefore meets a systematically wider, differently-shaped distribution in production. The standard stacking remedy applies: every residual the booster trains on should be out-of-sample for the baseline that produced it (rolling-origin refits within the training period). Both directions make the cross-validation pipeline more work to build than adding an ordinary feature.
  • No lookahead. Residual lags must obey the same nullification rule as raw power lags (_nullify_leaky_lags()). The expected-power values at past lag times must be hindcast from NWP runs that had been published by forecast time. The existing freshest-NWP-for-past-target-times join does not guarantee no lookahead — it selects the freshest run per past target time with no publication-time constraint, and is leak-free today only as a side effect of daily run cadence. The residual pipeline must therefore add an explicit availability cut, guarded by a leakage test in the spirit of the _nullify_leaky_lags tests. The natural home for that cut is a filter on the NWP frame before weather_utils.analysis_proxy.select_analysis_proxy reduces it — the shape single-run mode already uses for its ceiling. The residual pipeline runs in bulk mode, which applies no such cut today.
  • Cross-series features are new machinery. Neighbour residuals need the trial-area adjacency list (a dependency in Open items) plus a cross-series join in feature engineering. The feature-schema question (each series has its own neighbour set, of varying size) is answered by the pooled design below — a fixed handful of permutation-invariant pooled columns, never one column per neighbour.
  • Data volume. Learning multi-donor conservation implicitly from 32 series with ~10% event occupancy asks a lot of a tabular learner. Expect the model to learn "persist my own offset" easily and neighbour attribution only weakly. The closed-form detector exploits that structure directly, which is another reason the two-stage forecaster complements the detector rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Feature-design notes
docs.text:
• Event age, without a normality threshold. "How long has this series been abnormal?" is a natural feature, and it needs no hand-coded normality threshold. An XGBoost split is a learned threshold, so the model only needs continuous accumulator statistics of the normalised residual and it will pick its own cutpoints. The simplest basis: signed EWMAs (exponentially weighted moving averages) of the normalised residual at two or three half-lives (say 12 hours, 3 days, 2 weeks) — one ewm_mean per half-life, no thresholds anywhere. Duration is encoded in the relationship between the columns: a fresh event makes the short-half-life EWMA large while the long-half-life EWMA is still small. A weeks-old event saturates all of them. A two-sided CUSUM (cumulative-sum) statistic is the fancier alternative — its magnitude grows roughly as shift-size × duration and it self-resets at zero (its only parameter is the slack, set in normalised units), and "hours since the CUSUM last touched zero" gives a literal event age. Two disciplines apply. First, the accumulator must be computed only from residuals available at power_fcst_init_time — the same no-lookahead rule as every other lag feature.

    Second, feed the accumulators normalised residuals, never the detector's whitened innovations. It is easy to get this backwards, because whitening sounds like a strictly better input. The opposite holds here: whitening removes whatever was predictable from the residuals just before, and a persistent level shift is exactly the kind of predictable component whitening removes. So after an event's onset the whitened innovations fall back toward zero and an accumulator of them decays. The accumulator stops encoding age, which is the one quantity it exists to encode. The detector whitens because its question is "did a step occur just now". The accumulator's question is "how far from normal has the level been", and the persistence must be left in to answer it. The drawback of skipping whitening is that the accumulators also integrate slow NWP-error waves — acceptable for a feature (the booster holds the weather covariates and the neighbour pools that provide discriminating context) in a way it never would be for a detector that must control its false-alarm rate.

  • Pooled neighbour features, not per-neighbour columns. Neighbour context should enter as a fixed, small set of permutation-invariant pooled features rather than one input per neighbour: pooling keeps the feature schema identical for every series regardless of neighbour count (which is what lets the design survive to V2 scale). Permutation invariance matches the physics — which neighbour donated does not matter for forecasting this series; attribution is the detector's job.

    Compute the signed neighbourhood sum over raw MW, and rescale only after summing. The most informative pool is the signed neighbourhood sum, because it carries the conservation fingerprint: a transfer makes this series' residual and the neighbours' sum equal-and-opposite, while a regional NWP bust moves both the same way. Conservation holds in megawatts — a transfer moves the same MW out of one meter and into others — so the equal-and-opposite fingerprint exists only in MW. Summing per-series-normalised residuals looks more consistent with the other features but silently destroys the fingerprint whenever neighbours' noise scales differ: a 5 MW transfer between a noisy series and a quiet series sums to nowhere near zero in per-series σ-units. For fleet-wide comparability, normalise after summation — divide the MW sum by a combined neighbourhood spread (e.g. the root-sum-square of the members' MW spread estimates) — which rescales the whole signal without breaking the cancellation.

    Complement the sum with the most-anomalous neighbour's own signed residual. Select and express it in that neighbour's own normalised units, since "anomalous" is a per-series notion — the most-anomalous-neighbour feature covers the case the sum dilutes: one strongly anomalous neighbour among several quiet neighbours. Keep the sign, since whether that neighbour gained or shed load is exactly what predicts whether this series is about to give load back. The two families of features in these notes compose: the sum of neighbours' residual EWMAs is "how long has the neighbourhood been abnormal" in a single column.

  • Plot every one of these features before feeding it to a model. Residuals, event-age accumulators, and neighbour pools are all easy to build subtly wrong — a flipped sign convention, a mis-normalised spread, a missing availability cut — in ways a leaderboard metric will not surface. Each engineered feature should be inspected visually, on the same time axis as observed power and the model's forecast (and, in v1, the logged switching events), before it enters an experiment. The planned interactive feature-visualisation tool (#359) — likely an extension of the view-forecasts dashboard, with the switching labels overlaid — exists for exactly that inspection.

docs.title: When the two-stage forecaster runs, and the single-stage ablation control that precedes it
docs.text: The two-stage forecaster can begin as soon as the baseline exists (implementation step 2 below) and is itself implementation step 5, evaluated by cross-validation; its result also doubles as evidence of the baseline's quality. So that the work gets scheduled alongside the other forecaster experiments, the two-stage forecaster is also tracked on the XGBoost quick-wins backlog as the residual-lag features, where the horizon-band and init-time-anchoring interactions specific to that page are noted. Before any of that machinery is built, its config-only single-stage cousin should run first as the ablation control: aligned lagged-weather features (a quick win), which lets the booster judge each lag's normality without an explicit baseline and bounds how much of the anomaly signal a tabular learner extracts unaided.

docs.title: A second way to use the stage-1 baseline: correct a draft
docs.text:
The residual-lag design evaluates the stage-1 baseline at lag times, to tell stage 2 how anomalous each recent observation was. The same fitted baseline can also be evaluated at the target time, producing a "first-draft" forecast of the power we are trying to predict. Stage 2 then corrects the draft rather than forecasting from scratch. The draft is a design axis orthogonal to the residual lags: the residual lags concern what stage 2 receives as recent-observation features, while the draft concerns what stage 2 predicts and starts from. The two therefore compose (a booster can take a draft as its starting point and residual lags as features) rather than competing. The draft re-uses exactly the per-fold, out-of-sample hindcast machinery the residual lags already require, so the draft is easy to try once that machinery exists. There are two ways to hand stage 2 the draft:

  • Draft as an ordinary feature; stage 2 predicts total power. A soft specialisation: the booster usually latches onto the draft as a dominant split variable and spends the rest on corrections, but nothing forces it to. Draft-as-a-feature is close to the documented design plus one feature, and it keeps the main safety property — stage-1 error enters only as feature noise the booster can learn to down-weight.

  • base_margin; stage 2 predicts the correction (actual − draft). XGBoost's base_margin sets a per-row starting score. The trees therefore continue stage 1's boosting, and regularisation shrinks naturally toward "no correction". base_margin is the version that genuinely forces specialisation. The margin also degrades gracefully with horizon: as the anomaly signal decays and valid-time lags null out, the correction tends to zero and the forecast falls back to the draft.

    base_margin also sharpens interpretation, because the draft is an offset rather than a column and so never competes for splits. The trees' feature importances and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values therefore describe only what drives the correction — a cleaner read on the switching/anomaly signal than the soft variant, where the draft soaks up most of the gain and entangles everything else. (That interpretability win comes from predicting the correction, so the equivalent delta-regression shares the win. The interpretability win is a reason to prefer this hard corrector over draft-as-feature, not base_margin over the delta trick.)

What base_margin adds over predicting the delta directly. For plain squared-error regression, supplying the draft as base_margin is mathematically identical to training stage 2 on (actual − draft) and adding the draft back — same gradients, same trees. Under that objective, predicting the delta is fine and arguably more transparent. That equivalence is not special to squared error. The equivalence holds for any identity-link loss that is a function of the residual alone, including the pinball/quantile objective this project wants, because pinball loss is translation-invariant (ρ_τ(actual − draft − correction) = ρ_τ((actual − draft) − correction)): same gradients, same trees, and an identical early-stopping metric either way. The margin is only worth the extra machinery once the link is not the identity — a Poisson/Tweedie link (natural for a non-negative quantity), where the margin lives in log-space so the correction becomes multiplicative, the loss is no longer a function of actual − prediction, and the output cannot go negative. There the delta trick has no clean analogue and the margin is doing real work. The operational footgun is that the margin must be passed at both train and predict time; forgetting it at inference silently falls back to the default base score.

Drawbacks of the hard corrector, and the hedge. Because stage 2 starts from the draft, any stage-1 bias at the target time flows straight into the output unless stage 2 can see the raw inputs needed to fix the bias. The "no end-to-end optimisation" con therefore bites harder than in the residual-feature design. The hedge is to keep the weather/calendar inputs in stage 2's feature list even under base_margin, trading some of the specialisation for a route to correct draft bias.

Quantiles need care. The draft is a single deterministic number per row, so adding it shifts every quantile equally — \(Q_\tau(\text{actual} \mid x) = \text{draft} + Q_\tau(\text{correction} \mid x)\) holds exactly, for any fixed draft used as the margin. What this equivalence means is that correctness comes from training stage 2 per target quantile (each \(\tau\) its own pinball fit), not from any special choice of margin: a probabilistic version needs one stage-2 model per quantile, and using the corresponding stage-1 quantile as each model's margin is a warm-start convenience (smaller corrections), not a requirement. Stage 1's quantile spread then does double duty: as a stage-2 feature it supplies exactly the per-series "usual wobble" normalisation the residual lags already need.

The same no-lookahead discipline. The draft at the target time must be hindcast on NWP as available at that lead time, not on fresh analysis-like data, or stage 2 calibrates its corrections against a draft that is systematically better than the live draft — the same availability cut the residual-lag hindcasts and the freshest-run join require. The feature pipeline applies that cut in single-run mode, as a ceiling at the selected NWP run. The lead-time feature belongs in stage 1 so the draft's own attenuation with horizon is honest.

The prize — a plausible route to a global corrector. The correction target (actual − draft) has far smaller variance than raw power and is far more stationary across series: recent-anomaly persistence looks similar at a 200 MW grid supply point (GSP) and a 5 MW feeder once residuals are on a comparable scale. So a global corrector becomes plausible long before a global raw-power model does, sidestepping the per-series-level problem that is the global model's hard prerequisite. The global-model item notes the same base_margin move for its capacity-factor-normalised physics proxy.

docs.title: Attributing the uplift: calibration versus switching
docs.text:
A residual-lag booster would sharpen the forecast even on a grid that never switched, simply by telling the model how high or low the series is currently running relative to weather and clock — an inference-time calibration that corrects NWP bias, meter drift, distributed energy resource (DER) growth, or any persistent regime offset.
